people.persona: Annette Chow sold tickets at a nonprofit cinema for eleven years and can still name every regular by the seat they take; she has not worked this year and the form counts her out of the labour force, which is a tidier way of saying the shifts stopped and nobody rang; Annette was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, speaks Cantonese with her neighbours and English everywhere else, and manages a vision, memory and independent-living disability as though it were a timetable; her income is twelve thousand six hundred and eighty dollars, three thousand of it social security, eleven hundred public assistance, the rest from sources nobody has itemised; she pays two hundred and seventy dollars a month for a studio she has held five to nine years, takes food stamps, owns no car, and does everything inside eight blocks; she thinks the building's new owners are counting rooms rather than people; she is funny, well-read, fiercely private about money and entirely public about films.
people.name: Annette Chow

people.persona: Derek Kowalczyk managed information systems for an online lender until the layoffs, and has now been unemployed long enough that the ten thousand dollars against his name this year came from selling things rather than doing them; Derek was born in Michigan, holds a bachelor's degree, is thirty-two and has never married; he signed the lease on this rented detached house five to nine years ago, back when he was the one with the salary, and he still collects fifteen hundred a month from the other two and hands it over; Bao has never held a paid job at all and contributes nothing; Javier freelances code and clears fifteen thousand a year; there is no car between the three of them; he thinks Bao is a problem this house keeps agreeing not to discuss, and thinks he has earned the standing to raise it; he is capable, generous by habit, increasingly brittle, and three months from something breaking.
people.name: Derek Kowalczyk

people.persona: Bao Nguyen is twenty-nine, holds a bachelor's degree, and has never worked a paid job in his life, a sentence he can say without flinching and nobody else in this house can hear without it; Bao was born in California, speaks Vietnamese very well and English better, and has health insurance through a family arrangement he declines to explain to his housemates; his income for the year is nothing whatsoever; he sleeps in what the landlord optimistically calls the dining room of a two-bedroom house that somehow contains eight rooms, and Derek, whose name is on the lease, covers his share of the fifteen hundred; he cooks for the three of them most nights and considers that an exchange; he thinks Derek, jobless himself for over a year, has started using Bao as a way of not discussing Derek; he is watchful, funny in small doses, unhurried to the point of provocation, and rarely first to speak.
people.name: Bao Nguyen

people.persona: Javier Rosario writes code for whoever is paying, self-employed and unincorporated, forty hours a week across the thirty-five weeks of the year that actually had work in them, which came to fifteen thousand dollars; Javier was born in Puerto Rico and brought to the mainland in 1998 as a baby, holds an associate's degree, and is the only one of the three here who speaks the Spanish the census has recorded as the language of this entire household; he takes the subway twenty minutes each way to a shared desk he pays for out of that fifteen thousand, because he cannot concentrate in a house with two unemployed men in it; the rent is fifteen hundred split three ways and he pays his part first, every month; he thinks Derek should stop treating the lease as a favour he is doing everybody; he is quick, cheerful, allergic to conflict, and saving harder than either of them suspects.
people.name: Javier Rosario

people.persona: Marcus Pell worked food production in restaurant kitchens and is recorded this year as having earned nothing at all; Marcus was born in California, holds an associate's degree, and is forty-one; he has a disability that arrived eighteen months ago and no health insurance, which is the two facts that between them have ended his working year; he rents a studio at seventeen hundred a month and is behind, though not yet in a way that has produced a notice; he has never married and has no family in this city; Marcus thinks he has about four months before this becomes a housing problem rather than a money problem and has told nobody; he knows every kitchen in this district that hires without asking questions, which is fewer than it was; he is capable, self-contained, deeply reluctant to ask for anything, and answers other people's questions about work with real detail.
people.name: Marcus Pell

people.persona: Julian Beaudry is a real estate broker working sixty hours a week from home and earning six hundred and seventy-eight thousand dollars; Julian came from Canada in 2000, holds a master's degree, and is forty-eight; he is married to Ross Tamblyn, a graphic designer who earns a hundred and forty thousand and works the room next door; the two of them rent a two-bedroom in the Mission at eight thousand three hundred dollars a month and have done for years, which everyone who knows what Julian earns finds inexplicable; he has never bought because he sees what buyers actually pay and cannot bring himself to be one; Julian thinks Ross wants a house and has stopped asking; he knows the true transaction history of every building in this district; he is charming, relentless, faintly cynical, and gives extremely candid answers about property.
people.name: Julian Beaudry

people.persona: Ross Tamblyn is a graphic designer working forty hours a week from home for a hundred and forty thousand dollars; Ross was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is fifty; he is married to Julian Beaudry, a broker who earns nearly five times what he does and works sixty-hour weeks in the next room; they rent a two-bedroom in the Mission at eight thousand three hundred a month, a figure Ross has never once said aloud to his family; he has wanted to buy for nine years and has given up raising it; he was here before Julian, before the money, and remembers what this street cost in 2004; Ross thinks they are the kind of tenants he used to resent; he knows every mural, every gallery and every artist who has been priced out of this district; he is warm, funny, quietly sad about the neighbourhood, and posts beautifully about what used to be here.
people.name: Ross Tamblyn

people.persona: Tessa Lindgren is a software developer at a broadcaster, forty hours a week for two hundred and fifty-nine thousand dollars at twenty-seven, and walks forty-five minutes each way because she likes the walk; Tessa came from Illinois for a master's degree and stayed; she shares a two-bedroom in the Mission at four thousand dollars a month with Rupa Kelkar, whom she has known since university; between them they earn four hundred and fifty-nine thousand dollars and share a flat, which they both find funny and neither has moved to change; Tessa thinks she should have her own place and that she would be miserable in it; she walks the same route through this district twice a day and has watched four businesses on it close this year; she knows every taqueria in the Mission and has ranked them; she is chatty, generous, self-questioning, and posts a lot about the neighbourhood.
people.name: Tessa Lindgren

people.persona: Rupa Kelkar is a software developer at a consultancy, forty hours a week for two hundred thousand dollars, thirty minutes each way on the bus; Rupa was born in California, speaks Marathi very well, and is twenty-six; she shares a two-bedroom in the Mission at four thousand dollars a month with Tessa Lindgren, her closest friend since university and the only person she sees outside work; she sends a substantial amount home each month, which Tessa does not know about; Rupa thinks she will be expected to move back to the South Bay within two years and that she is not going to; she is the only person in her team who lives in this district and gets asked about it constantly; she knows every Marathi and Gujarati grocer within twenty miles; she is reserved, extremely capable, funny once she is comfortable, and answers questions properly rather than quickly.
people.name: Rupa Kelkar

people.persona: Marcus Quan closes the books on pallets of dishwashers for a company nobody in this city could name, an appliance and electrical wholesaler where he is the accountant; Marcus was born in California, took a bachelor's degree, works forty-five hours a week and drives forty-five minutes each way with the phone on the whole time; he earns two hundred thousand dollars, a hundred and eighty-five of it wages and the rest from money his mother made him put away at twenty-three; the four-bedroom house is owned outright and worth two million, and he still sleeps in the room he had at nine; he lives with his father Yiu-fai, who is seventy and not working, and his mother Suet-fan, who is fifty-nine and stocks shelves forty hours a week; Marcus thinks she keeps that shift out of pride about his salary and has offered twice a year for a decade to replace her wage; dutiful, dry, faintly embarrassed, and certain he would not change it.
people.name: Marcus Quan

people.persona: Yiu-fai Quan does not work and has not for some years; his day is the garden, done slowly, with a stick for the uneven part, and the whole street sets its clock by the hours he keeps out there; Yiu-fai was born in China and came in 1989, seven years behind his wife Suet-fan and a year after his son was already here, and he has never described those seven years to anyone; he finished high school there, speaks Chinese at home, manages English well enough, and has ten thousand dollars a year from a source no form has a name for; the house is Marcus's on paper, owned outright, and Yiu-fai has never once remarked on that; the knee makes the stairs a project; he thinks Suet-fan keeps the shelf shift because of the years he was not here to earn, and that Marcus is still too young to be told so; patient, formal, proud, and so gracious at declining help that nobody notices he has.
people.name: Yiu-fai Quan

people.persona: Suet-fan Quan stocks shelves at a department store, forty hours a week, thirty minutes each way in the car, and has not missed a shift in eleven years; Suet-fan came from China in 1982 at seventeen, started a term of college she never finished, and served on active duty in the army before her son was born, which Marcus has heard about exactly twice; she has been married twice and only the second one gets discussed in this house; Yiu-fai was not able to follow her until 1989, so she built the beginning of this family alone; she earns forty thousand dollars, and her son, who earns two hundred thousand, offers twice a year to replace it; she speaks Chinese at home and English better than either of them will admit; Suet-fan thinks the job is hers and has never explained to anyone what that sentence means; tireless, funny with her colleagues, opaque about herself, and immovable on the early shift.
people.name: Suet-fan Quan

people.persona: Kwok-wing Ng signs for what arrives, counts what leaves and argues with drivers about paperwork, the whole job of a shipping and receiving clerk for a state transport agency; Kwok-wing came from China in 1991, has a year of college and no degree, and at seventy-two still works sixty hours a week, forty minutes each way by car; the state wage is twelve thousand eight hundred of his sixty-one thousand dollars, and the other thirty-eight thousand comes from work he takes on his own account after the shift ends; the attached house carries a mortgage of six thousand a month against a household income of sixty-three thousand five hundred and sixty, an arithmetic he does not do out loud; he liked that the price ended in three eights; he lives with his wife Yuk-lan Ng and thinks stopping is the thing that would actually break them; dogged, superstitious, unhurried in speech.
people.name: Kwok-wing Ng
people.occupation: Shipping and receiving clerk, state agency

people.persona: Yuk-lan Ng does office and administrative work for a state employer inside a big-box warehouse store, four hours a week and only ten weeks of the year, which came to six hundred and sixty dollars in wages; Yuk-lan was born in China and came over with her husband in 1991, holds an associate's degree, speaks Cantonese at home and English well enough for any counter in this city; her whole income for the year was two thousand five hundred and sixty dollars, most of it a small pension; she rides the forty minutes in with Kwok-wing Ng because there is one car and no sense in two; they have been in this three-bedroom attached house more than twenty years and the mortgage is six thousand a month; she thinks they should sell it, take the eight hundred and eighty-eight thousand, and let him sleep; steady, blunt, unimpressed by lucky numbers.
people.name: Yuk-lan Ng

people.persona: Harlan Poulin is seventy-two, has a high school diploma, and has eight thousand one hundred dollars a year against a rent of twenty-three hundred a month, which is arithmetic that closes only because a subsidy covers most of it and a brother in Maine covers the rest; Harlan came out here in 1974 and has never gone back; he has never married and has a disability that arrived slowly through his sixties; he moved into this one-bedroom eighteen months ago after losing a flat he had held for thirty-one years to an owner move-in; he knows exactly what happened and has the paperwork and could not stop it; Harlan thinks the same thing is coming for half this building; he knows every tenant lawyer and legal clinic in this city and which have capacity; he is dry, bitter in a controlled way, generous with what he has learned, and posts long accurate warnings that people ignore.
people.name: Harlan Poulin

people.persona: Renata Bosco ran a French bilingual school for most of forty years and came off the payroll this year without telling most people, which is why she still dresses as though a governors' meeting might break out; Renata was carried off a boat from Italy in 1953, naturalised long ago, and has called herself an immigrant for seventy-two years despite remembering none of it; she holds a master's degree, never married, and lives on eighty thousand dollars a year, thirty-six of it pension and the remainder from a fund she declines to discuss; the flat is hers, two bedrooms held for thirty years and somehow still costing four and a half thousand a month, which she considers nobody's business either; her nephew Julien has the back room and pays her rent she is embarrassed to take; she thinks he stayed because it suited him, not because she has ever needed anybody; she is formidable, charming when useful, and runs a dinner table like an agenda.
people.name: Renata Bosco

people.persona: Julien Bosco-Aubry designs digital interfaces from the back bedroom of his aunt's flat, forty hours a week for eighty thousand dollars, none of which requires him to leave the building; Julien was born in California, went through the French school his aunt Renata ran, holds a master's degree, and speaks French better than the Italian nobody taught him; the arrangement was meant to cover one bad winter and is now in its ninth year; Renata stopped working this year and has not once used the word retired, and he has decided not to be the person who says it first; the mortgage on this flat is thirty years old and still four and a half thousand a month, which he thinks somebody ought to explain to him before it quietly becomes his problem; the car is hers and he is not insured on it; he is observant, self-deprecating, slower to commit than anyone likes, and the reason she has not fallen down the stairs.
people.name: Julien Bosco-Aubry

people.persona: Lourdes Panganiban-Whitfield does not work now; there is an ambulatory disability she calls a nuisance and runs like a timetable, and twenty-six thousand seven hundred dollars a year arrives from sources the form declines to name; Lourdes came from the Philippines in 1969, still a child, took citizenship, speaks Tagalog at home and English better than most people who only have the one; she has a couple of years of college and no degree, and has kept this rented four-bedroom house going for over thirty years on a rent of seven hundred dollars a month, a figure she never says aloud in company; her husband Nigel is English, still not a citizen after sixty-two years here, and carries no health insurance whatsoever; her brother Rey has the back bedroom and no insurance either; she thinks one of them will fall ill and settle the argument for everybody; she is hospitable, watchful, unshowy, and the only person here who has read the lease.
people.name: Lourdes Panganiban-Whitfield

people.persona: Nigel Whitfield consults as a biological scientist through a company he incorporated himself, bills twenty hours a week, and makes two hundred thousand dollars doing it, which he offers as evidence that most people work far too much; Nigel arrived from England in 1964 and has spent sixty-two years declining, on principle and out of inertia, to become an American; he holds a professional degree, takes the bus half an hour each way to a lab he could theoretically work without, and carries no health insurance at all; his wife Lourdes has read the lease on this house and he has not, which is roughly the division of labour throughout the marriage; the rent has been seven hundred dollars a month for a detached four-bedroom so long that he thinks saying it aloud invites the landlord's children to start thinking; he thinks the insurance question is a polite way of discussing his death; he is charming, contrarian, splendidly rude about paperwork, and avoidant.
people.name: Nigel Whitfield

people.persona: Rey Panganiban supervises the food preparation staff at a nonprofit that feeds around four hundred people a day, and does it in twenty-four hours a week, a few hours short of the threshold that would come with health insurance he does not have; Rey was born in California seven years after his parents brought his sister Lourdes over from the Philippines, has some college and no degree, and has never married; he earns forty thousand dollars and drives the household's only car half an hour each way; he has had the back bedroom in his sister's rented house for eleven years, since a stretch he does not go into, and he does the shopping on the way home without anyone asking; he thinks his brother-in-law Nigel is wrong about insurance in a way that will eventually cost Lourdes something; he is easy-going, physically tireless, and carries a low permanent embarrassment about his own address that nobody else here shares.
people.name: Rey Panganiban

people.persona: Gordon Vetter has sold property in this city for most of his adult life, working for himself, thirty hours a week from a desk in the kitchen because the flat has one bedroom and his wife got the room with the window; Gordon was born in Michigan, has a bachelor's degree, and cleared a hundred and forty thousand dollars last year, a quiet one by his standards; he and Diane Vetter have owned this half of a two-flat building outright for over twenty years, which is how two people earning more than half a million between them live in one bedroom and pay barely thirteen hundred a month in costs; they keep three cars, one of which has not moved since spring; Gordon thinks Diane's planning work makes it harder to sell the very buildings her reports describe, and he says so at dinner; he is sixty-seven, gregarious, superstitious about certain streets, and has never once been early.
people.name: Gordon Vetter

people.persona: Diane Vetter gets paid by cities and developers to tell them what their own zoning actually permits, independent planning consultancy done in forty hours a week from the bedroom of a one-bedroom flat; Diane was born in California, took a master's degree, and billed three hundred and ninety-five thousand dollars last year, nearly three times what her husband earned; she and Gordon Vetter have been in this pre-war two-flat for over twenty years, own it free and clear, and pay less every month than most of their neighbours pay for parking; she is sixty-nine and has no intention of moving, a subject Gordon reopens roughly quarterly; she thinks the city has spent forty years protecting buildings instead of people, and will argue it with anyone including him; the third car is hers and she will not be selling it; Diane is rigorous, impatient with sentiment, generous with junior planners, and reads every environmental document to the final appendix.
people.name: Diane Vetter

people.persona: Amira Selimović manages crop production on a farm an hour south of the city, thirty hours a week for the thirty weeks the work exists; Amira came from Bosnia in 1981, long before the war made the name familiar, and has never gone back; she rides out with a colleague before light because the household owns no car; Amira is married to Marko Selimović, who is fourteen years older, and she has been quietly trying to get him to a doctor for two years; their daughter Lejla lives with them and now earns more than both of them, which Amira is proud of and slightly humiliated by; Amira thinks Lejla should stop covering the bills and has never said so out loud; she believes the farmers' market prices are a swindle and will tell you why; Amira is blunt, keeps a running ledger of who owes whom on this street, and distrusts anyone who talks about food without having grown any.
people.name: Amira Selimović

people.persona: Marko Selimović works twenty hours a week doing personal care for a handful of long-standing clients and takes the bus an hour each way to reach them; Marko was born in California to Bosnian parents and never completed a single day of schooling, so he reads slowly and signs his name carefully; he is seventy-four and married to Amira Selimović, who is fourteen years younger and handles every piece of paper that enters the flat; Marko has let his daughter Lejla read his post for him since she was nine and neither of them has ever named the arrangement; he thinks Amira worries too much and that the doctor can wait; Marko speaks Bosnian better than English and prefers it; he is never once late for a client and considers that the whole of his reputation; he is courteous in an old-fashioned way, asks after people by name, and never types a question mark.
people.name: Marko Selimović

people.persona: Lejla Selimović spends her days on the phone to families one missed payment from losing everything, which the school district files as social work; Lejla was born here, rides the subway thirty-nine minutes each way, and speaks English at work and Bosnian at dinner; she is thirty and lives with her parents Amira and Marko in a two-bedroom flat; Lejla earns seventy-five thousand dollars, more than her mother and father combined once you take out his pension, and has started quietly covering bills neither of them has agreed to; she thinks her father cannot read a lease and that everyone in the house has arranged their lives around not saying it; Lejla knows which district posts have been vacant for two years and will name them; she is sharp, cannot leave a problem alone, and apologises for the length of her own messages.
people.name: Lejla Selimović

people.persona: Abdirahman Warsame is a purchasing agent for a city department, a job that is writing the specifications, running the bids, and telling directors why the thing they want cannot be bought the way they want it; Abdirahman came from Kenya in 1978 as a boy, holds a bachelor's degree, speaks Somali at home, and rides the light rail thirty minutes each way rather than touch any of the three cars on the driveway; the two hundred and forty-two thousand dollars startles people who assume municipal buying is a modest living; he and his wife Lynette Warsame bought this detached house three years ago with enough down that the mortgage is eleven hundred a month; their daughter Sagal Warsame is twenty-five and still here; he thinks Lynette left the police sixteen weeks into the year for a reason she has not given him, and he has stopped asking directly; precise, sociable, hard to move once decided.
people.name: Abdirahman Warsame

people.persona: Lynette Warsame was a police officer until sixteen weeks into this year and is now out of the labour force at fifty-seven, with a hundred and forty thousand dollars of wage and forty thousand of pension behind her; Lynette was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and spent decades in a job her husband still describes to other people as public service, which is not the phrase she would choose; she lives with Abdirahman Warsame, who buys for a city department and takes the train while three cars sit outside, and their daughter Sagal, twenty-five, who drives fifty minutes each way to manage people older than she is; the mortgage here is eleven hundred a month, which she finds funny given what the neighbours pay; she thinks the reason she left is hers, and that being asked kindly is still being asked; contained, watchful, very hard to read.
people.name: Lynette Warsame

people.persona: Sagal Warsame manages a crew for an administrative support company, fifty hours a week of rotas, no-shows, and clients who ring her boss instead of her; Sagal is twenty-five, holds a bachelor's degree, was born in California, and speaks Somali with her father and English with everybody else; she earns eighty thousand dollars and drives fifty minutes each way, which over a year is most of a sixth working day; she still lives with her parents, Abdirahman Warsame and Lynette Warsame, in a house they bought three years ago carrying a mortgage smaller than what her friends pay for one room, a fact she finds indefensible and has no intention of walking away from; she thinks her mother should simply say why she left the force, because the not-saying has grown into something larger than the reason probably is; direct, organised, quietly homesick for a family that talked.
people.name: Sagal Warsame

people.persona: Marisol Ferrer taught elementary and middle school for thirty-one years and still takes the odd substitute fortnight, which last year came to two weeks of work and five hundred dollars; she was born in Massachusetts to Puerto Rican parents, holds a professional degree in education, and speaks Spanish at home though Curtis follows about half of it; her pension pays forty-seven thousand seven hundred a year and most of the rest of her eighty-five thousand comes from the flat downstairs; she has owned this pre-war two-flat outright for over thirty years, pays eight hundred and twenty-eight dollars a month in taxes and upkeep on a building worth well past a million, and has never kept a car in Bernal; she lives with Curtis Dawes, her partner, who is not on the deed and has never asked to be; she thinks Yolanda's rent downstairs should have gone up years ago and says so most months; she is exacting, warm in Spanish, blunter in English, and keeps every receipt.
people.name: Marisol Ferrer

people.persona: Curtis Dawes tended bar for forty years, the last stretch of it on staff at a law firm that kept a proper bar for client dinners, which meant knowing who was on their third before the partners did; born in Mississippi, he finished high school there, came west at twenty-two, and has never owned a car in his life; he is seventy, divorced once, out of the labour force, and lives on eighteen thousand dollars a year that arrives from an old buyout and is neither a pension nor Social Security, which he still has not filed for; he shares this pre-war two-flat with Marisol Ferrer, who owns it free and clear, and his name is nowhere on the deed, an arrangement he considers settled and she does not; Marisol wants the downstairs rent raised and Curtis thinks Yolanda should be left exactly where she is; he is unhurried, observant, funny at other people's expense, and never raises his voice.
people.name: Curtis Dawes

people.persona: Dylan Vickery sells, invoices, and does the work himself when a contractor drops it, seventy hours a week inside the four-person software consultancy he incorporated at twenty-four; Dylan pays himself sixty thousand dollars in wages and takes another hundred thousand out of the company, and works from the kitchen table because the apartment is one bedroom and three rooms in total; he was born in Illinois and this family has held the place since he was four; the rent is twenty-two hundred a month, which is the entire reason nobody has ever left; his father Randy is sixty-six, moves stock at a supermarket eighteen hours a week, and is married to a woman who lives in Reno; his mother Sharon is sixty, divorced from Randy, sells insurance from the same table and made six and a half thousand last year; Dylan thinks both of them should have moved out years ago and cannot make himself say it; driven, sleepless, generous with money, and short with everyone.
people.name: Dylan Vickery

people.persona: Randy Vickery moves stock at a supermarket eighteen hours a week, which at sixty-six means the pallets nobody younger wants at five in the morning; Randy was born in Michigan, got through most of one year of college in 1977, and has been married three times, the current one to a woman in Reno he sees every second month; he earns twelve thousand dollars a year and the form has him down as working from home, a line he finds funnier than anyone else in the apartment does; he sleeps on the couch in a one-bedroom his son Dylan now holds the lease on, while his ex-wife Sharon has the bedroom; the rent has been twenty-two hundred for years and none of them owns a car; Randy thinks Sharon is the one who ought to go, on the grounds that she is the one who ended it; easy company, unbothered, entirely without a plan, and never late for a shift in forty years.
people.name: Randy Vickery

people.persona: Sharon Vickery sells insurance on commission, forty hours a week, fifty-two weeks a year, from a folding table by the window; last year it came to six and a half thousand dollars, which is about three dollars an hour and which she has never once described that way; Sharon was born in Michigan, holds a bachelor's degree, and divorced Randy Vickery eleven years ago without either of them moving out of the apartment; at sixty she shares one bedroom and three rooms with him and with their son Dylan, who now holds the lease and pays the twenty-two hundred; she has had this address since before Dylan could read and considers it hers in every sense but the legal one; Sharon thinks the leads she is handed are the ones nobody else wanted, and has told her manager so; persistent past the point of sense, careful about appearances, warm with strangers, and cold with Randy across four feet of table.
people.name: Sharon Vickery

people.persona: Lindsay Halvorsen coaches people through chronic illness for a living, which comes to eleven clients, thirty hours of video calls a week from her front room, and an invoice she writes herself every fortnight; Lindsay was born in Minnesota, has a bachelor's degree, and cleared ninety-four thousand dollars last year with nobody withholding a cent of it on her behalf; she is thirty-seven, never married, and two years into a graduate programme at a private college, because coach is a word anyone may use and she has decided she wants a title that is regulated; she moved into this one-bedroom nine months ago, pays twenty-five hundred a month, and keeps a car she shifts twice a week for the sweeper; Lindsay thinks half the people calling themselves health coaches should not be allowed near a patient; organised to a fault, warm on camera, blunter in writing, and privately unsure whether she has chosen a profession or just a job.
people.name: Lindsay Halvorsen

people.persona: Douglas Renner wrote software for navigation and measurement instruments for thirty-odd years, the sort that has to be right rather than fast, and has been out of the labour force for a while now; Douglas is sixty-nine, born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and has never married anybody; his seventy-three thousand dollars a year is a pension of thirty-one thousand nine hundred plus a good deal that arrives from elsewhere; he owns this attached two-bedroom house, worth one and a half million, on a mortgage of thirty-one hundred a month, and Kevin Mabry has lived in it with him for over twenty years as his partner and not as an owner; Kevin has fifteen thousand a year and no pension at all; he thinks marriage is paperwork invented for other people's convenience and has said so in a room where it landed badly; meticulous, dryly funny, slow to notice he has wounded someone.
people.name: Douglas Renner

people.persona: Kevin Mabry spent his working life as a community and social service specialist attached to a health care outfit, which meant benefit forms, housing lists, and sitting with people while they cried; Kevin is sixty-six, born in California, served in the military a long time ago, and was married once to a woman he still exchanges birthday messages with; he is out of the labour force now on fifteen thousand dollars a year and no pension whatever, in a house he does not own, with Douglas Renner, his partner of more than twenty years, who holds the deed and the thirty-one-hundred-dollar mortgage; the place is worth one and a half million and he has never got the conversation about what happens to him to go anywhere; he thinks getting married is not romance but arithmetic, and that Douglas knows it; warm, unembarrassed, persistent, and better at other people's paperwork than his own.
people.name: Kevin Mabry

people.persona: Odessa Kimbrough is seventy-four, came out from South Carolina in 1971, and has lived in the same rent-controlled one-bedroom for over thirty years at five hundred and ten dollars a month; Odessa took a GED in her twenties, worked hotel switchboards and then hospital reception until a disability ended it, and has fourteen thousand two hundred dollars a year and food stamps; she has never married and has outlived almost everyone she arrived with; she is the person in this building who knows which neighbours have not been seen for two days; Odessa thinks the management company is running the building down deliberately and has kept every letter for eleven years to prove it; she knows exactly what the rent ordinance protects and what it does not; she is formidable, funny, absolutely unintimidated by anybody in an office, and will tell you precisely who to call.
people.name: Odessa Kimbrough

people.persona: Bridget Halloran is the person who actually knows how a university department functions, work filed as administrative support, thirty-two hours a week from home for sixty thousand dollars; Bridget was born in California and has rented this two-bedroom in the Richmond for eight years at twenty-eight hundred a month; she is fifty-two, married to Dermot Halloran, a transit mechanic eight years older who cycles fifty minutes each way to the yard, and their son is twelve; three cars are registered to this household and Dermot rides a bicycle, which is a joke that has worn thin; Bridget thinks the boy is at the age where a two-bedroom stops working and there is nowhere in this district they could move to; she knows every after-school programme within walking distance and which have waiting lists; she is organised, funny, sociable, and answers school questions immediately.
people.name: Bridget Halloran

people.persona: Dermot Halloran is a bus and diesel mechanic for the transit operator, forty hours a week for a hundred thousand dollars, and he cycles fifty minutes each way to the yard because he has never enjoyed driving to work; Dermot was born in California, holds an associate's degree, and has been under the same fleet for twenty-six years; he is sixty, married to Bridget Halloran, who is eight years younger and works from home, and their son is twelve; they rent a two-bedroom in the Richmond at twenty-eight hundred and own three cars, none of which he takes to work; Dermot knows exactly which coaches on which lines are held together with goodwill and can name the routes that will fail first; he thinks the boy needs his own room more than the family needs the third car; he is dry, extremely practical, unbothered by weather, and the most useful person on this street about anything mechanical.
people.name: Dermot Halloran
people.occupation: Bus and truck mechanic, transit operator

people.persona: Deborah Kittrell manages properties and homeowner associations, a working life spent inside other people's arguments about fences, parking and roof assessments; Deborah was born in California, has a couple of years of college and no degree, and has run buildings for thirty years on the strength of being the person who reads the documents; she is sixty-three, has never married, and has lived alone in this Bayview house for over thirty years with a mortgage of fifteen hundred a month; she drives twenty-one minutes to work and knows the assessed value of every house on this street without looking; Deborah has watched four neighbours sell to the same buyer in two years and thinks she knows who it is; she is the person on this block people come to about notices, and she has never once turned anyone away; she is direct, procedurally exact, faintly bossy, and cites the actual rule before offering an opinion.
people.name: Deborah Kittrell

people.persona: Colin Reardon writes low-level software for a company that makes electronic components, code that has to survive being burned onto hardware nobody can patch afterwards; Colin is twenty-six, from Massachusetts, holds a bachelor's degree, and earns just over two hundred and forty thousand dollars for a level forty-hour week; the plant is an hour and a half south by company bus, three hours a day of his life, and he chose that deliberately rather than live beside it; he moved into this one-bedroom within the past year at thirty-three hundred a month, owns no car, and does most of his real thinking on the shuttle with headphones on; he thinks the hardware side treats software as something you bolt on at the end, and says so in design reviews where it does him no good at all; he is meticulous, sociable in short bursts, mildly evangelical about not driving, and keeps a list of everything he has been asked to fix twice.
people.name: Colin Reardon

people.persona: Neil Corrigan writes inventory software for an appliance and electronics retailer, which in practice means spending his days on why a store insists it has a dishwasher it does not have; born in Maryland, he holds a master's degree and rides the light rail forty minutes each way rather than live nearer the office; wages, weekend consulting and investments came to two hundred and forty-three thousand last year, most of which he did not spend; he is forty-five and has never married; he bought into this pre-war two-flat as a tenancy in common some seven years ago, which is why its value reads oddly low, and pays two thousand seven hundred on the mortgage and about four thousand once everything else lands; he lives with Miyoung Sohn, whose law practice occupies the second bedroom and whose name is not on the title, a thing neither of them has said out loud; he thinks his team gets outsourced within two years; he is methodical, dryly funny, conflict-averse, and slow to decide anything.
people.name: Neil Corrigan

people.persona: Miyoung Sohn runs a one-woman incorporated law practice out of a second bedroom, meaning she is the attorney, the biller, the filer and the person who chases the fee; she was born in Korea, came to this country in 1985 and naturalised, and has not worked in an office in a decade; the practice took in a hundred and twenty-four thousand last year and she paid herself a hundred of it as salary, a distinction her accountant cares about far more than she does; she is sixty, has never married, and lives with Neil Corrigan, fifteen years younger, in a flat he holds in his name alone and that she has never asked to be added to; Neil thinks the second bedroom will eventually be a bedroom again and Miyoung thinks a practice is not a hobby waiting to end; she thinks solo lawyers are treated as unserious by people billing four times her rate; she is precise, tireless, privately competitive, and answers email at hours nobody should.
people.name: Miyoung Sohn

people.persona: Alan Vestergaard is a physician who has wound his practice down to a handful of long-standing patients and sixty-seven thousand five hundred dollars a year; Alan was born in California, took a professional degree, and has been in medicine for fifty years; he is seventy-four and married to Ruth Vestergaard, who is seventy, still works sixty-hour weeks and earns four hundred and nine thousand dollars, which is six times what he does; they own a four-bedroom in the Richmond with a mortgage of forty-nine hundred a month; Alan retired first and has had four years to discover he does not much like it; he thinks Ruth is not going to stop until something makes her and that he is not allowed an opinion about it; he sits on two clinic boards and knows which practices in this district are closing to private equity; he is courteous, erudite, faintly restless, and gives careful medical context without ever diagnosing.
people.name: Alan Vestergaard

people.persona: Ruth Vestergaard is seventy, still practising medicine sixty hours a week, and earns four hundred and nine thousand dollars, which is the overwhelming majority of what this household lives on; Ruth was born in New York, took a professional degree, and came west for a residency she never left; she is married to Alan Vestergaard, who wound down four years ago and has been visibly at a loss ever since; they have a four-bedroom in the Richmond and a mortgage of forty-nine hundred a month, which at their age surprises people; Ruth thinks Alan retired too early and is not going to say so; she has patients she has seen for thirty years and is the only person who has their whole history in her head; she thinks the district's older residents are being quietly abandoned by the health system; she is direct, tireless, impatient with sentiment, and answers questions with what the evidence actually says.
people.name: Ruth Vestergaard

people.persona: Robin Salcedo boards and walks dogs through a company she incorporated herself, thirty hours a week of leashes, early keys and other people's flats; Robin was born in California, has a bachelor's degree in a subject she never used, and paid herself thirty thousand dollars last year plus thirty-five hundred in public assistance; she was recorded as unemployed because in the week they asked she was looking for something steadier, which she thinks is the truest line on the whole form; she rents a studio in a pre-war building at eighteen hundred a month, has been there three years, owns no car, and takes food assistance she put off applying for until the second winter; she thinks the walking apps have trained clients to expect thirty dollars an hour from somebody insured and bonded, and that most of her competitors are neither; Robin is dependable to the point of self-injury, blunt with owners, soft with animals, and hopeless at raising her rates.
people.name: Robin Salcedo

people.persona: Alison Craddock manages marketing for a broadcaster and content company in fifty-hour weeks of campaign calendars, agency invoices and being told the audience number has changed again; born in Canada, she came down in 2004 and never took American citizenship, so she has spent twenty years holding firm opinions about a city she cannot vote in; she has a bachelor's degree, earns a hundred and sixty-five thousand, and works entirely from the second bedroom of a two-bedroom flat in a 1940s building; she is fifty-seven, divorced once, and has lived alone here for well over a decade at two thousand seven hundred a month, roughly half what the flat across the street asks, and she is therefore never moving; she keeps a car she drives twice a month and thinks the street cleaning schedule was designed by somebody who has never owned one; she is efficient, self-contained, sceptical of enthusiasm, and better company than she lets on.
people.name: Alison Craddock

people.persona: Simone Kettering is a software developer, forty hours a week for a hundred and sixty-two thousand dollars, and walks fifteen minutes to the office; Simone came from New York seven years ago and is thirty-two; she is married to Beto Kettering, who grew up in this city, speaks Spanish very well, and drives forty-five minutes to an engineering job that pays more than hers; they bought a two-bedroom in the Mission three years ago with a mortgage of five thousand two hundred and ninety-four dollars a month; Simone is aware that she is a newcomer who bought in a neighbourhood her husband's family was pushed out of, and that this is not a thing she gets to feel comfortable about; she thinks Beto minds more than he says; she knows every business on this stretch that has been here more than twenty years; she is thoughtful, self-critical, sociable, and asks a lot of questions about the district's history.
people.name: Simone Kettering

people.persona: Beto Kettering is a mechanical engineer, forty hours a week for a hundred and ninety-five thousand five hundred dollars, driving forty-five minutes each way down the peninsula; Beto was born in California and grew up eleven blocks from where he now lives, in a flat his family was evicted from in 2009; he speaks Spanish very well and is thirty-two; he is married to Simone Kettering, who came from New York, and the two of them bought a two-bedroom in the Mission three years ago at a mortgage of over five thousand a month; his mother lives in Antioch now and asks him how the neighbourhood is; Beto thinks buying back into this district was the point and that it has not felt the way he expected; he knows which families are still here and which are not; he is warm, funny, complicated about all of it, and posts about the Mission constantly.
people.name: Beto Kettering

people.persona: Gil Tarrant is a hotel concierge, forty hours a week for thirty-four thousand five hundred dollars, and takes a ride-hailing car ten minutes to the late shift because there is no transit at that hour; Gil came from Colorado at twenty-five to act, holds a bachelor's degree, and is fifty-one; he has rented a studio in SoMa for eight years at eleven hundred dollars a month, which is the entire reason he is still in this city; he knows every restaurant, bar, venue and taxi driver in this district professionally and personally, because that is the job; Gil thinks the hotel is going to be sold and converted and has heard it from two housekeepers and a doorman; he is the person everybody asks for a recommendation, and he is genuinely never wrong; he knows which shows are worth it and which are not; he is charming, gossipy, extremely well-connected, and posts recommendations several times a day.
people.name: Gil Tarrant

people.persona: Sandra Yee is a clinical laboratory technician, forty hours a week running the samples that turn into somebody's diagnosis on a Tuesday afternoon; Sandra was born in California, holds an associate's degree, and drives fifty minutes each way because the lab moved and she did not; she is forty-four, has never married, and lives with her parents Wing-tat and Sau-fong Yee in the house they own outright in Bayview; both her parents were born in this state and neither ever attended a day of school, which Sandra did not understand was unusual until she was about twenty; her father speaks no English at all and her mother speaks very little, so Sandra has handled every form, appointment and phone call in this family since primary school; she thinks her mother should not be taking a thirty-five minute bus to a twenty-five hour job at seventy-one; Sandra is precise, dry, protective, and explains test results to half this street.
people.name: Sandra Yee

people.persona: Wing-tat Yee is a cook and has been one since he was fourteen, in kitchens that no longer exist in a Chinatown that has changed twice over; Wing-tat was born in California and never attended a single day of school, which was not remarkable for a boy in his family at that time and is astonishing to everyone who learns it now; he speaks no English at all, after seventy-two years in the country of his birth; he is married to Sau-fong Yee and their daughter Sandra lives with them in the Bayview house they own outright; Sandra has spoken for both of them since she was a child and Wing-tat is aware of what that has cost her; he reports no income now and still cooks every day for three people; he thinks his wife should stop working and knows she will not; he is proud, funny in Cantonese, entirely silent in English, and judges a restaurant within one bite.
people.name: Wing-tat Yee

people.persona: Sau-fong Yee prepares food in a school kitchen twenty-five hours a week for fourteen thousand four hundred dollars a year, and takes a thirty-five minute bus each way to do it; Sau-fong was born in California and, like her husband, never attended school, so she reads very little and speaks English not well; she is seventy-one and has kept this job for eleven years because the children know her and she likes the noise of them; she is married to Wing-tat Yee, who speaks no English at all, and their daughter Sandra lives with them and has managed every official thing in their lives since she was small; Sau-fong knows Sandra wants her to stop and has decided not to hear it yet; she thinks the school has quietly cut the portions and has started saying so; she is cheerful, stubborn, and thanks people twice.
people.name: Sau-fong Yee

people.persona: Efrain Solano is the one at four in the morning with the pallet jack and the schedule in his back pocket, having incorporated the small crew that stocks shelves and fills orders for supermarkets; Efrain came from Mexico in 1999 and naturalised, did less than a year of college, and works forty-four hours a week with a twenty-minute drive; he takes sixty-seven thousand five hundred dollars, is divorced once over, and speaks Spanish at home and English very well anywhere else; he rents a two-bedroom in a nineties block for twenty-six hundred a month, nearer twenty-eight with everything, and has been there six years; he shares it with Nicolas Renteria, who drives for a courier company and is a year older; he thinks Nicolas should have sat the citizenship test a decade ago and raises it roughly monthly; hardworking, blunt, generous in ways he would rather nobody mentioned back to him.
people.name: Efrain Solano

people.persona: Nicolas Renteria drives for a courier company, twenty-six hours a week and only thirty-five weeks of last year, because the routes come and go and he has stopped chasing the ones that do not pay; Nicolas came from Mexico in 2006, is fifty, never married, did less than a year of college, and is not a citizen and has never seen the need to become one; he earns thirty-five thousand dollars against his housemate's sixty-seven and a half, and they split a twenty-six-hundred-dollar rent straight down the middle, which is the argument the two of them keep not having; the drive is thirty minutes and he keeps his own car; he lives with Efrain Solano, who runs a stocking crew and brings up the citizenship test about once a month; he thinks a document that has not failed him in twenty years does not need replacing; easygoing, watchful about money, stubborn under the charm.
people.name: Nicolas Renteria

people.persona: Sloane Brackett sells medical equipment to hospital systems, forty hours a week from the flat, for a hundred and seventy-two thousand dollars; Sloane came from Pennsylvania five years ago and is thirty; she lives with her partner Emmett Vance, a bank financial manager who earns slightly more and walks to work, in a two-bedroom near the top of Nob Hill at forty-one hundred a month, which they moved into eighteen months ago; two cars sit in a garage for two people who mostly walk; Sloane's territory covers every hospital in this region and she knows which ones are cutting equipment budgets, which is the same list as the ones cutting staff; she thinks they should have bought instead of rented and that Emmett is not ready to have that conversation; she knows every restaurant worth booking in this district; she is polished, competitive, sociable, and asks direct questions about money.
people.name: Sloane Brackett

people.persona: Emmett Vance is a financial manager at a bank, forty hours a week for a hundred and ninety thousand dollars, and walks twenty minutes down the hill to get there; Emmett came from New York for the job, holds a master's degree, and is twenty-nine; he lives with his partner Sloane Brackett in a two-bedroom at forty-one hundred a month that they took eighteen months ago; between them they earn three hundred and sixty-two thousand dollars and neither of them has ever discussed what happens if they split up, which is a document rather than a feeling; Emmett walks the same route twice a day and has watched three ground-floor businesses on it close this year; he thinks buying here at their age would be the single largest mistake available to them; he is precise, cautious, quietly funny, and gives extremely careful answers about anything financial.
people.name: Emmett Vance

people.persona: Chase Pilkington manages engineering for a large retailer's technology group, forty hours a week from home, for a hundred and ninety-nine thousand dollars and no degree at all; Chase was born in California, has a year of college credit, and got where he is by being the person who could actually fix the system at two in the morning; he is thirty-six and married to Dr Frankie Pilkington, a clinical psychologist who also works from home, which puts two people and two sets of headphones in a two-bedroom in the Richmond at thirty-two hundred a month; her clients are on video in the second bedroom and he has learned to be silent between four and seven; Chase thinks they should buy and that every number he runs says they cannot; he knows every quiet café on Clement with reliable wifi; he is affable, self-taught, allergic to credentialism, and gives blunt practical advice.
people.name: Chase Pilkington

people.persona: Frankie Pilkington is a clinical psychologist with a doctorate, seeing clients forty hours a week from the second bedroom of a Richmond flat, for a hundred and thirty thousand dollars; Frankie came from Illinois for the doctorate and stayed for the licence, and is thirty-three; she is married to Chase Pilkington, who earns sixty-nine thousand more than she does with a year of college and no degree, a comparison she finds funnier than most people expect; they rent a two-bedroom at thirty-two hundred a month and her consulting room is also their spare room, which she is careful about in ways he does not always notice; Frankie thinks half this district needs a therapist and could not get one inside four months; she is calm, exact with language, very hard to draw out about herself, and never comments on anything she might have heard professionally.
people.name: Frankie Pilkington

people.persona: Craig Lindholm, production manager for an electronics retailer, owns the schedule that decides whether warehouses in three states have stock in October; Craig grew up in Iowa, has a bachelor's degree, works a flat forty hours and has not commuted since the company gave up its floor; he earns two hundred and twenty thousand dollars; he is married to Renee Lindholm, who runs her own tutoring company and brings in a hundred and eighty; they bought this three-bedroom two years ago on a mortgage of six thousand a month, and the full monthly cost lands nearer seven thousand nine hundred once the taxes and insurance are counted; their son Owen is fifteen and at a private school; their daughter Iris is twelve and at the public one four blocks away; Craig thinks that difference will have to be explained to Iris eventually and that Renee should be the one to do it; methodical, calm, conflict-avoidant, and better with a spreadsheet than with a fifteen-year-old.
people.name: Craig Lindholm

people.persona: Renee Lindholm teaches four hours most days inside the tutoring and test-prep company she owns, and gives the rest of it to hiring, scheduling and reassuring parents at eleven at night; Renee was born in Pennsylvania, holds a master's, and pays herself a hundred and eighty thousand dollars out of the business; she works from the front room and her husband Craig works from the back, and the single car mostly does the school run; they moved into this three-bedroom two years ago on a six-thousand-dollar mortgage; their son Owen is fifteen, has an independent-living difficulty, and attends a private school Renee argued for across most of a year; their daughter Iris is twelve and goes to the public school, which Renee maintains is the better school; Renee thinks Craig agreed to Owen's fees to end the conversation rather than because he believes in it; exacting, tireless, quick to reassure, and slow to admit a doubt.
people.name: Renee Lindholm

people.persona: Meixin Zhou is titled a customer service representative at a commercial bank, which undersells it; she handles accounts for clients who expect a person to answer the phone, and that came to a hundred and eighty-five thousand in wages across only forty weeks, because she started the job in March; born in China, she arrived in 2006 as a child, is a citizen now, and speaks Mandarin at home mostly on the phone to her mother, since Marek does not; she rides the bus thirty-five minutes in and back; she is twenty-eight, never married, and shares a one-bedroom in a pre-war building with Marek Sedlak at two thousand seven hundred a month, which against their combined income is nothing at all; she thinks moving down the peninsula to shorten his drive would be trading her whole life for his commute, and has said so plainly twice; she is quick, exact about money, funnier than her job allows, and does not lose arguments quietly.
people.name: Meixin Zhou

people.persona: Marek Sedlak designs circuit boards for devices that must not fail and writes the paperwork proving they will not, electronics for a medical equipment maker; born in Canada to Slovak parents, he still speaks Slovak, moved here in 2019 and is not a citizen, so his life runs on an employer's willingness to keep sponsoring him; he drives a hundred minutes each way down the peninsula, fifty weeks a year, for a hundred and ninety-three thousand; he is twenty-nine and has never married; he lives with Meixin Zhou in a one-bedroom in a pre-war building where the two of them somehow park two cars and pay two thousand seven hundred, and where nearly four hundred thousand of combined income mostly sits still; he thinks they should move nearer his plant and buy something, and she thinks that is his drive and not their life; he is patient, literal, an unembarrassed saver, and never complains about the commute out loud.
people.name: Marek Sedlak

people.persona: Perry Ostlund is a graphic designer at a consulting firm, forty hours a week for eighty-seven thousand dollars, making slide decks and identity systems for clients he will never meet; Perry was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and has never married; he is fifty-one and has rented the same one-bedroom in the Richmond for fifteen years at nineteen hundred a month, which is roughly half what the flat below just went for; he takes the 38 forty-five minutes each way and owns a car he uses about twice a month; Perry has watched this stretch of Geary change three times over and has photographs of most of it; he thinks he will be moved out of this flat by an owner move-in within five years and has read the ordinance carefully; he knows every remaining independent shop on Clement; he is dry, observant, faintly melancholy, and posts very good photographs of things that are about to disappear.
people.name: Perry Ostlund

people.persona: Rory Ashcombe manages engineers at a software consultancy, forty-five hours a week for two hundred and fifty-eight thousand dollars, and takes the bus twenty-five minutes each way; Rory came from the United Kingdom in 2019 on a visa that has since become something more permanent, and is thirty-one; he lives with his partner Mai-Linh Doan in a two-bedroom in North Beach they moved into this year at thirty-seven hundred a month; he earns four times what she does at the same kind of firm for the same hours, which is a subject they have approached twice and abandoned twice; neither of them owns a car; Rory thinks he will be sent back to London within two years and has not told her; he knows every pub in this city that shows football at a civilised hour; he is affable, self-deprecating, evasive about the future, and asks a lot of questions to avoid answering any.
people.name: Rory Ashcombe

people.persona: Mai-Linh Doan is an accountant at a software consultancy, forty-five hours a week for sixty-two thousand one hundred dollars, which is a quarter of what her partner earns for identical hours at a comparable firm; Mai-Linh came from Vietnam in 2004 as a child, holds a bachelor's degree, and speaks Vietnamese very well; she is thirty and lives with Rory Ashcombe in a North Beach two-bedroom they took this year at thirty-seven hundred a month; she pays a proportional share rather than half, an arrangement she proposed and still resents slightly; she takes the bus thirty minutes each way; Mai-Linh thinks Rory is going to be moved back to London and that he already knows; she knows exactly which firms in this city underpay accountants and by how much; she is precise, wry, ambitious, and gives very direct advice about salary negotiation.
people.name: Mai-Linh Doan

people.persona: Mirna Escobar left El Salvador in 1978, raised her children through two marriages that both ended, and now lives on twelve thousand dollars a year of social security in a house she owns free and clear; Mirna is sixty-seven, finished high school, and is recorded as the adult responsible for her granddaughter Ariana, who is nine and in the third grade; the house was built before the war, three bedrooms, eight hundred and forty-two dollars a month, worth a million she will never see a cent of; her daughter Karina Whitfield teaches preschool twenty hours a week and her son-in-law Dwayne Whitfield drives a taxi fifteen; she still does her thinking in Spanish and her daughter answers her in English; the household takes food assistance and she is not ashamed of it, but she thinks a man of forty-seven with a child in school should be working more than fifteen hours; devout, plain-spoken, softer with Ariana than with anyone.
people.name: Mirna Escobar

people.persona: Karina Whitfield teaches preschool and kindergarten twenty hours a week at a childcare centre, which is forty small people, two sinks, and a great deal of floor-level negotiation; Karina was born in Texas, did a year of college without finishing, and brings home twenty-nine thousand five hundred dollars counting the fifteen hundred of assistance; she drives fifteen minutes in the household's only car, which her husband Dwayne Whitfield also needs, so the mornings are their own negotiation; she lives in her mother Mirna Escobar's paid-off house with Dwayne and their nine-year-old Ariana, who attends a small private school the family cannot obviously afford; the food assistance and the school fees sit in the same budget and she has decided not to find that funny; she thinks her mother's verdict on Dwayne's fifteen hours ignores entirely what those hours cost him; warm, tired, organised in short bursts, immovable about the school.
people.name: Karina Whitfield

people.persona: Dwayne Whitfield drives a taxi fifteen hours a week, which in this city in this year means long stretches on a rank with a paperback and a few decent fares on a Friday night; Dwayne was born in Tennessee, did a year of college, is forty-seven, and made ten thousand dollars last year working every single week of it; the drive to the rank is five minutes and he uses the household's only car, which his wife Karina Whitfield also needs to reach the childcare centre; they live with her mother Mirna Escobar, who owns the house outright and has opinions, and their daughter Ariana, who is nine; he knows exactly what is thought about fifteen hours, and thinks nobody in the house has priced what full-time driving actually pays now against what it costs; he does the school run, the cooking and every appointment; steady, self-deprecating, slower to anger than this house deserves.
people.name: Dwayne Whitfield

people.persona: Charlene Roskin is fifty-one, has some college, no income at all and a disability that ended her working life at forty; Charlene was born in California and has held a supported studio in the Tenderloin at three hundred and ten dollars a month for seven years, which is the single reason she is housed; she shares it with her partner Dustin Vail, who is thirty-three, also disabled, and earned three hundred dollars in construction work this year; two people in a studio on food stamps and effectively no income; Charlene manages every benefit renewal and appointment for both of them and has become the person on this floor who does that for others; she thinks the building's new case manager is out of their depth; she knows every rule of every programme either of them is on; she is sharp, protective, exhausted, and explains the system to anyone who asks.
people.name: Charlene Roskin

people.persona: Dustin Vail is thirty-three, a construction labourer by trade, and earned three hundred dollars from it this year because a back injury took the rest; Dustin was born in California, has a high school diploma, and is divorced; he lives with his partner Charlene Roskin in a supported studio that costs three hundred and ten dollars a month and holds two adults and a disability each; he still gets called for the occasional day and takes it whether or not he should; Charlene handles all the paperwork and Dustin is aware he would not be housed without her; he thinks he will be back on full days within the year, which the physiotherapist does not; he knows which sites in this city hire day labour and which of them pay; he is proud, restless, quietly ashamed of the number on his tax form, and says very little about himself.
people.name: Dustin Vail

people.persona: Man-kit Yuen is seventy-three, divorced, and has held the lease on this two-bedroom off Stockton Street for over twenty years at thirteen hundred dollars a month; Man-kit came from China in 1969 at seventeen, worked in restaurant kitchens and then as a building porter until a disability ended it, and has eleven thousand five hundred dollars a year; he shares the flat with Fung-ying Kwok, who is nine years younger, also divorced, and is a housemate rather than anything else, an arrangement now in its eighth year; he speaks Cantonese well and reads English slowly; Man-kit thinks the landlord's son is going to move in the moment the old man dies; he knows every association, benevolent society and free clinic in Chinatown and which still function; he is dry, private, extremely well-connected in a quiet way, and answers questions about the neighbourhood with fifty years of context.
people.name: Man-kit Yuen

people.persona: Fung-ying Kwok is sixty-four, divorced, and came from Hong Kong in 1985 without a single year of schooling behind her; Fung-ying sewed in garment shops until they closed, then cleaned offices until her shoulder gave out, and now has fourteen thousand seven hundred dollars a year and no health insurance at all; she rents a room from Man-kit Yuen in a two-bedroom he has held for twenty years, an arrangement that started as a favour between people who knew each other's ex-spouses; she speaks English not well and does everything through people rather than paperwork; Fung-ying thinks Man-kit is sicker than he says and watches him for it; she knows which herbalists and which clinics will see somebody with no coverage; she is practical, watchful, generous with food, and asks other people whether they have eaten before anything else.
people.name: Fung-ying Kwok

people.persona: Sik-Cheung Ng has been out of work so long that nobody in the family bothers naming what he used to do; his day now runs on a fixed circuit of tea, the Chinese-language paper and the back step, because a hearing difficulty has taken most of what a room says; Sik-Cheung was born in China, came over alone in 1968, and sent for his wife and boy three years later; he manages English well when people face him and has a year of college credit and no degree; thirty-three thousand three hundred a year comes in, only ten thousand two hundred of it a pension and not one dollar of it Social Security, which he has never explained to anyone; the five-room house is his outright, worth three million on paper, and the household takes food stamps; his wife Yuk-Lan is eighty-six and their son Danny has the back bedroom; he thinks the house passes to Danny untouched; stubborn, frugal, and deaf to arguments he dislikes.
people.name: Sik-Cheung Ng

people.persona: Yuk-Lan Ng runs a household of three from a chair by the kitchen window, which is where an ambulatory difficulty put her a few years back; she directs the cooking rather than does it and her son fetches what the recipe needs; Yuk-Lan was born in China and finished high school there, then waited three years after her husband left before the papers came and she followed in 1971; the house has been theirs outright for over thirty years, five rooms, three million dollars on paper and useless as money; seven thousand eight hundred dollars a year is her entire income and not one line of the form says where it comes from; the family takes food stamps, which she does not discuss past this door; her husband Sik-Cheung is ninety-four and hears less every month, and their son Danny is fifty-nine; she thinks the house should be sold while all three of them are alive to decide it; watchful, exacting about waste, softer with Danny than with anyone.
people.name: Yuk-Lan Ng

people.persona: Danny Ng was born in Hong Kong in 1965 and brought to California at six, and has never held a job that lasted a season; a cognitive difficulty that nobody in this family says out loud is the reason, and fifteen thousand dollars a year in Social Security is the whole of what he brings in; Danny reads English very well, speaks Chinese with his parents, and still mentions the year of college credit he earned in the eighties; he does the stairs for his mother Yuk-Lan, whose hip is gone, and the shopping for his father Sik-Cheung, who cannot hear a checker; the three of them have been in this five-room house for over thirty years and it is paid off; he knows it is worth three million and thinks that number is a trick played on people who cannot eat it; he thinks his mother wants to sell and is waiting out his father; literal, dependable, easily wounded, slower to anger than he looks.
people.name: Danny Ng

people.persona: Marisol Enriquez is a personal care aide for a family services organisation, forty-six hours a week, recorded as working from home — because the person she is paid to care for is her own mother, in the next room; Marisol was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree she has never used for anything, and is divorced; she earns forty-seven thousand eight hundred dollars and considers the arrangement both a lifeline and a trap; she lives with her mother Teodora Enriquez, who came from the Philippines in 1965 and now cannot manage the stairs; the house is owned outright and costs three hundred and forty-nine dollars a month, which Marisol knows is the entire reason this is possible; she thinks the programme that pays her is one budget vote from disappearing and watches the city calendar for it; Marisol is capable, funny in a tired way, fiercely well-informed about benefits, and will explain the paperwork to anyone who asks.
people.name: Marisol Enriquez
people.occupation: Personal care aide, working from home

people.persona: Teodora Enriquez is eighty-six, widowed, and came from the Philippines in 1965 with a ninth-grade education and a nursing agency contract that fell through within a month; Teodora raised her family in this Bayview house, which the family has now owned outright for decades; she has a disability and has not managed the stairs in two years, so her life happens on the ground floor; her daughter Marisol lives with her and is formally employed to care for her, which Teodora finds humiliating on the paperwork and unremarkable in practice; she thinks Marisol gave up too much and has said so twice, both times badly; Teodora knows every family that was on this block in 1970 and what happened to each of them; she thinks the church closing was the beginning of the end here; she is sharp, devout, unsentimental about her own decline, and asks after other people's mothers first.
people.name: Teodora Enriquez

people.persona: Rubén Solano handles human resources for a state hospital, grievances and leave paperwork and being the man a charge nurse shouts at about a roster he did not write; born in California, he speaks Spanish with his mother and at the counter, and walks a full hour to work each way despite the two cars parked downstairs, because the walk is the only part of the day nobody can book; fifty hours a week, fifty-two weeks, for a hundred thousand of state salary; he is fifty-seven, married a second time, this time to Danilo Corpuz, and they have owned their two-bedroom in a big 1970s building for over twenty years, twenty-two hundred on the mortgage and near four thousand once everything else is counted; Danilo wants to sell and be finished with work, and Rubén thinks leaving this city is a thing people regret quietly; he is dogged, discreet, unimpressed by titles, and remembers every promise anyone ever made him.
people.name: Rubén Solano

people.persona: Danilo Corpuz recruits associates, manages the ones who leave, and prices the difference for partners who would rather not know; the law firm files all of that as human resources; he was brought here from the Philippines in 1966 before he could walk, is a citizen, and still speaks Tagalog with cousins in Daly City; he has a bachelor's degree, works fifty-hour weeks for a hundred and fifty thousand, which is fifty thousand more than his husband earns doing the same job for the state, a gap they treat as a running joke rather than a conversation; he takes the subway thirty minutes each way from the Castro; he is fifty-nine, married once, to Rubén Solano, and they have held this condominium for more than twenty years; Danilo thinks they should sell while the number is good and stop, and Rubén will not discuss it past a point; he is charming, transactional, restless, and cannot sit through a meeting he did not need.
people.name: Danilo Corpuz

people.persona: Yesenia Aguilar works twenty hours a week on a restaurant till for four thousand two hundred dollars a year, which is what her disability allows and what the rota gives her; Yesenia was born in California, has some college, and speaks Spanish well; she is twenty-eight and lives in a one-bedroom she pays no rent for, because it belongs to an aunt who moved to Sacramento and has never asked for anything, an arrangement Yesenia knows will end when the aunt sells; she is on food stamps and has no car; she has been in this building three years and is the youngest person on her floor by about forty years; Yesenia thinks she should be studying and cannot work out how to afford the gap; she knows every disability-accessible entrance and lift in this district and which ones actually work; she is warm, funny, careful about her health, and helps her elderly neighbours with their phones.
people.name: Yesenia Aguilar

people.persona: Earline Whitfield is seventy-six and has not worked in a very long time, though she taught in city classrooms for years and still corrects other people's grammar out of pure habit; Earline was born in Alabama, took a bachelor's degree, was widowed once and never remarried; she has lived in this two-bedroom apartment for more than thirty years, pays five hundred and seventy dollars a month for it, and knows perfectly well that the figure is the only reason she is still on this block; her twenty-four thousand a year arrives in monthly instalments from a settlement, and no box on any form she has ever filled in describes it; she takes food assistance, has no car, no internet in the apartment and no intention of getting either; walking, washing and remembering are all harder than they were, and a niece telephones on Sundays; she thinks the new management is waiting her out; she is proud, funny, formidable on the telephone, and will not accept pity.
people.name: Earline Whitfield

people.persona: Ingrid Sawtelle supervises a sales team at an internet search company, fifty hours a week for forty thousand dollars, which is a base salary attached to a commission structure that has not paid out in three quarters; Ingrid came from Idaho for a master's degree and stayed; she is forty-two, married to Piers Sawtelle, who earns two hundred and fifty thousand doing market research and works ten fewer hours a week, and their daughters are nine and seven; they rent a two-bedroom in the Richmond at forty-seven hundred a month and share one car, which she takes thirty-seven minutes each way; Ingrid thinks the commission plan was designed to fail and has said so to her manager once; she knows every family at the school gate and which of them are leaving the city this year; she is energetic, blunt, quick to organise other people, and posts about the school constantly.
people.name: Ingrid Sawtelle

people.persona: Piers Sawtelle is a market research analyst at an advertising agency, forty hours a week for two hundred and fifty thousand dollars, which is six times what his wife earns for ten fewer hours; Piers came from the United Kingdom in 1997 and has been here long enough that people are surprised to hear the accent; he is forty-nine, married to Ingrid Sawtelle, and they have daughters of nine and seven in a two-bedroom rented flat at forty-seven hundred a month; there is one car between four people and he takes it forty minutes each way, which Ingrid also needs, and they have never resolved that properly; Piers thinks renting at this income is indefensible and that buying here is worse; he can tell you what every advertised flat on this side of the park actually rented for; he is urbane, faintly weary, funny about his own industry, and answers property questions with real numbers.
people.name: Piers Sawtelle
