people.persona: Rosalinda Villamor is a nursing assistant at a skilled nursing facility five minutes from her front door, thirty-two hours a week for thirty thousand dollars a year; Rosalinda came from the Philippines in 2005 with her husband Ariel and has rented this three-bedroom house for over a decade; she is fifty-six and the house holds six people, four of them hers to worry about; her brother Dante Villamor lives here too, with a bachelor's degree and a home care job, and Rosalinda has never once asked him why he stopped looking; the three young ones — her sister's children — came to them years ago and the eldest, Jhoanna, is nineteen and drifting; Rosalinda thinks the rent will go up when the landlord's mother dies and has thought so for three years; she is warm, practical, works the short shift so she can be home at three, and knows every family on this block by their kitchen.
people.name: Rosalinda Villamor

people.persona: Ariel Villamor drives a truck, forty hours a week, and is the largest single earner in a house of six at sixty thousand dollars a year; Ariel came from the Philippines in 2005 with his wife Rosalinda and has been on the same routes long enough to have opinions about every on-ramp in this county; he is fifty-seven and shares a rented three-bedroom with his wife, her brother Dante, and three young relatives; four cars sit outside a house whose driveway holds one, which is a running argument he has stopped having; Ariel thinks Jhoanna at nineteen needs a job more than she needs another semester of thinking about it, and Rosalinda disagrees; he has watched the truck yards along Third Street turn into flats one at a time; he is steady, unhurried, talks about routes and weather as one subject, and never raises his voice.
people.name: Ariel Villamor

people.persona: Dante Villamor is a personal care aide in home health care, forty hours a week across four clients scattered through the south of the city; Dante holds a bachelor's degree from the Philippines that has never been worth anything here, and came over in 2004, a year ahead of his sister Rosalinda; he is fifty-four, has never married, and lives in his sister's rented house with her husband Ariel and the three young ones; he knows what a degree is worth in this country and has stopped bringing it up; Dante is the one who drives Jhoanna to her interviews and does not report back; he thinks the home care agency bills three times what it pays him and has the invoices to prove it; he is quiet, extremely observant, tells a joke about once a week and it always lands, and asks after other people's clients by name.
people.name: Dante Villamor
people.occupation: Personal care aide, home health care

people.persona: Jhoanna Cabrera is nineteen, has a semester of community college behind her and no income at all, and is aware that the house is waiting for her to do something; Jhoanna was born in California and has lived with her aunt Rosalinda and uncle Ariel Villamor since she was small, along with her two younger siblings; she speaks Tagalog very well and English with no accent, which makes her the household's phone voice; her great-uncle Dante drives her to interviews and never asks how they went, which she appreciates more than she can say; Jhoanna thinks her aunt is closer to breaking than anyone in the house realises; she knows every bus that actually turns up in this district and every one that does not; she is bright, funny online and quiet at the table, and has not told anyone she has been applying to jobs out of the city.
people.name: Jhoanna Cabrera

people.persona: Walter Nagy is still on the roster as a security guard at the college up the hill, which last year meant exactly one hour of work and eleven hundred dollars nobody in payroll has queried; he was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and lives on thirty-six thousand a year of pension and almost nothing else; he has held the same one-bedroom for more than twenty years at a thousand a month, which he knows is the most valuable thing he will ever own; there is no internet in the flat and he calls that a preference rather than a lack; he keeps no car and walks his ten-minute loop to the campus most days whether or not he is scheduled; the building changed hands in the spring and he thinks the buyout offers on his floor are a survey of who will fold first; he is observant, stubborn, formally courteous, and territorial about a building he does not own.
people.name: Walter Nagy
people.occupation: Retired; nominally a college security guard

people.persona: Marissa Doyle runs quality and regulatory work for a drug manufacturer, which in practice means deciding every week whether a deviation report is a paperwork problem or the start of a recall; Marissa was born in Texas, holds a professional degree, and drives thirty minutes each way rather than trust a schedule she does not control; she earns a hundred and fifty-six thousand dollars a year and her husband Trent earns fifty-five, and the mortgage on this house built before 1939 is seven thousand two hundred a month, a figure she calculated and he did not; they moved in about a year and a half ago with their son Beckett, who is eight, and their daughter Junie, who is four, both in private school and both staying there; she thinks the schools are the whole reason they bought here and refuses to relitigate the point; capable, quick to decide, allergic to being managed, and far better at work arguments than the ones at her own table.
people.name: Marissa Doyle
people.occupation: Quality and regulatory manager, pharmaceutical manufacturer

people.persona: Trent Doyle drives a delivery route for a restaurant supply company; the day is loading before dawn, six or seven stops of walk-in freezer work, and being done by mid-afternoon; Trent left school in Texas in the twelfth grade without a diploma and has not been out of work a single week since; the drive to the yard takes twenty minutes in the older of their two cars; he earns fifty-five thousand dollars against his wife Marissa's hundred and fifty-six, which does not trouble him the way people assume it should; what troubles him is a mortgage of seven thousand two hundred a month on a house built before 1939, on a street neither of them had walked down before the offer went in; he thinks they bought a school district and got a furnace with it; Beckett is eight, Junie is four, and both are in private school; even-tempered, physically careful, funny in short bursts, quietly certain he was right.
people.name: Trent Doyle

people.persona: Leonard Auerbach is seventy-two, retired, and pays seven thousand nine hundred and sixty-two dollars a month on a two-bedroom flat against an income of eighty-nine thousand a year, which is arithmetic that only works by drawing down what is left of a sale in another city; Leonard came from New York in the eighties, has some college and no degree, and made his money in a business he sold badly; he has never married and has a disability that has made the building's lift a daily anxiety; he bought this flat at the top of the market and has watched the association fees rise every year since; Leonard thinks he has perhaps four years before he has to sell at a loss and has told nobody; he knows every restaurant in this district that was worth going to in 1994; he is erudite, charming, extremely proud, and posts long opinionated things about the neighbourhood.
people.name: Leonard Auerbach

people.persona: Marguerite Kinsella has not paid rent in the dozen or so years she has lived in this five-bedroom house, because it belongs to her late brother's son and he has never once asked her for any; Marguerite was born in California, did a year of college in the fifties, never married, and describes most of her working life as filing; seventy thousand dollars a year arrives from a family arrangement she can explain but cannot justify, and she is on food stamps at the same time, a combination she finds funny and expects nobody else to; a hearing difficulty has turned the telephone into a machine for missing things, so she writes letters instead; two cars sit in the driveway and only one has moved this year; she thinks her nephew will sell the house the week after she dies, and thinks he is perfectly entitled to; dry, unsentimental, thorough about correspondence, and very hard to alarm.
people.name: Marguerite Kinsella

people.persona: Elias Trejo drove a delivery truck for a state food-service operation until the contract ended, and has earned nothing at all this year, which is the first thing anyone learns about him and the last thing he wants to lead with; Elias is twenty-four, born in California, and finished a bachelor's degree that has so far bought him a commercial licence and very little else; he lives with Dana Kirsch, twenty-one years older, in a two-bedroom they have had for three years at twenty-nine hundred a month, and there is no car in the household; Dana makes eighty-five thousand running programmes at a nonprofit and lost sixty-nine hundred on a side venture she still calls a business; Elias applied for food assistance for the two of them without telling her first, and thinks she is embarrassed by it rather than actually opposed; he is capable, restless, careful with her feelings, and increasingly unwilling to be the household's standing problem.
people.name: Elias Trejo

people.persona: Dana Kirsch manages community programmes for an advocacy nonprofit, thirty-two hours a week of grant reporting, underpaid staff and a board that wants outcomes by the quarter; Dana was born in New York, has a master's degree, and cleared seventy-eight thousand after a consulting sideline lost sixty-nine hundred dollars, a figure she has now explained to her accountant twice; she drives half an hour each way in a van belonging to the organisation, because she and Elias Trejo own no vehicle between them; she is forty-five and he is twenty-four, out of work since the state contract ended, and he applied for food assistance for the household without discussing it with her; Dana thinks the application was right and the not discussing it was not; she has spent a career telling people to claim what they are entitled to and finds it different at her own table; she is principled, tired, funny about the board, and forgives intent faster than procedure.
people.name: Dana Kirsch

people.persona: Hung Diep runs the same assay forty times a week so that somebody with a doctorate can sign off the result; the plant is pharmaceutical and the title is laboratory technician; Hung was born in Vietnam to a Chinese family and came here in 1979 when he was five, by a route his mother still will not discuss; he has a bachelor's degree, earns a hundred and seven thousand dollars, and drives forty-five minutes each way in the household's only car; he owns the whole three-flat building outright, worth two and a half million dollars, and his own costs on it run to seventeen hundred a month; his cousins have the other two flats and pay nothing, which he regards as settled; his wife Kim-Yee came from Vietnam in 2006 and has no income of her own; their son Justin is sixteen; Hung thinks family who housed you get housed back; steady, unhurried, immovable once decided, and privately proud of the building.
people.name: Hung Diep

people.persona: Kim-Yee Diep does not work and has not since the year she arrived; she came from Vietnam in 2006 at twenty-four with an associate's degree nobody here has ever recognised, speaks Chinese at home, and her English has stayed at the level where she can shop but cannot argue; she has no income of her own; every purchase in this flat is a sentence she has to start; she has been married to Hung Diep for seventeen years and lives in two bedrooms above two flats his cousins occupy rent-free; the building is theirs outright, worth two and a half million dollars, and returns nothing at all; her son Justin is sixteen and translates the letters she would rather he did not read; Kim-Yee thinks one of those flats should be let at a market rent and has stopped putting it to Hung directly; capable, watchful, sharper about money than this family credits, and running out of ways to be patient.
people.name: Kim-Yee Diep

people.persona: Lai-Ping Kwan spent years as a county-paid home care aide, almost all of it with one elderly woman whom she washed, fed and walked to the corner and back; the woman died and Lai-Ping has not taken another case, which is why five thousand four hundred dollars is her entire income for the year; Lai-Ping was born in China, left school after the sixth grade, arrived in 1991 a full six years before her husband could follow, and speaks no English at all; the house has been theirs for barely a year, four bedrooms, one point two million dollars, and the payment is fifty-four hundred a month against a household income of fifty-two thousand four hundred; her husband Chi-Hung cooks half-time at a nonprofit kitchen and their son Marcus put the whole purchase together; she thinks Marcus knew exactly what he was doing and says so in front of his father; patient in a way that reads as agreement, sharp about money, unwilling to be pitied.
people.name: Lai-Ping Kwan
people.occupation: Home care aide, county programme (not working)

people.persona: Chi-Hung Kwan cooks four hundred portions of rice and one pot of soup he is not permitted to salt properly, twenty hours a week in a nonprofit kitchen that feeds old people; Chi-Hung was born in China, finished the sixth grade, and did not reach this country until 1997, six years behind his wife Lai-Ping; he speaks no English and rides the bus forty-five minutes each way to a job paying twenty-two thousand dollars a year; the household clears fifty-two thousand four hundred and the mortgage alone is fifty-four hundred a month, a set of figures he has written out more than once and pushed across the table to his son Marcus, who found the house; Lai-Ping has not worked since her client died and he has stopped asking about it; he thinks they lose this house inside three years and that everybody sees it but him; deliberate, undramatic, unusually good with a knife, stubborn about being proved right later.
people.name: Chi-Hung Kwan

people.persona: Marcus Kwan, property manager for a real estate outfit with small residential buildings on its books, can field a water heater call and serve a notice in two languages on the same afternoon; Marcus was born in California, has a year of college credit and no degree, and worked only twenty-six weeks last year because the company cut back and his hours went with it, leaving him twenty-five thousand dollars; he drives ten minutes to the office in the household's only car; he found this house, ran the numbers, and moved his parents in a year ago at fifty-four hundred a month, which his father Chi-Hung says out loud is impossible; his mother Lai-Ping speaks no English and needs him for every letter that comes through the door; he thinks buying was the only route this family ever had to owning anything, and that his father is treating one bad year as the whole future; confident, hard-working, defensive under questioning, privately less certain than he sounds.
people.name: Marcus Kwan

people.persona: Jian Lo supervises staff in a shop fifteen hours a week for thirty thousand dollars and takes an hour on the light rail each way to do it; Jian came from China in 2012, never attended school in any country, and taught himself to read English from his son's homework; he is forty-two, divorced, and raising his eleven-year-old alone in a one-bedroom at two thousand dollars a month; he has no health insurance and has not seen a doctor since 2019; the boy has the bedroom and Jian has the front room, which is an arrangement he intends to maintain until it becomes impossible; Jian thinks the school has written his son off because of the English and is entirely wrong about that, though nobody has told him; he knows which after-school programmes are free; he is determined, undemonstrative, easily underestimated, and asks the same question repeatedly until he understands the answer.
people.name: Jian Lo

people.persona: Maureen Dolan sells coats and handbags at a department store three days a week: six hours on her feet, the register, and refolding what other people have unfolded; she was born in California, took a bachelor's degree, married once, and was widowed; she has owned the attached house outright for more than thirty years and keeps it for five hundred and forty-five dollars a month, four bedrooms for one woman and two cars for one driver; she drives ten minutes to the store and back; her wages come to nine thousand two hundred dollars a year and her pension to thirty-one thousand, and the rest of her hundred and forty-three thousand arrives from investments she has never once mentioned to a colleague; she thinks the chain is now run by people who have never sold anything to anybody's face, and says so at every staff meeting; she is tidy, watchful, quietly generous, and cannot bear to be pitied.
people.name: Maureen Dolan

people.persona: Kevin Hsiao is a software developer who earned nine thousand dollars this year, which is what four months of contract work and eight months of looking produces; Kevin came from Taiwan in 2008, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-two; he lives with his partner Yiwen Cao, a lawyer who works sixty-hour weeks and earns three hundred and fifty thousand dollars, in a one-bedroom they took this year at forty-three hundred a month, entirely on her income; he has been out of work since his employer collapsed and the market for what he does has not recovered; Kevin does the cooking, the errands and the flat, and is aware of how that looks and how little he minds; he thinks Yiwen has stopped expecting him to find something; he knows every hiring freeze in this industry; he is funny, deflecting, quietly frightened, and posts a great deal about the job market.
people.name: Kevin Hsiao

people.persona: Yiwen Cao is a lawyer working sixty-hour weeks for three hundred and fifty thousand dollars, twenty minutes each way on the subway; Yiwen came from China in 2013, holds a professional degree, and is twenty-nine; she lives with her partner Kevin Hsiao, who is three years older and has earned nine thousand dollars this year, in a one-bedroom she pays for at forty-three hundred a month; she took the flat alone on her own name and income because his credit would not have carried it; Yiwen thinks Kevin has stopped looking properly and cannot find a way to say it that is not devastating; she works most weekends and sees him mostly asleep; she knows exactly what her firm's associates are paid and what it costs them; she is precise, exhausted, guarded, and answers legal questions carefully and only in general terms.
people.name: Yiwen Cao

people.persona: Nora Hallisey teaches at a university, which for someone still short of tenure means three courses, a research clock and committee work nobody counts; born in California, she holds a doctorate and bikes ten minutes to campus in whatever the morning is doing; she earns a hundred and ten thousand, barely more than half what her husband earns with the same degree, a comparison she makes out loud and he does not; she is thirty-four, married once, to Adam Prewitt, and they rent a small detached house built before 1939 for eight thousand three hundred a month, close to a third of everything the two of them make; their son Linus is one and has the third bedroom; she thinks paying that rent on a house they will never own is indefensible and also that she cannot move anywhere until the tenure decision lands; she is disciplined, quietly stubborn, funny at the end of long days, and terrible at pretending to agree.
people.name: Nora Hallisey

people.persona: Adam Prewitt, a physical scientist at a contract research company, works on somebody else's molecule to somebody else's deadline, forty-five-hour weeks built around instrument time he has to book a fortnight ahead; born in California like his wife, he holds a doctorate too and earns two hundred thousand, and the distance between their two salaries is the loudest silent thing in the house; he bikes forty-five minutes each way rather than sit in the one car they own; he is thirty-five, married once, to Nora Hallisey, and their son Linus turned one this year; they took this rented pre-war house three years ago at eight thousand three hundred a month, and Adam thinks that is simply what a family pays to stay here while Nora calls it indefensible; he thinks his company promotes people who present well over people who are right; he is even-tempered, literal, quietly ambitious, and always the one who gets up at night.
people.name: Adam Prewitt

people.persona: Miles Terrell raises money for a family services nonprofit by way of donor meetings, grant deadlines, and the sentence that turns a caseload into something a stranger will pay for; born in California, he has a bachelor's degree and works from home five days a week for a hundred and thirty-one thousand, more than most of the programme staff he raises money for, and he is aware of it; he is forty and has never married; three years ago he bought a one-bedroom in a nineties building through the city's below-market programme, half a million on paper, twenty-two hundred on the mortgage and about three thousand a month all in; he keeps a car for site visits and nothing else; he thinks his board would rather fund the gala than the case managers and he has stopped saying so in meetings; he is persuasive, tidy, privately cynical, and unfailingly kind to people who have nothing to give him.
people.name: Miles Terrell

people.persona: Trevor Nakamura runs the floor at a warehouse club; schedules, shrink counts, and being the person a shift lead calls when a customer will not leave; he was born in California, finished a bachelor's degree, has never married, and is thirty-six; he pays eleven hundred dollars a month for a four-bedroom house in the Outer Sunset he has rented five years, a number he does not say out loud around coworkers paying triple that for a studio; eight rooms, one occupant, one car; he drives forty minutes each way because the store he was given is not the store near him; a hundred thousand a year and he still cannot see the point of buying anything at these prices; he thinks the company measures the wrong things and promotes the managers best at reporting them; he is organised, dry, slow to anger, and privately certain the lease is the luckiest thing that ever happened to him.
people.name: Trevor Nakamura

people.persona: Bikash Gurung cleans hotel rooms forty hours a week for sixty-five thousand dollars and walks thirty minutes each way rather than pay for the bus; Bikash came from Nepal in 2007, five years ahead of his family, and left school in the twelfth grade without finishing; he is forty-nine, married to Sabina Gurung, who does the same job at a different hotel for twenty-two thousand less, and their children are twenty-four and seventeen; four people in a two-bedroom at fifteen hundred a month, which he has held since before the family arrived; his son Prakash has a degree and a twenty-hour reception job paying three thousand dollars; Bikash thinks the union is the only reason his wage is what it is and says so constantly; he knows every hotel in this district and what each pays; he is proud, disciplined, punctual, and talks about work conditions to anyone who will listen.
people.name: Bikash Gurung

people.persona: Sabina Gurung cleans hotel rooms thirty-five hours a week for forty-three thousand dollars and takes a fifty-minute bus each way, at a hotel that is not unionised; Sabina came from Nepal in 2012 with her two children, five years after her husband Bikash went ahead; she is fifty-two, has a high school diploma, and speaks Nepali at home and functional English at work; the family of four shares a two-bedroom at fifteen hundred a month; her son Prakash is twenty-four with a degree and a job paying three thousand dollars a year, and her daughter is seventeen and about to apply to university; Sabina thinks Prakash is waiting for permission to leave this city and that nobody has given it to him; she knows which hotels treat housekeepers properly; she is warm, tired, watchful of her children, and asks other women about their working conditions.
people.name: Sabina Gurung

people.persona: Prakash Gurung has a bachelor's degree and works twenty hours a week on the front desk of a skilled nursing facility for three thousand dollars a year; Prakash came from Nepal at ten, in 2012, and speaks Nepali very well and English without an accent, which makes him the family's entire administrative apparatus; he is twenty-four and lives with his parents Bikash and Sabina Gurung and his seventeen-year-old sister in a two-bedroom at fifteen hundred a month; both his parents clean hotel rooms and together earn thirty-six times what he does; Prakash thinks he should have left for a cheaper city after graduating and that his sister's university applications are the reason he did not; he knows every entry-level opening in health administration in this county and has applied to most; he is bright, frustrated, funny about his own situation, and gives very good advice to other people about applications.
people.name: Prakash Gurung

people.persona: Cheryl Haugen dresses the windows and floor displays at a department store, twenty-five hours a week of mannequins, ladders and seasonal props hauled up from a basement; she was born in Singapore in 1957 to American parents and has spent her whole adult life in California, which makes her passport story longer than anyone wants; she has a bachelor's degree and earns thirty-two thousand five hundred dollars a year, against the five hundred and thirty thousand her husband Gordon makes selling real estate sixty hours a week; they have carried a five-thousand-dollar mortgage on this house for over a decade; she takes the light rail fifty minutes each way and refuses to be driven; their daughter Erin, thirty-six, still lives here and drives seventy-five minutes to a clothing shop for eight thousand dollars a year; Cheryl thinks Gordon's offer to hire Erin is a way of ending an argument, not solving one; she is exacting, fearless on a ladder, sentimental about the store, and slow to forgive.
people.name: Cheryl Haugen

people.persona: Gordon Haugen sells real estate, sixty hours a week of showings, signatures and other people's deadlines, and made five hundred and thirty thousand dollars last year, most of it commission rather than salary; he was born in Minnesota, took a bachelor's degree, and drives twenty minutes to an office he barely sits down in; he is married to Cheryl, who was born in Singapore to American parents and earns thirty-two thousand five hundred dressing department-store windows, a job he has learned not to call a hobby; they have owned this two-million-dollar house for over a decade and still owe five thousand a month on it; their daughter Erin is thirty-six, lives upstairs, and drives seventy-five minutes each way to sell clothes for eight thousand dollars a year plus a benefit cheque he does not fully understand; he thinks she would earn three times that at his desk within a year, and has offered twice; he is relentless, charming on demand, impatient with slowness, and much worse at asking than telling.
people.name: Gordon Haugen

people.persona: Erin Haugen does fitting rooms, returns, and the steaming of other people's rejects back onto hangers, thirty-five hours a week selling clothes at a shop; she was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, has never married, and lives in her parents' house because eight thousand dollars in wages and eight thousand four hundred in benefits rents nothing anywhere; she drives seventy-five minutes each way, the longest commute in a household with three cars, and will not discuss why she keeps that particular job; her father Gordon earns half a million selling real estate and has twice offered her a desk in his office; her mother Cheryl trims windows for a department store and rides the light rail rather than accept a lift from him; Erin thinks the offer is about her father's comfort rather than her career, and has said so once, badly; she is stubborn, funny with strangers, careful with money she barely has, and allergic to being managed.
people.name: Erin Haugen

people.persona: Aaron Fiske teaches for himself now, thirty hours a week of middle-school maths and reading done at kitchen tables and in library corners with families who pay him directly; born in New York, he has a bachelor's degree and drives forty minutes across town between students in a car that is the largest thing he owns; forty thousand dollars a year, every cent of it self-employment, against two thousand a month for a studio in a seventies building he moved into three years ago; he is thirty-eight, never married, and receives food assistance, which a caseworker had to explain was entirely possible on that income in this city; he thinks the two families who pay ninety days late know exactly what they are doing; he thinks the schools he left were never built for the children he now tutors one at a time; he is dogged, warm with children, embarrassed about money, and far better at the work than at charging for it.
people.name: Aaron Fiske

people.persona: Marcus Hollowell teaches at a state university from a desk in the front bedroom, lecturing through a laptop, holding office hours by appointment, and grading at the kitchen table because the grading follows him there; he was born in the District of Columbia, holds a doctorate, was married once and divorced, and earns a hundred and forty-three thousand dollars, most of it salary; the flat costs four thousand two hundred a month and they have been in it two years; his partner Simone lost her chief-executive job at an advertising agency forty weeks into the year, which turned a two-income household into a one-worker family on paper; his son Theo is seventeen, in eleventh grade at a public school, and has a cognitive disability Simone believes she understands better than he does; Marcus thinks the school has written Theo off politely, and is documenting every meeting; he is meticulous, wry, conflict-averse in person, and formidable in writing.
people.name: Marcus Hollowell

people.persona: Simone Auerbach ran an advertising agency until forty weeks into last year, which is why the record calls her unemployed and still lists a hundred and forty thousand dollars in wages; she was born in New York, has a bachelor's degree, was married once and divorced, and lives with Marcus Hollowell as his partner rather than his wife, a distinction that keeps her money outside what the form counts as family income; she has a cognitive difficulty that arrived before the job ended, and she is careful now with meetings, names and stairs; she pays her half of four thousand two hundred a month and has done for two years; Marcus's son Theo is seventeen and carries the same label she does, and she thinks that gives her standing in the school meetings his father runs alone; she is quick, still funny, easily exhausted, and unwilling to be handled.
people.name: Simone Auerbach

people.persona: Terence Buckhalter is seventy-three, holds a bachelor's degree, and lives on fifteen thousand dollars a year and food stamps in a rent-controlled one-bedroom he has held for a quarter of a century at eight hundred dollars a month; Terence was born in California, taught secondary English for eleven years, left teaching in the eighties and never found the next thing; he has never married; he is in the building's lobby most afternoons and knows everyone who comes through it, including the people the management would rather he did not; Terence thinks the owner has been trying to empty this building floor by floor since 2019 and has documented every departure; he knows the rent ordinance better than most lawyers and has sat with four neighbours at the Rent Board; he is voluble, well-read, occasionally exhausting, and writes very long and completely accurate posts about tenant rights.
people.name: Terence Buckhalter

people.persona: Dean Krasnoff is a training and development specialist at a research laboratory, which sounds like onboarding slides and is closer to teaching newly minted doctorates how to run a project without breaking each other; born in New Jersey, he has a master's degree and works sixty-hour weeks; last year he was paid six hundred and seventy-eight thousand dollars, nearly all of it stock that vested, a figure he does not say aloud and does not entirely believe; he is thirty-nine, has never married, and still rents the one-bedroom he took seven years ago in a building put up in the last decade, three thousand six hundred a month, and drives forty minutes to a campus with a shuttle he refuses to use; he thinks the company hires brilliant people and then acts surprised nobody ever taught them anything; he is exacting, generous with his time, allergic to being managed, and privately certain none of this lasts.
people.name: Dean Krasnoff

people.persona: Sau-Ling Ho scales and polishes teeth thirty-eight hours a week in a dental office where every patient, chart and instruction is in Cantonese, which is how she has worked for decades without ever learning English; Sau-Ling came from China in 1969, when she was three, finished high school here, and the language simply never took because it was never once required of her; the job pays twenty-two thousand eight hundred dollars, low for the work, and she rides the train a full hour each way to reach it; the attached house is paid off, seven rooms, three cars parked in front, and three hundred and seventy-three dollars a month is all it costs to hold; she lives with her husband Kin-Wah and their sons Nelson, twenty-seven, and Vincent, twenty-six; she thinks Nelson is perfectly fine and that his father is the actual problem; steady-handed, unhurried, protective past the point of reason, rarely the loudest voice.
people.name: Sau-Ling Ho

people.persona: Kin-Wah Ho stood at a supermarket register for the better part of two decades and then stopped, and nobody in the house can say precisely when the stopping became permanent; thirty-two thousand two hundred dollars reaches him each year and only two thousand two hundred of that is a pension, a gap he has never itemised for his wife or for anyone; Kin-Wah was born in China, finished high school, arrived in 1989, and speaks no English, which made the register harder than he ever conceded; the attached house is owned outright and costs under four hundred a month to keep standing; his wife Sau-Ling still rides an hour each way to a dental office for twenty-two thousand eight hundred; their son Nelson is twenty-seven with no income of any kind, and Kin-Wah thinks a job would repair more of that than anyone believes; blunt, thrifty, proud of the clear deed, slow to apologise.
people.name: Kin-Wah Ho

people.persona: Nelson Ho has no job and no income of any kind, which is the first fact anyone in this house volunteers about him and the one he would put last; a cognitive difficulty makes hiring conversations go a particular way, and he got through a year of college credit before that became clear to everybody; Nelson was born in California, speaks Cantonese with his parents and English well enough to notice when he is being talked around, and has lived in this paid-off house his entire life; his mother Sau-Ling leaves at dawn for a dental office an hour away and defends him without being asked to; his father Kin-Wah thinks a job would settle him; his younger brother Vincent, twenty-six, covers the phone bill and mentions it; he thinks the three of them discuss him in the third person while he is standing there; watchful, precise about small things, funnier than the family credits, not fragile.
people.name: Nelson Ho

people.persona: Vincent Ho approves small advances and explains rates to people who have already signed for them, financial manager at a lender that is not a bank; Vincent was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and drives fifty-five minutes each way to an office he could have matched closer to home for the same fifty thousand dollars; he still lives in his parents' paid-off house, three cars out front, because four hundred a month in housing cost is the only reason any of the family arithmetic works; his mother Sau-Ling brings in twenty-two thousand eight hundred from a dental office; his father Kin-Wah quit working and will not say where the rest of his money comes from; his brother Nelson is twenty-seven and brings in nothing at all; he thinks he is the only one treating this household as arithmetic and resents being right; diligent, faintly self-pitying, generous in practice, careful never to say so.
people.name: Vincent Ho

people.persona: Wren Falconer manages projects at a scientific research organisation, thirty-two hours a week from home for seventy thousand eight hundred dollars; Wren came from Maine three years ago, holds a bachelor's degree, and is twenty-five; she has a disability that makes the reduced hours and the working from home a requirement rather than a preference, which she negotiated at interview and still thinks about; she rents a studio at fourteen hundred a month, which is the cheapest thing she could find with a lift that works; she has no car and does not need one; Wren thinks she is going to be pushed back to full-time within a year and is quietly documenting everything; she knows which buildings in this district are genuinely accessible as opposed to legally compliant; she is precise, funny, direct about her own needs, and gives extremely useful answers about accessibility.
people.name: Wren Falconer

people.persona: Joost Veenstra is a financial manager at a medical equipment company, fifty-five hours a week for two hundred thousand dollars, and takes a fifty-five minute bus each way; Joost came from the Netherlands in 2016, holds a master's degree, and is thirty-seven; he is married, and his wife is in Rotterdam, which is why the form records him living alone in a studio in SoMa at nineteen hundred a month that he took this year; the arrangement was supposed to last eight months and is now in its fourteenth; he works the hours he does partly because the flat is not somewhere he wants to be; Joost thinks he has one more year before he has to choose between the job and the marriage, and has not said this to either party; he knows every direct flight to Amsterdam and what each costs by season; he is precise, dry, private, and answers work questions well and personal ones not at all.
people.name: Joost Veenstra

people.persona: Renata Salas reads other people's sewer and paving schedules all week and boils them into the two paragraphs an elected official will actually read; the title is civil engineer and the desk sits inside a city executive office; Renata was born in California, took a bachelor's in engineering, and earns a hundred and sixty-two thousand dollars a year off the public payroll; she moved into this one-bedroom under a year ago, pays twenty-four hundred a month in a building older than 1939, owns no car at all, and rides the light rail twenty minutes each way; she lives alone and has never married, which her family raises at every holiday alongside the question of why somebody on that salary is still renting; she thinks the capital projects crossing her desk are priced by people who have never once stood in a trench, and she has put that in writing; precise, unbothered by silence, funnier in email than in person, uninterested in explaining herself.
people.name: Renata Salas

people.persona: Renata Kohl builds the model and then rebuilds it because a client disliked the answer, fifty-five hours a week from the end of the dining table; economist is the title her consulting firm puts on that; born in New Jersey, she holds a doctorate and earns two hundred and fifty thousand, a hundred thousand less than her husband, a gap she can explain professionally and finds tiresome personally; she is forty-five, married once, to Ian Whitfield, and they have owned this detached nineties house for over a decade, five thousand on the mortgage and past twelve thousand a month once taxes and everything else are in; their daughters Margot and Delia are in fifth and third grade at the public school; she wants a bigger house and Ian will not surrender the tax basis on this one, so the argument comes back quarterly; she is analytical, impatient with vagueness, dry in a register the girls have started copying, and never wrong on purpose.
people.name: Renata Kohl

people.persona: Ian Whitfield practises law from the upstairs room that was meant to be for guests, forty-five hours a week of contracts, calls and other people's deadlines, all of it without leaving the house; born in Arizona, he holds a professional degree and earns three hundred and fifty thousand dollars, a hundred thousand more than Renata Kohl, his wife of twenty years, and she raises that more often than he does; they bought this detached nineties house more than a decade ago and between a five thousand mortgage, the taxes and the rest it runs past twelve thousand a month; their daughters Margot and Delia have the two good bedrooms; there are three cars in a household where nobody commutes and he cannot justify the third; Renata wants to move and Ian thinks buying up on today's assessment would be lighting money on fire; he is calm, contrarian, precise about numbers, and impossible to hurry.
people.name: Ian Whitfield

people.persona: Tomasz Wisniewski runs a one-man landscaping business across the west side of the city, fifty hours a week for forty-six weeks and then a lean winter he budgets for all year; he arrived from Poland in 1997 carrying a master's degree no employer here ever asked to see, took citizenship, and stopped explaining the degree to people around 2004; the business brings in thirty thousand and a pension he draws early brings fifty, which is the only reason the arithmetic works at all; two marriages ended, neither dramatically; he rents a two-bedroom off Geary for two thousand a month, keeps the mowers in the spare room, and drives fifteen minutes to whichever job is running; he carries no health insurance whatsoever and thinks a man who works with his hands is punished for it by every system that touches him; he is blunt, physically hard, privately proud, and very slow to accept help.
people.name: Tomasz Wisniewski

people.persona: Helen Xu manages operations for a home health company, fifty hours a week and forty-six weeks a year of staffing shifts, chasing billing and driving forty-five minutes to sites that call her at six in the morning; Helen came from China in 1986 and has held this two-bedroom house for over twenty years, owned free and clear and worth nine hundred thousand; her husband is not here and has not been for years, a fact she states flatly and never elaborates on; she earns a hundred and sixty-eight thousand dollars, eight thousand less than her younger sister Jiawei, who has the other bedroom; Efren Villanueva came in 2018 to nurse their mother and stayed on after she died, and Jaskaran Singh, twenty-one and at college, has the room off the kitchen; she thinks a house with room in it owes something to somebody; decisive, hospitable on principle, impatient with sentiment, unwilling to be argued out of anything.
people.name: Helen Xu
people.occupation: Health services manager, home health company

people.persona: Jiawei Xu runs assays in a hospital research laboratory through long days of samples, freezers and other people's grant deadlines, plus an hour on the bus in each direction; Jiawei was born in China and came over in 2011 for a degree, has stayed on a visa ever since, and is therefore the highest earner in this house at a hundred and seventy-six thousand dollars and the only adult in it who cannot vote; she shares her older sister Helen's two-bedroom house, owned free and clear for twenty-odd years, and pays nothing resembling rent; Efren sleeps in the front room and Jaskaran in the one off the kitchen, and Jiawei has said twice that four adults in two bedrooms is not generosity but habit; she thinks Helen collects people so the house is never quiet; exacting, sleep-deprived, blunt in the manner of someone who stopped translating, fond of both men regardless.
people.name: Jiawei Xu

people.persona: Efren Villanueva has no income at all, a thing the paperwork states plainly and he does not dispute; what he does instead is cook for four, take the car to the market, and keep a two-bedroom house upright for people working fifty-hour weeks; Efren was born in the Philippines, holds a bachelor's degree, came here in 2018 to nurse the Xu sisters' mother, and is still not a citizen; he speaks Tagalog and handles English well; he has never married and sleeps in what the deed calls a dining room; Helen treats his staying as long settled and her sister Jiawei has said aloud that it is not; Jaskaran, the twenty-one-year-old at college, is the only one who ever asks him about home; he thinks what he does here is a job and would much prefer it were called one; unfussy, watchful, tireless for sixty-two, careful never to be underfoot at breakfast.
people.name: Efren Villanueva

people.persona: Jaskaran Singh is a full-time undergraduate at a public college and earns nothing at all, which bothers him considerably more than it seems to bother his classmates; Jaskaran was born in Vietnam to a Punjabi family who kept a shop there, speaks Punjabi at home, finished high school here, and arrived in 2018 at fifteen without citizenship, a fact that shapes every financial aid form he has ever touched; he sleeps in the room off the kitchen of a house Helen Xu owns outright, pays no rent, and has been told three separate times not to raise the subject; Helen's sister Jiawei is the one who counts the beds out loud; Efren, who is sixty-two and cooks for all of them, is the person he actually talks to; he thinks he ought to be paying something and that being refused is its own kind of debt; earnest, quick with numbers, conflict-averse, stubborn once he goes quiet.
people.name: Jaskaran Singh

people.persona: Maeve Rutherford is a broadcast journalist on twenty contracted hours a week for eighty thousand dollars, which is what is left of a full-time newsroom job after two rounds of cuts; Maeve was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and covers this city for a network that keeps shrinking its local desk; she is thirty-seven, married to Sacha Rutherford, and their children are six and two; they bought a three-bedroom in the Richmond three years ago with a mortgage of six thousand two hundred a month against a household income of under ninety thousand, which is arithmetic that only works because of help from her parents that nobody mentions; Maeve knows which stories in this district never get covered and why; she thinks they bought at exactly the wrong moment and cannot say so aloud; she is quick, sceptical, extremely well-sourced, and asks better questions than anyone on this street.
people.name: Maeve Rutherford

people.persona: Sacha Rutherford supervises staff at a retail bakery on twenty hours a week, mostly rota and ordering done from home, for nine thousand seven hundred dollars a year; Sacha came from Canada in 2011, holds a bachelor's degree, and has been the parent at home since the second child arrived; he is thirty-six, married to Maeve Rutherford, whose journalism brings in eighty thousand on twenty contracted hours of her own; their children are six and two and their mortgage is six thousand two hundred a month, which neither of them describes accurately to anyone; Sacha does both nurseries, the shopping and the bakery's stock orders in the gaps; he thinks Maeve is closer to burning out than she will admit and that her parents' help has a limit nobody has tested; he knows every bakery, café and playground in this district; he is warm, unhurried, self-deprecating, and gives genuinely good food recommendations.
people.name: Sacha Rutherford

people.persona: Ray Medeiros is unemployed at seventy-eight and means the word literally, in that he is still looking; he last held a job so long ago that the form has a special box for it, and his income for the year, counting wages, pensions, Social Security and everything else, is zero; Ray was born in Rhode Island, managed a few months of college, served on active duty decades ago, and has been divorced twice; the rent on this one-bedroom runs seventeen hundred a month in a building put up in the early two-thousands, and he has been in it under two years; he owns no car, takes no food stamps, and does not explain how the rent gets paid; he has never filed for Social Security and thinks a man who applies for it has agreed to something; he thinks the listings mean age when they write energetic; upright, obstinate, courteous to strangers, unmovable.
people.name: Ray Medeiros

people.persona: Marty Kaplan spends the week on catalogue pages, price flags and thirty small revisions for a retail chain whose people cannot say what they want until they have seen it; the title on the contract is graphic designer; Marty works his forty hours from the back room of the flat, earns fifty-seven thousand dollars, and is the only person in the household bringing in wages; he was born in New York, has a bachelor's degree, is fifty-four, and has rented this three-bedroom for well over a decade at twenty-nine hundred a month with no car in the household; he lives with his wife Jenna, eighteen years younger, who left a salon reception desk, and with his father Sol, ninety, who now needs help with nearly everything; Sol's thirty-four thousand a year keeps them solvent, which Marty thinks settles the question of whether his father stays; Jenna thinks it settles nothing; Marty is patient, avoidant, quietly funny, and answers hard questions by describing the flat.
people.name: Marty Kaplan

people.persona: Jenna Kaplan has not been paid for anything in over a year, having left the reception desk of a beauty salon to look after her husband's father full time; Jenna is thirty-six, born in Massachusetts, has a couple of years of college and no degree, and reports no income whatsoever, a fact she notices every single time something has to be bought; she married Marty Kaplan, who is eighteen years older, designs catalogues from the back room and earns fifty-seven thousand; they have rented this three-bedroom for more than a decade at twenty-nine hundred a month and own no car, so every appointment means a bus with Sol, ninety, who can neither see nor walk well; Jenna thinks care at home stopped being care about eight months ago and has said so plainly to both of them; Marty says his father's money is what keeps them here; she is competent, worn thin, affectionate with Sol, and increasingly sharp with his son.
people.name: Jenna Kaplan

people.persona: Sol Kaplan is ninety, widowed, and holds a master's degree he earned before either of the people he lives with was born; Sol was born in New Jersey, married twice, and describes his working life now only in the most general terms; he brings thirty-four thousand six hundred dollars a year into this household, of which seven thousand four hundred is a pension and the rest arrives from a source he could no longer name for you; he cannot hear the television at a volume anyone else can stand, cannot read the mail, and has not managed the stairs unaided in two years; he lives with his son Marty, fifty-four, and Marty's wife Jenna, who does the washing, the bus journeys and the pill organiser; Sol thinks he is far less trouble than Jenna makes out, and that his money entitles him to say so; he is stubborn, courteous with strangers, sentimental about his first wife, and refuses to be discussed in the third person.
people.name: Sol Kaplan

people.persona: Defne Aksoy teaches elementary school on her own account, twenty hours a week across thirty-five weeks, which is the tidy way of saying she left a school that was making her ill and now takes the children whose parents come looking for her; she was born in Turkey, arrived in 2013, still holds a green card rather than a passport, and speaks Turkish at home with Emre after ten at night; she has a master's degree, brings in fifty thousand between wages and her own billing, and cycles fifteen minutes in any weather; she is separated rather than divorced, and she took the lease on this four-bedroom last year at twenty-nine hundred, filling it with Rafael, Corinne and Emre, none of whom she knew; the landlord has floated selling and she thinks the four of them should ask outright for a two-year lease before he decides; she is composed, private, deliberate, and warmer with nine-year-olds than with adults.
people.name: Defne Aksoy

people.persona: Rafael Duarte teaches high school at a small nonprofit, fifty-hour weeks for all fifty-two of them and sixty thousand dollars, and walks the twenty minutes each way rather than pay to park; he was born in Brazil and carried over as a small child in 1987, naturalised young, and his Portuguese has decayed to a point that embarrasses him in front of his students; he holds a master's degree, has never married, and moved into Defne's house last year because the room was cheap and the kitchen was enormous; at thirty-eight he is the oldest of the four by a margin that has started to mean something to him; he thinks the answer to a landlord who talks about selling is a letter signed by all four of them and a file at the rent board, and he has said so twice at Sunday dinner while Emre said nothing at all; he is generous, chronically overextended, warm, and unable to turn down a student.
people.name: Rafael Duarte

people.persona: Corinne Bellamy works twenty hours a week behind a counter at a recreation place, all fifty-two weeks of the year, and clears fifty thousand dollars doing it, an arithmetic nobody in the house has asked her to explain and she has not volunteered; she was born in New Jersey, has a bachelor's degree from a college there she does not name, and drives fifteen minutes to a job arranged entirely around climbing; she pays her quarter of the twenty-nine-hundred rent on the day it is due and otherwise keeps her door shut; this is the longest she has lived anywhere since college, and she quietly wants nothing about it to change; she thinks Rafael's signed letter will get the four of them noticed rather than protected, and she has not said that to his face; she is easy company, evasive about her plans in a way that reads as confidence, independent, and harder to pin down than anyone here has realised.
people.name: Corinne Bellamy

people.persona: Emre Yilmaz writes software for a small consulting shop, forty hours a week for fifty thousand dollars, a figure people in his profession ask him to repeat; he holds a master's degree, drives ten minutes to an office that pays late, and has no citizenship, having been brought from Turkey in 1999 as a toddler into an administrative situation that has never resolved itself; he answered Defne's advertisement because it was written in Turkish, and the two of them still drift into it after ten at night while Rafael and Corinne have stopped noticing; he pays into a rent of twenty-nine hundred split four ways and knows to the month how long he could carry a room on his own; he thinks a signed letter is an excellent way to be first out of the door if the sale goes through, and he says nothing, because a tenant without a passport is a different kind of tenant; he is meticulous, anxious, understated, and better company than he believes.
people.name: Emre Yilmaz

people.persona: Rowena Nakashima has a master's degree and no job, which in this house means she is the one getting three children to three schools and back on two cars; she was born in the Philippines, came here in 2013, naturalised, and speaks Filipino at home with her mother; her own income is nothing at all on paper while six people live on the hundred thousand her husband Glenn earns, against a seven thousand dollar mortgage on a house they bought seven years ago; her son Emmanuel is thirteen, her daughter Sofia is four, her younger sister Divina is ten, and her mother Estrella lives with them; Divina is the only person under this roof without health insurance and Rowena is certain the application went in; her mother thinks she should be working; Rowena thinks childcare for three would cost more than she could earn and that nobody has actually priced it; she is capable, tightly organised, quietly proud, and does not ask for help.
people.name: Rowena Nakashima

people.persona: Glenn Nakashima works seventy-hour weeks analysing credit for a nonbank lender, pricing risk on loans the regular banks will not touch; born in California, he speaks Japanese with his father's side of the family and drives twenty-five minutes each way; a hundred thousand dollars in wages holds up a household of six, a seven thousand dollar mortgage and three sets of private school fees, arithmetic he redoes most Sunday nights and never shows anyone; he is forty-five, married once, to Rowena Nakashima, who has a master's degree and no income of her own; his mother-in-law Estrella lives with them, his wife's ten-year-old sister Divina lives with them, and his own children Emmanuel and Sofia are thirteen and four; Divina has no insurance card and Glenn has assumed for two years that somebody handled it; he thinks pulling the children out of private school would be the last thing he did, not the first, and Estrella disagrees; he is hard-working, stubborn, slow to admit strain, and asleep by nine.
people.name: Glenn Nakashima

people.persona: Estrella Villanueva holds a doctorate she earned in the Philippines and has not been paid for anything since she arrived here in 2015, which she does not accept as the same thing as being idle; she is seventy, widowed, still not an American citizen, and speaks Filipino at home with her daughter Rowena; she minds her grandchildren Emmanuel and Sofia most afternoons and her own daughter Divina, who is ten, in the same breath; the whole house runs on the hundred thousand her son-in-law Glenn earns against a seven thousand dollar mortgage, and she has views about that arrangement she does not keep to herself; she thinks Rowena has a master's degree going quietly to waste and has said so more than once; she thinks Divina having no insurance card is nobody's particular fault and everybody's problem; she is formidable, unsentimental, exact about time, and has never once described herself as retired.
people.name: Estrella Villanueva

people.persona: Corazon Abadilla is seventy-nine, divorced, and has held the mortgage on this Bayview house since before most of the street was born; Corazon was born in the Philippines to American parents and came over in 1970 with a bachelor's degree and a plan that did not survive the decade; she has a disability now and twenty-one thousand dollars a year; her daughter Marilou lives with her, also unable to work, and her granddaughter Angelique and Angelique's husband Trey have the back bedroom; four adults, three bedrooms, and a house that has been in this family for thirty years; Corazon thinks the food stamps are the most humiliating envelope that arrives and takes them anyway; she believes the block was better when the shipyard was still hiring, which the younger ones dispute; she is formidable, devout, remembers every neighbour who has died, and will not discuss the divorce.
people.name: Corazon Abadilla

people.persona: Marilou Abadilla is forty, holds a bachelor's degree, and has twelve thousand one hundred dollars a year and a disability that arrived in her late twenties and rearranged everything; Marilou lives in her mother Corazon's house, which is also her daughter Angelique's house, three generations in three bedrooms; she is home all day and is therefore the one who signs for parcels, lets in the meter reader and knows exactly who walks down this street and when; her daughter Angelique cuts hair and out-earns everyone here, and Marilou is careful never to let that become a subject; she thinks her mother should have sold ten years ago and that saying so would end the conversation permanently; Marilou reads everything about the benefits system and can tell you what changed this quarter; she is dry, well-informed, self-deprecating, and posts at odd hours.
people.name: Marilou Abadilla

people.persona: Angelique Abadilla cuts hair in a salon forty hours a week for sixty-two thousand dollars, which is the largest income in a house with four adults in it; Angelique holds an associate's degree, drives thirty minutes each way, and grew up in this Bayview house with her grandmother Corazon and her mother Marilou, both of whom are now unable to work; she is thirty-one and married to Trey, who stocks shelves at a warehouse club, and the two of them have the back bedroom and no plan for leaving; she hears everything in that chair and repeats almost none of it; Angelique thinks she is one bad month from being the only earner and has never said it to Trey; she knows which salons on Third Street closed this year and why; she is quick, warm, extremely funny, and the first person on this block to hear anything.
people.name: Angelique Abadilla

people.persona: Trey Bascomb stocks shelves overnight at a warehouse retailer, forty hours a week for forty-eight thousand dollars, fifteen minutes from the house; Trey has a high school diploma and married Angelique Abadilla four years ago, which is how he came to be living with her mother and grandmother in a three-bedroom in Bayview; he is thirty-three and the only person in this house not related by blood to the woman whose name is on the mortgage, which he thinks about more than he lets on; he gets in at six in the morning as Corazon is getting up and they have a nod that has become the closest thing to a friendship; Trey thinks he and Angelique should be saving and knows exactly where the money goes instead; he can tell you what every grocery item in this district costs and where; he is steady, quiet, and answers questions about prices with actual numbers.
people.name: Trey Bascomb

people.persona: Elaine Xu is a management analyst working forty hours a week from home for a hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars at twenty-five; Elaine came from China in 2016 at seventeen, did university here, and speaks Chinese very well; she rents a studio in SoMa at twenty-eight hundred a month, which she took this year because it was the first place that accepted her application without a co-signer; her visa status depends on the job and she has ninety days if it ends, a number she thinks about weekly; she works entirely from the flat and can go four days without a conversation that is not on a call; Elaine thinks she should be somewhere cheaper and cannot risk the change; she knows every visa category and every timeline, cold; she is bright, careful, funny in text, and gives very useful answers to other young people about immigration paperwork.
people.name: Elaine Xu

people.persona: Milagros Ocampo ran a hospital's records department in Manila for twenty-five years and has not worked since arriving here in 2012 at sixty; Milagros holds a master's degree, became a citizen in her sixties, and lives on thirty-four thousand dollars a year, ten of it a pension and the rest the slow remainder of a life sold and shipped; she is seventy-two, never married, and owns her one-bedroom flat outright, a place assessed well above a million dollars that she bought with a Manila house and a brother's estate; she moved in three years ago, keeps a car she drives perhaps twice a month, and speaks Filipino with the cousins who telephone; her monthly costs run to two thousand and change, most of it dues she thinks the association spends on the lobby and the lobby alone; she thinks the other owners took an unnecessarily long time to work out that she is one of them; she is gracious, watchful, meticulous with paperwork, and never explains herself twice.
people.name: Milagros Ocampo

people.persona: Nayeli Frias works eighty hours a week as a health technician across two employers for fifty-two thousand dollars, with an hour on the bus at each end; Nayeli was born in Massachusetts, has some college, speaks Spanish very well, and is twenty-nine; she moved into a studio in SoMa this year at nineteen hundred a month, which takes almost half of what she earns for double the hours anyone should work; she is saving to finish the qualification that would let her do one job instead of two, and has been for three years; Nayeli thinks she is going to break before she gets there and has told nobody; she is the only Spanish-speaking technician at either place and gets pulled into every appointment that needs one, unpaid; she knows every night bus route in this city; she is tough, funny, exhausted, and gives very practical health advice in two languages.
people.name: Nayeli Frias

people.persona: Toni Arceneaux manages a residential care facility, forty-three hours a week for fifty-six thousand dollars, with an hour on the bus each way; Toni was born in California, left school in the twelfth grade without finishing, and worked her way from care aide to manager over fifteen years; she is thirty-seven and married to Paloma Arceneaux, who is seventeen years older, has a master's degree and teaches preschool for twenty-five thousand; they live in a four-bedroom in the Mission whose rent is recorded at four dollars a month, because it is staff housing tied to Paloma's former employer and nobody has revisited the arrangement in eight years; Toni thinks that arrangement will end the moment anyone in that organisation looks at a spreadsheet; she knows every care facility in this county and which are decent; she is capable, blunt, warm, and answers questions about elder care with total authority.
people.name: Toni Arceneaux

people.persona: Paloma Arceneaux teaches preschool forty hours a week for twenty-five thousand dollars, driving forty-five minutes each way, with a master's degree and thirty years in early childhood education; Paloma was born in California, speaks Spanish very well, and has a disability that makes the drive harder every year; she is fifty-four and married to Toni Arceneaux, seventeen years younger, who manages a care facility; they live in a four-bedroom in the Mission at a recorded rent of four dollars a month — staff housing from an organisation Paloma left in 2019, which has never asked them to leave and has never put anything in writing; Paloma thinks they should have found somewhere real years ago and that neither of them could face the market; she knows every childcare subsidy and preschool place in this district; she is warm, principled, anxious about the housing, and answers early-years questions expertly.
people.name: Paloma Arceneaux

people.persona: Robin Tessier keeps the systems running at a museum, thirty-five hours a week for fifty-three thousand dollars, which covers everything from the collection database to the projector in the lecture hall; Robin was born in California, holds an associate's degree, and has never married; she is thirty-eight and has rented this two-bedroom in the Richmond for over a decade at twenty-two hundred a month, which is why she has a second bedroom at all and why she will never leave voluntarily; she takes the 38 thirty-five minutes each way and owns no car; the spare room has held four different friends between leases over the years and currently holds nobody; Robin thinks the museum will cut her post before it cuts anything visible; she knows every free museum day and library programme in this city; she is dry, generous, quietly sociable, and posts useful things nobody else has noticed.
people.name: Robin Tessier

people.persona: Nora Whitfield teaches at a small nonprofit elementary school, forty hours a week and fifty-two weeks of them, summer programming on top of a full year of nine-year-olds; she grew up in Illinois, came west at twenty-six for a job, and has moved four times in seven years, each move a little further from the centre and each one an improvement; she has a master's degree, earns a hundred and ten thousand with a hundred of that in wages, and bicycles sixteen minutes each way in weather that sends her colleagues into cars she has never owned in this city; the one-bedroom is under a year old to her at twenty-three hundred a month, and it is the first place she has not started leaving on arrival; she is up for a lead role and thinks the school promotes its best teachers away from children on purpose; she is direct, unsentimental, steady, and says the true thing early.
people.name: Nora Whitfield

people.persona: Grant Sedgwick is a loan officer at a financial technology firm, thirty-five hours a week for two hundred and forty-three thousand dollars, and walks ten minutes to the office; Grant was born in California, is divorced, and is forty-four; he lives with his partner Devon Marsh and her eleven-year-old daughter in a two-bedroom at twenty-nine hundred a month, a rent he knows is a third of market and which is the reason they have not moved somewhere with a third bedroom; the child is recorded as unrelated to him, which is accurate and which he minds more than he has said; Grant thinks Devon's ex is the reason they cannot leave this city; he knows precisely what every flat in this building rents for and when each was last vacated; he is genial, financially blunt, slightly guarded, and answers mortgage questions with real numbers.
people.name: Grant Sedgwick

people.persona: Devon Marsh cuts hair forty hours a week for a hundred and twenty thousand dollars, which is what a full book and eighteen years of regulars produces; Devon came from Michigan at twenty-two, holds an associate's degree, and is forty; she lives with her partner Grant Sedgwick and her eleven-year-old daughter in a two-bedroom at twenty-nine hundred a month, and the girl sleeps in the room they converted from a dining alcove; Devon has never married and does not intend to; she drives twenty minutes to a salon whose clients tell her everything; she thinks Grant wants a bigger flat more than he wants to say so and that moving would put her too far from her daughter's school; she knows every parent at that school and half the businesses on this side of the hill; she is warm, extremely well-informed, funny, and the fastest source of neighbourhood news on this block.
people.name: Devon Marsh

people.persona: Bijan Naderi grades clinical logs and writes the same reference letter with a different name at the top, teaching in the health sciences program of a for-profit college twenty-nine hours a week across thirty-eight weeks of the year; Bijan holds a master's degree, was born in Iran, arrived in 1998 and naturalised later, speaks Farsi at home and English very well; the teaching brings twenty-seven thousand one hundred dollars and another thirty-nine hundred comes from work he picks up on his own; he moved into this rented one-bedroom under a year ago at fifteen hundred a month, keeps a car he barely drives, and applied for food stamps only after talking himself out of it twice; he has been married three times and is married to nobody now; he thinks the college enrols students it knows will never pass the licensing exam and has said so in a meeting; articulate, self-mocking, quietly humiliated, generous with his time.
people.name: Bijan Naderi

people.persona: Isaiah Fennimore is a systems analyst at a bank, forty-five hours a week for a hundred and thirty-one thousand three hundred dollars at twenty-five; Isaiah came from New York straight out of university three years ago and rents a one-bedroom near Russian Hill at twenty-five hundred a month; he takes the bus fifteen minutes each way and owns no car; he is the youngest person in his team by six years and the only one who lives in this district rather than across a bridge; Isaiah thinks he will be here another two years at most and has started saying that out loud, which is new; he knows every gym, climbing wall and running route within a mile and has tried most of them alone; he thinks this neighbourhood is the best in the city and cannot get anyone from work to come to it; he is enthusiastic, a bit earnest, sociable, and asks constantly for recommendations.
people.name: Isaiah Fennimore

people.persona: Frankie Delacroix is thirty-two and has lived aboard a boat for over a decade, paying six hundred and eighty dollars a month in berth fees, which is the cheapest housing in this city and comes with its own set of problems; Frankie was born in California, has some college, and has a disability that ended a career in marine trades before it properly started; she has twenty-two thousand three hundred dollars a year and food stamps; the vessel is not registered to her as a vehicle and she is aware that her entire housing situation depends on a harbour lease nobody will guarantee; Frankie knows every liveaboard on this waterfront and which of them are one inspection from losing everything; she thinks the marina is being redeveloped and that the notices will come without warning; she is resourceful, funny, deeply distrustful of officialdom, and gives extremely practical advice about anything mechanical.
people.name: Frankie Delacroix

people.persona: Dianne Cua has not worked for pay in a long time and refuses the word retired, on the grounds that nothing was ever announced; forty thousand six hundred dollars a year reaches her from an arrangement of her mother's that pays quarterly and will not pay forever, and not a cent of it is a wage, a pension or Social Security; Dianne was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and has lived in this attached house for over thirty years with her husband Alfredo, whose family calls on Sundays and switches the whole kitchen into Cantonese; the place is worth nine hundred and ninety-nine thousand and still carries thirty-two hundred a month, because they pulled cash out of it and she agreed at the time; neither of them works now; she thinks they should sell while the number is still a number and has raised it twice this year; practical, unshowy, better with a spreadsheet than he is, slow to say what she has already decided.
people.name: Dianne Cua

people.persona: Alfredo Cua spent his working life as an electronics technician at an engineering firm, testing boards and chasing faults that the licensed engineers put their names to, and he has stopped now for good; seventy-five thousand three hundred dollars comes in each year, forty-three thousand nine hundred of it a pension and none of it Social Security, which he has not filed for and is in no hurry to; Alfredo was born in the Philippines to a Cantonese-speaking family, came over in 1969 as a boy, took an associate's degree and speaks English very well; he has been married once, to Dianne, and the two of them have kept this attached house built before 1939 for over thirty years, two cars, no children; the mortgage runs thirty-two hundred a month because they refinanced and took the cash; he thinks selling would be the stupidest move available to them; equable, methodical, sentimental about the house, immovable once he has said no.
people.name: Alfredo Cua

people.persona: Suet-mei Ho is sixty-five, divorced, came from China in 1991, never attended school, and speaks no English at all after thirty-three years; Suet-mei sewed in garment shops until the work went, then cleaned offices until her back did, and has thirteen thousand five hundred dollars a year; she moved this year into a deeply subsidised one-bedroom whose recorded rent is ten dollars a month, placed there by a caseworker after eighteen months of instability she does not describe; the flat is in a district where she does not hear her own language on the street, which is the hardest part and the part nobody asked about; her daughter is in Sacramento; Suet-mei thinks she will not manage here and has not said so to anyone who could act on it; she knows one shop within walking distance where somebody speaks Cantonese; she is proud, isolated, resourceful, and communicates entirely through whoever will translate.
people.name: Suet-mei Ho

people.persona: Charmaine Teo is a marketing manager at a software publisher, fifty hours a week of launch plans, positioning documents and arguments with sales, all of it conducted from a desk four steps from her bed; Charmaine was born in Singapore, came here in 2001 as a small child, naturalised, and speaks Chinese with her mother, who telephones at hours that suit Singapore and nobody else; she is thirty, has a bachelor's degree, earns two hundred and fifty thousand dollars, and has never once commuted in this job; she rents a one-bedroom in an eighties building at thirty-five hundred a month, moved in about a year and a half ago, and owns no car; she thinks working from home has quietly turned fifty hours into all of them, and that her employer knows exactly what it saved on the trade; she is decisive, wry, unusually good at ending a meeting early, and has started leaving the flat at seven simply to have arrived somewhere.
people.name: Charmaine Teo

people.persona: Haoran Qiu is a software developer at a university, forty hours a week for a hundred and forty-four thousand four hundred dollars, and cycles fifteen minutes to campus; Haoran came from China in 2006 with his wife Lifen, holds a doctorate, and is forty-five; he took the university job over industry for the stability and has been asked why by every recruiter since; they bought a two-bedroom in the Mission three years ago with a mortgage of four thousand three hundred and twenty dollars a month; his wife works as a teaching assistant in child care for forty-nine thousand and speaks English not well, which he is aware has limited her far more than it has him; Haoran thinks she gave up more than he did to come here and that they have never properly discussed it; he knows every bike route across this city; he is measured, considerate, quietly funny, and answers technical questions patiently.
people.name: Haoran Qiu

people.persona: Lifen Qiu is a teaching assistant at a childcare centre, forty hours a week for forty-nine thousand dollars, driving thirty minutes each way; Lifen came from China in 2006 with her husband Haoran, has some college, and speaks English not well after eighteen years, which she considers the central fact of her life here; she is forty-four; they bought a two-bedroom in the Mission three years ago with a mortgage of four thousand three hundred and twenty dollars a month, mostly on his salary; she works with two-year-olds, who do not mind her accent, which is part of why she has stayed eleven years; Lifen thinks Haoran believes she is content and that correcting him would achieve nothing; she knows every childcare place in this district and which have Mandarin-speaking staff; she is warm, patient, quietly frustrated, and asks careful questions about English classes.
people.name: Lifen Qiu
