people.persona: Chi-Keung Lau has not worked in years and lives on twenty-six thousand a year in retirement money and a little interest on top, which is the whole of what he brings into a house that costs more than that to keep; he came from China in 1986, finished high school there and went no further, and took citizenship in the years when that still felt like an achievement; he speaks Chinese at home because his English never got past poor, and he is married to Yuk-Fong Lau, who followed him over eight years later and earns nothing at all; their daughter Amanda, twenty-eight, pays for most of this two-bedroom house and works at its kitchen table; Chi-Keung thinks they should sell, take the million the place is now worth, and go somewhere that is not twelve hundred a month against a fixed income; Yuk-Fong will not discuss it; he is stubborn, thrifty to the point of comedy, early to bed, and keeps a running total of everything in his head.
people.name: Chi-Keung Lau

people.persona: Yuk-Fong Lau has no income of her own and has not had any since the sewing work dried up, which the Census records as nothing and which in this house means every meal, every errand and every appointment she takes her husband to; she was born in China, finished high school there, and came over in 1994, eight years after Chi-Keung, a gap nobody in the family has ever explained in front of her; she is a citizen now, sixty-one, speaks Chinese at home, and her English is poor enough that her daughter Amanda still makes the phone calls; she has lived in this two-bedroom house for well over ten years and thinks Chi-Keung's plan to sell it is the idea of a man who has never once packed a box; she wants Amanda to stay and says so openly; she is watchful, quietly funny, busy from six in the morning, and does not forget a slight.
people.name: Yuk-Fong Lau

people.persona: Amanda Lau spends whole days on calls persuading brands to attach their names to things nobody has finished editing; she sells advertising for a company that makes video content; she was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and speaks Chinese to her parents and English to everybody else, though on paper her English is only rated as good; she earns seventy-eight thousand a year and works from home, which in practice means the kitchen table, because both bedrooms in this house are spoken for; she brings in three quarters of what the household lives on and neither parent has ever put it that way out loud; her father Chi-Keung wants to sell the house and move somewhere cheap, and Amanda thinks that would end any chance she has of owning anything in this city; her mother Yuk-Fong is on her side, loudly; she is capable, funny on the phone, tired most evenings, and slower to leave than she tells people.
people.name: Amanda Lau

people.persona: Desmond Pryor spends his days watching login attempts against control systems designed before anyone thought to lock them, information security analysis for the city's power and gas utility; Desmond was born in Washington, D.C., has a master's degree, and has worked for local government his whole career because he wanted the pension and says so without embarrassment; he earns two hundred thousand dollars a year, forty hours a week, fifty-two weeks of them; he rides the bus forty-five minutes each way while his wife takes the household's only car fifteen minutes; he is married to Alison Pryor, a market research analyst on the city's consulting side who earns forty thousand a year more than he does; they pay eight thousand three hundred a month for the upper flat of a two-unit building and Desmond thinks that is money set on fire, and has run the mortgage numbers at her twice; he is methodical, unhurried, dryly funny, and keeps score quietly.
people.name: Desmond Pryor

people.persona: Alison Pryor is a market research analyst inside a city agency that sells its services to other departments; the surveys she runs go unread until somebody finally reads one and she has to defend the methodology; Alison was born in Rhode Island, has a bachelor's degree, and is on her second marriage, a fact she mentions early rather than late; she earns two hundred and forty thousand dollars a year, forty thousand more than her husband Desmond, who has never once made it strange; she drives the couple's one car fifteen minutes to work while he takes a forty-five minute bus, an arrangement she did not ask for and has stopped apologizing for; three bedrooms, no children, eight thousand three hundred a month, two years in the flat; Desmond wants to buy and Alison will not, because she has already divided one house with a lawyer in the room; she is exact, socially warm, allergic to sunk-cost arguments, and slower to trust than she looks.
people.name: Alison Pryor

people.persona: Jocelyn Espiritu, a physical therapist assistant for a home health agency, drives to strangers' houses and gets people who have had hips replaced to stand, walk to the door and back, and do it again tomorrow; she was born in Mississippi, took a bachelor's degree, and speaks Tagalog on the phone to her mother every Sunday without fail; thirty-eight and never married, she lives alone in the upper flat of a two-unit house built in the forties, twenty-one hundred a month before the utilities that push it nearer twenty-four; she has been there barely two years and drives twenty minutes to the first visit of the day; she is paid eighty-five thousand for thirty-five hours that are never thirty-five, and thinks the schedulers plan routes as though this city had no hills and no traffic; she is warm with patients, blunt with the office, superstitious about her car, and cannot sit still on a day off.
people.name: Jocelyn Espiritu

people.persona: Rafael Otero runs operations for a newspaper publisher, thirty-five hours a week spent deciding which part of a shrinking business gets cut next, and he drives it in fifteen minutes from the Bayview house he learned to ride a bike outside; born in California to a Nicaraguan mother, he speaks Spanish at home, holds a master's degree, and has never married; he reports three hundred and fifty thousand dollars, two hundred and ninety of it wages and the rest from things he bought young; he took over the mortgage in his twenties and still sends twenty-nine hundred a month, which his younger brother Danny experiences as a standing debt and he treats as weather; their mother Estela, seventy-four and widowed, holds the kitchen; three adults, one bedroom on the plan, and no car registered to any of them; he thinks the paper has about two years left and says it only to people who cannot repeat it; decisive, dry, over-responsible, and awkward when thanked.
people.name: Rafael Otero
people.occupation: General and operations manager, newspaper publishing

people.persona: Danny Otero reconciles other people's money at an investment firm, forty-eight hours a week matching figures that were already supposed to match, plus two hours daily on a bus that takes a full hour in each direction; he was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, speaks Spanish with his mother and English everywhere else, and has never married, though he still calls the end of one long thing a divorce; his seventy-five thousand dollars would be comfortable in almost any other city and here it buys the utilities and the groceries, a contribution he keeps a private tally of; his older brother Rafael carries the mortgage on the house they share with their mother Estela, and the temporary arrangement is in its second decade; Danny cannot account for this household being recorded as taking food assistance and thinks somebody's paperwork is simply wrong; observant, wry, conflict-avoidant, and quietly tired of feeling like a guest at forty-seven.
people.name: Danny Otero

people.persona: Estela Otero left Nicaragua in 1965 with nine years of schooling and a sister already settled in the Mission, and she has held citizenship here longer than either of her sons has been alive; she is seventy-four and widowed, raised both boys in this detached house and buried their father out of it; her own income is twelve thousand dollars a year and everything beyond that comes from Rafael, who pays the mortgage, and Danny, who buys the food, an arrangement she permits without ever discussing; Spanish is the language of her kitchen and her English is good enough to out-argue a pharmacist; she cooks Sunday dinner and treats attendance as settled law; Estela thinks her sons circle each other like men waiting for permission, and that Rafael's talk of a job in another city is a question he wants her to answer for him; stubborn, devout, funnier than either boy credits, and saying nothing lately about the stairs.
people.name: Estela Otero

people.persona: Claire Mackey sees trauma and substance-use clients for twenty paid hours a week and writes up another unpaid stretch of notes nobody reimburses, her own practice contracted to an outpatient clinic; Claire was born in California, holds a master's degree, and works entirely from the second bedroom of a two-bedroom apartment; sixty-five thousand of her seventy thousand dollars arrives through the practice and only five as wages, which makes every April a project; she is married to Mauricio Escalante, who directs information systems for a nonprofit, earns sixty-five thousand, and works from home as well; they moved in less than a year ago at two thousand seven hundred a month, a number everyone tells them is impossible; the room she needs shut from ten until four is the room he needs for calls, and Claire thinks a closed door during a session is not a negotiation; she is soft-spoken, stubborn about boundaries, funnier at home than at work, and terrible at resting.
people.name: Claire Mackey

people.persona: Mauricio Escalante is the help desk, the security policy and the man who negotiates the software renewals at a small nonprofit, running its information systems for sixty-five thousand dollars a year; Mauricio was born in El Salvador and came to this country in 2015; he is a permanent resident and not a citizen, which comes up at work more often than he would like; he has a bachelor's degree and puts in forty hours a week at the kitchen table, because the second bedroom belongs to his wife Claire Mackey's therapy practice from ten until four; Claire earns seventy thousand on twenty hours and he has done that arithmetic more than once; they signed this lease under a year ago at two thousand seven hundred a month; Mauricio thinks a nonprofit that cannot pay market rate should stop pretending the mission makes up the difference; he is even-tempered, quietly competitive, generous with his time, and keeps his own counsel.
people.name: Mauricio Escalante

people.persona: Meredith Hollins owns the accountancy firm with her name on it and works fifty-five hour weeks of other people's returns, payroll filings and phone calls that open with please don't be angry; Meredith was born in Ohio, has a bachelor's degree, and cleared six hundred and seventy-eight thousand dollars last year, which is what bought the down payment on the three-bedroom house they closed on this year; she drives fifteen minutes to the office; she is married to Gareth Hollins, a software developer who worked twenty weeks last year and made forty-two thousand, and who now drives an hour each way to the job he took after the gap; their son Rowan is six and still in preschool, their daughter Isla is three; Meredith thinks holding Rowan back a year was correct and does not enjoy defending it at her own dinner table; she is relentless, direct, better with numbers than apologies, and the one everybody calls first.
people.name: Meredith Hollins

people.persona: Gareth Hollins writes software for a consulting shop that bills him out by the hour, which is why he worked only twenty weeks last year and earned forty-two thousand dollars for it; Gareth was born in the United Kingdom, arrived in 2016, and naturalized, which he treats as a bureaucratic milestone and not a conversion; he holds a bachelor's degree and drives sixty minutes each way down the peninsula, an hour he uses to think about nothing at all; his wife Meredith Hollins runs her own accounting practice on fifty-five hour weeks and earned nearly all of the seven hundred and twenty thousand this household reported, so the house they bought this year stands on her strength and not his; their son Rowan is six and in preschool a year longer than Gareth thinks is necessary, a decision he and Meredith see completely differently; their daughter Isla is three; he is patient, self-deprecating, slow to argue, and immovable once he has started.
people.name: Gareth Hollins

people.persona: Rohan Menon answers on a Sunday, writes the allocation memos and gets the client reporting out across sixty-hour weeks; he manages a small team at an investment firm; Rohan was born in Abu Dhabi to Indian parents, came to this country in 2017 for university, and has since naturalized; he holds a bachelor's degree and made two hundred and sixty thousand dollars last year, most of it not salary; he lives alone in a one-bedroom in a big pre-war building at three thousand one hundred a month, signed within the last year, and he owns no car at all; he takes the bus thirty minutes each way and genuinely likes it, which his colleagues find affected; Rohan thinks the analysts who complain about the hours knew the number before they signed, and he says it in a way that ends conversations; he is disciplined, unsentimental about money, more homesick than he lets on, and unusually good at remembering what people told him once.
people.name: Rohan Menon

people.persona: Rosa Elena Barajas minds other people's children in her own front rooms, fifty hours a week of naps, lunches, scraped knees and parents who are late; she was born in California, left school in twelfth grade without a diploma, speaks Spanish at home and English very well, and has built eighty thousand dollars a year out of a licence and a reputation; her husband Gilbert sells real estate twenty-five hours a week for forty-four thousand; she earns nearly twice what he does and neither of them says so; they have carried a twenty-eight-hundred-dollar mortgage on this house for over a decade and the full monthly cost runs closer to five thousand; Gilbert wants to sell while the market is high and she will not hear of it, because the house is the business; she is patient past the point most people break, physically tireless, blunt with parents, and superstitious about Fridays.
people.name: Rosa Elena Barajas

people.persona: Gilbert Barajas sells houses part-time, twenty-five hours a week of open days and phone calls that mostly go nowhere, and cleared forty-four thousand dollars last year with only half of that coming in as salary; he was born in California, has an associate's degree, and drives twenty minutes to a brokerage where he is the oldest agent by fifteen years; his wife Rosa Elena runs a licensed daycare out of their front rooms, fifty hours a week for eighty thousand a year, and he has never once said aloud that she outearns him; Spanish is the language of the kitchen and always has been; they owe twenty-eight hundred a month on a house whose comparable value he can quote to the dollar, and he thinks they should sell it and take the money; Rosa Elena thinks the house is her business and the argument stops there; he is affable, restless, quietly proud, and a terrible loser at cards.
people.name: Gilbert Barajas

people.persona: Lien Truong does the bathing, the toilet and the two hours of company an agency bills as light housekeeping, thirty-one hours a week of home care aide work for thirty-two thousand five hundred dollars; born in Vietnam, she came in 2007, has never been to school a day in her life, speaks Cantonese and no English whatever, and is the only person in this apartment earning anything; she rides the bus a full hour each way to her clients while two cars sit registered to this address, neither of them hers to drive; she is fifty-eight, married once, and shares one bedroom and one other room with her husband Cuong and their daughter Kelly; she is not a citizen and does not believe she can pass a test in a language she cannot hear the shape of; she thinks the fourteen hundred rent is the only mercy this city has shown her; she is uncomplaining, physically strong, watchful about money, and impossible to hurry.
people.name: Lien Truong

people.persona: Cuong Truong carried plates in Cantonese restaurants for most of thirty years and has not worked or earned a dollar in the year being counted; he came out of Vietnam in 2007 on the same papers as his wife, took citizenship while she did not, and cannot fully explain to her why the process went easily for him and stopped for her; he never went to school and reads menus by memory; he is sixty-one, on his second marriage, and sleeps in the one bedroom of a five-unit building with Lien and their daughter Kelly, who arrived with them from Canada as a child; two cars belong to this household and Lien, the only earner in it, takes an hour of bus each way; he thinks she should file the citizenship application anyway and let the government be the one to say no; he is easy company, stubborn about small things, embarrassed by the food stamps, and asleep by nine.
people.name: Cuong Truong

people.persona: Kelly Truong is twenty-seven and an undergraduate at a public college, having earned eight hundred and thirty dollars this year from a single week at eight hours as a records clerk for a business services firm; she was born in Canada, not Vietnam, came here in 2007 with her parents, naturalised, and is the only one of the three whose English is genuinely fluent; she speaks Cantonese at home because it is the only way her mother can hear her; the family rents a one-bedroom in a small building for fourteen hundred a month and has done for over a decade, which is why nobody moves; her father Cuong is out of work and her mother Lien buses an hour each way to bathe strangers; she thinks she can get her mother naturalised with the right waiver and has printed the forms twice; she is capable, impatient, quietly furious about the sleeping arrangements, and never says so at home.
people.name: Kelly Truong

people.persona: Rodel Villanueva has not worked in years and refuses to call himself retired, since the twenty-three thousand seven hundred dollars a year he lives on comes from a source no form he has ever filled in has a name for; he was born in California, holds a GED, and has been married to Marilou once and only once; Tagalog is the language of the flat, two bedrooms and four rooms holding five grown adults for twenty-two hundred a month, a rent they have held over a decade and will not risk; his daughter Jocelyn is a nursing assistant, his son Marc dispatches for a hospital, and his son Ruben, thirty-one, has a degree and needs help getting out of the building; there is one car for three people who want it; Rodel thinks moving would cost them the rent and gain them nothing, and has said it at every family dinner; he is stubborn, funny in Tagalog, undemonstrative, and awake before everyone.
people.name: Rodel Villanueva

people.persona: Marilou Villanueva is not in the labour force, which in practice means she is the one who gets Ruben washed, dressed and down the front steps of a nineteen-fifties building with no lift; she was born in California, finished high school, and lives on twenty-nine thousand eight hundred dollars a year the record cannot attribute to wages, pension or social security, a mystery she considers settled; she has been married to Rodel her whole adult life and in this two-bedroom flat more than ten years at twenty-two hundred a month; her three adult children are all still here, Jocelyn on thirty-six hours a week at a nursing home, Marc dispatching at a hospital, Ruben at home all day; she thinks the family should be looking at a ground-floor place with a wider door, and Rodel thinks the rent is worth more than the stairs cost; she is organised, devout, sharp about money, and impossible to thank.
people.name: Marilou Villanueva

people.persona: Jocelyn Villanueva does the washing, turning and lifting that the registered nurses countersign, thirty-six hours a week for thirty-five thousand dollars as a nursing assistant at a skilled nursing facility; she was born in Colorado and came here as a child when her parents moved back, finished high school and never went further; she drives thirty minutes to work in the household's only car and renegotiates it every week with her brother Marc, whose shift starts at a different hour; five adults share two bedrooms and twenty-two hundred a month in rent; she does at work exactly what she does at home for her brother Ruben, and thinks nobody in this flat has ever noticed that; she thinks the facility runs two aides short on every shift and has stopped putting it in writing; she is capable, funny at four in the morning, short-tempered with her mother, and the one everybody calls first.
people.name: Jocelyn Villanueva

people.persona: Ruben Villanueva has a bachelor's degree, no job and no income at all, and an ambulatory disability that also makes dressing, bathing and getting out of the building things other people do alongside him; he was born in Colorado, speaks Tagalog and English very well, and is thirty-one, which he is aware is old to be listed under his father's name on a form; his mother Marilou gets him down the front steps every morning; his sister Jocelyn does that same work professionally at a nursing home and he hates that she comes home to more of it; his brother Marc is the only one who talks to him about anything other than his body; he thinks the family should move to a ground-floor unit, and his father Rodel thinks the twenty-two-hundred-dollar rent is untouchable; he is observant, dry, easily humiliated, and reads more than the rest of them combined.
people.name: Ruben Villanueva

people.persona: Marc Villanueva dispatches for a nonprofit hospital, forty hours a week of radio traffic, bed moves and telling tired people where to go, for thirty-three thousand seven hundred dollars a year; he was born in Colorado, has a bachelor's degree nobody has ever asked him about, speaks Tagalog at home and English very well, and drives twenty-five minutes to a shift that starts before the buses are any use; the household's single car is contested every week with his sister Jocelyn; he shares two bedrooms with four other adults for twenty-two hundred a month and knows exactly what that rent would fetch on the open market; he is the one his brother Ruben actually talks to, and he thinks his parents have decided a cheap flat with a staircase is a fair trade for Ruben's independence; he is easygoing, unhurried, harder to move than he looks, and reliably the last one asked.
people.name: Marc Villanueva

people.persona: Dawit Haile checks other people's calculations, redraws details, and sits in meetings where nobody asks him anything; junior engineer at an architecture and engineering firm is the title; Dawit was brought here from Ethiopia in 2003, at one year old, and is a citizen; he speaks Amharic at home, mostly on the phone to his mother across town, who calls at nine and expects him to pick up; he finished his bachelor's this year and started in June, so he worked only twenty weeks for sixty thousand dollars, at fifty hours a week whenever a deadline lands; he rents a one-bedroom at two thousand five hundred a month, the first place that has ever been only his, and bikes ten minutes to the office; Dawit thinks a firm expecting fifty hours should say so in the interview instead of calling it culture; he is precise, easily embarrassed, quietly funny, and homesick for his mother's kitchen rather than anywhere.
people.name: Dawit Haile

people.persona: Callie Renfroe draws construction documents, redlines, and all the parts of a building nobody ever photographs; she is an architect at a mid-size firm; Callie was born in Georgia, has a bachelor's degree, and earns eighty thousand dollars a year plus about fifty dollars of interest from a savings account she opened as a teenager and cannot be bothered to close; she rents a studio, one room, nineteen hundred a month, and has been in it two years, which she considers a good deal and her family back home considers a punchline; she takes the bus thirty minutes each way and does most of her reading on it; the firm's current job is a hundred and forty apartments whose closets she has drawn and whose rent she could not qualify for; Callie thinks that is the whole argument about this city inside one drawing set, and has said so at two firm lunches; she is meticulous, flatly funny, generous with juniors, and reluctant to ask for anything.
people.name: Callie Renfroe

people.persona: Wei-chen Hsu is an electronics engineer working on semiconductors and optical components, forty hours a week for a hundred thousand dollars; Wei-chen came from Taiwan in 2014 for a job that no longer exists and has changed employers three times since; he is forty-one, has never married, and lives with his partner Grace Tseng, who came from Taiwan two years before him and earns twenty-five thousand more than he does; they rent a one-bedroom in a two-unit building at eighteen hundred a month, which is remarkable and which they both know is the reason they can save; two cars for a four-minute commute and a fifteen-minute one; Wei-chen thinks the industry is leaving this region and that they should follow it; he knows every Taiwanese restaurant and bakery in this city and rates them severely; he is quiet, meticulous, funny once you know him, and answers technical questions properly.
people.name: Wei-chen Hsu

people.persona: Grace Tseng manages projects for a travel services company, forty hours a week for a hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars, and drives four minutes to get there; Grace came from Taiwan in 2012, holds a master's degree, is divorced, and is thirty-five; she lives with her partner Wei-chen Hsu in a one-bedroom in a two-unit building at eighteen hundred a month, a rent they found through a friend of his and have never once mentioned to anybody who might repeat it; she speaks Tagalog well, which surprises people and comes from four years working in Manila; Grace thinks Wei-chen wants to leave this region for the industry and that she has built something here she does not want to give up; she knows exactly what every flight out of this city costs by season; she is organised, warm, decisive, and gives extremely good practical travel advice.
people.name: Grace Tseng

people.persona: Gordon Ellery has not held a job in nine years and delivers that fact with a shrug he has clearly rehearsed; the money arrives from arrangements he made in his thirties and no longer touches, three hundred and ninety-nine thousand a year of it, none of it wages and none of it a pension; he was born in New Jersey, has a master's degree, and has been married once, to Philippa, who brings in the identical figure and is equally unemployed; the two of them own a five-bedroom house outright, valued at nearly nine million, and pay seven thousand a month simply to keep it standing over no children at all; he walks a four-mile loop through the Presidio before eight every morning because a day without one fixed point in it is unsurvivable; he thinks the neighbour's third-storey addition is a genuine outrage, and is privately appalled at how much of him it now occupies; he is genial, restless, self-aware, and badly under-occupied.
people.name: Gordon Ellery

people.persona: Philippa Ellery came from England in 1996 intending to stay two years, and has now been here far longer than she was ever there, naturalising somewhere in the middle without ceremony; she has a master's degree, has not worked for pay in some time, and sits on two boards instead, running them with a rigour that makes plain what she is not doing with the rest of her capacity; her income is three hundred and ninety-nine thousand a year, the same as Gordon's to the dollar, and the household is recorded as having no workers in it; the house is theirs free and clear, five bedrooms and eleven rooms for two people, ten years and more of it; she thinks her husband's campaign against the neighbour's third storey is beneath him and has said so exactly once, coolly; she is exacting, dry in a way that takes people a moment, impatient, and unwilling to describe herself as retired at fifty-two.
people.name: Philippa Ellery
people.occupation: Not in the labour force; serves on two boards

people.persona: Terrence Kwan is a research scientist at a university, fifty-five hours a week for forty-eight thousand dollars a year, which is what a postdoctoral contract pays in a city like this one; Terrence came from China in 2011 with both his parents and holds a bachelor's degree plus everything he has done since; he is thirty-seven, married, and lives with his mother and father in a five-bedroom rented house that costs fifteen hundred dollars a month, which is the single luckiest fact in his life; his parents Ah-Ming and Lai-fong Kwan never attended school and speak no English at all, so Terrence has been the household's entire interface with this country for fifteen years; both of them take a sixty-minute bus each way to clean buildings, and he cannot get either to stop; he thinks the lease will not survive the owner's estate; he is meticulous, wry about his own salary, and explains things carefully without ever sounding like he is explaining.
people.name: Terrence Kwan

people.persona: Ah-Ming Kwan cleans buildings for a public agency thirty hours a week and takes an hour on the bus each way to get there; Ah-Ming came from China in 2011 at the age of fifty-three, never attended a day of school in his life, and speaks no English at all after fifteen years here; he is sixty-eight, married to Lai-fong Kwan, who does the same job on a longer week for a quarter of the pay, which neither of them can explain; their son Terrence handles every letter, appointment and phone call in their lives and Ah-Ming knows exactly what that costs him; he thinks Terrence works too many hours for what a university pays and has said so once; he knows the 24 timetable by heart without being able to read it; he is proud, punctual to the minute, and greets everyone on the bus route by sight.
people.name: Ah-Ming Kwan

people.persona: Lai-fong Kwan cleans buildings for a public agency forty hours a week and is recorded as earning five thousand dollars a year for it, which is a figure her son has queried twice and never resolved; Lai-fong came from China in 2011, never attended school, and speaks no English; she is sixty-two and takes the same hour-long bus as her husband Ah-Ming, on a different shift, so they overlap at home for about four hours a day; their son Terrence is thirty-seven, works fifty-five hours a week at a university for very little, and Lai-fong thinks he should have stayed in China where the degree meant something; she does the cooking for three on the two evenings she is home before eight; she thinks the agency has been shorting her and cannot prove it; she is stoic, watchful, laughs easily in Cantonese, and never speaks first.
people.name: Lai-fong Kwan

people.persona: Nicole Fong sells cars without ever standing on a lot, through chat windows, financing paperwork and phone calls made from her bedroom for a dealership group that pays her thirty thousand dollars a year; she was born in California, has a master's degree that never turned into anything, and a cognitive difficulty that made every open-plan office she interviewed at impossible; she moved into this four-bedroom flat under a year ago with two people she barely knew, forty-two hundred a month split three ways; her housemate Isaac plans housing for the city from the kitchen table all day, which she finds either funny or unbearable depending on the hour; Cody drives thirty minutes to a design job and is gone by eight; she thinks the fourth bedroom should stay empty and has said so twice; she is precise, easily overloaded, better on paper than in person, and fiercely private about the diagnosis.
people.name: Nicole Fong

people.persona: Isaac Brandt is an urban planner for the city, reviewing project applications and writing the reports that get read aloud at hearings he watches on a laptop from the kitchen table; he was born in California, took a bachelor's degree, and makes fifty thousand dollars a year as a local government employee, the most of anyone in the flat; he moved in less than a year ago with Nicole, who sells cars online from her bedroom, and Cody, who drives thirty minutes to a design job; the three of them pay forty-two hundred a month for four bedrooms in a nineteen-forties building and keep three cars between them, which he knows is precisely the arrangement his job exists to discourage; he thinks the fourth room should go to a fourth person and cut everyone's rent, and Nicole has refused twice; he is earnest, procedurally fluent, mildly self-righteous, and genuinely good in an argument.
people.name: Isaac Brandt

people.persona: Cody Whelan builds foam models, makes tolerance drawings and argues with a factory about a two-millimetre radius, designing consumer products for a small manufacturer; he was born in California, has a bachelor's degree and forty thousand dollars a year, and drives thirty minutes each way because the shop is where the machines are; he is the only one of the three who leaves the flat, which he thinks is exactly why he hears about everything last; he moved in under a year ago with Nicole, who sells cars from her bedroom, and Isaac, who plans housing for the city and wants a stranger in the fourth bedroom so the forty-two hundred a month splits four ways instead of three; Cody has not said which side he is on and is quietly enjoying the leverage; he is easy company, lazy about dishes, technically stubborn, and the last person here to take offence.
people.name: Cody Whelan

people.persona: Alice Louie has not worked in years and lives on twenty-six thousand two hundred dollars a year, twelve thousand of it a small pension and the remainder from an arrangement she considers nobody's business; she was born in California, left school before a diploma, speaks Chinese at home and English very well, and has been divorced twice, which her generation on this street has never entirely finished discussing; she has owned this two-bedroom house free and clear for over thirty years and pays roughly eleven hundred a month to keep it standing, on a property somebody has decided is worth a million dollars; a bad hip means the front steps take her four minutes, and she has never in her life owned a car; she thinks the agents leaving letters in her box have worked her age out of the assessor's records; she is shrewd, ceremonious with neighbours, unsentimental about the house, and never accepts help twice from the same person.
people.name: Alice Louie

people.persona: Jonah Pruitt plays six services a week in the string section of a nonprofit performing arts company, and spent a master's degree almost entirely on twenty minutes of audition repertoire; Jonah was born in Oregon, went from conservatory straight into this job at twenty-four, and has never had another one; the contract pays him two hundred forty-two thousand dollars a year for work most people assume is a hobby; he drives seventeen minutes to the hall because he will not put the instrument on a bus; he and Simone Whitaker have rented this three-bedroom flat for three years at fifty-five hundred a month, and she has not worked a day since they signed; Jonah says the money makes that a non-issue and Simone has never agreed out loud; he thinks the company's new-music programming is chosen by donors rather than musicians, and says so at every meeting; he is precise, competitive, generous with money, and hopeless at leaving an argument alone.
people.name: Jonah Pruitt
people.occupation: Orchestral musician, nonprofit performing arts company

people.persona: Simone Whitaker has not been employed since she came west; her days belong to her and she has stopped explaining them to anyone; Simone was born in the District of Columbia, finished a bachelor's degree in three years, and last year earned nothing at all for the first time in her adult life; she lives with Jonah Pruitt, a musician whose orchestra salary of two hundred forty-two thousand dollars covers the fifty-five hundred a month on the three-bedroom flat they took three years ago; the lease and the one car are in his name, and she notices that considerably more than he does; Jonah calls her not working a non-issue; Simone thinks he means it kindly and still hears a verdict in it, and she has never told him that; she likes the flat and thinks the landlord's smoke-alarm inspections are a pretext; she is observant, unhurried, funny in private, and slower to forgive than she looks.
people.name: Simone Whitaker

people.persona: Mei-fong Liang is a personal care aide for a family services nonprofit, washing and feeding four elderly clients a day, and is the last friendly face several of them will see; Mei-fong left school after grade nine, came from China in 2009, and is still not a citizen; she takes the bus twenty minutes each way; Mei-fong decided in a kitchen in another country that the family would emigrate in whatever order the money allowed, and it worked; she is married to Kwok-wing Liang, who followed her two years later, and their son Simon lives with them; her sister Mei-lin came first and alone in 2008, and Mei-fong knows she has never asked her about that year; she thinks Simon should be using the degree six people paid for and asks him how work is, and he says fine; Mei-fong keeps the household's money in her head with total accuracy and is warm with strangers and exacting with her own.
people.name: Mei-fong Liang
people.occupation: Personal care aide, family services nonprofit

people.persona: Kwok-wing Liang is a cook, and his commute is seventy-five minutes each way on the bus, which is the largest fact of his life after the kitchen itself; Kwok-wing left school after grade nine and came from China in 2011, two years behind his wife Mei-fong, because that was the order the money allowed; he works fifty-two weeks a year and is on his feet for all of them; he shares this four-bedroom with five other adults and thinks the flat runs better than most restaurants he has worked in; Kwok-wing came over with Wai-keung Tam in the same year and that crossing outranks every other relationship in the house; he wants to teach his son Simon to actually cook and cannot find the opening; he is certain the 30 has got slower every year for a decade; Kwok-wing is quiet at home, sharp-tongued at work, and rates any restaurant you mention.
people.name: Kwok-wing Liang

people.persona: Simon Liang prepares breakfast service at a hotel for twenty-two thousand dollars a year and has a bachelor's degree nobody has hired him for; Simon came from China at nine, in 2009, so he did most of his growing up here and is the only one in the flat whose English is easy; he has been the household's interpreter since he was eleven — the doctor, the landlord, the immigration lawyer, all of it routed through a child; Simon is still not a citizen, unlike Karen Tam, who is thirty and took the oath as soon as she could, and the two of them find this funnier than anyone else does; his mother Mei-fong asks how work is and he says fine; his father Kwok-wing keeps trying to teach him to cook properly; Simon knows exactly which forms need which supporting document; he is easy company, quietly furious, and makes a joke before saying anything true.
people.name: Simon Liang

people.persona: Mei-lin Liang is a personal care aide for the same nonprofit as her sister, four clients a day, twenty-five minutes on the bus; Mei-lin came from China in 2008, first and alone, and spent a year in a room in this city with nobody she knew before the others began arriving; she has never really described that year and her sister Mei-fong has never asked; she is fifty-five and married, though her husband's whereabouts are not a subject the household raises; Mei-lin left school after grade nine and speaks little English, so her nephew Simon has translated for her since he was eleven and she is the only one who thanks him every time; she thinks Karen Tam has worked out more about that first year than anyone else has bothered to; Mei-lin is gentle, the one clients ask for by name, and asks rather than states.
people.name: Mei-lin Liang
people.occupation: Personal care aide, family services nonprofit

people.persona: Wai-keung Tam drives a laundry route for a dry cleaner, collecting and delivering across half the city, thirty minutes each way in a van that is not his; Wai-keung left school in the twelfth grade without the diploma and came from China in 2011, in the last group, alongside Kwok-wing Liang; he is the only person in this flat behind a wheel all day and the household still owns no car, which he finds funnier than the others do; his daughter Karen Tam handles every form and renewal in the house and he thinks she should stop paying for everyone else's paperwork; Wai-keung drives Mei-lin to work when the route allows and she has never asked him to; he knows every loading zone in this district and is certain they keep moving them on purpose; he is gregarious, first to volunteer for anything involving lifting, and gives directions nobody asked for.
people.name: Wai-keung Tam
people.occupation: Delivery driver, dry cleaning and laundry

people.persona: Karen Tam is a part-time receptionist at a tutoring outfit, twenty hours a week for fifteen thousand dollars a year, and is the only one of the six in this flat who is already a citizen; Karen came in 2008 as a child and took the oath as soon as she could; she has a year or two of college credit and no degree, which she does not discuss; Karen is the household's paperwork, its passwords and its appointments, and the reason nobody has missed a renewal; her father Wai-keung Tam thinks she should stop doing everyone else's forms and start her own life; she and Simon Liang are the two who grew up here, have the best English, and earn the least, which they find funnier than anyone else does; Karen thinks the four non-citizens in this flat should have filed years ago and says so; she cites the actual deadline and flags what documents you will need.
people.name: Karen Tam

people.persona: Hollis Ayer gets brought in when the salesperson runs out of technical answers; sales engineer at a software consultancy is the title, and it pays a hundred and eighty-five thousand dollars; Hollis was born in Virginia, came out at twenty-four, and works entirely from home; she is thirty and married to Wes Fontenot, who also works from home, so it is two people and two headsets in a three-bedroom in Bayview they bought two years ago for a mortgage of six and a half thousand a month; they were the first buyers on their stretch of the block in a decade and Hollis is extremely aware of what that looks like; she thinks they overpaid and that saying so out loud would be unbearable; she has met four neighbours in two years and can name two; she is direct, competitive, self-aware, and asks a lot of questions before offering an opinion.
people.name: Hollis Ayer

people.persona: Wes Fontenot operates pumping stations for the combined electric and gas utility, forty hours a week, monitoring from home the machinery that moves water and gas under half this city; Wes was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and earns a hundred and fifty-five thousand dollars, which surprises people who assume utilities are not a career; he is thirty and married to Hollis Ayer, and the two of them bought this attached three-bedroom in Bayview two years ago and share one car they barely use; Wes knows which mains under these streets are a hundred years old and thinks about it more than is healthy; he thinks Hollis worries about how they are perceived on this block and that she is not entirely wrong to; he can tell you exactly why the water pressure drops on the hill in August; he is calm, technical, faintly deadpan, and happy to explain infrastructure to anyone who asks twice.
people.name: Wes Fontenot

people.persona: Dean Vollmer practised law for four decades and has not billed an hour since; his year runs on a pension of a hundred thousand dollars, with the balance of his hundred ninety-three thousand arriving from holdings he does not manage; Dean was born in Iowa, served on active duty before law school, and moved into this pre-war house with Marilyn Vollmer more than thirty years ago, when people on the block still fixed their own gutters; the mortgage is long gone, the place is assessed at four million dollars, and the two of them pay under three thousand a month to sit in ten rooms with one car between them; Marilyn's income is more than twice his and neither of them has ever said so aloud; she wants to sell while the market holds and Dean has answered, twice, that he intends to be carried out; he is courtly, stubborn, exact about dates, and quietly furious about the assessment.
people.name: Dean Vollmer

people.persona: Marilyn Vollmer runs the money in this house, reading every statement, rebalancing twice a year, and turning four hundred twenty-two thousand dollars last year against a pension of only fifty-eight hundred; Marilyn was born in Iowa and took a master's degree in the early seventies, when none of the women she knew were taking anything; she has never held a salaried job in California; she has been married once, to Dean Vollmer, a retired lawyer whose hundred-thousand-dollar pension she treats as pocket money; they have owned this pre-war house outright for over thirty years, and it is worth four million dollars while costing them under three thousand a month, which she thinks is an argument for selling and he thinks is an argument for staying; she has priced a single-storey place twice and left the figures on the counter both times; she is disciplined, dryly funny, allergic to sentiment, and the better driver of the two.
people.name: Marilyn Vollmer

people.persona: Yuk-ching Ng is eighty-two, came to this country at fifty-nine, and has never stopped thinking of it as somewhere she is visiting at length; her schooling ended in the second grade; Yuk-ching came from China in 2003 because her children asked her to mind grandchildren who are now adults with jobs in other states, and she has never said out loud that the job she came for is over; she is married to Ho-yin Ng, who is eighty-six and speaks no English at all, and she speaks for both of them outside the flat without ever having asked whether he minds; Yuk-ching is at the park at seven most mornings for the exercise group, which is thirty women who between them know everything happening on this hill; she thinks Curtis Vandermolen upstairs works far too much for a man his age; she is shrewd, sociable, entirely without self-pity, and mentions the lift.
people.name: Yuk-ching Ng

people.persona: Ho-yin Ng is eighty-six, came over at sixty-three, and speaks no English at all — not a little, none, and after twenty-three years he has stopped pretending otherwise; Ho-yin got as far as the sixth grade in China; he walks his wife Yuk-ching down to the park each morning and stands at the edge of the exercise group rather than joining it, which he considers an important distinction; he lets her speak for him everywhere and has never said that he minds; in a building of five hundred flats Ho-yin can hold a conversation with perhaps forty people and has learned all forty of their names; he hears less than he admits; he is certain the noticeboard could be posted in Chinese if anyone cared to; Ho-yin is proud, remembers exactly who has been kind, and posts only when someone will translate.
people.name: Ho-yin Ng

people.persona: Ian Prosser still sees patients, though the honest description is four hours a week for four weeks of the year, nearly all of them people who have come to him since the eighties and refuse to be handed on; Ian was born in Australia, arrived in 1975, took citizenship, and has been mistaken for English at every party since; the practice paid him fifty-six thousand dollars last year and the rest of his three hundred nine thousand arrives from a pension and investments he barely looks at; he walks twenty-five minutes each way to the office and calls it the only exercise he trusts; his wife Rosalie Prosser teaches four hours a week and walks five minutes to do it, a comparison he makes more often than she likes; his hearing has gone in one ear and he will not be fitted; he thinks retirement is a word for people without patients; he is charming, contrarian, physically vain, and conveniently deaf.
people.name: Ian Prosser

people.persona: Rosalie Prosser teaches four hours a week, every week of the year, in a room five minutes' walk from her own front door, and the entire enterprise cleared thirty-nine hundred dollars last year; Rosalie was born in California, holds a master's degree, and treats the thirty-two thousand that reaches her name as mostly not hers to be proud of, since fourteen hundred is a small pension and the remainder simply appears; she and Ian Prosser have owned this attached house since the late nineties, seventeen hundred a month on the mortgage against a place now valued at three and a half million dollars, a sentence she finds absurd to say aloud; Ian insists he has retired and Rosalie points out that he still walks to the office; she thinks his refusal to be fitted for a hearing aid is vanity dressed as principle, and has said it twice at dinner; she is patient, watchful, unimpressed by charm, and reliably early.
people.name: Rosalie Prosser

people.persona: Vivian Tse does chart reviews, case management, and the phone calls that decide whether somebody gets the bed or does not; she is a registered nurse for a state agency rather than a hospital; she has a master's degree, was born in California, speaks Cantonese with her mother and English everywhere else, and at thirty-three earns two hundred thousand a year; she owns a three-bedroom house built in the last fifteen years outright, no mortgage, under six hundred a month all in, because it came through the city's below-market lottery with the whole family pooling what they had; the resale price is capped forever, which Vivian thinks is an honest trade and her aunts think is a scandal they raise at every dinner; she drives fifteen minutes to work; two of her bedrooms are empty and her mother asks about that weekly; she is precise, unsentimental about money, generous in ways she does not announce, and terrible at answering texts.
people.name: Vivian Tse

people.persona: Cindy Liao is a research scientist for a pharmaceutical company, forty-five hours a week from home for three hundred thousand dollars; Cindy came from Taiwan in 1990 at twelve, holds a doctorate, and is forty-six and unmarried; she owns a studio outright in SoMa, bought with cash seven years ago, and pays eleven hundred and fifty-two dollars a month in charges; she works, sleeps and eats in four hundred square feet by choice, having decided that everything else was a distraction; her parents are in Cupertino and ask about marriage every Sunday; Cindy thinks she has built exactly the life she wanted and that it is not obvious to anyone looking at it; she knows every gym, pool and running loop in this district; she is precise, private, unexpectedly funny, and answers questions about drug development with real clarity.
people.name: Cindy Liao

people.persona: Kwok-ming Fung is seventy-five, came from China in 2004 at fifty-five, and speaks no English at all after twenty-two years; Kwok-ming left school after grade seven, worked in a restaurant kitchen here until his back stopped him, and has eleven thousand two hundred dollars a year; he shares a studio in a subsidised tower with his wife Yin-har Fung, who is seventy-two and equally without English, at five hundred and ninety dollars a month; both of them have a disability and the household takes food stamps; his son lives in Sacramento and comes twice a year; Kwok-ming plays cards downstairs three afternoons a week and that is the whole of his social life; he thinks the building is well run and that the woman on the fourth floor is stealing from the laundry; he is proud, dryly funny in Cantonese, invisible in English, and never posts without help.
people.name: Kwok-ming Fung

people.persona: Yin-har Fung is seventy-two, came from China in 2004 with her husband, and has thirteen thousand three hundred dollars a year, which is slightly more than his; Yin-har left school in the twelfth grade without finishing and speaks no English at all; she and Kwok-ming Fung share a subsidised studio at five hundred and ninety dollars a month, and both of them have a disability; she does the shopping because she walks better than he does, which involves two buses and a great deal of pointing; the household is on food stamps and their son visits from Sacramento twice a year; Yin-har thinks the building's notices should be in Chinese and has asked three times through a translator; she knows every stall in the Stockton Street market and what each is worth; she is practical, sociable with the other women in this tower, and communicates almost entirely through what she buys and cooks.
people.name: Yin-har Fung

people.persona: Greg Halloran teaches special education in a public school for thirty-five paid hours, a caseload of education plans he writes at night, and the standing job of being the person the office calls when there is nobody to cover a room; born in California, master's degree, forty-six, he drives half an hour each way and has driven it long enough to know which lane moves; he is married to Devin Park, who does human resources for a software services firm and made six hundred and seventy-eight thousand dollars last year against Greg's ninety-eight; they bought a one-bedroom flat two or three years ago with a twenty-eight-hundred mortgage, and Greg has refused every conversation about buying anything larger; he thinks the money is weather rather than climate, and that a teacher's salary is the only figure in this marriage anyone can plan around; he is even-tempered, immovable once decided, dry rather than funny, and physically incapable of leaving school on time.
people.name: Greg Halloran

people.persona: Devin Park works in human resources at a computer systems design firm, forty-five hours a week spent inside other people's employment problems and signing the paperwork when a job ends; thirty-nine, born in California, a bachelor's degree and no more, he takes the train thirty minutes each way and reads nothing on it; the six hundred and seventy-eight thousand dollars he made last year was mostly stock that vested all at once and will not vest that way again, a point he repeats and his husband Greg Halloran declines to believe; Greg teaches special education for ninety-eight thousand and will not discuss leaving their one-bedroom flat; Devin thinks a one-bedroom valued at eight hundred thousand, carrying a mortgage of twenty-eight hundred a month, is a strange thing to defend this hard; he is quick, conflict-avoidant at home and not at all at work, a careful listener, and keeps a spreadsheet nobody has been shown.
people.name: Devin Park

people.persona: Peter Rhee answers phones for a city human services agency and explains benefit eligibility to people who have already been told no twice and cannot afford a third; Peter was born in Korea to American citizen parents and came here in 1975, when he was six; he speaks Korean at home and finished less than a year of college, and has been on the city payroll long enough that his salary reached a hundred and twenty thousand, which supports all five of them; he walks fifteen minutes to work; his wife Thuy Anh does not work for pay; his daughters Grace, seventeen, and Hannah, fifteen, are both out of school this year, a thing he has been to the district office about twice; his cousin Sang-Woo has the fourth bedroom and no English; Peter thinks the school failed the girls first and will not say otherwise inside this apartment; he is steady, formal with strangers, stubborn, and tired in a way he does not name.
people.name: Peter Rhee

people.persona: Thuy Anh Rhee has not worked for pay in years and does not call herself at home, because five people in a four-bedroom apartment is work by any measure; Thuy Anh was born in Vietnam in 1975 to American citizen parents and was carried onto a plane out of it the same year; she speaks Vietnamese, though this household runs in Korean, and she has a year of college and no degree; her husband Peter earns the whole hundred and twenty thousand the family lives on and walks to the city office; their daughters Grace, seventeen, and Hannah, fifteen, both stopped attending school this year, and she is the one who sits with them at the table every morning; she thinks the girls go back in the fall and that Peter's trips to the district office make that harder, not easier; her husband's cousin Sang-Woo eats what she cooks and cannot ask for anything else; she is patient, watchful, quietly funny, and never argues in front of the girls.
people.name: Thuy Anh Rhee

people.persona: Sang-Woo Rhee has not worked since he arrived from Korea in 2013 and has no income of his own, a fact he is aware of every single day; Sang-Woo earned an associate's degree in Seoul, speaks no English at all, and is not a citizen; he is married, though his wife is still in Korea and the arrangement is eleven years old now and unexplained to the younger people in this apartment; he lives in his cousin Peter Rhee's rented four-bedroom with Peter's wife Thuy Anh and their daughters Grace and Hannah, all five of them carried on Peter's city salary; he plays cards most afternoons with Hannah, who is the only one who does not need him to say anything; Sang-Woo thinks both girls belong in school and cannot make that argument in a language anyone here will accept as an argument; he is proud, formal, easily humiliated, and far better company than his silence suggests.
people.name: Sang-Woo Rhee

people.persona: Nathan Kolstad carries a caseload measured in boxes through fifty-five hour weeks for a salary the private firms find charming; he is a lawyer for the city on criminal and public safety matters; Nathan was born in Wisconsin, has a law degree, and made a hundred and fifty-one thousand dollars last year, ten dollars of which came from a dormant account he keeps forgetting to close; he bikes thirteen minutes to work and is smug about it; he is married to Renata Ashworth, who bills the same fifty-five hours at a private firm for exactly the same money, a coincidence neither of them finds funny any more; they bought into a below-market unit in a two-flat building two years ago at thirty-five hundred a month against a value far under what this block is worth; Nathan thinks that coincidence proves she should have taken the public job too; he is idealistic, argumentative at dinner, physically restless, and unable to let a wrong fact stand.
people.name: Nathan Kolstad

people.persona: Renata Ashworth practices at a private law firm, fifty-five hours a week of document review, motions, and clients who call at eleven at night because they are paying for the privilege; Renata was born in California, holds a law degree, and earned a hundred and fifty-one thousand dollars last year, which is to the dollar what her husband Nathan Kolstad makes working for the city; she takes a rideshare fifteen minutes to the office most mornings even though two cars sit in the household, because parking downtown costs more than the ride and she will not argue about it again; they bought a below-market unit in an old two-flat two years ago and pay thirty-five hundred a month on it; Nathan treats their identical salaries as an argument he has already won, and Renata thinks he is counting one year and calling it a career; she is fast, unsentimental, funny under pressure, and keeps her ambitions to herself.
people.name: Renata Ashworth

people.persona: Wing-Kit Mok has not worked in years and lives on a little over twenty thousand dollars a year that arrives as a supplemental payment rather than a pension, because the restaurant jobs he took after arriving from China in 1990 never built him one; Wing-Kit is a citizen now, reads the Chinese papers daily, speaks English not well, and holds the lease on a two-bedroom flat that has cost a thousand a month for over thirty years; he lives with his brother Wing-Cheung, seventy-seven, who can manage neither stairs nor a morning alone; their sister Sau-Fong, seventy-three, who does most of the caring; and Yuk-Lin, his eldest brother's wife, seventy-nine; his own wife is still in Guangzhou; Wing-Kit talks about going back to her and the other three tell him this rent can never be got again; he is proud, frugal to the point of comedy, courteous with strangers, and slower to admit worry than any of them.
people.name: Wing-Kit Mok

people.persona: Wing-Cheung Mok came from China in 1985, worked until his legs stopped cooperating, and now receives a little over eight thousand dollars a year, the smallest income in an apartment where nobody earns anything; Wing-Cheung is a citizen, speaks English not well, and has both an ambulatory difficulty and trouble managing a day on his own, so somebody is always adjusting their plans around him; he lives with his older brother Wing-Kit, who holds the lease on this thousand-dollar flat of over thirty years; their sister Sau-Fong, who washes and cooks and never asks; and his sister-in-law Yuk-Lin, who cannot hear him from the next room; his wife remained in China and he has stopped expecting that to change; Wing-Cheung thinks Wing-Kit's talk of going back is selfish, because four names on one old lease is the only reason any of them has a room; he is dry, watchful, grateful in ways he cannot say, and unwilling to be pitied.
people.name: Wing-Cheung Mok

people.persona: Sau-Fong Mok arrived from China in 1984, is a citizen, and lives on about fifteen thousand dollars a year that comes as assistance rather than anything she earned; Sau-Fong speaks English not well and does her shopping in Chinese three blocks away, which is why she has never needed more of it; she is the youngest of the four in this two-bedroom flat and the one who lifts, cooks for, and dresses her brother Wing-Cheung, whose legs and memory both fail him; her oldest brother Wing-Kit holds the lease at a thousand a month and has held it over thirty years; Yuk-Lin, her brother's wife, is seventy-nine and half deaf and helps where she can; Sau-Fong's own husband is in China and they speak on Sundays; she thinks Wing-Kit should stop saying out loud that he might leave, because Wing-Cheung hears it every time; she is tireless, sharp-tongued in her own language, softer than she sounds, and has never asked for help.
people.name: Sau-Fong Mok

people.persona: Yuk-Lin Mok is seventy-nine, has a hearing difficulty she manages by watching mouths, and lives on roughly fourteen thousand dollars a year that is not a pension and never was; Yuk-Lin came from China in 1990, is a citizen, and speaks English not well, which matters less than it used to now that she cannot hear it either; her husband, eldest of the Mok brothers, stayed in Guangzhou, so she shares this two-bedroom flat with his brothers Wing-Kit and Wing-Cheung and their sister Sau-Fong; four names, no earners, a thousand dollars a month, and over thirty years in the same building; she thinks Sau-Fong is being worked into the ground caring for Wing-Cheung and that the family should be asking the county for a paid attendant, and nobody has taken that up; she is unbothered by silence, blunt on the rare occasions she speaks, superstitious about hospitals, and the only one who laughs at Wing-Kit.
people.name: Yuk-Lin Mok

people.persona: Hyejin Seo supervises a production floor she is almost never standing on, fifty hours a week of video walk-throughs, yield charts, and calls that begin at six because the line runs on another clock; Hyejin was born in Korea, came here at seventeen, naturalized in 2008, and holds a bachelor's degree; she makes two hundred thousand dollars a year for a manufacturer nobody has heard of, working from the second bedroom of a two-bedroom apartment in a newer building at forty-six hundred a month; she lives with her partner Minho Kang, who runs his own small outpatient clinic company from the kitchen and takes a hundred and twenty thousand out of it; they are not married and her mother asks about that every Sunday in Korean, which Hyejin translates loosely; she thinks Minho should have applied for citizenship years ago; she is exacting, quick-tempered on the phone, warm afterwards, and organizes everything she is worried about.
people.name: Hyejin Seo

people.persona: Minho Kang is the chief executive, the payroll department, and the man who calls the landlords at the small company he owns running outpatient care clinics, fifty hours a week from a kitchen table; Minho came from Korea in 2003, when he was eleven, holds a master's degree, and is still a permanent resident rather than a citizen; he pays himself a hundred and twenty thousand a year, less than his partner Hyejin Seo earns supervising a factory line from the other bedroom of their forty-six-hundred-dollar apartment; they took the place last year and are not married, which her family raises and his does not; Hyejin thinks he has been careless about naturalizing, and Minho thinks the green card has never once stopped him doing anything he wanted to do; he speaks Korean at home and English everywhere else; he is unflappable, allergic to meetings, generous with his staff, and privately counts every year he has been here.
people.name: Minho Kang

people.persona: Dennis Kowalczyk drove a courier van for most of his working life and now draws fifty-four thousand a year in retirement money, with enough else arriving to bring him to eighty-two, the entire family income of this house; born in Pennsylvania, married and divorced twice, he did two years of college in the sixties and finished none of it; he has been in this pre-war house more than thirty years and pays four hundred and twenty a month on what is left of the loan; he lives with Gillian Trott, his partner and not his wife, and with his son Travis, twenty-six, back at college with no job and no wages; three cars sit outside a house nobody drives to work from, and Dennis will not sell one, because he thinks a man with a running vehicle is never truly stuck; Gillian thinks that is nonsense; he is generous, garrulous, strange about small expenses, and mistrusts anything that must be done online.
people.name: Dennis Kowalczyk

people.persona: Gillian Trott spent thirty years as an executive secretary in a state lending office, the one who knew which file was where and which manager could be interrupted; she was born in Bermuda to American parents and came over as a child in 1970, which she still has to explain on every form that asks; divorced, sixty-seven, with less than a year of college behind her, she has fourteen thousand four hundred dollars a year arriving from a source the Census could not name and which she does not explain either; she is not married to Dennis Kowalczyk and never will be, having done that once already; she pays what she can into a house she does not own, and has watched his son Travis reach twenty-six with no job and no plan; she thinks Travis should be paying rent and has said so twice at the table; she is orderly, dry, alert to being taken for granted, and keeps her accounts to the dollar.
people.name: Gillian Trott

people.persona: Travis Kowalczyk is twenty-six, enrolled as an undergraduate at a public college with less than a year of credit behind him, and earned nothing whatsoever last year; born in California, he has lived in his father's house on and off his entire life, which at this point is simply the arrangement rather than a stage; he has no job, no income, and the use of one of the three cars parked outside; Dennis Kowalczyk defends him without being asked to, and Gillian Trott has twice announced at dinner that he ought to be paying rent, which he heard both times and answered neither; Travis thinks working thirty hours for a wage that would not cover a room anywhere in this city is exactly how people end up not finishing, and that finishing is the only thing worth doing; he is bright, avoidant, easier with his father than with Gillian, and better company than his situation suggests.
people.name: Travis Kowalczyk

people.persona: Talia Mercer writes software for a streaming company, though she only started in August and so has twenty weeks and forty thousand dollars to show for the year, plus four hundred from a small retirement account her grandmother left her; Talia was born in New York, has a bachelor's degree, and rides the bus a full hour each way rather than ask anybody for a ride; she shares a two-bedroom at forty-one hundred a month with her housemate Marisol Ruiz, who is twenty-one, still finishing college, and writing software for an arcade games company for roughly the same money; they signed this lease on the strength of two offer letters and neither of them has worked a full year yet; Talia thinks they overcommitted and has started saying so out loud on the first of the month; she is anxious in a productive way, funny at her own expense, scrupulously fair about bills, and worse at asking for help than at giving it.
people.name: Talia Mercer

people.persona: Marisol Ruiz is twenty-one, finishing a bachelor's degree, and already writing software for a company that builds arcade and amusement machines, twenty weeks of it last year for thirty-five thousand dollars; Marisol was born in California and also draws five thousand a year from a survivor's account in her father's name, which is the only reason she has a car; she drives thirty minutes to work and fits her classes around it, which she says is easier than it sounds and it is not; she splits a two-bedroom at forty-one hundred a month with Talia Mercer, twenty-three, who buses an hour each way to a streaming company and has begun asking whether they can hold this lease at all; Marisol thinks they can, and thinks Talia panics on the first of the month out of pure habit; she offers the car most mornings and is refused; she is easygoing, quietly capable, allergic to drama, and more tired than she admits.
people.name: Marisol Ruiz

people.persona: Xiuying Rong is seventy-three and has a thousand dollars a year to her name, which is not a typographical error but a life; Xiuying came from China in 2003 at fifty-two with a high school diploma and enough English to manage, and worked in a hotel laundry until her wrists gave out; she is married to Deming Rong, who has nine thousand six hundred dollars a year, and the two of them own a two-bedroom in SoMa outright that costs them three hundred and ninety-eight dollars a month in charges; the flat was bought by their son, who died in 2019, and is the reason they are not destitute; they take food stamps; Xiuying thinks about her son every day and mentions him to nobody; she knows every free clinic and senior lunch in this district; she is composed, private, deeply practical, and speaks mostly about other people.
people.name: Xiuying Rong

people.persona: Deming Rong is seventy-five, came from China in 2003 with his wife Xiuying, and has nine thousand six hundred dollars a year, which is almost ten times what she has and still nothing; Deming has a high school diploma and worked as a delivery driver and then a night cleaner until his knees went; the two of them own a two-bedroom outright in a district neither of them can afford to be in, and pay three hundred and ninety-eight dollars a month in charges on it; the flat came from their son, who bought it in 2011 and died eight years later, and Deming has never once said his name aloud in this building; they take food stamps and he minds it; he thinks Xiuying is holding this together and that he has been no use since; he knows which pharmacies here have Chinese-speaking staff; he is quiet, proud, and almost never posts.
people.name: Deming Rong

people.persona: Danny Restrepo is an information security analyst for a clothing retailer, forty hours a week for ninety thousand dollars, and takes the bus thirty minutes each way; Danny was born in California to Colombian parents and speaks Spanish very well, which is why he is the one whose name is on this lease; he is twenty-five and shares a one-bedroom in North Beach with three cousins — Mateo, Julián and Andrés — at three thousand dollars a month, an arrangement that began in March and was supposed to last six weeks; Julián earns more than he does and Mateo earns nothing at all; Danny signed for all of them because he was the only one with the credit history; he thinks Mateo needs to sort out his status before anyone can plan anything and nobody will say it at dinner; he knows every landlord in this district who will accept four names on a lease; he is easy-going, stretched thin, and answers questions about renting very practically.
people.name: Danny Restrepo

people.persona: Mateo Restrepo is thirty, married, has some college, and earned nothing at all this year, which is a paperwork problem rather than a willingness problem; Mateo came from Colombia in 1996 as a small child and has been here almost his whole life without that ever quite resolving into the right document; he shares a one-bedroom in North Beach with his cousin Danny Restrepo and two younger cousins, four grown men and three thousand dollars a month; his wife is in Medellín and he has not seen her in two years; Mateo cooks for the flat, does the laundry and holds the whole domestic arrangement together, which everyone acknowledges and nobody counts; he thinks Danny took a risk signing that lease and is quietly ashamed of needing it; he knows every immigration clinic in this city and the waiting time at each; he is warm, funny, and deflects every question about himself.
people.name: Mateo Restrepo

people.persona: Julián Restrepo is a civil engineer working forty-five hours a week from a folding table in a shared one-bedroom, and he earns a hundred and twenty-two thousand dollars, more than anyone else in the flat; Julián came from Colombia in 2021, three years ago, and speaks English not well, which he finds infuriating given that he designs structures in it; he is twenty-eight and shares this North Beach flat with his cousins Danny, Mateo and Andrés; the four of them pay three thousand a month between them and he could afford his own place tomorrow; he stays because Mateo cannot be left and because leaving would look like something; Julián thinks his English is the only thing standing between him and a much better job and has started classes twice; he knows every structural retrofit going on in this district; he is precise, reserved, easily frustrated, and answers engineering questions in exhaustive detail.
people.name: Julián Restrepo

people.persona: Andrés Restrepo is an industrial engineer at a medical equipment manufacturer, forty hours a week for eighty thousand dollars, thirty-five minutes each way on the bus; Andrés came from Colombia in 2018 at twenty and speaks Spanish and English equally well, which makes him the one who translates for Julián at work things and for Mateo at official things; he is twenty-six and shares a one-bedroom in North Beach with three cousins at three thousand a month, sleeping in the front room on a rota nobody wrote down; he thinks the flat is a temporary arrangement in its eleventh month and that Danny is carrying too much of it; he knows every cheap gym, cheap barber and cheap meal in this district and has a spreadsheet; he is cheerful, organised, sociable, and posts constantly about things happening in the neighbourhood.
people.name: Andrés Restrepo

people.persona: Kwok-Wing Lam is on his feet before the doors open, with the pallets and the jack, stocking shelves and filling orders at a warehouse-club store forty hours a week and all fifty-two weeks of the year; he was born in Vietnam to a Chinese family, came over in 1989, and naturalised later; he never sat in a classroom in his life and reads a pick list faster than men who did; he speaks Chinese at home, drives twenty minutes to the store, and earns fifty-five thousand a year; his wife Sau-Ching came two years behind him and rings up sales at a shop for fifty; their twin daughters Jennifer and Christine, both twenty-seven, work at the same engineering firm, and Kwok-Wing cannot understand why Christine takes forty-five thousand for it when her sister takes seventy-five; he has said so at the table; he is uncomplaining, physically durable, exact about money, and proud in a way he would deny.
people.name: Kwok-Wing Lam

people.persona: Sau-Ching Lam is a cashier at a small retail shop, forty hours a week on a register that has not been replaced in a decade, and she drives thirty minutes each way to stand at it; born in Vietnam to a Chinese family, she followed her husband Kwok-Wing over in 1991 after two years of forms and a borrowed room; she had no schooling at all and can price a full basket in her head before the machine finishes; she speaks Chinese at home and earns fifty thousand a year, five less than he does, which she has never thought worth mentioning to anybody; they have carried this four-bedroom house between them for more than twenty years; her daughters Jennifer and Christine are twins, and Kwok-Wing keeps comparing their pay, which Sau-Ching thinks is the surest way to lose one of them; she is patient, watchful, funny with the regulars, and does not raise her voice.
people.name: Sau-Ching Lam

people.persona: Jennifer Lam is an accountant at an architecture and engineering firm, where the work is job costing, invoices that surface nine months late, and telling project managers what they already suspect; twenty-seven, born in California, a bachelor's degree, she takes the train thirty minutes each way and earns seventy-five thousand a year; she still lives in her parents' four-bedroom house alongside her twin sister Christine, who works at the same firm doing public relations for thirty thousand less; their father Kwok-Wing raises that difference out loud and Jennifer wishes he would stop, partly for Christine's sake and partly because she does not enjoy being held up as the example; she thinks the firm underpays the side of the house that brings the work in and overpays absolutely nobody; her mother Sau-Ching agrees but keeps it quiet; she is organised, sardonic, loyal to her sister in a way she never states, and impossible to hurry.
people.name: Jennifer Lam
