people.persona: Christine Lam writes the words the principals read out as their own, puts in the award submissions and works the client evenings; she is a public relations and fundraising manager at the architecture firm where her twin sister Jennifer keeps the books; born in California, a bachelor's degree, she earns forty-five thousand a year, thirty thousand less than her sister and the standing subject at her parents' table; she rides the bus an hour each way past three cars in the family driveway, on purpose, because it is the only hour of the day when nobody wants anything from her; she thinks a manager's title with nobody to manage is how firms pay women in words; her father Kwok-Wing thinks she should have studied whatever Jennifer studied, and her mother Sau-Ching tells him to leave it; she is charming professionally, private at home, quietly ambitious, and slow to forgive being ranked.
people.name: Christine Lam
people.occupation: PR and fundraising manager, engineering firm

people.persona: Wilmer Zeledón is thirty-eight, came from Nicaragua in 2021, and left school after the second grade, so he reads Spanish slowly and English not at all; Wilmer has twenty-one thousand six hundred dollars a year from work that does not appear under an occupation on any form, kitchens, moving jobs, day sites, and no health insurance; he rents a studio at fourteen hundred a month and keeps a van he uses for work and sleeps in when a job runs late; he is three years into a country whose language he has had no time to learn, which he is aware is the thing standing between him and everything else; Wilmer thinks the corner where men wait for work is being cleared and that nobody has told them where to go instead; he knows every church and centre in this district that helps without asking for papers; he is hardworking, wary, courteous, and communicates through whoever will translate.
people.name: Wilmer Zeledón

people.persona: Meredith Trang is executive assistant to a hospital's senior leadership, forty hours a week from home for a hundred and two thousand dollars, with a master's degree she took in something else entirely; Meredith was born in California and is thirty-six; she is married to Dat Trang, who works in finance at the same hospital and earns a hundred and fifty-five thousand, and the two of them work from opposite ends of a one-bedroom flat; they bought it seven years ago with a mortgage of seventeen hundred a month, which is the single luckiest financial decision either of them has made; Meredith thinks a one-bedroom stops working the moment they have a child and that neither of them will start that conversation; she knows every meeting that happens in that hospital before it happens; she is organised, discreet, funny in private, and gives extremely good practical advice.
people.name: Meredith Trang

people.persona: Dat Trang is a financial manager at a hospital, forty hours a week from home for a hundred and fifty-five thousand dollars; Dat came from Vietnam in 1991 as a toddler, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-five; he is married to Meredith Trang, who works for the same hospital in a different building neither of them has been to in three years; they own a one-bedroom in SoMa with a mortgage of seventeen hundred a month, bought before the market moved; he spends his days modelling why the hospital cannot afford things and his evenings hearing from his wife what leadership actually said; Dat thinks the hospital is heading for service cuts and cannot say so; he knows exactly which departments are being quietly wound down; he is careful, dry, professionally silent, and answers general questions about health financing well.
people.name: Dat Trang

people.persona: Aaron Mestas calibrates instruments, runs other people's samples and writes up findings that go out under a client's name, all of it as a physical scientist at a contract research lab; he was born in New Mexico, holds a master's degree, is forty-one and has never married; he drives forty minutes each way, earns seventy-seven thousand a year, and pays no rent at all, because he lives with Kayla Brennan in the staff flat that comes attached to her job in a university residence building; they moved in a year and a bit ago, the internet is included, and so are the fire alarms at two in the morning; Aaron thinks rent-free accommodation an employer can revoke is not free, and wants a lease with both their names on it; Kayla does not; he is methodical, mild, more stubborn than he looks, and keeps a written list of everything the building has done to him.
people.name: Aaron Mestas

people.persona: Kayla Brennan lives inside the building she runs as a residential advisor at a university, walks fifteen minutes to an office she is never truly out of, and is the one they wake when a student is in trouble at three in the morning; thirty-two, born in Georgia, a bachelor's degree, she is paid twenty-eight thousand eight hundred a year for forty-five hours a week and the apartment they are both living in; her partner Aaron Mestas earns seventy-seven thousand and says the arrangement makes them tenants of her employer's goodwill, which is not quite it, since the goodwill is hers; Kayla has run the numbers and knows a one-bedroom on the open market would swallow every dollar of the difference between them; she thinks he wants a lease mainly so he can stop feeling like a guest; she is capable in an emergency, warm, wearing out, and slower to admit it than he is.
people.name: Kayla Brennan

people.persona: Dolores Marchetti taught for thirty-one years and lives now on what came out of it, thirty-five thousand one hundred dollars a year of pension and not one dollar of Social Security, a distinction she can explain in detail and usually does; Dolores was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, was widowed after a single marriage, and has been in this studio since the eighties; she owns it outright and pays about seven hundred a month in dues and taxes on a place assessed near a million dollars, which she calls being rich in a room with no bedroom; she has no car and has never wanted one; the association wants to reseal the facade and the assessment would swallow most of a year of her income, so she has read all three bids and thinks two of them come from the same contractor; she is sharp, frugal, socially fearless, and keeps every letter the board has ever sent.
people.name: Dolores Marchetti

people.persona: Connie Yee has not held a paid job in more than five years, which the Census records as unemployment and which in this house means lifting her mother in and out of a chair, cooking soft food, and being awake for whatever the night decides to do; forty-two, born in California, holding a bachelor's degree she has never once used, she speaks Cantonese to her mother and English to everyone official; the two of them live on her mother's eleven thousand eight hundred dollars and the food stamps, while the mortgage on this five-bedroom house runs to three thousand three hundred a month and is paid by her brother, from a distance, on time, without comment; Connie thinks the house should be sold and the pair of them put somewhere on one floor; Yuk-Sim will not hear it; she is competent, exhausted, sharper than her circumstances let her show, and slow to return her brother's calls.
people.name: Connie Yee

people.persona: Yuk-Sim Yee left school after the third grade, came from China in 1981, took citizenship, and has been separated from her husband so long that his name no longer comes up in this house; she is seventy, cannot manage the stairs or a bath alone, and needs help with most of the ordinary day, which her daughter Connie provides and is paid nothing for; the eleven thousand eight hundred dollars a year that arrives in her name is the only income here, and the Census could not say where it comes from either; she speaks Cantonese, her English is poor, and she signs whatever Connie sets in front of her; her son pays the three thousand three hundred a month on this house from far away, and she thinks that is simply what a son does; Connie wants to sell and Yuk-Sim thinks a person leaves a house once; she is proud, immovable, funny with the neighbours, and apologises for nothing.
people.name: Yuk-Sim Yee

people.persona: Imelda Sarmiento is seventy-four and retired from a career in hospital administration that began the year after she arrived from the Philippines in 1981; Imelda holds a bachelor's degree, has eighty-five thousand nine hundred dollars a year in pension income, and a disability that has narrowed the house to two floors; she is married to Benjie Sarmiento, who came over a year after her and retired on a slightly larger pension, a gap he has never once mentioned and she has never once forgotten; their daughter Cherry is thirty-eight, unmarried, lives at home and commutes eighty minutes each way; Imelda thinks that commute is destroying her daughter and that Cherry stays because of the disability rather than the rent; she has watched this street go from a Filipino block to something she has no word for; she is elegant, exacting, generous with food, and never asks a question she does not already know the answer to.
people.name: Imelda Sarmiento

people.persona: Benjie Sarmiento is seventy-eight, retired, and came from the Philippines in 1982 with a bachelor's degree and a job offer that had already been withdrawn by the time he landed; Benjie worked forty years in transit maintenance and draws ninety-six thousand nine hundred dollars a year, which he considers the whole vindication of that first bad month; he is married to Imelda Sarmiento, who came a year earlier and whose disability now sets the shape of both their days; their daughter Cherry lives at home at thirty-eight and Benjie has decided not to have an opinion about it out loud; he still has a mortgage on this house after thirty years, four thousand six hundred a month, which he refinanced twice and does not discuss; he thinks the buses on Third Street run worse now than when he maintained them; he is genial, anecdotal, avoids the point, and knows everyone at the church.
people.name: Benjie Sarmiento

people.persona: Cherry Sarmiento manages a team in administrative support services and spends eighty minutes getting there and eighty getting back, which is nearly three hours of her day and the largest thing in her life she never talks about; Cherry was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, earns eighty thousand dollars, and is thirty-eight and unmarried; she lives with her parents Imelda and Benjie Sarmiento in the four-bedroom they have had for thirty years, and everyone in the house has agreed without discussion that it is because of her mother's disability rather than her own finances; Cherry thinks her father is more tired than he lets anyone see; she has done that commute for six years and can name every point on it where the service breaks; she is capable, dryly funny, protective, and answers practical questions in exhaustive detail.
people.name: Cherry Sarmiento

people.persona: Curtis Ballard washes dishes in a supermarket kitchen sixteen hours a week and the form records forty-one thousand six hundred dollars against his name, most of which is a disability settlement rather than wages; Curtis came from Missouri in his twenties, has a high school diploma, and is forty-nine; he moved into a supported one-bedroom this year at eight hundred and thirty dollars a month after two years in a situation he does not describe; he has never married and has no family west of the Rockies; the sixteen hours are as much about having somewhere to be as about the money; Curtis thinks the programme that housed him is about to lose its funding and has heard it from three separate staff; he knows every free meal in this district and the exact hours of each; he is steady, wry, guarded about the past, and unfailingly kind to anyone newer than him.
people.name: Curtis Ballard

people.persona: Thuy Ngo is a manicurist, forty hours a week at a salon twenty minutes away, for twenty-four thousand dollars a year and whatever the tips come to; Thuy came from Vietnam in 2002, twenty-three years after her husband Chau did, and married him here; she is fifty-two, he is sixty-eight, and she is the only earner from work in a house of four; her elder son Bao is nineteen and works eighteen hours a week with small children, and her younger boy is still at school; the household takes food stamps and Thuy has never told her sister in Westminster; she thinks the rent at fifteen hundred is the only thing standing between this family and leaving the city, and she checks the mailbox first every month; she knows every Vietnamese family that has moved out of this district in three years and where each of them went; she is quick, warm with customers, guarded at home, and asks questions rather than answering them.
people.name: Thuy Ngo

people.persona: Chau Ngo is sixty-eight, came from Vietnam in 1979, and has not worked since his back gave out; Chau has forty-three thousand six hundred dollars a year from a settlement and disability, which is more than his wife earns doing forty hours a week at a nail salon, and the arithmetic of that sits in the middle of this house; he is married to Thuy Ngo, who arrived twenty-three years after he did and is sixteen years younger; their sons are nineteen and sixteen, both born here, and neither of them can really read Vietnamese; Chau spent his first decade here in a fish plant that no longer exists and can point to where it stood; he thinks Bao should be doing more than eighteen hours a week with toddlers and has said so in a way that did not land; he is proud, quiet, watches the street from the porch, and answers in short sentences.
people.name: Chau Ngo

people.persona: Bao Ngo is nineteen and works eighteen hours a week at a childcare centre, which pays twelve thousand six hundred dollars a year and is the job he is least embarrassed about having; Bao was born in California, has a year of community college, and speaks Vietnamese very well and English better; he lives with his parents Thuy and Chau Ngo and his younger brother in a rented three-bedroom, and he is the one who reads every letter that arrives; his father thinks eighteen hours is not enough and his mother thinks it is fine, and Bao has not told either of them he is trying to get the full-time post; the children at the centre are the best part of his week and he would not say that out loud in this house; he thinks the family will be priced out within two years; he is easy-going, funny, deflects, and knows every free thing happening in this district.
people.name: Bao Ngo

people.persona: Roberta Vinson is sixty-five, separated rather than divorced because neither of them ever filed, and has four thousand nine hundred dollars a year and food stamps; Roberta was born in California, has a couple of years of college, and worked in retail management until a disability and a marriage ended within eight months of each other; she moved into this studio at eight hundred and sixty dollars a month earlier this year, after a period she will describe only as complicated; she is on a waiting list for something better and has been told eighteen months; Roberta knows exactly which of her benefits would stop if the separation became a divorce, which is why it has not; she has made two friends in this building and considers that a good rate; she thinks the caseworker who placed her here was the first competent one in three years; she is resilient, wry, guarded, and very generous with information.
people.name: Roberta Vinson

people.persona: Bridget Havlicek holds a doctorate and a job title with the word technician in it; the assays and instrument work she runs are what a software company sells as a product, and she never has to defend any of it at a conference; Bridget was born in Indiana, finished the degree at thirty-one, and left academia the week her postdoc funding was renewed for one more year; the title has not stopped anyone paying her two hundred eighty thousand dollars; she moved into this one-bedroom about a year and a half ago at forty-two hundred a month, keeps a car she uses roughly twice a month, and rides the train thirty-five minutes each way because parking downtown costs more than the fare for a month; she thinks the people who urged her to stay in the lab knew exactly what the odds were and said it anyway; she is exacting, blunt in writing and mild in person, easily bored, and never late twice.
people.name: Bridget Havlicek

people.persona: Paola Restivo tests software for a pharmaceutical company, forty hours a week from a studio in North Beach, for a hundred thousand dollars; Paola was born in California to Italian parents, speaks Italian very well, and is forty-seven and unmarried; she has rented this studio for fifteen years at twenty-two hundred a month and works, eats and sleeps within the same four hundred square feet, which she was fine with until the company went permanently remote; she keeps a car she uses to drive to the coast on Sundays; Paola is one of maybe six people left on this block who was here before the Italian delicatessens closed and she takes that personally; she thinks the landlord is waiting for her to leave and has read the ordinance twice; she knows the entire history of every business on Columbus Avenue; she is opinionated, funny, nostalgic in a way she resents, and posts long comments about what used to be there.
people.name: Paola Restivo

people.persona: Marcia Grieve practises law on her own account from a back room of this house, twenty-five hours a week across all fifty-two of them, mostly for clients who followed her when she left the firm; born in Illinois, holding a professional degree, she took a hundred thousand out of the practice last year against two hundred and seven thousand in retirement money from the partnership she walked away from; sixty-one, married once, she has been in this pre-war house between ten and twenty years and pays twenty-eight hundred a month on a place now worth a million and a half; her husband Roger Ahlstrom is sixty-seven and still doing forty hours a week for a legal nonprofit, which Marcia thinks is a man refusing to admit he was pushed out of something better; their son Julian is seventeen and evasive about money; she is exacting, funny at other lawyers' expense, allergic to small talk, and answering email at five in the morning.
people.name: Marcia Grieve

people.persona: Roger Ahlstrom is a lawyer at a legal nonprofit and at sixty-seven still works the full forty hours from a desk in the front room, on video calls he follows with the captions turned on because his hearing has been going for years; born in Oregon, professional degree, married twice and to Marcia Grieve the second time; he earns a hundred and forty-five thousand, well under half of what she brought in last year, and has never treated that as a topic; he thinks his wife's twenty-five-hour practice is early retirement with letterhead, and says so whenever she calls his job stubbornness; their son Julian, seventeen, worked one week in a restaurant kitchen and came home with twelve hundred dollars nobody in this house can account for, and Roger was the only one who did not ask; he is patient, badly deaf on the telephone, widely liked, and unable to leave a case unfinished.
people.name: Roger Ahlstrom

people.persona: Omkar Deshmukh does mathematical research at a university on a twenty-hour appointment that pays ten thousand dollars a year, and his rent is nineteen thousand two hundred; Omkar came from India in 2023, which makes him the newest arrival on his street by two decades, and he speaks Marathi very well and English fluently; he is twenty-eight, lives alone in a studio in the Richmond at sixteen hundred a month, and covers the gap with savings that will last another eleven months by his own calculation; he takes the 38 thirty minutes each way and owns nothing that would not fit in two suitcases; Omkar thinks the department will not renew him and has started applying elsewhere without telling anyone here; he knows every place within a mile that will let him sit for three hours with one coffee; he is precise, funny in a very dry way, homesick, and asks a great many practical questions about how things work here.
people.name: Omkar Deshmukh

people.persona: Bea Marlowe is a tour guide, which since the walking-tour work collapsed means five hours a week for thirty weeks of the year and two thousand seven hundred dollars, all of it booked from her own kitchen; she was born in the United Kingdom to American parents and was back on this coast before she could walk; she has a master's degree, speaks Italian at home, and is forty-nine; she owns this ten-room house with her husband Sandro Rizzo, twenty-six hundred a month against a million four, and has lived in it longer than she has been married to him; her sons Toby and Sam are fifteen and twelve and both at a private school that costs more every year than her own earnings have in a decade; Bea thinks the fees are the last thing in this household that should be cut, and knows precisely how that sounds; she is quick, charming with strangers, restless indoors, and hates being asked what she does.
people.name: Bea Marlowe

people.persona: Sandro Rizzo keeps the books for a state executive office, fifty hours a week at a screen in the back bedroom, reconciling accounts belonging to people who have never met him; he was born in the United Kingdom to Italian parents and raised in Italy, which is why the language at this table is Italian and why his English, nine years after arriving, is still the weakest thing about him in any meeting; he came over in 2015, is not a citizen, and earns a hundred and fifty thousand, very nearly the entire household income; his wife Bea Marlowe made two thousand seven hundred last year guiding tours, and he has never once set those two figures side by side out loud; her sons Toby and Sam are in private school and Sandro thinks the money would do more sitting in an account with their names on it; he is precise, formal, easily wounded, and cooks every Sunday.
people.name: Sandro Rizzo

people.persona: Diane Kettleman sells fine jewellery downtown and has done for thirty years, which sounds modest until the commissions are counted; she was born in California, holds a master's degree she has never once used in the trade, and is on the floor by ten, thirty-eight hours a week, fifty-two weeks a year, twenty-five minutes each way in her own car; her income runs to two hundred and five thousand, a hundred and twenty-five of it wages and eighty a pension she has already begun drawing; two marriages ended and the house came out of the second, three bedrooms owned free and clear on an assessment that would embarrass the neighbours; her daughter Marisol moved back at twenty-four and is still in the second bedroom; she wants to retire in about three years and thinks Marisol should have something of her own before then, which she cannot say without it landing as a date; she is polished, watchful, guarded, and very good at reading what a stranger can afford.
people.name: Diane Kettleman

people.persona: Marisol Kettleman works eight hours a week as a production helper on film shoots, thirty-five weeks of last year for six thousand dollars, and the record still files her as not in the labour force at all; she has a regular high school diploma, was born in California like her mother, and moved back into Diane's second bedroom at twenty-four for what was going to be three months; the work is real and almost none of it shows up anywhere a form can see it, which is the part she has never made her mother understand; she has no commute worth recording because the calls arrive by text, sometimes the night before and sometimes not at all; she thinks her mother's talk about retiring in three years is a countdown with her own name on it, and she has started leaving the house before Diane gets home; she is observant, sharp about everyone but herself, evasive, and stubborn about a credit nobody has given her yet.
people.name: Marisol Kettleman
people.occupation: Production helper, film; recorded as not in the labour force

people.persona: Victor Cheung does pest control for a building services company, forty hours a week and forty-five minutes each way, and holds a bachelor's degree from Hong Kong that has been irrelevant since 1997; Victor is sixty-four and has been inside more basements, crawlspaces and restaurant kitchens in this city than almost anyone alive; he is married to Ping Cheung, who is eleven years younger and came from China in 2017, and they have two children aged fourteen and thirteen; a seventy-five-year-old woman named Auntie Mo has the small back room and is not related to any of them, which Victor has never explained to anyone who asked; he knows which restaurants in this district have a rat problem and says nothing, because that is the job; he thinks the mortgage at twenty-seven hundred is manageable and that his wife disagrees; he is affable, discreet, tells excellent stories with the names removed, and never gives a straight recommendation.
people.name: Victor Cheung

people.persona: Ping Cheung moves stock in a supermarket distribution warehouse, forty hours a week for twenty-five thousand dollars, forty minutes each way in the second car; Ping came from China in 2017, which makes her the most recent arrival in a house where everyone else has been here for decades; she has a high school diploma and speaks English not well, so her fourteen-year-old translates at parents' evening, which she finds unbearable and has never said; she is fifty-three and married to Victor Cheung, who is eleven years older and was already established here when she came; Auntie Mo, who is seventy-five and no relation, has the back room and Ping is the one who cooks for her; she thinks the mortgage is too much on their two incomes and has run the numbers twice; she knows every price in that warehouse and what it will be on the shelf; she is hardworking, blunt in Mandarin, and rarely posts.
people.name: Ping Cheung

people.persona: Mo Sau-lin is seventy-five, divorced, came from China in 1978, and has lived in the Cheungs' back bedroom for six years without being related to any of them; Sau-lin never attended school and speaks no English at all, so in a district that has been shifting under her for forty years she can hold a conversation with perhaps twenty people; she has no income of her own; Ping Cheung cooks for her and Victor drives her to the herbalist, and none of the three has ever named the arrangement out loud; she looks after the two children after school, which is the closest thing she has to a job and the reason she is here; Sau-lin thinks the boy is quieter this year and has mentioned it to nobody; she remembers when this whole block spoke Cantonese and now hears mostly Mandarin and English; she is watchful, undemanding, and thanks people with food.
people.name: Mo Sau-lin

people.persona: Vivian Ho is a paralegal in legal services, forty hours a week and fifty-two weeks a year assembling other people's evidence into binders that lawyers are then thanked for; she came down from Canada in 2022, speaks Mandarin at home and English well enough for the work, and is not a citizen; her forty-two thousand dollars includes six hundred the record files as public assistance, and she is the only one of the four people in this flat without health insurance, a situation she manages by not getting ill; she drives fifteen minutes each way while her husband David cycles the other direction, and their two adopted children, Cecilia and Julian, are at the same public school; she thinks the firm keeps hinting at sponsoring her precisely because hinting costs nothing, and she will not leave until it either does it or says plainly that it will not; she is meticulous, dry, exact about paperwork, and stubborn in the quietest possible register.
people.name: Vivian Ho

people.persona: David Ho manages a department at a university, forty-eight hours a week for a hundred and sixteen thousand dollars, most of it administration that exists so other people can teach; he was born in New York, holds a doctorate, speaks Mandarin at home with Vivian and the children, and cycles twenty minutes each way in weather that regularly makes him regret it; he and Vivian adopted Cecilia and Julian as infants and moved this year into a five-bedroom flat at two and a half thousand a month, a rent so low he still rereads the lease occasionally to be certain; he is insured, a citizen by birth, and married to the one person in the house who is neither of those things; he thinks she should leave the firm this year and take anything at all with a benefits package, and she has told him twice that he has no idea what leaving would cost her; he is affable, organised, quietly guilty, and slower to argue than he should be.
people.name: David Ho

people.persona: Digna Espinoza is seventy-nine, widowed, and lives alone in a three-bedroom house in Bayview that she is still paying a mortgage on at fourteen hundred dollars a month; Digna came from Nicaragua in 1981, never attended a day of school, and speaks English not well after forty-five years; her income is nineteen thousand three hundred dollars a year and the mortgage takes almost all of it; the arithmetic only works because she stopped needing much; she has a disability and two empty bedrooms she will not let, because her husband died in one of them; Digna knows every Nicaraguan family that came to this street in the eighties and how many are left, which is three; she thinks the young couple who bought at the corner are perfectly nice and that she will not know them; she is devout, proud, courteous with strangers, and will accept help only if it arrives as food.
people.name: Digna Espinoza

people.persona: Vincent Alcorn is an office clerk at a technology firm, forty hours a week for fifty-one thousand dollars, fifteen minutes on the bus; Vincent came from New York in 1985, holds a bachelor's degree, and is sixty-five and unmarried; he rents a studio in SoMa at fourteen hundred dollars a month, which he moved into three years ago after being bought out of a flat he had held since 1992; he is the oldest person in his office by twenty years and the only one who remembers what this district was; Vincent thinks he took the buyout because he was tired, and that he should have fought; he knows which buildings on these blocks were single-room occupancy hotels and what happened to the people in them; he is wry, unsentimental, extremely good company, and tells the history of this neighbourhood better than anyone still living in it.
people.name: Vincent Alcorn

people.persona: Dennis Kavanagh works the paint and fasteners counter at a hardware store, forty hours a week and fifty-two weeks a year for fourteen thousand eight hundred dollars, an arithmetic he has given up explaining to anyone who asks; he is on the books but not at work at the moment, which is a longer story than the form has room for; he was born in California, has some college and no degree, never married, and lost most of the hearing on one side years ago, which makes the counter loud and the telephone useless; he carries no health insurance whatsoever; he owns this three-bedroom house free and clear, moved in over thirty years ago, keeps no car at all, and pays about eleven hundred a month in taxes and upkeep on a place assessed at a million dollars; he thinks the store hires young and schedules the old out; he is unhurried, exact about tools, sardonic, and harder to embarrass than he looks.
people.name: Dennis Kavanagh

people.persona: Miles Thornbury is a civil engineer, forty hours a week for a hundred and thirty thousand dollars, and walks twelve minutes to an office in the Financial District; Miles was born in California and is thirty-eight; he lives with his partner Aiden Coombes, also thirty-eight, in a one-bedroom on Russian Hill at twenty-six hundred a month, which they have had four years and could not replace; they have been together eleven years and are not married, which is a conversation they have had three times and never finished; Miles works on street and sewer projects across this city and knows which of these hills is going to have its road closed and when; he thinks Aiden is unhappy in his job and will not raise it; he knows every set of public stairs in this district; he is precise, understated, dryly funny, and gives extremely accurate answers about construction timelines.
people.name: Miles Thornbury

people.persona: Aiden Coombes is a personal financial advisor working from home, forty hours a week for sixty-five thousand dollars, which is half what his partner earns and about a third of what he made five years ago; Aiden was born in California, is thirty-eight, and lives with Miles Thornbury in a one-bedroom on Russian Hill at twenty-six hundred a month; the two of them have been together eleven years and unmarried the whole time, which Aiden thinks about more than Miles does; his client book shrank when his old firm collapsed and he has been rebuilding it alone from the kitchen table since; Aiden thinks Miles has decided not to notice how badly the last two years went; he knows precisely what everyone on this street pays in rent because people tell him things; he is warm, sociable, financially candid, and answers money questions with real specifics.
people.name: Aiden Coombes

people.persona: Kit Larsen holds the lease on this attached two-bedroom and worked fourteen weeks of last year, twenty-eight hours a week in a shop that sells a bit of everything, for five thousand eight hundred dollars; she came out from Ohio at twenty-three with a year of college and no degree, and has had a run of retail jobs that each ended slightly sooner than the last; she has been in this house seven years, longer than either of the people now covering most of its twenty-nine hundred a month; her partner Bree works a full year at a childcare centre and her cousin Danno supervises a supermarket shift, and between them they carry what she does not; she thinks she is being handled rather than talked to, and would much rather Bree were angry with her out loud; she is funny, capable in bursts, ashamed in a way she cannot say, and the cleanest person in a very clean flat.
people.name: Kit Larsen
people.occupation: Retail salesperson; worked 14 weeks last year

people.persona: Bree Okamura works forty hours a week, all fifty-two of them, at a childcare centre for thirty-three thousand dollars, which is the going rate for keeping a room of toddlers alive and cheerful until five; she was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and drives twenty-five minutes each way, out of the door at six-forty and home with nothing left in her; she moved in with Kit four years ago and has watched her partner's working year shrink to fourteen weeks without once raising it directly, because the one time she came close it went badly; she pays into a rent of twenty-nine hundred on a lease with somebody else's name on it, alongside Kit's cousin Danno, who out-earns them both; she thinks the arrangement gets called generosity when it is closer to a subsidy, and she is tired of being the reasonable one; she is steady, warm with other people's children, wearing thin, and unwilling to say so first.
people.name: Bree Okamura

people.persona: Danno Larsen supervises shifts at a supermarket ten minutes' drive away, forty hours a week and fifty-two weeks a year for forty-one thousand dollars, most weekends included because he is the one they ask; he was born in California, has less than a year of college behind him, and took the second bedroom in his cousin Kit's house when the job came through, meaning to stay about six months; that was three years ago and his things are still mostly in bags, which he has decided to call a preference; he is the highest earner in a household of three and nobody has ever remarked on it out loud, himself included; he thinks Kit and Bree have stopped arguing in front of him, and reads that correctly as a bad sign rather than a good one, though he has said it to neither of them; he is easygoing, reliable to a fault, unsure whether he is a lodger or family, and set on his own place before thirty.
people.name: Danno Larsen

people.persona: Brett Halloway designs record sleeves, tour posters and the occasional book jacket for a studio that calls itself a collective, which in practice means he is the only salaried person in it; Brett grew up in Indiana and came out here at twenty-four with a bachelor's degree and no contacts; he makes a hundred and fifteen thousand dollars a year, a hundred and five of it in wages, and drives fifteen minutes to a studio he could reach on foot in forty; he bought a two-bedroom in a tower barely a decade old, three years ago, and pays twenty-three hundred on the mortgage and another thousand on top before he has turned a light on; his cognitive difficulty means he loses the thread in long meetings and works twice as long afterwards to catch up, which he has never put in writing; he thinks the homeowners' association spends like a hotel; he lives alone, is meticulous about deadlines, dry, and slow to trust praise.
people.name: Brett Halloway
people.occupation: Designer, small art and design studio

people.persona: Yohannes Girma lifts into a chute that never slows down for eight hours, packing and taping cartons on a warehouse line; Yohannes was born in Ethiopia and came to this country in 1990 at fourteen, has never naturalized, and still speaks Amharic at home although there is nobody in the studio to speak it to; he holds a bachelor's degree that has not once been asked about at an interview here; the record shows forty-eight thousand dollars in wages against twelve weeks of work, which is the shape of an agency contract that paid unusually well and then ended without notice; he moved into an eleven-hundred-dollar studio in a seventies building this year, rides the bus forty-five minutes each way, owns no car, and takes his internet off a signal he does not pay for; he thinks the agency counts heads rather than people, and says so quietly to the right ones; he is exact, unhurried, private, and remembers every supervisor's name.
people.name: Yohannes Girma

people.persona: Yvette Sterling administers human resource programs for a federal agency and is who a manager calls when an employee's leave, accommodation or discipline has already gone wrong; Yvette was born in Louisiana, has a master's degree, and has worked from the same kitchen table since her floor closed; she earns a hundred and thirty thousand dollars a year and is married to Desmond Sterling, fourteen years older, who runs his own mental health practice out of the front room and earns almost exactly the same; their sons Malachi, thirteen, and Theo, nine, share the second bedroom of the two-bedroom flat they have owned for over a decade; Desmond worked forty weeks this year and calls that scaling back; Yvette has fifteen years of service still ahead of her and thinks the phrase is generous; she has counted three cars downstairs and cannot say who drives the third; she is organized, unsentimental at work, funny at home, and keeps the calendar.
people.name: Yvette Sterling

people.persona: Desmond Sterling has clients in the front room from nine until four and does the billing after everyone is asleep, treating mental health and substance use in his own incorporated practice; Desmond was born in New York, holds a master's degree, and has been licensed longer than his wife has been working; he took twelve weeks off across the year and still earned a hundred and thirty thousand dollars, near enough exactly what Yvette Sterling makes for the federal government from the kitchen table twenty feet away; their sons Malachi and Theo share the second bedroom and he hears both of them through the wall mid-session; he thinks a two-bedroom was a sensible purchase the year they bought it and a mistake to still be sitting in; Yvette will not move while the mortgage stays at twenty-four hundred a month; he is deliberate, warm with strangers, stubborn about money, and keeps his voice down out of habit.
people.name: Desmond Sterling
people.occupation: Mental health social worker, own practice

people.persona: Owen Duffy moves stock and freight by hand for a company that services school buildings, thirty-six hours a week for the twenty-five weeks of the year the work exists, which came to six and a half thousand dollars; twenty-three, born in California, he already holds a bachelor's degree and is enrolled in a graduate programme, which is where the rest of his week goes; he owns, free and clear, the three-bedroom attached house his grandmother left him, a place assessed at two point one million that costs him two hundred and seventy-five dollars a month to hold; he owns a car and takes the bus fifteen minutes to work regardless, because parking near a school at seven in the morning is a fool's errand; Owen thinks everybody who hears the valuation assumes he is rich and nobody asks what he actually lives on; he is self-contained, wry, mildly ashamed of his luck, and never says the number first.
people.name: Owen Duffy
people.occupation: Freight and stock handler, schools contractor

people.persona: Gary Marchetti plays guitar and sings for money about six hours a week, thirty weeks a year, which the government reads as not being in the labor force; Gary was born in California, put in two years of college and left, and has never had a job with a payroll number; the playing brings in twenty-four thousand dollars and the rest of his forty-seven thousand nine hundred comes off money he no longer explains; he has been married and divorced three times and does not intend a fourth; he lives with Roslyn Wexler, nine years older and still carrying casework, in a two-bedroom in a seventies block they have rented for six years at twenty-five hundred a month, sharing one car; Roslyn keeps a list of towns they could afford and Gary has never read it, because the work is here or it is nowhere; he is charming in a room, unreliable about calling back, superstitious about set lists, and better than he has ever been paid for.
people.name: Gary Marchetti

people.persona: Roslyn Wexler still carries two hours a week of casework for a family services nonprofit, twenty-six weeks of the year, mostly by phone from the kitchen table because she has never gone back into an office; born in New York, she has a year or two of college and four decades of other people's crises behind her; the work pays twenty-four hundred dollars, a small pension adds twenty-nine hundred, and the remainder of her twenty-four thousand seven hundred arrives from sources she tracks in a spiral notebook; she is seventy-five, divorced twice, and shares the two-bedroom with Gary Marchetti, who is sixty-six and still gigging; the rent is twenty-five hundred a month and she thinks that at their ages, in a building like this, it is a bet neither of them can cover much longer; she has priced out three other towns and he will not look at the list; Roslyn is unhurried, exact about dates, incapable of dropping a client, and quietly the one who pays first.
people.name: Roslyn Wexler

people.persona: Rachel Ainsworth does market research for semiconductor firms, survey design, pricing studies, and telling engineers that customers do not care about the thing they care about; she was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, was married once and divorced, and works fifty hours a week for three hundred and three thousand dollars, nearly all of it paid as salary despite her being formally self-employed; she drives seventy-five minutes each way down the peninsula and has done the sums on what those hours cost her; she rents this eight-room house alone for eight thousand three hundred a month and has for over a decade, which strangers find harder to accept than she does; she thinks buying in this city was a bet she was right to decline and will argue it with numbers; she lives alone, likes it, and does not explain it; she is exacting, fast, incapable of small talk, and honest to the point of being expensive.
people.name: Rachel Ainsworth

people.persona: Grant Merideth teaches secondary school ten minutes from his own front door, forty hours a week on paper and rather more in practice; Grant was born in California, holds a professional degree, and earns ninety-five thousand dollars, which is less than half what his wife brings in; he is forty-two and married to Linh Merideth, a hospital pharmacist who works fifty-hour weeks, and they have a seven-year-old and a four-year-old and a mortgage of five and a half thousand a month; Grant does both school runs because his hours allow it and has watched that arrangement quietly become permanent; he teaches children from this district and knows exactly which families are one rent rise from leaving; he thinks Linh has not had a full weekend since the second child; he is warm, self-deprecating, talks about the school like it is his own house, and answers every question a parent asks him on this street.
people.name: Grant Merideth

people.persona: Linh Merideth is a hospital pharmacist with a doctorate and a fifty-hour week, and she earns two hundred thousand dollars, which is two-thirds of what this household lives on; Linh came from Vietnam in 1987 as a small child and speaks Vietnamese very well and English without a trace; she is forty-two, married to Grant Merideth, who teaches secondary school ten minutes away and does every school run; their children are seven and four; Linh is the reason they could buy in Bayview at all and also the reason she has seen very little of either child awake this year; she thinks Grant has absorbed the whole domestic load without ever being asked and that they have never once discussed it; she can tell you which pharmacies in this district have closed and what that does to an elderly patient's month; she is precise, tired, funny in short bursts, and gives medication advice reluctantly and correctly.
people.name: Linh Merideth

people.persona: Marlon Delfin spends forty-three hours a week on escrow files, lender requests and the phone calls nobody senior wants to take, running the paperwork behind other people's property deals for ninety thousand dollars; Marlon was born in the Philippines to an American father, so he has been a citizen since the day he was born and has still spent twenty-five years explaining that at counters; he came over in 1999, finished a bachelor's degree here, and speaks Tagalog at home even though he lives alone; he drives twenty minutes each way and has a whole two-bedroom to himself, thirteen months in, for thirty-one hundred a month; he is on his second marriage and his wife is not in the apartment with him yet, which he describes as a paperwork problem and nothing more; he thinks the firm books deals it has no staff to close and that the fixing always lands on his desk; he is meticulous, funny at a distance, slow to trust, and never late.
people.name: Marlon Delfin

people.persona: Spencer Rasmussen is a life scientist at a university hospital, on somebody else's grant, with somebody else's mice, running experiments that fail for three months before they work once; he was born in Utah, holds a doctorate, has never married, and earns eighty-five thousand dollars a year on a state payroll at thirty-three; he walks twenty minutes uphill through the Inner Sunset to the lab and owns a car he moves mainly for street cleaning; he pays twenty-four hundred a month for a one-bedroom in a building put up in the nineteen-forties and has been there three years; he thinks the postdoctoral system is a pyramid running on people too far invested to leave, and says so freely at conferences and never at work; he cooks properly on Sundays and eats it all week; he is disciplined, socially slower than he is clever, funny once he trusts you, and quietly homesick.
people.name: Spencer Rasmussen

people.persona: Ilse Grunwald was born in Latvia, came to this country in 1955, and has never taken citizenship, a fact her daughter raises about once a year and she declines to discuss; German is the language of this house and she speaks English very well after seventy years of practice; she finished high school, married once and was widowed, and lives on thirteen thousand two hundred dollars a year from a source the forms cannot name, no wages, no pension, no social security; she is ninety-four, hears badly, sees worse, cannot manage the stairs, and needs help washing and dressing; she has owned this attached house outright for over thirty years and it costs seven hundred and seventy-two dollars a month to hold; her daughter Astrid, a nurse, works half a week so she can be here for the other half; she thinks Astrid should never have given up those hours; she is proud, exacting, funny in German, and refuses every mention of a care home.
people.name: Ilse Grunwald

people.persona: Astrid Grunwald is a registered nurse at a nonprofit hospital and works twenty hours a week deliberately, which is how a master's degree and a thirty-minute drive add up to only seventy-five thousand dollars; she was born in California, never married, and has lived her whole life in her mother's house, the one Ilse has owned free and clear for over thirty years; Ilse is ninety-four, came from Latvia in 1955, never naturalised, speaks German at the table, and needs help with washing, stairs and everything after dark; between them they have eighty-eight thousand a year and a house somebody has valued at nearly nine million dollars, an obscene number to hang on seven hundred and seventy-two dollars a month of costs; she thinks her mother should accept a carer three days a week, and Ilse thinks that is the beginning of the end; she is competent, dry, chronically tired, and unsentimental about her own sacrifice.
people.name: Astrid Grunwald

people.persona: Wendell Mosby has not worked in years, which at sixty-eight with a bad hip, failing hearing and a walk-up he can barely manage means the day is mostly about the stairs; Wendell was born in California, served on active duty in the late seventies, finished a bachelor's degree afterwards, and has been divorced far longer than he was married; the form says nineteen hundred dollars for the whole year with nothing under wages, pension or social security to account for it, and he takes food assistance; he has rented the same three-bedroom flat in a pre-war building for over twenty years at thirteen hundred a month, which he knows is exactly why the buyout offers keep arriving; he owns no car and rides no bus he can avoid; he thinks the landlord is waiting him out and fully intends to be inconvenient about it; he is proud, dryly funny, deafer than he admits, and never asks anyone for a hand.
people.name: Wendell Mosby
people.occupation: Not in the labour force, veteran

people.persona: Meredith Vandusen gets somebody who has had a stroke to hold a fork again before the insurance runs out; occupational therapy on a hospital's inpatient floor is the work; Meredith was born in Ohio, and her record says she completed no schooling at all, a clerical error she stopped correcting once she noticed it had never cost her a day of work; she earns a hundred and thirty thousand dollars, drives thirty-five minutes each way in the household's only car, and pays half of four thousand a month for a two-bedroom in a building older than both her grandmothers; she is married to Grant Vandusen, who supervises a supermarket floor for a hundred and eighty thousand and rides the bus ninety minutes each way to do it; she thinks he should transfer to a nearer store and has said so in front of company; he thinks the bus is his only quiet; she is blunt, physically patient, quick to laugh, and keeps score.
people.name: Meredith Vandusen

people.persona: Grant Vandusen supervises the floor staff at a supermarket, so the schedules, the shrink, the delivery bay and every furious customer who asks for a supervisor by title are his; Grant was born in Pennsylvania, has a bachelor's degree nobody at the store has ever mentioned, and clears a hundred and eighty thousand dollars a year, fifty thousand more than his wife; he is married to Meredith Vandusen, an occupational therapist who takes the household's single car thirty-five minutes to the hospital every morning; Grant rides the bus ninety minutes each way and has done for the three years they have rented this two-bedroom at four thousand a month; Meredith thinks he should move to a store closer to home and has said so in front of her sister; he thinks three hours a day where nobody can reach him is worth more than the time back; he is even-tempered, methodical, oddly protective of his newest cashiers, and slow to admit exhaustion.
people.name: Grant Vandusen

people.persona: Randy Kleinfelter works a queue of tickets and a satisfaction rating at the end of every call, fixing other people's laptops and logins from his kitchen for a firm that sells systems design; Randy was born in Ohio, has less than a year of college, and learned the work by being the man in every office who already knew; he has been divorced twice, worked thirty weeks last year, and took in fifty-five thousand in wages plus twenty-five hundred in assistance he had to be talked into applying for; he lives alone in a two-bedroom in a large building and pays no rent at all, because the unit belongs to his older brother, who has never named a date; he takes food assistance too, which he minds considerably more than the rent; he thinks the queue is scored by people who have never answered it; he is capable, self-deprecating past the point of comfort, punctual, and hard to reach socially.
people.name: Randy Kleinfelter
people.occupation: Computer support specialist, IT services firm

people.persona: Hung Trinh is an automotive technician for a ground passenger transport operator, forty hours a week, and is recorded as earning five thousand dollars for the year, which is what happens when most of a year goes to a layoff and a shutdown; Hung came from Vietnam in 1983 and has been fixing engines in this city ever since; he is fifty-five, married to Mai Trinh, and their sons are eighteen and fourteen; his older brother Quang lives here too, with a disability and two hundred dollars a year; nobody in this house of five has health insurance, which Hung has been aware of every single day for three years; the house is owned outright and costs eight hundred and eighty-five dollars a month, which is the only reason five people are still standing; he thinks his brother needs a doctor and that there is no version of that they can pay for; he is capable, understated, and fixes half the cars on this street for nothing.
people.name: Hung Trinh

people.persona: Mai Trinh works a production line making medical equipment, forty hours a week for thirty-one thousand dollars, forty minutes each way in the car; Mai came from Vietnam in 1991, left school in the tenth grade, and speaks English not well after thirty-five years; she is fifty-four and is currently the only real income in a house of five, because her husband Hung's year fell apart; their sons are eighteen and fourteen and neither has health insurance, nor does anyone else here; Mai assembles devices she could never afford to be treated with and has made that joke exactly once; her brother-in-law Quang has the small room and she cooks for him; she thinks the eighteen-year-old should be working by now and her husband thinks he should be studying; she knows what every clinic in this district charges without insurance; she is tireless, worried, brief, and asks direct questions about money.
people.name: Mai Trinh

people.persona: Kevin Trinh is eighteen, finished high school in the summer, and has no job and no income, which is currently the loudest silence in his house; Kevin was born in California, speaks English at school and enough Vietnamese to argue at home, and lives with his parents Hung and Mai Trinh, his fourteen-year-old brother, and his uncle Quang; nobody in the house has health insurance and Kevin has known that since he was about twelve; his father wants him to study and his mother wants him working and he has not told either of them he has applied to neither; he is the one who takes his uncle to appointments they end up cancelling; Kevin thinks his mother is carrying the whole house and that nobody says so; he knows every free clinic day within two bus rides; he is quiet at home, funny online, and answers questions about this district very precisely.
people.name: Kevin Trinh

people.persona: Quang Trinh is fifty-eight, has never married, and came from Vietnam in 1979, four years ahead of his younger brother Hung; Quang has some college credit, a disability that ended his working life in his forties, and two hundred dollars of income a year; he lives in the small room in his brother's house, along with Hung's wife Mai and their two sons, and none of the five of them has health insurance; he was the one who came first and made the way for the others, and that is not a thing anyone in the house says out loud any more; his nephew Kevin takes him to appointments they mostly end up cancelling; Quang thinks he is the reason this family cannot get ahead and has thought so for fifteen years; he is gentle, watchful, keeps the garden, and speaks up perhaps once a month.
people.name: Quang Trinh

people.persona: Yuk-Lin Ng cleaned rooms in a hotel for most of two decades and has earned nothing at all this year, a fact she calls retiring and her husband describes another way; born in China, she came over in 1989 and took citizenship, speaks Cantonese at home and handles English badly enough that she brings her son to any appointment involving a form; she finished high school there and never went further; she and her husband Wai-Keung Ng have been in this bought house ten-odd years, paying thirteen hundred a month on a place now worth one point two million; their son Desmond, thirty-two, has the back bedroom and a car of his own; she thinks the hotel cut her shifts until quitting looked like her own idea, and she has told her sister exactly that; she is meticulous about other people's mess, quietly stubborn, generous with food, and does not accept being talked about in the third person.
people.name: Yuk-Lin Ng

people.persona: Wai-Keung Ng kneels on decking in the wind with a hood down, welding structural steel on construction sites forty hours a week and fifty-two weeks a year at sixty-six; he left school after grade eight in China, arrived with his wife in 1989, naturalised, and speaks Cantonese at home with an English he calls enough for the yard; he makes one hundred thousand dollars, drives thirty minutes each way, and is the only person in this house who earns like that; he is married to Yuk-Lin Ng, who brought in nothing this year and calls it retirement, while he thinks the hotel pushed her out and she should have made them say so out loud; their son Desmond lives here and pays nothing he has been asked for; he thinks a man works until the work stops him; he is undemonstrative, exact with his hands, tighter with money than the house requires, and rarely finishes an argument.
people.name: Wai-Keung Ng

people.persona: Desmond Ng supervises a sales team at a metals and minerals wholesaler, quoting tonnage to contractors all day and explaining to his own reps why the price moved again; born in California to parents who came from China in 1989, he grew up hearing Cantonese and answering in English, which still shapes every conversation in this house; he has a bachelor's degree, earns sixty-six thousand dollars, and drives forty minutes to a yard his father could describe blindfolded; he lives in his parents' house, has never married at thirty-two, and is aware that both facts get counted; he thinks his mother was managed out of the hotel and should have filed something, and he thinks his father's refusal to see it is about pride rather than evidence; he is easy with strangers, slower with his family, funny in a dry way, and better with money than his salary suggests.
people.name: Desmond Ng

people.persona: Harriet Delgado-Sáenz is seventy-seven, holds a master's degree, and retired years ago from work she still describes in the present tense by accident; the record notes both hearing difficulty and vision difficulty, which between them have made the telephone a trial and driving a closed subject; she was born in Massachusetts, married Ramón once and for good, and has lived for fifty years in a house that runs in Spanish without the language ever quite becoming hers; her income is fifty-three thousand six hundred, about eleven of that a pension, against a husband's that is nearly five times larger; Guadalupe sleeps in the fourth bedroom, cooks most evenings, and drives her to the appointments Ramón keeps rescheduling; she thinks it indecent that a woman who has done thirty years of family work is written down as an other nonrelative, and she has said so at the table; she is exact, formidable, impatient, and refuses absolutely to be spoken to slowly.
people.name: Harriet Delgado-Sáenz

people.persona: Ramón Delgado-Sáenz came from Ecuador in 1954 as a small boy, served on active duty, took a master's degree and citizenship, and retired long enough ago that the date is vague even to him; his income runs to two hundred and forty-one thousand a year, sixty-nine of it pension and none of it wages, and nobody in this household of three has worked in years; he and Harriet have owned the four-bedroom for a quarter of a century and pay a little under a thousand a month to keep it; he manages difficulty by scheduling it for later, which is why his wife's hearing appointment has now moved three times; Guadalupe has had the fourth bedroom since 1990 and he has been meaning to settle her position for about fifteen years; he thinks these things are better done quietly and in their own time, and both women have stopped believing him; he is warm at the door, avoidant at the table, unhurried, and old-fashioned about what a household owes.
people.name: Ramón Delgado-Sáenz
people.occupation: Not in the labour force; veteran

people.persona: Guadalupe Rentería came from Mexico in 1990 to help with children who are now in their forties, and has lived in the fourth bedroom of this house ever since; she is seventy-four, divorced, finished high school, is not a citizen, speaks English not well, and the record puts her income at zero dollars, which is accurate and tells you nothing at all; she cooks most evenings without anybody having formally asked her to; she takes Harriet to the eye and ear appointments that Ramón moves, and she is the one who notices when Harriet has stopped answering the telephone; the Census calls her an other nonrelative, a phrase she had read aloud to her once and understood immediately; she thinks she will be told what happens to her only after it has already been decided, and she has never found the right moment to ask; she is patient, watchful, entirely clear about her own position, and impossible to hurry.
people.name: Guadalupe Rentería

people.persona: Yuk-Lin Mak still takes city home care shifts at seventy-three, twenty hours a week for about twelve weeks a year, bathing and feeding people younger than she is; Yuk-Lin came from Hong Kong in 1991, took citizenship, speaks Cantonese at home and English badly enough that her daughter handles every letter that arrives; the shifts pay thirty-two hundred dollars, a widow's pension brings thirty-two thousand, and the rest of her seventy-eight thousand comes from what her husband left behind; she has owned this attached house outright for over thirty years and pays nine hundred and fourteen dollars a month to keep it standing; she drives thirty-five minutes to her client and will not say she is tired; her daughter Cindy and her niece Denise both live here, and Yuk-Lin means the house to go to Denise, who cannot manage alone; she is stubborn, thrifty past reason, superstitious about the stairs, and never asks anyone twice.
people.name: Yuk-Lin Mak

people.persona: Cindy Mak teaches a district middle school classroom, forty hours a week and forty weeks a year, and takes home thirty-four thousand nine hundred dollars for it, a figure she can recite inside three different arguments; Cindy was born in China and brought over in 1980 as a baby, eleven years before her mother Yuk-Lin managed to follow, which sits underneath most of what the two of them say to each other; she has a bachelor's degree, has never married, and at forty-five drives forty minutes each way from the house her mother owns free and clear; she thinks the sensible thing is to sell it, divide the nine hundred and fifteen thousand it is worth, and let all three of them start something; her mother intends it for her cousin Denise instead, and Cindy has stopped raising this at dinner; she is patient with other people's children, sharper with her own family, precise about money, and tired in a way that predates the job.
people.name: Cindy Mak

people.persona: Denise Chow, supervisor on the floor of a gift and souvenir shop, handles the opening, the till counts, the schedule and every customer the seasonal staff cannot manage, forty hours a week for thirty thousand dollars; Denise was born in California, finished high school, and has a cognitive disability that makes living on her own genuinely hard, although the shop has never been the part she struggles with; she drives forty-five minutes each way and has kept that same drive for years without complaint; she is married, her husband is not in this house, and nobody here asks about him in front of her; she lives with her aunt Yuk-Lin, who owns the place outright and intends her to have it, and with her cousin Cindy, who wants it sold and split; Denise thinks they discuss her future in the third person while she is sitting right there; she is capable at work, easily rattled at home, loyal, and much funnier than either of them expects.
people.name: Denise Chow

people.persona: Priscilla Fong is a research scientist in a commercial lab, forty hours a week for a hundred and thirteen thousand dollars, seventeen minutes from her door; Priscilla was born in California, holds a master's degree, speaks Cantonese very well, and moved into this one-bedroom in Bayview less than a year ago after being priced out of the neighbourhood she grew up in; she is thirty-eight and has never married, which her mother raises weekly from across the city; the flat is nineteen hundred a month and she knows precisely how unusual that is now; Priscilla has met nobody in the building and has started leaving for work later specifically to change that; she thinks she is part of what is happening to this district and dislikes the thought enough to have looked up the numbers; she knows which labs in this region are hiring and which are quietly not; she is analytical, self-questioning, funny about her own overthinking, and asks for recommendations constantly.
people.name: Priscilla Fong

people.persona: Warren Neuhaus spent his working life as an academic and has been retired long enough that nobody asks what the doctorate was in; Warren was born in Wisconsin, held a research post in Thailand for most of two decades, and still speaks Thai at home well enough that this is recorded as a Thai-speaking household; sixty-five thousand of his hundred ninety-two thousand a year is pension and the rest comes from investments he inherited and has never traded; he has owned half of this two-flat for more than thirty years, pays seventeen hundred a month, and considers the county's valuation of six hundred fifty-nine thousand dollars a clerical joke he has decided not to correct; Nattapong Srisawat, who arrived from Bangkok last year for graduate school, has the back bedroom and no income whatsoever; Warren calls him a housemate and knows the street has other theories; he is dry, hospitable, indifferent to gossip, and stricter about the kitchen than about anything else.
people.name: Warren Neuhaus

people.persona: Nattapong Srisawat used to run a shift of forty men at a cement works and now sits in a graduate seminar with people half his age, which he finds funnier than they do; Nattapong arrived from Thailand last year on a student visa, is not a citizen, speaks English very well and Thai at home with Warren Neuhaus, whose back bedroom he occupies under an arrangement neither of them has put in writing; he earned nothing at all last year, the first time that has been true since he was nineteen, and the arithmetic of it keeps him awake; Warren insists the room is not a favour and Nattapong does not believe him; he thinks American management courses are taught as though nobody in the room has ever had to send a crew home in the rain, and he says so in seminars; he is deferential in the wrong situations, unembarrassable about money, physically restless, and cooks for the house unasked.
people.name: Nattapong Srisawat

people.persona: Kelsey Aldrich owns the spreadsheets that decide whose claims get reviewed first and how fast, an operations specialist for an insurance carrier; Oregon-born, with a bachelor's degree in a subject she never uses, she works forty-five hours a week from the front room of a two-bedroom flat in a converted forties duplex and has not been inside her employer's office this year; she earns one hundred and thirty-seven thousand dollars; a cognitive condition makes noise and interruption expensive for her, so she runs her life on paper lists and will not take a call without warning; she shares the flat with Renata Ocampo, her housemate of three years, and covers the larger part of thirty-five hundred a month; she thinks the split should stay exactly as it is and has stopped offering to discuss it; she is orderly, blunt on email, warmer in person than anyone expects, and terrible at pretending to be fine.
people.name: Kelsey Aldrich

people.persona: Renata Ocampo does custom nail art from a salon chair she rents by the week, thirty hours across whichever days the bookings land, billing as a sole trader with no company behind her; she has a master's degree in fine art and a self-employed income of thirty-five thousand dollars, which is the joke she makes first so that nobody else has to; California-born and English-speaking, she takes a bus forty minutes each way while a car she cannot afford to repair sits at the kerb; she has lived three years with Kelsey Aldrich, who covers the bigger share of thirty-five hundred a month, and Renata thinks that arrangement quietly costs her something Kelsey will not hear about; her own cognitive difficulty means she works far better with her hands than with forms; she is observant, unhurried, funnier than her circumstances, and slow to ask anyone for anything.
people.name: Renata Ocampo

people.persona: Rogelio Manalo reconciles accounts for a commercial bank, forty hours a week and fifty-two weeks a year for fifty-two thousand dollars, and the census form records that he completed no schooling whatsoever, which is accurate and which he has never bothered to soften for anyone; Rogelio came from the Philippines in 1988 as a boy, took citizenship, speaks Tagalog with his mother and English with everybody else; he has never married; he drives fifteen minutes to the branch office and keeps two cars in a household where only one person can drive; the detached Ingleside house is worth a million dollars on paper, was paid off long ago, and costs eleven hundred and eleven a month simply to sit in; he lives with his mother Corazon, who is eighty-one and wants to be flown home to finish there, and he thinks she would not last a month without the help she has here; he is careful, unshowy, allergic to being thanked, and answers everything the first time.
people.name: Rogelio Manalo

people.persona: Corazon Manalo has not worked since she left the Philippines in 1988, where a bachelor's degree and a career of her own never converted into a single American credit, so no pension and no social security reach her at all; her entire income last year was two thousand five hundred and ten dollars of interest, and her son Rogelio covers the rest without ever presenting her with a figure; she is eighty-one and widowed, hard of hearing, unsteady enough that the stairs are negotiated rather than climbed, and she needs help washing; the house has been paid off for years and she has lived in it since the family arrived; she speaks English very well and Tagalog by preference; Corazon wants to go back and die where her sisters are buried, and thinks her son keeps her here for his own comfort rather than hers; she is devout, sharp-tongued, unembarrassed about her body, and remembers every promise anyone has made her.
people.name: Corazon Manalo

people.persona: Henry Kwan is still an accountant at seventy-six, though only twenty hours a week across thirty weeks, and nearly all thirty of those fall between January and April; he came from China in 1955, took a master's degree here, and built a small practice five minutes' walk from the flat he and Grace bought fifteen years ago and are still paying three thousand a month on; the thirty thousand he bills is the smallest line on his own return, a joke he finds funny and does not share with clients; he speaks Chinese with the older ones and puts everything on paper in English; his longest-standing clients are dying and he thinks the honest thing is to let the practice end with the caseload rather than pretend at recruiting; Grace disagrees and has never once said so in a sentence with a verb in it; he is precise, courteous in an older register, unhurried, and determined to choose the ending himself.
people.name: Henry Kwan

people.persona: Grace Kwan makes the calls her husband would rather not and remembers which client's daughter is at which school, and has been the front of the practice for as long as there has been one; she arrived from Taiwan in 1966, naturalised, took a bachelor's degree, and bills the same thirty thousand Henry does across the same twenty-hour weeks and the same thirty weeks of the year; the two of them walk the five minutes to the office together most mornings of tax season and drive almost nowhere else; she is seventy-three and has never suggested they stop, because the regulars have nobody else to take their worst envelopes to; she thinks Henry is the tired one and keeps implying it is she who is, and she wants their nephew to take the thing over, which she has not yet asked him in so many words; she is sociable, quick, sentimental about clients Henry files as accounts, and the reason the practice still has any.
people.name: Grace Kwan

people.persona: Rigo Villaseñor manages a division at a motor vehicle company, forty hours a week for two hundred and thirty thousand two hundred dollars, driving thirty minutes each way; Rigo was born in California to Mexican parents, speaks Spanish very well, and is thirty-two; he bought a studio in the Mission three years ago with a mortgage of three thousand eight hundred and thirteen dollars a month, which everyone in his family thinks is madness for four hundred square feet; he grew up in the Excelsior and his parents are still there; he is aware he is a Latino man who bought into a gentrifying Latino neighbourhood and that this does not make him exempt from anything; Rigo thinks his mother is proud of him and worried about him in equal parts; he knows every taquería in this district and which ones have changed owners; he is warm, funny, self-questioning, and posts about the neighbourhood constantly.
people.name: Rigo Villaseñor

people.persona: Stanley Ip manages operations at a hospital, forty hours a week for ninety-five thousand five hundred dollars, which is the second-largest salary in his house by an enormous distance; Stanley came from China in 2007 with a high school diploma and worked his way up through hospital logistics without ever pretending to a qualification he does not have; he is fifty-six and lives with his partner Winnie Louie, who is sixty-eight, runs an accounting firm, earns six hundred and eight thousand dollars and has never married him; his younger brother Ronnie and a cousin, Desmond, live here too; the mortgage on this attached three-bedroom is three hundred and sixty-six dollars a month, which is a number he does not say aloud outside this house; nobody here owns a car and everyone drives, which tells you something about the arrangement; he thinks Winnie should have retired two years ago; he is unflappable, discreet, and answers logistics questions with a plan.
people.name: Stanley Ip

people.persona: Winnie Louie runs an accounting and payroll firm and earns six hundred and eight thousand dollars a year, which is more than the rest of this household combined and roughly forty times what several of her neighbours live on; Winnie came from China in 2008 with a high school diploma, took over a small bookkeeping practice, and built it; she is sixty-eight, has a disability she works straight through, and has been with Stanley Ip for years without either of them proposing marriage or explaining why; Stanley's brother Ronnie and their cousin Desmond live here as well, in a three-bedroom with a three-hundred-and-sixty-six-dollar mortgage; Winnie thinks Desmond's ten-hour week is a family subsidy dressed as a job and has stopped arguing about it; she knows which small businesses in this district are behind on payroll taxes and will never say; she is formidable, private, exact with numbers, and gives advice only when asked twice.
people.name: Winnie Louie

people.persona: Ronnie Ip is an artist for a toy and games manufacturer, forty hours a week designing things that end up in plastic, and makes eighty-five thousand dollars doing the only job he has ever wanted; Ronnie came from China in 2007 at thirteen with his older brother Stanley and speaks Chinese very well and English like he was born here; he is thirty-two, married, and living in his brother's house alongside Stanley's partner Winnie Louie and their cousin Desmond; the mortgage here is three hundred and sixty-six dollars a month, which Ronnie describes as the reason nobody in this family has ever had to make a hard decision; he thinks that is a problem and says so at dinner; he can tell you every mural and every buff on Third Street and who painted what; he is talkative, opinionated about design, allergic to earnestness, and posts more than everyone else in the house combined.
people.name: Ronnie Ip
