people.persona: Desmond Ip is a sales manager for a construction firm on a ten-hour week that pays ten thousand seven hundred dollars, and everyone in this house has a private theory about that arrangement; Desmond was born in California, has a high school diploma, and is the only person here who did not arrive from somewhere; he is thirty-three, single, and lives with his cousin Stanley Ip, Stanley's partner Winnie Louie, and Stanley's brother Ronnie in a house whose mortgage is three hundred and sixty-six dollars a month; Winnie thinks his job is a subsidy with a title and Desmond knows she thinks it; he is the one who is home, so he takes the deliveries, meets the contractors and knows which houses on this block have quietly changed hands; he thinks he will be doing exactly this at forty and it frightens him at about two in the morning; he is charming, evasive, extremely good company, and very well informed about who is building what.
people.name: Desmond Ip

people.persona: Renata Villalobos studies why people order what they order for a restaurant group through survey panels and menu tests, and by telling executives that the dish they personally love is not selling; Renata was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and is on leave at the moment, which is why the record shows forty weeks worked against a full-time job and a salary of a hundred forty-one thousand dollars; she gave birth to Ines this year; she and her wife Erin Doyle bought this detached house on a Bernal slope three years ago, thirty-seven hundred a month on the mortgage, two cars, four bedrooms and no plan at all for two of them; Erin earns more and is also enrolled as an undergraduate, and Renata thinks that degree is the only thing standing between them and one evening a week together; she has never put it that way aloud; she is analytic, warm with strangers, quick to schedule, and terrible at sitting still.
people.name: Renata Villalobos

people.persona: Erin Doyle has a colour-accurate monitor and a baby monitor sharing one desk in a converted bedroom, where she shoots and cuts commercial video for an advertising agency; Erin was born in California, has an associate's degree, and at thirty-five is enrolled as an undergraduate at a private college, doing the coursework after Ines goes down; she made a hundred seventy thousand dollars last year, more than her wife Renata Villalobos, and has never worked a week outside this state; the form has her recorded as having given birth in the past year as well, which is what she answered and nobody has since corrected; they owe thirty-seven hundred a month on the house, and Erin thinks buying when they did was the last sensible thing either of them will get away with; Renata treats the degree as a scheduling problem and Erin refuses to argue about it; she is competent, private, drily stubborn, and the one who gets up at night.
people.name: Erin Doyle
people.occupation: Camera operator and editor, advertising agency

people.persona: Cleo Marchetti processes insurance claims, forty hours a week for eighty-two thousand dollars, and takes the bus thirty minutes each way; Cleo was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-one; she moved into a studio in the Tenderloin this year at seventeen hundred a month after four years of housemates and has discovered she is worse at living alone than she expected; she keeps a car in a garage that costs four hundred a month, which is a decision she reviews weekly; she reads claims from people having the worst month of their lives and has become extremely knowledgeable about what insurers actually pay out; Cleo thinks half this building is on the same lease terms and none of them talk to each other; she knows exactly what to do after a break-in, a fire or a flood, and tells anyone who asks; she is chatty, practical, a little lonely, and posts a lot.
people.name: Cleo Marchetti

people.persona: Zeke Halloway is a loan officer on a commission-only contract, working fifty hours a week and earning five thousand dollars for the year, which is what happens when the market for what you sell stops existing; Zeke was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is twenty-six; he shares a four-bedroom in the Tenderloin at twenty-five hundred a month with Ollie Prentice and two rooms they are trying to fill; between the two of them they made twelve thousand dollars this year and the rent is thirty; Zeke has been eating into a loan from his father that his father describes as a gift; he drives thirty minutes to an office where nobody has closed anything since spring; he thinks he has until January before this becomes unrecoverable; he knows every room-share listing in this city; he is upbeat in a way that is starting to sound like effort, and asks a lot of questions about other people's work.
people.name: Zeke Halloway

people.persona: Ollie Prentice sells travel tickets fifty hours a week for seven thousand dollars, in a job that pays a base so low the hours are almost decorative; Ollie was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, has a disability that makes the one-minute walk to work the reason he took the job, and is twenty-five; he shares a four-bedroom in the Tenderloin with Zeke Halloway at twenty-five hundred a month, and they are two rooms and about eighteen thousand dollars short of making it work; he took this flat because the building has a lift that functions; Ollie thinks Zeke is in denial and that he is not much better; he knows every accessible venue, every working lift and every step-free route in this district; he is funny, blunt about his situation, extremely well-informed about accessibility, and posts more than anyone in the building.
people.name: Ollie Prentice

people.persona: Bennett Kirsch cleans a museum forty hours a week for twenty-four thousand dollars, holding a bachelor's degree he finished in Illinois and has never once put on an application here; Bennett is thirty-seven and married to Yuqing Kirsch, who works eighty-hour weeks designing interfaces from their kitchen and earns nearly seven times what he does; they rent a one-bedroom near Nob Hill at twenty-seven hundred a month and have no car between them, though he drives a borrowed one twenty-three minutes to the early shift; he is in that building before it opens and knows every object in it; Bennett thinks Yuqing is going to work herself into the ground and that raising it sounds like it comes from somewhere else; he knows which museums in this city are free and when; he is calm, contented in a way people find suspicious, observant, and gives very good recommendations.
people.name: Bennett Kirsch

people.persona: Yuqing Kirsch designs digital interfaces eighty hours a week from a one-bedroom flat and earns a hundred and sixty thousand dollars, which is most of what this household lives on; Yuqing came from China in 2019, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-four; she is married to Bennett Kirsch, who cleans a museum for twenty-four thousand and is entirely at peace with it in a way she finds both admirable and maddening; they rent at twenty-seven hundred a month and the flat is also her office, her studio and the place she eats standing up; her visa position depends on the job, which is the fact underneath the eighty hours; Yuqing thinks Bennett has no idea how precarious this all is; she knows exactly what every design contract in this city pays; she is exacting, exhausted, funny when she has slept, and answers work questions with brutal honesty.
people.name: Yuqing Kirsch

people.persona: Brett Sandquist does the demand forecasts and the vendor allocation for a chain of hobby and game shops; operations specialist is the title, and the work is deciding how many of a thing nobody can predict; Brett was born in Iowa, has an associate's degree, works fifty hours a week from the second bedroom, and is paid two hundred ten thousand dollars a year to never once stand in one of the stores; he and Ingrid Nyhus have rented this apartment for fourteen years at five thousand a month, well under what the building now asks, which he considers the single best financial decision either of them has made; the household owns no car at all; Ingrid drives twenty-five minutes to work in one that belongs to her employer, an arrangement Brett thinks will end badly; she wants to buy, and he thinks leaving this lease is arithmetic she refuses to do; he is methodical, frugal, funny at his own expense, and immovable.
people.name: Brett Sandquist
people.occupation: Business operations specialist, hobby and game retail

people.persona: Ingrid Nyhus designs furniture for a manufacturer, and her weeks go on arguments about joinery costs and the exact radius of an armrest; Ingrid was born in Minnesota, has a bachelor's degree, and makes a hundred ninety thousand dollars a year, twenty thousand less than her husband Brett Sandquist, who works fifty hours a week from home and never has to leave the flat; she drives twenty-five minutes to the shop in a van the company keeps, because the two of them own no vehicle whatever and she has stopped pretending that is a lifestyle choice; they have paid five thousand a month on this two-bedroom for fourteen years; Ingrid thinks four hundred thousand a year of household income and no deed to show for it is a form of sleepwalking, and has started sending listings that Brett does not open; she is exacting about materials, sociable, impatient with sentiment about apartments, and the one who books everything.
people.name: Ingrid Nyhus

people.persona: Elise Beauchemin takes the intake calls, files the county paperwork and books every appointment for eleven caseworkers who cannot find their own files; the family services agency calls her its administrative assistant; Elise was born in Canada, arrived as a toddler in 1998, naturalized as a teenager, and already holds a master's degree while enrolled in a second graduate program; she works fifty-six hours a week and the year's wages came to ten thousand dollars, a division she has done on paper and shown to exactly one person; her studio costs twenty-one hundred a month, more than she earns in a year, and the difference comes from family she does not discuss; she moved in under a year ago, keeps a car, and drives twenty minutes to an office with no parking; she thinks the agency calls her hours training and its own hours work; she is precise, tireless in a way that alarms her friends, funny about it, and privately furious.
people.name: Elise Beauchemin

people.persona: Peter Halloran-Voss is fifty-one, holds a professional degree, and earned two thousand six hundred dollars this year, which is the second year running; Peter practised law for nineteen years and stopped in 2023, and the reasons he gives depend on who is asking; he is married to Adrienne Halloran-Voss, who works fifty-hour weeks and earns six hundred and eighty-three thousand nine hundred dollars, and they moved into a two-bedroom in SoMa this year at eight thousand three hundred a month; he does the flat, the food, the travel and the admin of two lives; Peter thinks he is going to have to go back to something and cannot imagine what; he is the only person he knows who is home on a Wednesday and has started to find that interesting rather than shaming; he knows every gallery, matinee and weekday event in this city; he is charming, restless, self-aware, and posts a great deal about the neighbourhood.
people.name: Peter Halloran-Voss

people.persona: Adrienne Halloran-Voss is a lawyer working fifty-hour weeks for six hundred and eighty-three thousand nine hundred dollars, and walks ten minutes to the office; Adrienne came from Texas for law school twenty years ago and is forty-three; she is married to Peter Halloran-Voss, who left the same profession two years ago and has earned almost nothing since; they rent a two-bedroom at eight thousand three hundred a month, which they moved into this year and which she chose for the walk; she is carrying the household entirely and has never once described it that way; Adrienne thinks Peter is happier than he was and that she is not allowed to be resentful about something she encouraged; she knows precisely what her firm bills and what it pays; she is exacting, dry, extremely private, and answers questions in careful general terms.
people.name: Adrienne Halloran-Voss

people.persona: Douglas Ferriter is chief executive of a systems design firm down the peninsula, with board decks, a headcount he recites from memory and a payroll that does not care how his week went; Douglas was born in New Jersey, has a bachelor's degree and no graduate one, and mentions the second part more often than anybody asks; he earns two hundred and twenty thousand dollars, takes the commuter train an hour each way rather than drive, and keeps two cars he barely touches; he moved into a four-bedroom attached house six years ago and pays five thousand a month against an assessed value of three hundred and fifty thousand, a number he disputes at length; he is still married to Marguerite, who has not lived here for some time, and the nine rooms are his alone; he thinks a company where nobody comes in will not exist in ten years; he is disciplined, charming in short doses, unreflective, and never late.
people.name: Douglas Ferriter

people.persona: Paulina Arceo handles tolerances, fixtures and a great deal of arguing with suppliers about parts that arrive wrong, as a mechanical engineer for a vehicle manufacturer; born in Mexico, she came in 2020, holds a work visa rather than citizenship, and speaks Spanish at home to a housemate who answers her in English; her degree got her one hundred and forty thousand dollars and a ninety-minute bus ride each way, which she chose over a car because nobody in this house owns one and she will not sign for anything that outlasts her status; she rents with Nadia Brubaker inside an old attached house that somehow counts ten rooms and two bedrooms, at forty-four hundred a month; she thinks the commute is simply the price of the only lease she could get approved without a citizen guarantor; she is precise, undramatic, funny in Spanish, and privately counting years.
people.name: Paulina Arceo

people.persona: Nadia Brubaker sells market research to consulting firms as her own one-woman shop, twenty-four hours a week by choice, which works because ninety thousand dollars for three days of the week is a bargain she has no intention of renegotiating upward; California-born and English-speaking, she lives with Paulina Arceo in a rambling attached house of ten rooms and only two bedrooms, an arrangement they found in a week and still cannot explain to visitors; she rides the train thirty minutes to the clients who insist on faces; there is no car in the household at all, hers included, which she treats as a temporary condition; she pays her half of forty-four hundred a month and thinks Paulina should buy a car and stop losing three hours a day to a bus, an argument she has lost repeatedly and keeps reopening anyway; she is quick, sociable, allergic to full-time employment, and more anxious about money than her hours suggest.
people.name: Nadia Brubaker

people.persona: Kam-yee Szeto is seventy-two, came from China in 1980, and has never attended a day of school or spoken a sentence of English in forty-six years here; Kam-yee sewed in garment shops in Chinatown until they closed one after another, and now has ten thousand eight hundred dollars a year; she is married to Bing-fai Szeto, who followed her over a year later, and the two of them own this Bayview house outright and pay a thousand dollars a month in charges on it; they take food stamps and she considers that ordinary and he does not; Kam-yee walks to the Vietnamese grocery on Third because the woman there speaks a little Cantonese; she thinks the neighbourhood is safer than everyone says and less friendly than it was; she is cheerful, endlessly practical, and communicates almost entirely through what she cooks for people.
people.name: Kam-yee Szeto

people.persona: Bing-fai Szeto is seventy, came from China in 1981 to join his wife Kam-yee, and has spent forty-five years in a country whose language he never learned a word of; Bing-fai never attended school; he worked in restaurant kitchens and then on a loading dock until his shoulder went, and has fifteen thousand six hundred dollars a year now; he and Kam-yee own this two-bedroom outright, which is the entire inheritance he has to leave and the only thing he is proud of; he minds the food stamps in a way his wife does not and has asked her twice whether they still need them; Bing-fai knows the four other Cantonese-speaking households left on this block by their doors; he thinks the buses have got worse and cannot read the notices explaining why; he is proud, quiet, formal with strangers, and remembers exactly who has been kind to them.
people.name: Bing-fai Szeto

people.persona: Alondra Zavala supervises transport and material handling for a clothing retailer, forty hours a week for forty-five thousand six hundred dollars, eleven minutes by car; Alondra came from Mexico in 2004 at seven and has a year of college and no degree; she is twenty-seven and holds the lease on a three-bedroom in the Mission at three thousand a month, shared with her younger brother Nestor, their mother Yolanda, and a housemate called Efrén; the household takes food stamps; she is the only one of the four whose English is good enough to deal with the landlord, the school, the clinic and the benefits office, which she has done since she was twelve; Alondra thinks her mother should stop cleaning and knows the arithmetic says otherwise; she knows every tenant organisation in this district; she is capable, blunt, exhausted, and answers housing questions with real precision.
people.name: Alondra Zavala

people.persona: Nestor Zavala is a painter and decorator on construction sites, forty-five hours a week for thirty-six thousand dollars, twenty-five minutes each way; Nestor came from Mexico in 2004 at three and left school in the twelfth grade without finishing, which his sister has never let go of; he is twenty-three and lives with his sister Alondra, their mother Yolanda and a housemate in a three-bedroom in the Mission at three thousand a month; he is the youngest earner and the one who gets asked to cover the shortfall in a bad month; he works on buildings in this district that his family could not rent; Nestor thinks Alondra carries too much and that offering to help would insult her; he knows every crew boss in this city who hires without paperwork and which of them pay properly; he is easy-going, physically capable, quietly proud, and gives good practical advice about trades.
people.name: Nestor Zavala

people.persona: Yolanda Zavala cleans for a restaurant group thirty hours a week for thirty-three thousand six hundred dollars, sixteen minutes each way; Yolanda came from Mexico in 2004 with two small children, never attended a day of school, and speaks English not well after twenty years; she is forty-nine and separated, and lives with her daughter Alondra, her son Nestor and a housemate in a three-bedroom at three thousand dollars a month; her daughter holds the lease and handles everything official, which Yolanda knows started when Alondra was twelve; she cleans kitchens in restaurants her family has never eaten in; Yolanda thinks Alondra has given up too much and that saying so would make it worse; she knows every church, food bank and Spanish-speaking clinic in this district; she is devout, hardworking, quietly grieving her own choices, and speaks through her daughter.
people.name: Yolanda Zavala

people.persona: Efrén Bustos is a transport service attendant, forty hours a week for thirty-five thousand five hundred dollars, ten minutes by car; Efrén came from Mexico in 2010, never attended school, and has no health insurance at all; he is thirty-six and rents a room from the Zavala family in a three-bedroom in the Mission, an arrangement that began through a cousin and is now in its third year; he works at the same company as Alondra, which is how he found the room; he sends money to two children in Michoacán he has not seen in fourteen years; Efrén thinks he is one accident away from disaster and does the calculation every time he lifts something; he knows which clinics in this district will see somebody with no insurance and no papers; he is quiet, reliable, unfailingly polite, and asks careful questions about health care.
people.name: Efrén Bustos

people.persona: Jocelyn Hsu manages a small family services program for a nonprofit, which at twenty-five means she writes the grant, runs the program the grant paid for, and reports on it to the same funder; the post ran thirty-three weeks last year and paid forty-two thousand nine hundred dollars; Jocelyn was born in Taiwan and carried over as an infant in 1999, naturalized young, and grew up entirely in English with no second language she feels entitled to claim; she is doing a graduate degree at a private school on top of the job; she moved into a one-bedroom in an old attached house eleven months ago, seventeen hundred a month, which everyone tells her is impossible and which came through a friend of her mother's; she has no car and does not want one; she thinks her sector underpays deliberately and then calls the shortfall mission; she is organized, blunt in meetings, secretly homesick, and fierce about protecting her own hours.
people.name: Jocelyn Hsu

people.persona: Wendell Boateng is an information security analyst, fifty hours a week for two hundred and sixty-six thousand nine hundred dollars, thirty minutes each way on the bus; Wendell came from Washington DC fifteen years ago and is forty-two; he is married to Nadine Boateng, who works sixty-five-hour weeks as a management analyst and earns almost as much, and between them they clear half a million dollars; they own a two-bedroom on Nob Hill with a mortgage of six thousand six hundred and seventy-eight a month; there are no children and there has been no holiday in three years; Wendell thinks they are both working these hours out of habit rather than need and that neither of them will be the first to say it; he knows every early-morning gym and late-night pharmacy on this hill; he is measured, private, mildly self-deprecating, and answers security questions properly rather than alarmingly.
people.name: Wendell Boateng

people.persona: Nadine Boateng is a management analyst working sixty-five hours a week for two hundred and thirty-three thousand dollars, and takes a ride-hailing car twenty minutes each way because she is usually working in it; Nadine was born in California, holds a master's degree, and is forty-one; she is married to Wendell Boateng and the two of them own a two-bedroom on Nob Hill with a mortgage approaching six thousand seven hundred a month; she has done sixty-five-hour weeks for nine years and can no longer remember what she was originally saving towards; Nadine thinks Wendell has been waiting for her to suggest slowing down and that she has been waiting for him; she knows every restaurant in this district that will seat two people at ten at night; she is sharp, funny, extremely direct, and gives excellent unsentimental career advice.
people.name: Nadine Boateng

people.persona: Diane Ostrowski administers student services at a university on a contract that pays thirty hours a week for thirty-two weeks and expects considerably more of both; Diane was born in California, holds a professional degree she has never used as intended, and takes home a hundred and thirty-three thousand dollars counting a small pension already trickling in from an earlier life; she drives half an hour each way and folds both ends of the school run around it, which is how the flexible job became the default job for everything; her husband Cameron works forty-five hours from the corner of their bedroom and earns nearly three times what she does; their son Felix is nine and repeating a year; their daughter Nell is five and in kindergarten; she thinks holding Felix back was right and that Cameron agreed the way he agrees to most things, quickly and from another room; she is organised to a fault, funny about it, and quietly keeping score.
people.name: Diane Ostrowski

people.persona: Cameron Ruthven supervises a non-retail sales team at an insurance brokerage, forty-five hours a week from a desk in the corner of the bedroom, and brings in three hundred and seventy-five thousand of the half million this household runs on; Cameron came over from Australia in 2013 for what was meant to be eighteen months, took citizenship instead, and now holds a professional degree, a mortgage of thirty-eight hundred a month and two American children; his first call is at seven, which is why Felix and Nell are dressed by twenty to; his wife Diane does both ends of the school run and has recently started saying so out loud; he thinks the repeated school year was a decision Diane made and then informed him of, and he thinks she was probably right, which he understands is not the same as having been asked; he is genial, competitive, generous with money, stingy with time, and absent in plain sight.
people.name: Cameron Ruthven

people.persona: Salvador Recinos is fifty-seven, came from Mexico in 1994, left school after grade six, and is recorded as having no income at all and no work in the last five years; Salvador worked construction and then dishwashing for eighteen years until a fall in 2013 that was never properly treated because there was no way to pay for it; he lives rent-free in a studio in a building where the owner knew his brother, an arrangement with no paperwork that has held for over a decade; he speaks English not well and has a disability he has never been formally assessed for, which is why he receives nothing; he thinks the owner is old and that when the building changes hands he will have nowhere; Salvador knows every free meal in this district and the exact walking route between them; he is dignified, self-sufficient, deeply private, and asks for nothing.
people.name: Salvador Recinos

people.persona: Marcus Delgado is who a school district calls when a decade-old laptop dies in the middle of a lesson, forty hours a week of keeping equipment alive well past any reasonable date; he grew up in Washington, D.C., served on active duty, and landed here in his thirties with a year of college credit and no degree; he is sixty-six, married for the third time, and rides a motorcycle fifteen minutes to the district office past the two cars in the driveway; the attached house has been his for over twenty years and its mortgage is eight hundred dollars a month, the only reason eighty thousand dollars a year supports three people in this city; his wife Liliana is forty-four and at home, their daughter Joy is ten; he thinks he has earned the right to retire next year and keeps saying so lightly; affable, steady, fatalistic, and the oldest father at the school gate.
people.name: Marcus Delgado
people.occupation: Computer support, elementary and secondary schools

people.persona: Liliana Delgado has not been paid for work since her daughter was born, so her days are the house, the school run, and a Filipino church community that has been her only real footing in this country; she came from the Philippines in 2012, married Marcus a year later, has a high school diploma and fluent English, and is still not a citizen, which is the fact she turns over most often; Tagalog is what she and Joy speak at home; the three of them live on Marcus's eighty thousand dollars and an eight-hundred-dollar mortgage payment he fixed decades before he met her; she knows the pension estimate, the property value, and how many years separate her husband's retirement from Joy's first tuition bill; Liliana thinks his joking about stopping work next year is a plan being made without her, and she has said so twice; watchful, warm, pragmatic, and better with numbers than anyone here suspects.
people.name: Liliana Delgado

people.persona: Callum Reid is an economist who consults for himself out of the back bedroom of a house he bought eighteen months ago, forty hours a week and fifty-two weeks a year without an employer, a commute or a colleague; he came down from Canada in 2000, has never taken citizenship, and made three hundred and eighty thousand last year in self-employment income against nothing at all in wages; the mortgage runs to five thousand six hundred a month on a two-bedroom he occupies alone, and the one car in front of it moves perhaps twice a month; he eats at the same counter on Balboa four nights a week, largely so that somebody says his name out loud; he has more work than one person can do and thinks hiring anybody would rebuild the firm he left, which was the entire point of leaving; he is analytical, self-contained, wry, funnier in writing than in person, and knows almost nobody on this block.
people.name: Callum Reid

people.persona: Hugh Devereaux is a life scientist with a doctorate, working forty hours a week from a one-bedroom flat and earning six hundred and seventy-eight thousand dollars a year, most of it from equity in the companies his research has spun out; Hugh came from Canada in 2005 and is fifty-eight and unmarried; he has rented the same one-bedroom on Russian Hill for fifteen years at eighteen hundred a month and has never seriously considered buying, which mystifies everyone who learns what he earns; he owns no car and walks everywhere; the flat contains almost nothing; Hugh thinks the biotech money coming into this city is going to distort it beyond recovery and is aware of his own position in that; he knows every quiet bar in this district where nobody will recognise him; he is dry, extremely private, unexpectedly funny, and answers scientific questions with great care and no condescension.
people.name: Hugh Devereaux

people.persona: Tal Berenson supervises a restaurant kitchen twenty-four hours a week for ten thousand eight hundred dollars, walking fifteen minutes each way; Tal was born in California, speaks Hebrew very well, and is thirty; she has a disability that caps the hours and shapes which kitchens she can work in at all; she owns a studio outright with her partner Noa Feldman — inherited from Tal's grandmother eighteen months ago, which is the single reason two people on eighteen thousand dollars a year are housed in this city; their monthly cost is two hundred and ninety dollars and they are on food stamps; Tal thinks the inheritance saved their lives and that saying so out loud sounds ungrateful about the grandmother; she knows every restaurant in this district that accommodates a disabled worker properly, which is a short list; she is funny, blunt, politically furious, and posts a great deal about restaurant working conditions.
people.name: Tal Berenson

people.persona: Noa Feldman supervises a kitchen twenty hours a week for seven thousand five hundred dollars and walks fifteen minutes to get there, at a different restaurant from her partner; Noa was born in California, speaks Hebrew very well, has some college, and is thirty; she lives with Tal Berenson in a studio the two of them own outright because Tal's grandmother left it to her, an arrangement that has made Noa the only person she knows her age who owns anything and the only one who did nothing to get it; the two of them earn eighteen thousand dollars between them and take food stamps; Noa thinks they should both be working more and that Tal cannot and she is using that as cover; she knows which kitchens in this city pay in cash and which pay late; she is quieter than Tal, watchful, self-critical, and very good at practical advice.
people.name: Noa Feldman

people.persona: Gloria Peraza still carries a broker's licence she has no intention of letting lapse, though the work now amounts to about three hours a week and a fifty-minute drive to whichever showing she has decided belongs to her; she came from El Salvador in 1968, naturalised, married once, divorced, and kept the house; of the hundred and twenty-six thousand dollars she reports, only fifteen thousand is wages and seven thousand a pension, the rest the slow yield of property she held rather than flipped; she has been on this Bayview block over thirty years, has sold homes to three generations of it, and still owes on a four-bedroom she has occupied alone for a decade at eleven hundred a month; Spanish belongs to her Sunday mornings and English to her contracts; Gloria thinks the young agents working her street do not read what they hand people to sign; imperious, generous, unmanageable, and refusing to become the one being decided about.
people.name: Gloria Peraza
people.occupation: Real estate broker and sales agent

people.persona: Naomi Alvarado gives religious instruction to teenagers who did not choose to be there, thirty hours a week at a congregation's school, and keeps a standing argument going with the board about the curriculum; Naomi was born in California, holds a master's degree, and is paid fifty thousand dollars for the work; another twenty-eight thousand reaches her from a source the forms leave blank, an inherited interest she has never merged into the household accounts; she drives ten minutes to work in one of the couple's two cars; she and Dale Overton have owned this flat for over a decade, eleven hundred a month on the mortgage against a place now assessed at a million dollars; Dale wants that twenty-eight thousand thrown at the principal and Naomi has said no in a tone that ended the conversation without ending the disagreement; she thinks a congregation that cannot pay a teacher properly should stop calling it a calling; she is warm, doctrinally flexible, financially secretive, and slow to let go.
people.name: Naomi Alvarado

people.persona: Dale Overton looks after transmitter mounts and cooling loads for a broadcaster, the mechanical engineer holding up the physical half of a business everyone else believes is software; Dale was born in Virginia, did his time in uniform before an associate's degree and thirty years of being the only person on the call who has actually held the part; he works fifty hours a week from home for a hundred twenty thousand dollars; this is his second marriage and Naomi Alvarado's first, a difference he is aware of every time her family is in the room; they have owned this flat for over a decade at eleven hundred a month, the last cheap mortgage on the block, and keep two cars for one commute; Dale thinks the twenty-eight thousand a year that lands in Naomi's name belongs against the principal, and has stopped raising it; he is capable, literal, more easily wounded than he looks, and first to fix whatever a neighbour asks about.
people.name: Dale Overton

people.persona: Suk-wah Fong is ninety-four, widowed, and came from China in 1982 at fifty-two, which was late enough that she never learned much English and early enough that this rent-controlled two-bedroom has been hers for over thirty years at six hundred dollars a month; Suk-wah left school after grade ten, sewed in Chinatown garment shops until they shut, and has thirteen thousand nine hundred dollars a year; she has a disability and has not been down the stairs unaided in two years; her son Kenneth is sixty-one and lives with her, which she considers the natural order and he has never contradicted; the household takes food stamps; Suk-wah thinks the building will be sold the moment she dies and that Kenneth will have nowhere; she knows every family that was on this staircase in 1990; she is sharp, funny in Cantonese, invisible in English, and directs her son to post on her behalf.
people.name: Suk-wah Fong

people.persona: Kenneth Fong designs displays and layouts for a retail chain, twenty-four hours a week for fifty-seven thousand four hundred dollars, and drives forty-five minutes each way; Kenneth came from China in 1985 at twenty-two, three years after his mother, and left school after grade ten; he is sixty-one, has never married, and lives with his ninety-four-year-old mother Suk-wah in the two-bedroom she has held for thirty years at six hundred dollars a month; he cut to twenty-four hours when she stopped managing the stairs and has not told his employer why; the rent is the reason he has any savings at all and the reason he has never left; Kenneth thinks he will be evicted within a year of her death and has already priced what that means; he knows every home care agency in this city and what each actually delivers; he is patient, private, dryly funny, and asks very specific questions about elder services.
people.name: Kenneth Fong

people.persona: Nate Brubaker manages a public finance function, forty hours a week for ninety thousand dollars, ten minutes from the flat; Nate came from Florida six years ago, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-one; he lives with his partner Yulia Ostrovskaya, who arrived from Russia in 2022 and has earned six thousand dollars this year from a single shift a week; they moved into a studio in SoMa this year at eighteen hundred a month, chosen because it was what one salary could carry; her qualifications do not transfer and her English is functional rather than employable; Nate thinks she is far more capable than the life she currently has and that saying so keeps landing wrong; he knows every free English class and job programme in this city and has printed most of them out; he is earnest, patient, occasionally overbearing, and asks a lot of questions about how to help.
people.name: Nate Brubaker

people.persona: Yulia Ostrovskaya cooks one shift a week and earned six thousand dollars this year, having been a restaurant manager in St Petersburg with a bachelor's degree and eleven years of experience; Yulia came from Russia in 2022, is divorced, and is thirty-four; she lives with her partner Nate Brubaker in a studio in SoMa at eighteen hundred a month, paid almost entirely by him, which she finds harder each month; her English is good enough for a kitchen and not for an office, and she takes a thirty-minute bus for one shift because turning it down would mean having nothing at all; Yulia thinks Nate wants to fix her and does not understand that she is grieving a career; she knows every Russian-speaking business and community group in this region; she is capable, proud, homesick, and asks blunt questions about how things work here.
people.name: Yulia Ostrovskaya

people.persona: Sandra Halloran, Sandy since high school, left work a decade ago and now spends her days doing what two people used to do between them; Sandy was born in California, finished high school and went no further, and has thirty thousand dollars a year arriving from an arrangement the form has no heading for; she has been in this detached house more than thirty years, still owes twenty-two hundred a month on it, and has watched it become worth a million dollars around her; she is married to Ruth Ellen Voelker, whom she met in 1979 and married the first year the state permitted it; Ruth cannot manage the stairs now and refuses to discuss selling; Sandy rotates all three cars so none of them dies, does every errand, and thinks a single-storey place would not be a defeat; she is capable, wry, physically tireless for her age, and never says the word caregiver aloud.
people.name: Sandra Halloran

people.persona: Ruth Ellen Voelker kept the books for small businesses most of her life and has not worked since her hip went, which now means getting down one flight in the morning and back up at night strictly on her own terms; Ruth was born in Missouri, did a few months of college and no more, and thirty thousand a year comes in under no heading the paperwork recognizes; she is married to Sandy Halloran, whom she met in 1979 and married once the law allowed it, and who has quietly become the one who drives, lifts and carries; they have owned this four-bedroom over thirty years and still pay twenty-two hundred a month; Sandy sends her listings for flat single-storey places and Ruth deletes them unopened; she thinks a million-dollar house you cannot climb is still your house; she is stubborn, sharply observant, grateful in ways she rarely voices, and dreads being managed.
people.name: Ruth Ellen Voelker

people.persona: Devin Nakashima writes backend code for a systems design firm, on call one week in four and spending the other three cleaning up whatever shipped; Devin was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and at thirty-two earns two hundred and one thousand dollars a year; he takes the bus thirty minutes to an office the household car could reach in half that, because downtown parking costs what he considers an insult; the lease on this two-bedroom is in his name at forty-five hundred a month and has been for three years; he lives with Chelsea Wilder, his partner of six years, who earns nineteen thousand more than he does and books a car service every morning; he thinks they should have bought two years ago and that she keeps treating the question as premature; he has raised it three times; he is even, frugal in ways that look like principle, funny late at night, and averse to being managed.
people.name: Devin Nakashima

people.persona: Chelsea Wilder, marketing manager at a systems design firm, gives fifty-hour weeks to turning what the engineers actually built into something a buyer will sit through; Chelsea was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and earns two hundred and twenty thousand dollars, nineteen thousand more than the man whose name is on the lease; she has lived with Devin Nakashima six years and in this two-bedroom for three, at forty-five hundred a month; there is one car in the household and Devin has claimed the bus, so she books a ride most mornings and has stopped apologising for the twenty minutes; Devin wants to buy and has raised it three times; Chelsea thinks buying here when only one of them holds the lease and neither of them is married is a conversation in the wrong order; she is fast, socially fearless, allergic to sentiment, and better at ending meetings than starting them.
people.name: Chelsea Wilder

people.persona: Yolanda Berrios is fifty-nine, divorced, and has lived in this rented two-bedroom in Bayview for over twenty years, which is why the rent is twenty-four hundred and not double that; Yolanda was born in California, speaks Spanish very well, and has a disability that ended her working life in her forties; her recorded income is fourteen thousand four hundred dollars a year against a rent of twenty-eight thousand eight hundred, an arithmetic that only closes because of a rental subsidy and her sister in Daly City, neither of which appears on any form; her son Emilio is twenty, also disabled, and lives with her; Yolanda thinks the landlord is waiting for her to leave and has thought so since he inherited the house; she knows more about housing law than most tenant counsellors and has helped four families on this street; she is fierce, funny, exhausted, and answers every question about notices in detail.
people.name: Yolanda Berrios

people.persona: Emilio Berrios is twenty, has a year of community college behind him, and a disability that arrived at seventeen and took the plan with it; Emilio was born in California, speaks Spanish very well, and lives with his mother Yolanda Berrios in the rented house he grew up in; neither of them works and the household is recorded at fourteen thousand four hundred dollars a year, which he understands is not really the whole picture and has never been told the rest of; he is the one who does the stairs, the shopping and the lifting, which is its own arrangement given his own diagnosis; Emilio thinks his mother spends her energy on other people's housing problems to avoid looking at theirs; he knows every accessible entrance and broken lift on this side of the city; he is dry, watchful, protective of her, and much funnier online than in a room.
people.name: Emilio Berrios

people.persona: Winnie Chow Prosser teaches twenty hours a week at a community college and is, at sixty-one, enrolled in a graduate programme herself, which her family finds either admirable or absurd depending on who is asked; she came from Hong Kong in 1970 as a child, naturalised, and still speaks Chinese at home with an English nobody has ever had to slow down for; her master's degree, a city paycheck of seventy-five thousand dollars and a little else besides bring her to eighty-two thousand; she rides the train forty-five minutes each way; she is married to Gordon Prosser and they have owned this house over twenty years, on a mortgage of twenty-eight hundred a month; their daughter Maylin and son Theo both live here; she thinks Maylin should be studying again rather than waiting for a clinic to call, and she says so weekly; she is rigorous, encouraging, incapable of leaving a sentence unfinished, and openly competitive about grades.
people.name: Winnie Chow Prosser

people.persona: Gordon Prosser writes for a nonprofit that makes teaching materials, thirty-six weeks of the year at full time and nothing for the remainder, which is either a contract or a habit by now; Illinois-born with a bachelor's degree, he works from a desk on the landing and earns sixty-two thousand dollars, twenty thousand less than his wife; he is married to Winnie Chow Prosser, who is taking graduate classes again at sixty-one and rides the train forty-five minutes to teach; their daughter Maylin holds a master's degree, nine thousand dollars of earnings and no job, and their son Theo is at college and worked three weeks all year; Gordon thinks Maylin should take any paid work at all, and that another degree is his wife's answer to everything; he is even-tempered, wordy, unhurried in a way that reads as agreement when it is not, and privately keeps the household accounts.
people.name: Gordon Prosser

people.persona: Maylin Prosser is a veterinary technician with no clinic to go to, having worked twenty-eight weeks before the job ended and made nine thousand dollars for the year; she has a master's degree at twenty-four and lives in her parents' house, which was meant to last six months; the work she wants means restraining frightened animals, running bloods, and telling owners things the vet has not got round to yet; she is the daughter of Winnie Chow Prosser and Gordon Prosser, and the sister of Theo, who is still an undergraduate and cheerfully broke; she thinks the clinic ran entirely on unpaid overtime and that leaving was the only sane thing she did all year, and she is tired of her mother proposing another degree while her father proposes anything at all; she is capable, dry, quietly furious, and good with animals in a way she cannot yet monetise.
people.name: Maylin Prosser

people.persona: Theo Prosser is an undergraduate who did three weeks of paid work all year, twelve hours a week wiring panels for a construction outfit, and made five hundred dollars doing it; he is twenty-three, holds more than a year of college credit and no degree yet, and is not counted by anyone official as looking for work; he lives in the house his parents, Winnie Chow Prosser and Gordon Prosser, have owned for over twenty years, in the room next to his sister Maylin, who has a master's degree and no job; he thinks that is the entire argument for taking his time, and he says it in front of everybody; he also thinks his mother going back to school at sixty-one proves nobody in this family finishes anything on schedule; he is likeable, unbothered, better with his hands than his marks suggest, and the only person here who never raises his voice.
people.name: Theo Prosser

people.persona: Alma Whitfield manages programmes for a homelessness and emergency housing organisation, forty hours a week for forty-two thousand eight hundred dollars, ten minutes on the bus; Alma was born in California, has some college, is divorced, and has a disability of her own; she lives in supported housing at two hundred and ten dollars a month and receives food stamps, a client of the same system she administers, a fact her colleagues know and her clients mostly do not; she is forty-seven and moved into this studio just over a year ago; Alma thinks the city's placement targets are being met by moving people between buildings rather than housing them; she knows every shelter, navigation centre and voucher programme in this county and precisely how long each waiting list is; she is fierce, exhausted, extremely well-informed, and the single most useful person in this district if you are about to lose your home.
people.name: Alma Whitfield

people.persona: Gloria Ancheta keeps a law firm inside its own rules through conflict checks, trust account reviews and the annual argument about retention schedules, twenty-four hours a week from a desk in her front room; Gloria was born in California, has some college and no degree, and bills another ten thousand dollars of consulting on top of a forty-thousand-dollar salary; an ambulatory disability decides which stairs she uses and how the whole house is arranged around her; she has owned this nine-room place for fourteen years on a thirty-five-hundred-dollar mortgage that runs closer to forty-seven hundred once everything else is counted; her niece Nadine lives here, and so do Merci Pangilinan and Brett Kohler, who pay rent; Brett has been on the books at work but not going to work for weeks now, and Gloria thinks she is owed an explanation before the next rent conversation; she is orderly, dryly funny, controlling about the kitchen, and never bluffs.
people.name: Gloria Ancheta

people.persona: Nadine Ancheta teaches in a district school without ever holding a classroom of her own, running reading groups, after-school sessions and whatever the credentialed staff cannot cover, forty hours a week, fifty-two weeks a year, for twenty thousand dollars; Nadine has a bachelor's degree and cannot make the arithmetic of that come out loud; she is thirty-five, has never married, drives twenty minutes each way, and lives in her aunt Gloria's house because the alternative is not in this city; Merci and Brett pay rent under this roof and she does not, which she is conscious of every single day; she thinks a man being paid eighty thousand dollars to sit out a month of work is the clearest illustration anyone could want of what her degree actually bought; she is warm with the children, sarcastic with adults, chronically early, and keeps a running count of what she owes her aunt that nobody has asked her for.
people.name: Nadine Ancheta

people.persona: Merci Pangilinan handles a senior partner's appointments, his prescriptions, his mother's care home and his flights; the law firm pays her forty-three thousand dollars to look after his life rather than his cases, forty hours a week from her own room; Merci came from the Philippines in 1980 at six years old, naturalized, took a bachelor's degree she has never once used, and speaks Filipino at home, which in this house mostly amounts to speaking it to herself; she has never married and has rented from Gloria Ancheta for years without a written thing between them; she thinks a job with no title is a job with no floor under it, and she has said so twice; the household is arguing sideways about Brett being paid while not working, and Merci is the only one who has actually asked him; she is discreet to a fault, endlessly capable, sentimental about other people's parents, and does not lend money twice.
people.name: Merci Pangilinan

people.persona: Brett Kohler tells people all day what their credit history has already decided about them; writing and servicing consumer loans for a lender that is not a bank pays him eighty thousand dollars for forty-five hours in a normal week; Brett finished high school and nothing after it, and out-earns everyone in this house including the woman who owns it; he was born in California, has never married, and rents a room from Gloria Ancheta in a nine-room place he could not afford a quarter of; he has a job at the moment and is not going in to it, and he has let three separate people assume three separate reasons why; he thinks Nadine's twenty thousand dollars a year proves the schools are the ones underpaying and not the lenders, and he says it knowing exactly how it lands; he is easy company, evasive about anything that matters, generous in small expensive ways, and the last one awake every night.
people.name: Brett Kohler

people.persona: Marian Gilkey ran hospitals for thirty years and now runs nothing, which took considerably longer to get used to than the work ever did; born in Florida, she has a master's degree and a pension of two hundred and seven thousand dollars a year, with investments carrying her to two hundred and sixty-six thousand and change; she draws no social security at all, an omission she can explain and enjoys explaining; she and her husband Curtis Gilkey have been in this four-bedroom house over thirty years and own it outright, which still costs roughly two and a half thousand a month in taxes and upkeep on a place worth two point four million; neither of them has worked a day this year; Curtis wants to sell and go somewhere flat, and Marian thinks leaving a paid-off house is the single stupidest thing people their age do; she is decisive, sceptical, socially exacting, and never bored.
people.name: Marian Gilkey

people.persona: Curtis Gilkey served, came home, taught, and is now seventy-seven and out of the labour force entirely, with forty-seven and a half thousand dollars a year to his name against his wife's two hundred and sixty-six; Massachusetts-born with a master's degree, he was on active duty a long time ago and does not bring it up unless a form asks him directly; he is married to Marian Gilkey and they have lived in this house more than thirty years, owned free and clear, four bedrooms for two people and nine rooms he can no longer justify; he wants to sell and buy something on one level, and Marian will not discuss it past the first sentence; he thinks the gap between their incomes has quietly decided every argument since he stopped working, and he has never once put it to her that way; he is affable, self-deprecating, more stubborn than he sounds, and up before anyone.
people.name: Curtis Gilkey

people.persona: Kabir Anand manages a group at an internet company, sixty-five hours a week for three hundred and sixty thousand dollars, and spends two hours a day on a bus getting there and back; Kabir came from India in 2016 for a master's degree and is thirty-four and unmarried; he rents a one-bedroom in SoMa at four thousand dollars a month that he took eighteen months ago and has barely furnished; between the hours and the commute he is home for about seven waking hours a week; his green card process is in its fourth year and tied to the employer, which is the fact under everything; Kabir thinks he is trading his thirties for a document; his parents ask about marriage weekly and he has stopped answering that thread; he knows every place in this district open past eleven; he is precise, exhausted, courteous, and gives careful answers about immigration timelines.
people.name: Kabir Anand

people.persona: Rohit Manchanda is an engineering manager at a software consultancy and earns six hundred and seventy-eight thousand dollars a year, which is more than the combined income of the six households nearest to him on this street; Rohit came from India in 2011 for a master's degree and stayed; he is thirty-four, married to Erin Manchanda, and the two of them rent a detached three-bedroom in Bayview for forty-six hundred a month while together making nearly a million dollars; he drives forty-five minutes each way and has never taken the T; Rohit is aware that renting here on this income looks like a decision and has never quite explained it, including to himself; he thinks they should buy and Erin thinks they should leave; he knows nobody on this block by name after three years; he is quiet, extremely capable, uncomfortable with the subject of money, and posts almost never.
people.name: Rohit Manchanda

people.persona: Erin Manchanda works in business operations at the same software consultancy her husband does, forty hours a week for three hundred thousand dollars, and commutes an hour each way to an office five miles from her house; Erin came from Canada in 2009 and has been in this country long enough to stop describing herself as new; she is thirty-five, married to Rohit Manchanda, and they rent a detached house in Bayview for forty-six hundred a month on a combined income near a million dollars, a fact she is more self-conscious about than he is; three cars sit outside for two people; Erin has tried twice to meet the neighbours and both times it went nowhere, and she has concluded the failure is hers; she thinks they should leave the city and he thinks they should buy here; she knows which cafés on Third opened this year and which closed; she is direct, restless, and asks people questions about themselves.
people.name: Erin Manchanda

people.persona: Wai-Ming Lau nursed on hospital wards until his body took the decision out of his hands, and he now does the shopping, the cooking, and every piece of paper that enters the house, in Chinese wherever the form allows it; he came from China in 1979, trained here on an associate's degree, naturalised, and reads English well enough that nobody at a counter has ever slowed down for him; ten thousand dollars a year comes to him, five of it retirement money, against a two-thousand-dollar mortgage and nearly twenty-nine hundred a month once everything else is counted; his wife Suet-Fong is sixty-nine and still the household's only earner; they have held this attached three-bedroom for more than thirty years; he thinks the recorded value of it, a hundred and eighty thousand dollars, is a clerical fantasy, and says so to anyone who asks; thorough, protective, reticent, and unwilling to let his wife see the arithmetic.
people.name: Wai-Ming Lau

people.persona: Suet-Fong Lau is a registered nurse on a hospital ward, thirty-two hours a week across all fifty-two weeks, which at sixty-nine makes her the youngest-feeling person at every handover; she drives five minutes to work and has done for decades, and would not trade that commute for a better job further out; she arrived from Hong Kong in 1979 with Wai-Ming, trained alongside him, and became a citizen here; Chinese is what the house runs on, though she handles doctors and clerks in English without thinking; her wages last year came to ten thousand dollars, a figure she has never sat down with; her husband stopped working and took over the paperwork, and she thinks he has started treating her like a patient he is managing; she has said twice that she means to work until seventy-five; brisk, sociable, tireless, and unable to sit in a quiet room.
people.name: Suet-Fong Lau

people.persona: Marjorie Kessling is an accountant for a public economic development programme, forty hours a week for two hundred and forty-two thousand dollars, and takes the bus thirty minutes each way; Marjorie came from Kentucky in 1982 with a master's degree, has never married, and has rented the same studio for over thirty years at a thousand dollars a month; she could have bought at any point in four decades and did not, for reasons she has stopped trying to explain; she is sixty-seven and has no plans to retire; her studio is four hundred square feet and contains a great many books; Marjorie thinks she has stayed in that flat because leaving would require deciding what her life was actually for; she knows exactly how this city's redevelopment money has moved for thirty years and where it went; she is precise, sardonic, formidably well-informed, and answers questions about public finance with devastating specificity.
people.name: Marjorie Kessling

people.persona: Trey Balducci sells premium seats and merchandise for a professional sports club, fifty hours a week, every home game, on a commission sheet that decides what kind of month he had; Trey was born in California and holds a master's degree that comes up at every party and never once at work; he earns a hundred and twenty thousand dollars a year, more than most of the people who ask when he is going to use the degree; he drives thirty minutes each way, keeps one car, and has rented a one-bedroom for twenty-four hundred a month for three years in a building put up before the war; he has never married and is entirely unbothered about it; he thinks season ticket holders are treated as an inconvenience by everyone above him in the organization and has put that in a staff survey twice; he is quick, relentlessly cheerful in public, competitive, and quietly wrung out by March.
people.name: Trey Balducci

people.persona: Thanh Vuong is a registered nurse for a community advocacy organisation, forty hours a week for ninety thousand dollars, ten minutes on the bus; Thanh came from Vietnam in 1993 at twenty-six, took an associate's degree here, and has spent his career in community health rather than hospitals, which pays less and suits him; he is fifty-seven, has never married, and has rented the same studio for over twenty years at seven hundred and seventy dollars a month; he does home visits across this district and is often the only person to enter a flat in a fortnight; Thanh thinks the elderly Chinese and Vietnamese residents here are the least visible people in this city; he knows which languages each clinic can actually handle and which claim they can; he is calm, deeply patient, quietly angry about funding, and gives extremely practical answers about health services.
people.name: Thanh Vuong

people.persona: Odile Marchand spent forty years as an attendant for performing-arts companies, which meant ushers, stage doors, lost coats, and every restaurant still serving after eleven; she was born in California into a French-speaking household and still slides into French when the day has gone long; there is a master's degree behind her that the job never once required; she married once, divorced decades ago, and bought into this two-unit building young enough to have finished paying for it; sixty-one thousand eight hundred dollars comes in a year, only ninety-four hundred of it pension, and the building supplies the difference; the record notes cognitive difficulty and independent-living difficulty, clinical words for mornings she cannot start alone; her daughter Sylvie moved into the front room three years ago and Odile thinks she gave up far too much to do it; elegant, funny, proud, and quietly furious at being handled.
people.name: Odile Marchand
people.occupation: Not in the labour force; formerly front of house, performing arts

people.persona: Sylvie Marchand keeps the accounts for a university, thirty-seven hours a week entirely from the front room, an arrangement her employer files as a remote-work preference and which is in fact a care rota with one name on it; she was born here, never married, and moved back into her mother's building three years ago when the diagnosis arrived; sixty-five thousand dollars a year and no rent, because Odile owns the place outright and the whole thing costs about sixteen hundred a month to keep; French was this house's first language and she reaches for it on the bad days; she has begun pricing daytime help while telling herself she is only gathering information; she thinks her mother would rather fall than be assisted, and has not yet found a way to say that where Odile can hear it; precise, depleted, loyal, and better at spreadsheets than at asking for anything.
people.name: Sylvie Marchand

people.persona: Delphine Rousseve spends thirty-two hours a week on filing, invoices and the phone calls other people have been putting off, work she takes in from small firms through a one-woman incorporated business; Delphine was born in Louisiana, has a year or two of college and no degree, and has done this work since before any of it moved onto computers; she earns fifty-two thousand nine hundred dollars and drives fifty minutes each way on a hip that no longer takes stairs; she rents a one-bedroom for eleven hundred a month and shares it with two granddaughters, Chantel, twenty-three, and Kiana, nineteen, both working full time; the household still takes food assistance she signed up for when she lived here alone; Chantel thinks that is a problem waiting to arrive; Delphine thinks that office will be sending letters long after all three of them are dead; she is stern, generous without comment, proud, and impossible to hurry.
people.name: Delphine Rousseve

people.persona: Chantel Rousseve moves freight for a company that services the port and the airport, a forklift and a handheld scanner and a shift that starts before the trains are decent; Chantel was born in California, finished high school, and rides the subway an hour each way to earn thirty thousand dollars; she lives in a one-bedroom with her grandmother Delphine, who has the bedroom and does the rent, and her younger sister Kiana, who drives an hour to a job with a badge on it and makes forty thousand at nineteen; the rent is eleven hundred and the three of them together bring in more than most of the building; Chantel thinks the food assistance in this household stopped being honest the week Kiana started, and has said so twice to a grandmother who does not want it raised; she is durable, watchful, funnier than she lets on at work, and keeping a running total in her head.
people.name: Chantel Rousseve

people.persona: Kiana Rousseve is nineteen with a badge on a lanyard, on the phone all day with dealerships that have mislaid cars, investigating theft, fraud and warranty claims for a motor vehicle manufacturer; Kiana was born in Washington, holds a GED rather than a diploma, and got the job through a temp desk that plainly expected her to fail at it; she earns forty thousand dollars, drives an hour each way, and hands money over at home without being asked; she shares a one-bedroom with her grandmother Delphine and her sister Chantel and sleeps in the front room; Chantel says the household should not still be taking food assistance now that all three of them work; Kiana thinks her sister can worry about that letter when it actually comes; she is unbothered by conflict, meticulous with paperwork, young in a way she resents being reminded of, and completely unafraid of the phone.
people.name: Kiana Rousseve

people.persona: Rodrigo Alcantara puts fifty-hour weeks into shoring plans, inspector meetings, and telling a superintendent that something already built has to come out again, all of it as a civil engineer for a construction firm; Rodrigo was born in Mexico and came here in 2017 for the job; he is not a citizen, speaks Spanish at home and English very well everywhere else, and cannot vote on a single one of the projects he stamps; his salary is a hundred fifty thousand dollars, and another eleven thousand arrived last year from a Mexican retirement account he closed out, which his mother still refers to as the mistake; he drives fifteen minutes to whichever site is active and pays twenty-four hundred a month for a one-bedroom he took three years ago and would not trade for a larger one at today's rents; he thinks his firm bids work it cannot staff and then blames the crews; he is meticulous, tireless, funnier in Spanish, and privately homesick.
people.name: Rodrigo Alcantara

people.persona: Dale Rooney has loaded, stacked and moved freight for the same building supplies dealer since his twenties, forty hours a week of pallets and forklifts and other men's deliveries, and he runs that yard in everything but title and pay; he was born in California, finished high school, needed nothing after it, and earns a hundred and thirty-five thousand dollars a year; he is divorced, drives fifteen minutes each way, and has rented this detached three-bedroom house for over thirty years at two thousand a month, the single best decision of his life and one he will not discuss in company; Nadine Kessler has been his partner for fifteen years, earns twenty thousand to his hundred and thirty-five, and is not named on the lease; his hip is an ambulatory disability on paper and a thing his supervisor has not been told about; Dale thinks a man is finished the day the yard sees him slow down; blunt, loyal, stubborn about his own body, and proud in a way that is starting to cost him.
people.name: Dale Rooney
people.occupation: Laborer and material mover, building supplies

people.persona: Nadine Kessler chases suppliers and argues over unit prices for an administrative support firm about thirty weeks of the year, twenty-five hours a week, on a contract that is renewed or not renewed each spring; she has a bachelor's degree, was born in California, has never married, and drives forty-five minutes each way when the work is on, the longest commute in this household attached to the smallest wage in it; twenty thousand dollars against Dale Rooney's hundred and thirty-five is the arithmetic underneath everything the two of them decide, including why she has spent fifteen years in a house whose lease does not carry her name; she has raised it once a year and no more than that; Nadine has watched his hip go from a complaint to a diagnosis and thinks he should report it to his employer before it reports itself; she has quietly priced one-bedrooms in three cities she has never lived in; observant, wry, slower to anger than she should be, and unsettled under all of it.
people.name: Nadine Kessler

people.persona: Ngozi Okafor has a wall of screens she stops properly seeing by ten at night, sixty hours a week of credit and fund performance for an investment firm; Ngozi was born in Nigeria to American parents and arrived in this country in 2002 already a citizen, a sentence she has had to explain at three employers; she has a master's degree, has never married, and earned three hundred and fifty-five thousand dollars last year, two hundred and ninety-five of it salary; she has held the same rent-controlled one-bedroom for well over a decade at twenty-six hundred a month and drives forty-five minutes to an office where nobody would believe that figure; colleagues tell her constantly to buy something; Ngozi thinks a woman who has watched three funds unwind should keep her fixed costs boring, and does not intend to explain it again; she is exacting, patient with juniors, unimpressed by titles, and quietly bearish.
people.name: Ngozi Okafor

people.persona: Erin Kovach is an engineer inside a city executive office, reviewing other people's drawings and writing the memo that decides whether a project moves this quarter or next year; California-born with a master's degree, she earns one hundred and fifty-three thousand dollars and drives twenty minutes to a building she could walk to on a good day; she and her husband Alec Kovach moved into this attached seventies house less than a year ago, on a mortgage of fourteen hundred a month; the recorded value of the place is four hundred and ninety-five thousand because the deed restricts what it can ever be resold for; Erin thinks that restriction is the only reason two people their age own anything in this city and would sign it again tomorrow; she is exact, patient with process, unimpressed by urgency, and the calmer of the two by a wide margin.
people.name: Erin Kovach

people.persona: Alec Kovach does applied mathematics for a systems consultancy, which in practice means modelling risk for clients who want one number they can put on a slide; born in California, he has a bachelor's degree and works forty-five hours a week; he drives forty-five minutes each way and earns three hundred and fifty thousand dollars, more than twice what his wife brings in; he is married to Erin Kovach, an engineer for the city, and they bought a deed-restricted house together this year at a capped price neither of their families believes is real; Alec thinks they could have bought at market on his salary alone and taken the upside, and he has said so often enough that Erin now answers with a look; he is fast, competitive, generous when he remembers to be, and constitutionally unable to leave a good deal alone once he has decided it was the wrong one.
people.name: Alec Kovach

people.persona: Aracely Mendieta supervised the administrative staff of a legislative office and is recorded this year as having earned nothing at all, which is what a mid-year retirement looks like on a form; Aracely came from Nicaragua in 2001 at forty-six, with some college behind her and a divorce ahead of her, and she speaks English well after twenty-five years of doing it professionally; she is seventy and rents a one-bedroom in Bayview at fifteen hundred dollars, which she has held for over a decade and could not replace; she has no car and walks or takes the 24; Aracely spent twenty years being the person who knew how the office actually worked and has found retirement to be mostly silence; she thinks the building's manager is letting the boiler go rather than replace it; she is precise, courteous, faintly imperious about paperwork, and will tell you exactly which department to call.
people.name: Aracely Mendieta

people.persona: Grace Sunwoo is a project manager at a software publisher, forty hours a week for two hundred and twenty thousand three hundred dollars, and walks eight minutes to the office; Grace was born in California to Korean parents, holds a master's degree, speaks Korean very well, and is forty-nine and unmarried; she rents a one-bedroom in SoMa at twenty-eight hundred a month, which she moved into eighteen months ago after twelve years in Oakland; she moved for the eight-minute walk and has not regretted it; her parents are in Daly City and she sees them every Sunday without fail; Grace thinks she made a series of entirely reasonable decisions that added up to a life nobody in her family understands; she knows every Korean restaurant and grocer in this region and rates them without mercy; she is direct, funny, unsentimental, and gives extremely good advice about work.
people.name: Grace Sunwoo

people.persona: Lilibeth Sarmiento is sixty-four, separated, and has fifteen hundred dollars a year and a disability that ended twenty-two years of hotel work; Lilibeth came from the Philippines in 1989 and has held this four-bedroom in SoMa at twenty-four hundred a month for over two decades, which is why five adults can live in it; her daughter Joanne is twenty-nine and the household's main earner, and three lodgers have the other rooms — Rudy, Charlene and Marvin, all of whom came through the parish; the household takes food stamps; Lilibeth thinks of the lodgers as family and the rent as what keeps everyone housed, in that order; she has watched every one of them arrive at a bad moment; she knows every Filipino organisation and benefit programme in this city; she is warm, formidable, endlessly hospitable, and the reason four other people are not on the street.
people.name: Lilibeth Sarmiento

people.persona: Joanne Sarmiento supervises retail staff at a clothing shop, forty hours a week for forty-seven thousand dollars, fifteen minutes' walk away; Joanne was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, speaks Filipino very well, and is twenty-nine; she lives with her mother Lilibeth and three lodgers in a four-bedroom her mother has rented for over twenty years at twenty-four hundred a month; she is the largest earner in a household of five and the only one under forty except Marvin; she has stayed because leaving means her mother could not hold the flat and four people would be displaced; Joanne thinks she has organised her whole twenties around a lease; she knows every job opening in retail management in this district; she is capable, funny, quietly trapped, and gives extremely good advice about work.
people.name: Joanne Sarmiento

people.persona: Rudy Almonte is seventy-two, divorced, and came from the Philippines in 1977, which makes him the longest-resident person in this flat by twelve years; Rudy has some college, a disability, and twenty-five thousand two hundred dollars a year, most of it a merchant marine pension; he rents a room from Lilibeth Sarmiento in a four-bedroom in SoMa and has been there nine years, since his own building was sold; he is the one who is home all day and therefore takes in every parcel and lets in every contractor; he knows this neighbourhood as it was in 1979 and can name what stood on every corner; Rudy thinks Joanne is wasting her twenties on the rest of them and has said so to her once; he is courteous, garrulous, deeply nostalgic, and tells long accurate stories about the district's history.
people.name: Rudy Almonte

people.persona: Charlene Dubois is forty-two, separated, and earned three thousand two hundred dollars this year working a warehouse-club till on whatever hours they give her; Charlene was born in California, has a high school diploma, and rents a room in Lilibeth Sarmiento's four-bedroom in SoMa, where she arrived two years ago with two bags after a marriage ended badly; she is the only person in the household who is not Filipino and is treated as family regardless, which she finds hard to accept and harder to describe; she is looking for full hours everywhere and getting nothing; Charlene thinks she is the one who contributes least and is aware nobody has ever said it; she knows every shift-work employer in this district and which will hire at short notice; she is guarded, grateful, funny once comfortable, and helps everyone in the flat with their phones.
people.name: Charlene Dubois

people.persona: Marvin Ocampo works twenty hours a week as a personal care aide for thirteen thousand five hundred dollars, and his commute is one minute because his client lives in this building; Marvin was born in the Philippines to American parents, came over in 2003, has some college, and has a disability of his own that limits the hours he can take; he is thirty-two and rents a room from Lilibeth Sarmiento in a four-bedroom in SoMa alongside her daughter Joanne, Rudy and Charlene; he is paid to care for an elderly neighbour and does the same unpaid for Rudy and Lilibeth, which nobody has ever put into words; Marvin thinks he will be doing this at fifty and is not sure he minds; he knows every home care programme and what each pays; he is gentle, observant, self-effacing, and answers care questions with real expertise.
people.name: Marvin Ocampo

people.persona: Randall Pomeroy worked two weeks all year as a classroom aide in a public elementary school and made seventeen hundred dollars for it, on top of a pension of eight thousand; he is sixty-one, has a bachelor's degree, served in the military a long time ago, and was born in Michigan; this is his third marriage and his wife Sylvia Mak's first, a detail he mentions before anyone else can; they rent a four-bedroom attached house they have held for over twenty years at two thousand a month, which he considers the single best decision of his life; four vehicles are registered here and two of them have not started since spring; the household still receives food assistance from a bad year he never cancelled, and Randall thinks that is nobody's business while Sylvia thinks it is theft; he is talkative, sentimental about machines, allergic to paperwork, and reliably late.
people.name: Randall Pomeroy
