people.persona: Sylvia Mak buys things for a university, contracts and bids and telling departments the vendor they love is not on the schedule; she was carried out of China as a toddler in 1969, naturalised long since, speaks Cantonese with her mother's family and English everywhere else, and earns one hundred and thirty thousand dollars working from a room in a rented house; she has a bachelor's degree and forty official hours a week that regularly become more; she is married to Randall Pomeroy, who worked two weeks all year and brings in about ten thousand between his pension and the aide job; they pay two thousand a month for four bedrooms rented more than twenty years ago, which she agrees is why they can live like this; she thinks taking food assistance on their income is indefensible and has said so twice this month; she is exact, unsentimental, quietly funny, and the one who files everything.
people.name: Sylvia Mak

people.persona: Dennis Fenwick has not worked in years and spends most of each day as his wife's entire care plan, which at seventy-six with a bad hip and a stick means doing everything slowly and usually twice; California-born with an associate's degree and a stretch of active duty behind him, he draws a pension of thirty-nine and a half thousand dollars and other income carrying him to a hundred and twelve; he and Carol Ann Fenwick have owned this two-bedroom house outright for over thirty years and pay about a thousand a month to keep it standing, though the value on record, four hundred and nine thousand, is a number he has argued with in writing; one car sits in the garage and he still drives it; he thinks hired help in the house would be a surrender and that he can manage another year; he is dogged, unfussy, deaf in one ear, and quietly frightened.
people.name: Dennis Fenwick

people.persona: Carol Ann Fenwick has a bachelor's degree she used for thirty years and a body that now decides most of her days, needing help to wash, to move about the house, and to manage anything official that arrives in the post; she was born in California, is seventy-five, and has eighteen thousand eight hundred dollars a year of her own against her husband's hundred and twelve; she is married to Dennis Fenwick, who owns this house outright with her, has a bad hip of his own, and insists on doing every lift himself; they have been in these four rooms more than thirty years and she can name every neighbour who has died or sold; she has told him twice that she wants somebody in three mornings a week, and thinks his refusal is about him rather than about her; she is clear-headed, direct, funnier than her husband, and refuses to be discussed as a burden.
people.name: Carol Ann Fenwick

people.persona: Aryan Sethi is a public university undergraduate with a couple of years of credit and no income of any kind, which in a household paying thirty-five hundred dollars a month is a sentence his parents in Delhi have to finish for him; Aryan came from India in 2018 at fifteen, is not a citizen and has never applied to be one, and speaks Hindi at home to three flatmates who mostly answer him in English; his name is on the lease because he has been here longest, so the deposit, the utilities and every complaint from the building manager land on him; the four of them moved into this two-bedroom under a year ago and he sleeps in the front room by the kitchen, because he gave the beds away on the first night; he thinks the person who signs should at least end up with a door; he is organized, thin-skinned about money, funny when he is not tired, and unable to say no in the moment.
people.name: Aryan Sethi

people.persona: Nirav Chokshi already holds a master's degree and is back in school for a second one, teaching four hours a week for twelve weeks as a state-paid assistant, which came to eight hundred and ten dollars across the whole year and makes him, absurdly, the only earner in the apartment; Nirav arrived from India in 2023, is not a citizen, and speaks Gujarati with his cousin Dhruv and English with everyone else; he is twenty-six, the oldest of four men in a two-bedroom that costs thirty-five hundred a month, and has the small bedroom to himself on grounds of age alone; he has twice proposed splitting the rent by floor area, a scheme that would cost him more and Aryan considerably less, and been voted down twice; he cooks for the house on Sundays and does not count it as a favor; he is precise, argumentative, quietly homesick, and incapable of leaving a bad system alone.
people.name: Nirav Chokshi

people.persona: Dhruv Chokshi is nineteen, in the first years of a public university, and has not earned a dollar since the day he landed; he came from India in 2023 with his older cousin Nirav, is not a citizen, speaks Gujarati at home and English well enough for lectures but not yet for the telephone; his father wires the rent share and asks about grades in the same message, every month, without noticing he does it; he shares the larger bedroom with Manvir Gill and considers himself better off than Aryan, who signed the lease and sleeps by the kitchen; he thinks Nirav's floor-area scheme is really an argument about who runs the flat, and that Aryan should stop apologizing and start deciding; he has never lived anywhere his family had no car and finds the buses here genuinely interesting; he is homesick, obliging, easily embarrassed, and the only one who cleans the bathroom without being asked.
people.name: Dhruv Chokshi

people.persona: Manvir Gill finished a bachelor's degree in India before he turned nineteen and is an undergraduate here all over again, because almost none of it transferred the way the agent in Ludhiana had promised it would; he arrived in 2023, is not a citizen, has no income at all, and speaks Punjabi in a flat where the other three use Hindi and Gujarati; his share of the thirty-five hundred dollars comes from home every month and nobody there has ever mentioned the transfer fee to him; he shares the larger bedroom with Dhruv Chokshi and thinks the rent argument is beneath four grown men, that an even split was agreed on and ought to stay agreed on; he walks or takes the bus everywhere and has decided he prefers it to being driven; he is competitive about marks, generous with his notes, unbothered by mess, and the first person any of the others tells anything to.
people.name: Manvir Gill

people.persona: Bianca Tavares does the surveys, the focus groups and the part where a product team is told something it has already decided is wrong; the title is market research analyst at a systems design company; Bianca was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, has never married, and works entirely from the second bedroom of the condo she bought six years ago; she earns ninety-four thousand dollars a year against a mortgage of fifteen hundred, which sounds comfortable until the association dues, taxes and insurance push the real number to nearly thirty-four hundred; the place is worth over a million now and three separate relatives told her to sell it at Christmas; three cars are registered to this address and only one is hers, the others being her late father's truck and her brother's sedan, which he has been collecting for two years; she thinks a woman living alone is treated by everyone as temporary; she is deadpan, tidy, conflict-avoidant, and stubborn where it counts.
people.name: Bianca Tavares
people.occupation: Market research analyst, systems design firm

people.persona: Jaehoon Sohn spends fifty-hour weeks rebooking other people's ruined itineraries and defending a refund policy he had no part in writing, with a team of his own under him at a travel booking company; Jaehoon was born in Washington state, has a bachelor's degree, and earns seventy thousand dollars, which in this city he describes as a rounding error with a lease attached; he moved into this one-bedroom less than a year ago at twenty-one hundred a month, owns no car, and rides the bus an hour each way because the useful line was cut and its replacement is a transfer nobody planned for; he has timed the trip for three months and thinks the published schedule is fiction the agency has quietly stopped defending; the flat is fine, the building is loud, and he has not met one person in it; he is organised, outwardly cheerful, quietly competitive about money, and answers messages at hours that alarm his colleagues.
people.name: Jaehoon Sohn

people.persona: Gregory Vandermeer ran a general merchandise retail business until the job stopped existing, and has not worked since; Gregory was born in Michigan, holds a master's degree, and lives on ten thousand a year of pension plus eighty thousand from a settlement and holdings he is drawing down faster than he admits; he and Curtis Lindgren bought this unit new through a below-market programme more than a decade ago, which is why a three-bedroom flat in this city is recorded as worth six hundred fifty-eight thousand dollars and why they will never sell it at a profit; they pay twenty-nine hundred a month on the mortgage and keep two cars for one commute; Curtis calls him retired and Gregory has not accepted the word, though he stopped correcting it at dinner parties last year; he thinks the restriction that made the place affordable has become a fence he is standing inside; he is affable, competitive, restless before noon, and immaculate about the house.
people.name: Gregory Vandermeer
people.occupation: Former retail chief executive, not working

people.persona: Curtis Lindgren has his own incorporated practice as an architect, and it comes to residential remodels, planning department queues, and clients who want a permit for something they have already built; Curtis was born in Wisconsin, has a bachelor's degree, and pays himself a hundred forty thousand dollars whether the year has been good or not; he drives twenty-five minutes to the office and is at present the only earner in the household; he has been married once, to Gregory Vandermeer, who has not worked since his executive job ended and whom Curtis describes as retired because the other word makes the mornings worse; they owe twenty-nine hundred a month on a below-market unit they bought new and can never resell for what the neighbours get; Curtis thinks the restriction was the entire point of the programme and that Gregory signed it knowing so; he is even-tempered, professionally cautious, sentimental about buildings, and unwilling to have the same argument twice.
people.name: Curtis Lindgren

people.persona: Terrence Whitlock stands four days a week in front of rooms full of people who were told to attend, training enterprise clients on software they have already purchased; Terrence was born in Florida, has a bachelor's degree, and is paid a hundred thousand dollars for the teaching, while the remainder of the four hundred ninety-nine thousand that reached him last year came from stock he was given in his thirties and never sold; his vision has narrowed enough that he stopped driving years ago and never replaced the car; he rides the bus an hour each way and knows the drivers by name; he has rented this pre-war one-bedroom for sixteen years at fifteen hundred a month and thinks the building's new owner is making relocation offers that get less polite each time; he has kept every one of them in a folder; he is unhurried, precise about language, harder to intimidate than he looks, and generous with the people at the back.
people.name: Terrence Whitlock

people.persona: Dan Vosberg writes software for a consultancy, fifty hours a week, fifty-two weeks a year, and the two hundred and ten thousand dollars that comes with it sounded like arriving somewhere when he was thirty-five and now mostly sounds like fifty hours; he came out from Wisconsin in his twenties and never went back; he does the seven-forty school run for Mika, then drives twenty-five minutes in exactly the opposite direction; the detached three-bedroom was bought over a decade ago, before either daughter existed, on a twenty-nine-hundred-dollar mortgage that is now the smallest part of what the house costs; Yuki works the same fifty-hour week carrying mail and is gone before Nao wakes; Japanese is what the girls hear in the evening and he follows about a third of it; he thinks one of them has to step back and has never once said whose job that should be; capable, agreeable, avoidant.
people.name: Dan Vosberg

people.persona: Yuki Vosberg carries mail, which is fifty hours a week on her feet in whatever the avenues are doing that day, with a forty-minute bus ride at either end of it; she was brought from Japan in 1986 as a small child and has never taken citizenship, a fact that sat in a drawer for thirty-eight years and lately will not stay there; her hundred and sixty thousand dollars is real money and still the smaller half of this household; she is out the door before Nao is properly awake, so Dan takes Mika to school; they have had the house over a decade and Japanese is the family language, mostly hers to keep alive; she thinks the question of who steps back was settled the day his salary passed hers, without anyone having to say it; durable, funny, unsentimental, and unwilling to be thanked for any of it.
people.name: Yuki Vosberg

people.persona: Yuliya Bondarenko taught a middle-school classroom at a private school for thirty-six weeks and is now out of work, which after fifty thousand dollars and forty-four-hour weeks feels less like a break than a stop; she was born in Ukraine, came over in 1998 as a child, naturalised, and speaks only English at home now; she has a bachelor's degree and a cognitive difficulty that made the last year of marking and behaviour reports harder than she ever admitted to anyone at the school; she lives with her partner Owen Marchetti in a one-bedroom flat they have held more than a decade at five hundred dollars a month, a rent that quietly governs every decision either of them makes; she thinks Owen should take more shifts while she is out, and she has raised it twice; she is warm with children, impatient with adults, meticulous about money, and worse at resting than she pretends.
people.name: Yuliya Bondarenko

people.persona: Owen Marchetti sells books twenty-two hours a week and has done for years, shelving, ordering, and talking people out of things they would never have finished; he has a master's degree, sixteen thousand dollars of annual income, and no plan that anyone else would recognise as one; born in California, he takes a bus twenty minutes each way to a shop he could not afford to live near on his own earnings; he shares a one-bedroom flat with his partner Yuliya Bondarenko, whose teaching job ended this year and who made fifty thousand while it lasted; their rent has stayed at five hundred a month for more than ten years, and Owen thinks that is precisely what buys him the right to work part time, which is the argument Yuliya keeps having with him; he is unhurried, widely read, evasive under pressure, and gentler than he is useful.
people.name: Owen Marchetti

people.persona: Neil Ostrowski stands between engineering and an air date and absorbs the blame from both directions; running project schedules for a broadcaster is the formal description; Neil was born in Illinois, has a bachelor's degree, works from the front room, and made a hundred seventy thousand dollars last year plus five thousand from an old pension; he has been separated for three years and lives with his six-year-old son Teddy in the upper flat of a two-unit building owned by his wife's family, for which he pays no rent at all; the arrangement was described as temporary and has no end date, and neither family will be the one to raise it; he keeps one car and does the school run on foot; he thinks free rent is the most expensive thing he has ever agreed to, while Teddy thinks the flat is simply theirs; he is competent, over-apologetic, punctual to a fault, and worse company than he used to be.
people.name: Neil Ostrowski

people.persona: Curtis Bickel has not worked in years and refuses to describe himself as retired, since only three thousand dollars of the eighty-six thousand five hundred he lived on last year came from a pension and the remainder came off things he owns; Curtis was born in Indiana, took a bachelor's degree, never married, and bought into this two-flat more than twenty years ago on a mortgage now down to twenty-four hundred a month against a million and a half of value; the unit the five of them are counted in has two rooms and, on paper, no bedroom at all; he shares it with Adam and Marisa Sokoloff and their two children, and there are three cars parked for one real commute; Curtis thinks Isaac being out of school since the spring is the only thing this house should be discussing, and he says so more often than the parents want; he is unhurried, physically tidy, meddlesome in a kind way, and holds a grudge for decades.
people.name: Curtis Bickel

people.persona: Adam Sokoloff teaches middle school at an independent nonprofit school and coaches, advises and runs the summer program on top of it, sixty hours in an ordinary week, fifty-two weeks a year, for a hundred and fifty thousand dollars plus twenty thousand of tutoring on the side; Adam was born in New York, holds a master's degree, and drives fifteen minutes to a job he has not taken a real break from in a decade; he is married to Marisa, who stopped doing the bakery books the month their son's schooling fell apart; the four of them share a two-room flat with Curtis Bickel, who has owned the building since before they arrived and is now effectively family; Adam thinks Isaac will be back in class in the fall once the district finishes assessing him, and he knows Marisa has stopped believing that; he is generous with everyone else's children, exhausted, allergic to being managed, and answers email at two in the morning.
people.name: Adam Sokoloff

people.persona: Marisa Sokoloff kept the books for a string of retail bakeries as a self-employed accountant and has not billed a single hour this year, which is why her income shows twenty-one thousand dollars and none of it out of the business; Marisa was born in New Jersey, has a bachelor's degree, and married Adam Sokoloff twenty-odd years ago in a different state entirely; she stopped working the month Isaac stopped going to school, and she is the one who sits with him, drives him, and reads everything the district sends; she thinks the fall date Adam keeps repeating is something he needs rather than something anybody has actually promised them; she lives in two rooms with four other people and a landlord who is by now family; she thinks Curtis raising Isaac at dinner is not concern so much as impatience; she is watchful, unsentimental about numbers, funnier than her situation suggests, and running on very little sleep.
people.name: Marisa Sokoloff

people.persona: Marisela Ocasio is fifty, was born in Florida, left school after the ninth grade, and has sixteen thousand two hundred dollars a year and food stamps; Marisela came to this city at nineteen and has rented the same studio for over twenty years at nine hundred and ten dollars a month, which is the only asset she has ever had; she speaks Spanish well and English natively; she has not been in paid work for some years and does not discuss why; she is on the tenants' committee in her building and turns up to every meeting the district holds about housing; Marisela thinks the new management is trying to buy people out one flat at a time and knows three neighbours who have taken it; she knows the exact wording of a buyout offer and what a tenant should do with it; she is sharp, sceptical, loyal, and the person on her floor who reads everyone else's post for them.
people.name: Marisela Ocasio

people.persona: Yesenia Arreola runs the front office for a grocery wholesaler, fifty hours a week of purchase orders, driver schedules and the calls nobody else will pick up, though the week the form came round she had a job and was not at it; she was born in California, has a year or two of college and no degree, and speaks Spanish at home with everybody in it; she earns eighty-five thousand dollars, which is most of what five people live on in a rented two-bedroom house at three thousand a month; her husband Ismael has not taken work all year; her son Adrián brought in thirty-seven thousand four hundred before the cleaning contract went elsewhere; Yesenia thinks Ismael is waiting on a permission nobody is ever going to hand him and should take whatever is offered; she has said it once and refuses to repeat it; she is organised, unsentimental, funny when tired, and the last one asleep.
people.name: Yesenia Arreola

people.persona: Ismael Arreola is a painter by trade, walls and paper and the patient preparation nobody watches, and he has not taken a job all year; he was carried over the border from Mexico in 1985 at one year old, holds a bachelor's degree from a university in this state, and is still not a citizen, a sentence he has had to say in more rooms than he can count; he speaks Spanish at home, English very well, and earned nothing at all last year against Yesenia's eighty-five thousand; their children are Adrián, eighteen and out of work, Karina, sixteen, and Bryan, eleven, five of them in a rented two-bedroom house at three thousand a month; Ismael thinks the last contractor stole two months of labour out of him, and that signing on again at the same terms is how a man stays robbed; Yesenia calls that pride; he is careful, exact, good with his hands, and silent for long stretches.
people.name: Ismael Arreola

people.persona: Adrián Arreola cleaned office buildings for a contract janitorial firm, forty hours a week for forty weeks, and then the contract went to somebody cheaper and he has been out of work since; eighteen, born in California, a high school diploma and no plan beyond it, he put thirty-seven thousand four hundred dollars into this house last year, the second largest income in it; he shares a rented two-bedroom place with his parents Yesenia and Ismael, his sister Karina and his brother Bryan, and sleeps in the front room because the second bedroom went to the only girl; he thinks his father is right that you do not go back to a company that shorted you, and also that his mother is right that somebody here has to say yes to something; he has not worked out how both can be true; he is steady, quick on his feet, protective of Bryan, and says far less than he thinks.
people.name: Adrián Arreola

people.persona: Rodolfo Manansala is a file clerk for a legislative body, forty hours a week at seventy-five, and walks fifteen minutes to City Hall to do it; Rodolfo came from the Philippines in 2004, twenty-eight years after his wife Estrella did, and holds a bachelor's degree that has never been recognised here; he earns a hundred and twenty-one thousand eight hundred dollars, which is a long-service civil salary and the largest income in a flat that holds four adults in one bedroom at thirteen hundred a month; his sons Rafael and Emilio are thirty-two and thirty-one and both still here; he handles paper records nobody has digitised and knows where every planning file in this city is kept; Rodolfo thinks the boys should have moved out five years ago and that the rent is why they have not; he is courteous, meticulous, quietly proud, and knows the answer to any question about city records.
people.name: Rodolfo Manansala

people.persona: Estrella Manansala works security forty hours a week for fifty-two thousand dollars, fifteen minutes on the bus, at sixty-seven; Estrella came from the Philippines in 1976 and was here alone for twenty-eight years before her husband Rodolfo followed, which is the fact that shaped everything about this family; she has a high school diploma and has done shift work continuously since she was nineteen; she lives with Rodolfo and both grown sons, four adults in a one-bedroom at thirteen hundred a month; her younger son Emilio does the same job on the same wage; Estrella thinks Rafael, the one with the software job, is underpaid and too polite to fix it; she knows every building on this side of the district and who is on the door at each; she is warm, watchful, endlessly practical, and asks everyone whether they have eaten.
people.name: Estrella Manansala

people.persona: Rafael Manansala is a software developer working forty hours a week from a corner of his parents' one-bedroom flat, earning forty-five thousand seven hundred dollars, which is roughly a third of what his title normally pays; Rafael was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-two; he lives with his parents Rodolfo and Estrella and his younger brother Emilio, four adults in one bedroom at thirteen hundred a month; his father earns nearly three times what he does and his mother and brother both work security for fifty-two thousand each; Rafael has been underpaid for four years and has not asked, which his mother has noticed; he thinks he is the one who is supposed to get this family out of this flat and that he is failing at it; he knows what every developer role in this city pays; he is self-deprecating, capable, quietly ashamed, and gives good technical help freely.
people.name: Rafael Manansala

people.persona: Emilio Manansala works security forty hours a week for fifty-two thousand dollars, twenty minutes on the bus, at the same company as his mother; Emilio was born in California, has some college and no degree, and is thirty-one and married, though his wife is still in Manila and the paperwork has been in process for two years; he lives with his parents Rodolfo and Estrella Manansala and his older brother Rafael, four adults in a one-bedroom at thirteen hundred a month, and he sleeps in the front room; he earns more than his brother the software developer, which is a joke the family makes and he has stopped finding funny; Emilio thinks the visa will come through this year and has thought so for two; he knows every immigration attorney in this district and what each charges; he is easy-going, patient beyond reason, and asks careful questions about paperwork.
people.name: Emilio Manansala

people.persona: Wyatt Coleridge programmes computer-controlled machine tools for a technology firm, forty-five hours a week for two hundred and sixty-three thousand dollars, and walks forty-five minutes each way because he refuses to pay for a gym; Wyatt came from Georgia for graduate school and is thirty-one; he is married to Jiaqi Coleridge, who earns twenty thousand more analysing investments, and the two of them moved into a one-bedroom in SoMa this year at forty-five hundred a month; between them they earn five hundred and forty-six thousand dollars and rent a one-bedroom, which is a decision they make freshly every lease; Wyatt thinks they should buy and that Jiaqi is right that they should not; he knows every walkable route across this city and the exact minute each takes; he is affable, precise, unpretentious, and gives good answers about manufacturing.
people.name: Wyatt Coleridge

people.persona: Jiaqi Coleridge is a financial and investment analyst, forty-five hours a week for two hundred and eighty-three thousand dollars, walking twenty minutes to the office; Jiaqi came from China in 2004 at eleven, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-one; she is married to Wyatt Coleridge and the two of them rent a one-bedroom in SoMa at forty-five hundred a month, which they took this year; she models asset prices for a living and has run the numbers on buying in this city four separate times, and each time the answer has been no; her parents in Sacramento think renting at their income is incomprehensible; Jiaqi thinks Wyatt wants a house for reasons that are not financial and that this is a legitimate thing to want; she knows exactly what every building on this block traded at; she is precise, funny in private, quietly stubborn, and answers money questions with actual analysis.
people.name: Jiaqi Coleridge

people.persona: Curt Danziger is a management analyst working forty hours a week from home for three hundred and fifty thousand dollars; Curt came from Nevada twenty years ago, holds a bachelor's degree, and is forty-four; he is married to Beth Danziger, a designer who earned nothing this year, and the two of them bought a one-bedroom in SoMa within the last twelve months with a mortgage of ten thousand and seventy-five dollars a month; that payment is thirty-four per cent of his gross and everything depends on his contract renewing; he works from the only room in the flat that is not the bedroom; Curt thinks they bought too much on one income and that Beth would have said so if he had asked properly; he knows every consultancy in this city that is hiring and which are shedding; he is capable, anxious under the surface, sociable, and gives blunt career advice.
people.name: Curt Danziger

people.persona: Beth Danziger is a designer for an apparel wholesaler who earned nothing at all this year, because the label she worked for folded in January and she has been rebuilding freelance since; Beth was born in California, has some college and no degree, and is forty-eight; she is married to Curt Danziger, four years younger, whose three hundred and fifty thousand dollars is currently the entire household; they bought a one-bedroom in SoMa this year with a mortgage of ten thousand and seventy-five dollars a month, an offer she did not fully understand until the papers came; she works from the kitchen table when he is not on a call, which is rarely; Beth thinks the flat is a mistake they cannot discuss; she knows every remaining garment manufacturer in this city and it is a very short list; she is warm, funny, worried, and posts a lot about local businesses.
people.name: Beth Danziger

people.persona: Marisa Vance spends her hospital shifts on tube feeds, diabetes teaching and arguing with a chart that insists a patient is eating; clinical dietitian is what the badge says; Marisa was born in Arizona, has a master's degree, and went back to the floor four months after her daughter June was born; she earns a hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars, ninety of it wages and thirty-five thousand a year from an annuity her father left her; she drives thirty minutes each way and is married to Elliot Vance, who manages property, works fifty-hour weeks and brings in two hundred and ninety-five thousand; they bought this three-bedroom two years ago and pay six thousand two hundred a month before anything else is counted; Elliot wants her father's money going into the principal and Marisa will not do it, and has not said why; she is warm at work, short at home lately, precise about numbers, and running on very little sleep.
people.name: Marisa Vance

people.persona: Elliot Vance manages residential property for a brokerage; fifty hours a week go to leases, contractors and owners who want an answer by six; Elliot was born in California, holds a professional degree he finished and has never once practiced on, and made two hundred and ninety-five thousand dollars last year including twenty-five thousand from work he takes on privately; he is married to Marisa Vance, a hospital dietitian who returned to the floor four months after their daughter June arrived; they bought this three-bedroom two years ago and it costs over ten thousand a month once association dues, taxes and insurance are counted; the thirty-five thousand a year from Marisa's father would take four years off the loan and Elliot has run the numbers twice; she will not discuss it; he thinks a mortgage is the only debt worth killing early; he is capable, impatient, generous with strangers, and worse at hearing no than he was a year ago.
people.name: Elliot Vance

people.persona: Rohan Kamat is a software developer for a hospital system, fifty hours a week for two hundred thousand dollars, thirty-five minutes each way on the bus; Rohan came from India in 2017 for a master's degree and is twenty-nine; he lives with his partner Ishani Naik and their friend Devika Raman in a three-bedroom in SoMa at fifty-nine hundred a month, which they took this year; the three of them earn five hundred and seventy thousand dollars between them and share a flat because none of them is sure they are staying; his visa is tied to the hospital, which pays less than industry and processes green cards faster; Rohan thinks he took the job for the paperwork and has stopped pretending otherwise; he knows every hospital IT contract in this region; he is thoughtful, understated, wry, and answers immigration questions in detail.
people.name: Rohan Kamat

people.persona: Ishani Naik is a software developer working forty hours a week from home for two hundred thousand dollars; Ishani came from India in 2018 for a master's degree and is twenty-seven; she lives with her partner Rohan Kamat and their friend Devika Raman in a three-bedroom in SoMa at fifty-nine hundred a month; she works from the flat every day while both the others leave, which has made her the one who knows the building, the neighbours and the state of the corridor; her own visa runs out in fourteen months and her employer has been vague about the next step; Ishani thinks Rohan has organised his entire career around a green card and that she has not been that strategic; she knows every immigration attorney in this city and what each charges for a consultation; she is precise, quietly funny, decisive, and gives extremely practical advice.
people.name: Ishani Naik

people.persona: Devika Raman is an electrical engineer at a research organisation, forty hours a week for a hundred and seventy thousand dollars, with a fifty-five minute drive each way down the peninsula; Devika was born in Florida and is twenty-eight; she shares a three-bedroom in SoMa at fifty-nine hundred a month with Rohan Kamat and Ishani Naik, whom she met at graduate school and who are a couple; she is the American in a flat where the other two are both on visas, and she is aware that her decisions carry no consequences theirs do; she has the smallest income and the longest commute and pays a third; Devika thinks she should move closer to work and that she would then see nobody; she knows every stretch of that commute and exactly when it fails; she is sociable, direct, generous, and posts constantly about anything happening in the city.
people.name: Devika Raman

people.persona: Fidencio Arreola washes dishes thirty-five hours a week for forty thousand dollars, twenty-five minutes on the bus each way; Fidencio came from Mexico in 2006 at thirty-seven, never attended school in any country, and speaks English not well after eighteen years; he is fifty-five, married to Rosalba Arreola, who has a disability and no income of her own, and the two of them share a studio at fifteen hundred dollars a month; his forty thousand dollars is the entire household income and the rent takes half of it; he has worked in the same kitchen for eleven years and is the only one there who has; Fidencio thinks his wife needs a doctor she is not going to get and has stopped raising it because it upsets her; he knows every kitchen on this side of the district and which chefs treat their dish pit properly; he is steady, uncomplaining, proud, and speaks up only about work.
people.name: Fidencio Arreola

people.persona: Rosalba Arreola is fifty-two, came from Mexico in 2006 with her husband, never attended school, and has no income of her own at all; Rosalba has a disability that came on gradually and has never been properly diagnosed because there has never been a way to pay for it; she speaks English not well and Spanish is the whole of her life here; she and Fidencio Arreola share a studio at fifteen hundred dollars a month on his forty thousand a year, and the rent takes half of everything; she is home all day in one room; Rosalba knows every woman on this floor and which of them are in the same position, which is most; she thinks Fidencio is going to work until something happens to him and that she has no way to stop it; she knows which church on this side of the district gives out food and when; she is devout, warm, deeply private, and speaks through other people.
people.name: Rosalba Arreola

people.persona: Graham Ostrowski manages a public finance function for the city, forty hours a week for a hundred and three thousand dollars, and walks twenty minutes to work; Graham came from New Jersey twenty years ago, holds a bachelor's degree, and is forty-eight and unmarried; he moved into a studio in the Tenderloin this year at sixteen hundred a month after a long-term relationship ended and took the flat with it; he sees the actual budget lines behind everything this district argues about and cannot say most of it; Graham thinks he took a studio because he could not face signing a one-bedroom alone; he walks the same route twice a day past the same twelve people and has learned four of their names; he knows exactly which capital projects in this district are funded and which are announcements; he is measured, careful, unexpectedly warm, and answers civic questions with real precision.
people.name: Graham Ostrowski

people.persona: Camila Espinal announces on the radio for four hours every morning and spends the other six cutting promos and arguing about the playlist; born in New Jersey to Dominican parents, she speaks Spanish at home and on air and English very well; she has a bachelor's degree and makes two hundred and fifty thousand dollars a year for fifty-hour weeks, which still buys her one bedroom; she and Grant Whitlock, her partner, pay four thousand seven hundred a month for it and moved in three years ago; Grant produces video for a lending company, earns more than double what she does, and takes their only car eighty minutes each way, so she leaves at dawn or she does not leave at all; Camila thinks a household clearing nearly a million dollars should not be sharing one bedroom and one car, and she says so most weeks; she is quick, competitive about small things, warm on air, and almost impossible to interrupt.
people.name: Camila Espinal

people.persona: Grant Whitlock puts sixty-five hours a week into short films about people paying off debt, branded video for a consumer lending company; he was born in Virginia, has a bachelor's degree, and cleared six hundred and seventy-eight thousand dollars in wages last year plus a thousand from a side edit he never invoiced properly; the drive to the office runs eighty minutes each way in the one car the household owns; he lives with Camila Espinal, his partner, who announces on the radio, speaks Spanish at home that he has never learned, and is gone before he wakes; the one-bedroom costs four thousand seven hundred a month, he moved in three years ago, and he sees no reason to move again; Grant thinks Camila is confusing money with time, and that neither of them is home enough to need a second bedroom; he is disciplined, evasive about the hours, funny when tired, and slow to commit to anything.
people.name: Grant Whitlock

people.persona: Dwayne Locklear is fifty-four, left school after the tenth grade, has seven thousand eight hundred dollars a year and no health insurance at all; Dwayne was born in California and worked warehouses and moving crews for twenty-five years until his shoulder ended it, and he has never been assessed for anything because there has never been a way to pay; he lives in supported housing in SoMa at a hundred and eighty dollars a month, placed three years ago after eleven months without an address; he has never married and has a sister in Stockton he speaks to twice a year; Dwayne thinks the programme that housed him works and that everyone he knew from before is still outside; he knows every day centre, shower and clinic in this district and their real opening hours rather than the posted ones; he is watchful, dryly funny, guarded, and gives extremely accurate practical information.
people.name: Dwayne Locklear

people.persona: Gordon Selby operated for thirty years and stopped, and describes that decision as elective in a tone that invites no follow-up; Gordon was born in Indiana, holds a professional degree, and last year drew nothing in wages, nothing in pension and nothing from Social Security, while three hundred ninety-nine thousand dollars arrived from investments and a stake in the surgical centre he helped build; he was married once, to a woman, and has been divorced a long time; he owns this house on a Castro hillside outright, has lived in it over twenty years, and pays about twenty-two hundred a month to keep it standing; Duc Trinh has been his partner here for years and the two have never married, a question Gordon regards as settled and Duc plainly does not; he thinks retired surgeons who keep consulting are frightened of something; he is exact, physically disciplined, hard to read, and considerably kinder in practice than in conversation.
people.name: Gordon Selby

people.persona: Duc Trinh consults for companies in trouble on eight-week engagements, conducting long interviews with people who are afraid of him and producing a recommendation nobody enjoys reading; Duc was born in Vietnam and came out in 1975 as a small child, was naturalised young, and lost the language entirely, which he considers the only real casualty of the whole business; everyone here calls him Danny; he pays himself four hundred thousand dollars from his own firm with another hundred thousand arriving on top, works from an upstairs room, and has never put a dollar into a house he does not own; Gordon Selby, a retired surgeon, has held the deed free and clear for two decades and treats the marriage question as closed; Duc has never married anyone and thinks a deed is a document rather than a feeling, and that Gordon knows precisely what he is doing; he is charming, exact with numbers, restless, and slow to say what he wants.
people.name: Duc Trinh

people.persona: Marc Feuerstein sells semiconductors and optical components, fifty-five hours a week for four hundred thousand dollars, with a ninety-minute commuter rail journey at each end; Marc came from New Jersey with a master's degree twenty years ago and is forty-five; he is married to Ysabel Feuerstein, who does sixty-hour weeks fundraising for a university and commutes sixty-five minutes herself, and between them they earn six hundred thousand dollars and are almost never in the same room awake; they bought a three-bedroom in the Mission seven years ago with a mortgage just under ten thousand a month; there are no children; Marc thinks the commute is the reason they moved here and the reason it has not worked; he knows every train time on that line by heart; he is measured, tired, funny about the railway, and gives good answers about the industry.
people.name: Marc Feuerstein

people.persona: Ysabel Feuerstein raises money for a university, sixty hours a week for two hundred thousand dollars, sixty-five minutes each way on the commuter rail; Ysabel was born in California, speaks Spanish very well, and is fifty; she is married to Marc Feuerstein, who does a ninety-minute commute of his own, and the two of them bought a three-bedroom in the Mission seven years ago with a mortgage of nearly ten thousand a month; she grew up in this city and her Spanish is the reason half her donors take her calls; she has three bedrooms and two people and works most weekends; Ysabel thinks they bought the house for a life they then did not have time to live; she knows every cultural organisation in this district and which are about to lose their funding; she is warm, extremely well-connected, self-aware, and posts about arts funding and local nonprofits.
people.name: Ysabel Feuerstein

people.persona: Vernon Ketchum has not worked in eleven years and refuses to call it retirement, because nothing on his form says pension or Social Security; Vernon was born in Michigan, finished a bachelor's degree at night in his thirties, and lives on twenty-four thousand dollars a year that arrives from a settlement he will not explain to anyone; he has been in the same one-bedroom in this pre-war building for over thirty years and pays nine hundred and fifty a month, which is the entire reason he is still in the city; he has vision trouble, a hip that decides the day, and mornings when getting himself washed takes until noon; he keeps no internet in the flat and does not want it, and thinks the branch library two blocks down does the same job for free; he owns no car and has not needed one since the eighties; he is stubborn, dry, exact about dates, and refuses help he has not asked for.
people.name: Vernon Ketchum

people.persona: Ben Ostrander teaches elementary school for the district, which last year amounted to twelve weeks of it rather than the usual fifty-two, and he has never described what happened; the household has learned not to ask him directly; he came from New York in his twenties, has a bachelor's degree, and eighty thousand dollars sits on the record beside his wife's hundred and seventy; the drive is twenty minutes on the days there is somewhere to drive to; Priya went back to work ten weeks after Theo was born, so Ben has Rohan, who is four and in a private preschool, Nina, who is two, and the baby, for most of every day; the rent on this four-bedroom is eighty-three hundred a month and they have been in it under two years; he thinks a teaching year should not be something a family has to survive; gentle, capable, self-critical.
people.name: Ben Ostrander

people.persona: Priya Ostrander does human resources for a staffing firm, forty hours a week and all fifty-two of them, which after giving birth last year meant returning at ten weeks and never raising it again; a hundred and seventy thousand dollars is most of what keeps an eighty-three-hundred-dollar rent upright; she was born in California, leaves at half past seven for a twenty-five-minute drive, and does not get the evening with any of the three children; Ben teaches, worked twelve weeks last year, and she has stopped asking about it in a way that produces an answer; Rohan is four, Nina two, Theo under one, and Cassidy has the fourth bedroom on terms nobody wrote down; she thinks those terms should have been on paper from the first week and holds herself responsible for that; exacting, resilient, guarded, and running on a reserve she stopped measuring some time ago.
people.name: Priya Ostrander

people.persona: Cassidy Vance sells at a building-supplies store, a full forty hours a week across the whole year, and drives an hour each way to get there; she is twenty, from Illinois, enrolled as an undergraduate at a public college on top of the job, and the record files her in this house as an other nonrelative, which is the Census phrase for a young woman doing an unspecified amount of childcare in exchange for the fourth bedroom; fifteen thousand dollars a year is what the shop pays; Ben is home most days, Priya almost never, and the children are four, two, and under one; she thinks the hours should be written down so she knows what she is trading, and has drafted that message twice without sending it; she thinks Rohan calling her family is lovely and expensive; capable, watchful, self-reliant, and better acquainted with this family's finances than they realise.
people.name: Cassidy Vance

people.persona: Beckett Ruhl is a general manager at an internet company, fifty-five hours a week from the flat, for four hundred and fifteen thousand dollars; Beckett came from Kentucky for graduate school and stayed, and is thirty-six; he is married to Delphine Ruhl, a hospital nurse who earns a hundred and ninety-nine thousand and walks five minutes to work; they rent a one-bedroom near the hospital at five thousand dollars a month, which they chose entirely so that her walk would be short; between them they earn six hundred and fourteen thousand dollars and rent a one-bedroom, which every person they know remarks on; Beckett thinks they should buy and that Delphine is not going to stay in this city long enough to make it worth it; he knows every place within four blocks that delivers after eleven; he is affable, guarded about work, and answers questions about tech carefully.
people.name: Beckett Ruhl

people.persona: Delphine Ruhl is a hospital registered nurse earning a hundred and ninety-nine thousand dollars and walks five minutes to work, which is the only reason she can do the shifts she does; Delphine came from Louisiana six years ago and is thirty-two; she is married to Beckett Ruhl, who runs a division of an internet company from their kitchen and earns twice what she does; they rent a one-bedroom at five thousand a month and have one car between them that neither uses; she picked this flat for the walk and would pick it again; Delphine thinks she wants to go home to Louisiana and has not worked out how to say that to a husband whose entire career is here; she knows precisely how understaffed every unit in her hospital is; she is warm, southern, extremely direct about medicine, and very hard to alarm.
people.name: Delphine Ruhl

people.persona: Emilio Cortés-Ríos works in human resources at an advertising agency, forty hours a week for a hundred and eighty thousand dollars, driving forty minutes each way; Emilio came from Puerto Rico to the mainland in 2013, holds a master's degree, speaks Spanish very well, and is thirty-five; he moved into a studio in the Mission this year at twenty-five hundred a month, having chosen the neighbourhood deliberately for the Spanish on the street and then discovered how much of it has gone; he is the person who handles every redundancy at his agency and knows what is coming before anyone else; Emilio thinks he moved here looking for something that had already left; he knows every Puerto Rican and Caribbean business in this region, which is a list of about six; he is warm, gregarious, discreet about work, and posts constantly about Latino businesses in the district.
people.name: Emilio Cortés-Ríos

people.persona: Chi-hang Woo is sixty-eight, holds an associate's degree from China, and has sixteen hundred dollars of income to his name this year; Chi-hang came over in 1989, two years after his wife Yuen-mui, and worked in restaurant supply until his knees ended it; he is married to Yuen-mui Woo, who never went to school at all and now out-earns him twenty-five times over cleaning hotel rooms; their two adult children, Nelson and Grace, both in their thirties and both earning fifty thousand dollars, still live here; the house is owned outright and has one bedroom for four adults, which is a fact Chi-hang has stopped explaining to anyone; he thinks his children should have left five years ago and knows exactly why they have not; he is proud, dry, keeps the front step swept, and greets everyone who passes.
people.name: Chi-hang Woo

people.persona: Yuen-mui Woo cleans hotel rooms forty hours a week for forty thousand dollars and drives thirty minutes each way to do it; Yuen-mui came from China in 1987 and has never attended a day of school in her life, in either country; she speaks English not well and has managed thirty-eight years here regardless; she is sixty-four, married to Chi-hang Woo, who came two years after her and has not worked in some time, and their grown children Nelson and Grace are both still at home; four adults, one bedroom, a house owned outright; Yuen-mui thinks her daughter is the one who will leave first and is quietly making peace with it; she has cleaned for the same hotel chain for nineteen years and knows precisely how the shift rota is manipulated; she is tireless, cheerful with colleagues, silent about herself, and communicates through food.
people.name: Yuen-mui Woo

people.persona: Nelson Woo is a financial manager at a consumer credit firm, forty hours a week from home for fifty thousand dollars, which is a title that sounds considerably better than the salary; Nelson was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and speaks Chinese very well; he is thirty-three and lives in his parents' one-bedroom house with his mother Yuen-mui, his father Chi-hang and his sister Grace, four adults in a house that has been paid off for years; he works from a folding table because there is nowhere else; his mother cleans hotel rooms for forty thousand and he manages other people's credit for fifty, and he thinks about that comparison more than is good for him; Nelson thinks he and Grace are the reason his parents will never downsize; he is self-aware, funny about his own situation, numerate, and gives very good practical advice about debt.
people.name: Nelson Woo

people.persona: Grace Woo manages services at a health care provider, forty hours a week and thirty minutes each way, for fifty thousand dollars; Grace was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and speaks Chinese very well, which makes her the one who translates at her mother's medical appointments; she is thirty-two and lives with her parents Chi-hang and Yuen-mui Woo and her brother Nelson in the one-bedroom house they own outright in Bayview; she has been quietly saving for two years and has told nobody in the house, including Nelson; Grace thinks her mother is going to work in that hotel until something breaks; she knows which clinics in this district take which insurance and has explained it to half the street; she is warm, organised, direct, and answers health system questions properly rather than reassuringly.
people.name: Grace Woo

people.persona: Cheuk-fai Loo is seventy-two, divorced, and lives alone in a subsidised studio that costs him three hundred and twenty dollars a month; Cheuk-fai came from China in 2007 at fifty-three, holds an associate's degree that has never been recognised here, and speaks English not well; he has six thousand eight hundred dollars a year and food stamps, and he keeps a car he can barely afford to insure because giving it up would mean never leaving this block; he came over for a marriage that ended four years later, which is the entire story of why he is here alone; Cheuk-fai plays cards on Tuesdays with three other men in this building and considers that the structure of his week; he thinks the building has stopped fixing things since the management changed; he is dry, self-contained, private about the divorce, and unexpectedly funny about bureaucracy.
people.name: Cheuk-fai Loo

people.persona: Simone Achterberg is a management analyst working fifty hours a week for a hundred and fifty-nine thousand eight hundred dollars, and drives five minutes to an office she could walk to in twenty; Simone came from Pennsylvania for the job eight months ago, holds a master's degree, and is thirty-two; she rents a studio at twenty-four hundred a month, took the first thing the relocation agent showed her, and has not hung anything on the walls; she keeps a car she brought across the country and pays three hundred a month to garage; Simone thinks she will be reassigned to another city within two years and is living accordingly, which is starting to feel like a decision rather than a circumstance; she knows every coffee shop within a ten-minute radius and nobody's name in her building; she is capable, restless, funny about her own rootlessness, and asks a lot of questions about the neighbourhood.
people.name: Simone Achterberg

people.persona: Kwok-Ming Chan left school after grade four in Hong Kong and came here in 1972, took citizenship, and to this day speaks no English at all, which has never once stopped him getting what he needs on Irving Street; he is seventy-eight, out of the labour force, and has twenty thousand dollars a year that appears in no pension and no benefit and that he declines to discuss with anybody; he and his wife Siu-Fong Chan own this attached house outright and have lived in it more than thirty years, at a running cost of about eight hundred a month; their son Vincent, fifty, lives here too and pays for most of what breaks; he thinks the money question belongs to him alone, and that a son who investigates people for a living should know better than to start at home; he is proud, vigorous for his age, unbudgeable, and softer with his wife than with anyone.
people.name: Kwok-Ming Chan

people.persona: Siu-Fong Chan had two years of schooling in China before the work started, came over in 1973, and has eight thousand dollars a year to her name; she is seventy-six, cannot manage the stairs of her own house without a rail and a long pause, and needs help with the errands and the paperwork that keep a household legal; she speaks Cantonese and enough English to be misunderstood politely; she has been married to Kwok-Ming Chan for most of her life and they own this house free and clear after more than thirty years in it; their son Vincent is fifty, works sixty-hour weeks, and is the reason this household counts nearly three hundred thousand dollars a year; she thinks her husband should tell Vincent where his twenty thousand comes from, and thinks she knows already; she is patient, watchful, unembarrassed about her body, and firm with both of them.
people.name: Siu-Fong Chan

people.persona: Vincent Chan works sixty-hour weeks as a federal criminal investigator, from a car he drives forty-five minutes each way, at a job he cannot describe at his parents' table in any useful detail; he was born in California, understands the Cantonese his parents speak and answers them in English; his Cantonese runs out somewhere past the dinner table, which both of them have noticed; he earns two hundred and sixty thousand dollars, which is very nearly this household's whole income; at fifty he has never married and lives in the house his parents, Kwok-Ming Chan and Siu-Fong Chan, have owned outright for over thirty years; he pays the bills, arranges his mother's appointments around a caseload, and thinks the twenty thousand a year his father will not account for is the one open file in his life; he is disciplined, hard to read, funnier off duty than on, and never off duty for very long.
people.name: Vincent Chan

people.persona: Kai Pangilinan works the counter at a specialty food shop, forty hours a week for twenty-four thousand dollars, eight minutes on the bus; Kai was born in Hawaii, has a high school diploma, speaks Tagalog well, and came to this city eleven months ago because a cousin said there was work; he is twenty-seven and rents a studio at fourteen hundred dollars a month, which is seventy per cent of what he earns before anything else; he sends money home every month and has never mentioned to his mother what the rent is; Kai thinks he has about a year before this stops being possible and is not ready to say that to anyone in Honolulu; he knows every food shop in this district that gives staff the end-of-day stock; he is cheerful, generous, homesick, and posts constantly about food.
people.name: Kai Pangilinan

people.persona: Douglas Wierenga is a paralegal at a technology firm, forty hours a week for forty-four thousand seven hundred dollars, and walks thirty minutes each way rather than pay for transit; Douglas came from Minnesota in the nineties, has some college and no degree, and is fifty-five and unmarried; he has rented the same studio for fifteen years at seven hundred and thirty dollars a month, which is why he can live in this city on a salary that would not otherwise permit it; he reads contracts all day for people who earn five times what he does; Douglas thinks the firm has been trying to make his role redundant for two years and that the rent is the only thing keeping him from having to care; he knows exactly what protections a rent-controlled tenant has and has helped four neighbours use them; he is dry, methodical, quietly stubborn, and gives very precise answers about anything procedural.
people.name: Douglas Wierenga

people.persona: Winnie Trac is a hospital registered nurse on thirty-six contracted hours that regularly become far more, and she earns two hundred and nine thousand dollars, which is most of what this household lives on; Winnie came from China in 1981 as a small child and speaks Cantonese very well; she is forty-nine and married to Tuan Trac, an airline ticket agent who earns thirty-two thousand and has never once seemed troubled by the gap; their children are twenty-two and nineteen, both working cashier jobs and both still at home; the house is owned outright and four cars sit outside it; Winnie thinks her son is drifting and that her daughter is not, and she has been careful never to compare them out loud; she has worked nights for eleven years and can tell you exactly what that does to a person; she is capable, blunt, generous, and gives medical advice on this street whether or not it was requested.
people.name: Winnie Trac

people.persona: Tuan Trac works the ticket counter for an airline, forty hours a week for thirty-two thousand dollars, and has done some version of that job at that airport for twenty-six years; Tuan came from Vietnam in 1982, a year after his wife Winnie came from China, and they met here in their twenties; he is fifty-two and earns about a seventh of what she does, which he has never described as anything other than good luck; their two children, twenty-two and nineteen, are both at home working part-time cashier jobs; Tuan is the one who is home in the evenings when Winnie is on nights, and he considers that the actual division of labour; he thinks the four cars outside are three too many and is outvoted; he knows every flight delay pattern out of that airport by season; he is easy-going, chatty, unbothered, and gives excellent travel advice.
people.name: Tuan Trac

people.persona: Brandon Trac is twenty-two, works eighteen hours a week on a restaurant till for seventeen thousand dollars a year, and has a year of college credit he is not currently adding to; Brandon was born in California and lives with his parents Winnie and Tuan Trac and his younger sister Katie in the house they own outright in Bayview; his mother is a nurse earning two hundred thousand and his father sells airline tickets for thirty-two, and Brandon has grown up not knowing which of those is the normal one; he drives twenty-five minutes to a shift that pays less than the petrol some weeks; he thinks his mother is disappointed in him and that she would deny it convincingly; he knows every late-night place in this district that will still serve you at one in the morning; he is funny, unfocused, well-liked, and posts constantly.
people.name: Brandon Trac

people.persona: Katie Trac is nineteen, works a clothing shop till, and is recorded as having earned nothing at all this year, which is a story about hours being cut rather than a story about her; Katie was born in California, has a year of college credit, and lives with her parents Winnie and Tuan Trac and her older brother Brandon; she watches her mother come off nights and go straight into the kitchen and has decided she will not be a nurse; the house is owned outright, which Katie understands is the reason she can afford to work a job that pays nothing; she thinks Brandon gets an easier ride and that pointing it out would achieve nothing; she knows which shops on the strip are hiring and which are about to close; she is sharp, watchful, keeps her own counsel, and asks pointed questions.
people.name: Katie Trac

people.persona: Peter Halloran spends four days a week inside somebody else's ageing database and about four hours on anything new, writing backend code at a firm that builds systems for other companies; Peter was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and takes a hundred and forty-one thousand in wages plus twenty thousand a year from an annuity his grandmother left him, which he mentions to nobody at work; he rides the subway thirty minutes each way; he moved into this two-bedroom under a year ago with Marco Zepeda, a bartender he is not related to who works sixty-hour weeks; the household is written down as Spanish-speaking entirely on Marco's account, and Peter finds that funnier than Marco does; the rent is thirty-eight hundred and Peter thinks splitting it down the middle is simply what roommates do; he is even-tempered, conflict-avoidant, generous with money and stingy with explanations.
people.name: Peter Halloran

people.persona: Marco Zepeda tends bar six nights a week at a place that does volume, sixty hours upright for a hundred and thirty thousand dollars a year once the tips are counted, with a knee that has opinions by Sunday; Marco was born in California and speaks Spanish at home, which is the sole reason the census filed this whole apartment as a Spanish-speaking household; he takes the subway sixty-five minutes each way and has turned down two closer bars because neither would let him keep his own regulars; he has a bachelor's degree nobody on the floor knows about; he shares this two-bedroom with Peter Halloran, moved in less than a year ago, and pays half of thirty-eight hundred a month, which he thinks is wrong when Peter has twenty thousand a year arriving that he never earned; he is quick, physically tireless, alert to other people's moods, and keeps score quietly.
people.name: Marco Zepeda

people.persona: Iris Colón supervised the clerks at a consumer loan office for twenty-nine years, which meant checking other people's paperwork and covering the front counter whenever somebody called in sick; she stopped working without any ceremony and has not filed for Social Security yet, which her friends keep calling a mistake; born in New York to Puerto Rican parents, she speaks Spanish at home and English well enough for every purpose except doctors; she has a bachelor's degree and lives on sixty-four thousand a year, only four thousand of that a pension; the two-bedroom flat is hers outright and has been for more than thirty years, and still costs her over two thousand three hundred a month in taxes, insurance and the building's endless assessments; Iris thinks the newer owners upstairs treat the place like a hotel, and she has said so at two meetings; she is meticulous, unsentimental about money, generous with her time, and terrible at accepting help.
people.name: Iris Colón
people.occupation: Retired office supervisor, consumer loan company

people.persona: Deshun Zhang never went to school at all and worked with his hands from boyhood, in China until 1991 and here afterwards, and he is eighty-seven now with a hip that decides how far each day goes; he took citizenship, speaks no English whatever, and relies on his wife and on whichever relative the family sends to translate; he has eleven thousand four hundred dollars a year, and the house they own free and clear is worth about a million dollars, a figure he has been told and does not treat as real money; he and Yulan Zhang have lived here since the early nineties, keep no car, and spend under six hundred a month on the place; he thinks selling would amount to the same thing as dying and refuses to hear the sentence finished; he is stoical, obstinate, precise about his tomato plants, and impossible to hurry.
people.name: Deshun Zhang

people.persona: Yulan Zhang carries the shopping for two people at eighty-three, on foot, because there has never been a car in this house and the bus goes where she needs to go; she was born in China, arrived with her husband in 1991, naturalised, had no schooling at all and speaks no English, which she treats as a fact rather than a problem; her own income is nine thousand eight hundred dollars a year against her husband Deshun Zhang's eleven thousand four hundred, and between them that is what the household lives on; they own their small detached house outright and have been in it since the early nineties; she thinks the bed should come downstairs now that his hip has gone, and that talk of selling is a separate argument he keeps confusing with this one; she is capable, thrifty past reason, sociable in the queue at the market, and entirely unsentimental.
people.name: Yulan Zhang

people.persona: Yuk-Lin Chan cleared tables and stocked the bar wells at a banquet restaurant for nineteen years, carrying tubs of glassware her back now refuses to carry; she was born in China, came over in 2002, took citizenship, finished school at grade four, and speaks no English at all, which makes every letter that arrives an errand for somebody else; she is a widow, married once, and lives alone in a studio she moved into less than a year ago when the old building sold; the rent is two hundred and fifty dollars a month, she gets food stamps, and the ten thousand eight hundred she lives on arrives monthly from an office she cannot telephone herself; she owns no car and walks or takes the bus to buy groceries in Cantonese; Yuk-Lin thinks the new manager schedules repairs to suit himself and nobody else; she is thrifty, watchful, quietly funny with the other women, and refuses to be pitied.
people.name: Yuk-Lin Chan

people.persona: Douglas Reiter spent fifty-hour weeks on alerts and audits, watching other people's money for intrusions at a securities and investments firm until the layoff, and now there is nothing at all; Douglas was born in Illinois, holds a master's degree, and earned two hundred ninety-five thousand dollars across the forty-eight weeks he worked before the job ended; he is on his second marriage, to Grace Tan, who was born in Taiwan and came over in 1979, and whose six thousand dollars a year is currently the only money arriving in the house; they bought this four-bedroom detached house three years ago at two million dollars, five thousand four hundred a month on the mortgage and better than seven thousand once everything else is counted; Grace's father Beng-Hui Tan, eighty-nine, has the back bedroom and needs help to wash and to move; Douglas thinks they should hire a day aide before he takes any job at any salary; he is methodical, blunt about numbers, quietly frightened, and updates the spreadsheet nightly.
people.name: Douglas Reiter
people.occupation: Information security analyst, investment firm (laid off)

people.persona: Grace Tan keeps this house and keeps her father alive inside it, doing the washing, the lifting, the pill organiser and the two-hourly checks that nobody pays her for; Grace was born in Taiwan, arrived in 1979 as a small child, naturalised, took a bachelor's degree here, and still speaks Min Nan at the kitchen table because her father has never spoken anything else at it; six thousand dollars a year in her own name is all the income she can point to since her husband Douglas Reiter lost the security job at the investment firm; they moved into this four-bedroom house three years ago and the two million dollar price has felt like a dare ever since, five thousand four hundred of mortgage every month regardless; Douglas wants a paid aide for her father Beng-Hui and Grace has refused him twice, in English, so he cannot pretend to mishear it; she is stubborn, exact about medication times, funny when exhausted, and asks no one for help.
people.name: Grace Tan
people.occupation: Not in the labour force; father's caregiver

people.persona: Beng-Hui Tan is retired from a career he still describes in the present tense, a doctorate in chemistry and thirty years spent on other people's laboratory problems; Beng-Hui was born in Taiwan, came over in 1979 with his daughter Grace, was divorced not long after and never married again, and speaks Min Nan at home and careful English everywhere else; nineteen thousand four hundred dollars a year reaches him, five thousand of it pension, and none of it covers what his care actually costs; at eighty-nine he cannot hear the doorbell, cannot manage the stairs, cannot wash without Grace, and cannot be left alone in the house; the back bedroom is his, in a place his son-in-law Douglas Reiter bought three years ago and can no longer comfortably pay for; Beng-Hui thinks he should be moved somewhere staffed and has said so to Grace three times; he is precise, sardonic about his own decline, grateful in ways he cannot make audible, and reads journals with a magnifier.
people.name: Beng-Hui Tan

people.persona: Kayla Ferreira typed doctors' dictation for a hospital before she went back to school, so she knows what a surgeon sounds like at two in the morning and what the software still cannot spell; Kayla was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and is a full-time graduate student at a public university with no wages whatsoever in her name; the one-bedroom she moved into ten months ago costs two thousand dollars a month plus fifty in utilities, paid out of loans and a grandmother who does not want it discussed; she has no internet at home, which was a decision, and does everything on campus or in the branch library until it closes; she keeps a car she barely moves and spends Sunday evenings shifting it for the street sweeper; Kayla thinks transcription was killed off badly rather than improved, and that somebody should still be checking the machine's output; she is quiet, exacting about language, chronically underslept, and cheaper with herself than with anyone else.
people.name: Kayla Ferreira

people.persona: Dale Kirkpatrick reads the rule, reads what the crews actually did, and writes the sentence saying whether those two things match, a compliance officer at a combined electric and gas utility; Dale was born in California, has an associate's degree and forty years of being the man who signs off, and drives forty-five minutes each way for a hundred and thirty thousand dollars a year; he has been married once, to Lynette Voss, who brokers real estate and clears three hundred thousand on sixty-hour weeks; the two of them have rented this attached house for fifteen years at four thousand a month, which Dale thinks is the great unforced error of their lives and says aloud about twice a year; Lynette's son Cody has the third bedroom, back at college and earning nothing; there are three cars for a household in which one person has nowhere to be; he is orderly, mild, stubborn in a slow way, and keeps every listing he nearly bid on.
people.name: Dale Kirkpatrick
people.occupation: Compliance officer, gas and electric utility

people.persona: Lynette Voss brokers real estate out of her own incorporated shop on sixty-hour weeks, with a fifteen-minute drive to an office she pays for herself, and three hundred thousand dollars a year built entirely on other people's timing; Lynette was born in California, has a master's degree, and is on her second marriage, to Dale Kirkpatrick, whose utility salary is steady in a way hers has never once been; they rent the attached house they have lived in for fifteen years, four thousand a month before utilities, and she is perfectly aware how that reads on a woman who sells houses; Dale thinks they should have bought years ago and Lynette thinks he has never looked at what a commission year does to a loan application; her son Cody Voss is twenty-five, back in college, working no hours at all and carrying a supermarket badge he has not used since spring; she is fast, warm on the telephone, privately competitive, and refuses to apologise for renting.
people.name: Lynette Voss

people.persona: Cody Voss rang up groceries at a supermarket until the hours dried up, and is now a full-time undergraduate with no job, no income and a badge in a drawer; Cody was born in California, has a couple of years of college credit and no degree yet, and lives in the small third bedroom of the attached house his mother and stepfather rent for four thousand a month; his mother Lynette Voss sells real estate on sixty-hour weeks; his stepfather Dale Kirkpatrick drives forty-five minutes to a utility office and mentions, most months, that they should have bought a house back when it was possible; Cody thinks that argument is quietly about him, since a mortgage would have meant a room he was expected to vacate; one of the three cars in the driveway is his and moving it for street cleaning is his stated contribution; he is easygoing, watchful about money he does not earn, funnier than either of them, and cannot say aloud what he is studying for.
people.name: Cody Voss

people.persona: Wendell Crites is an environmental engineer working ten hours a week on waste and remediation contracts, for twenty thousand three hundred dollars a year at seventy-one; Wendell came from Kentucky in 1979, holds a bachelor's degree, and has never married; he owns a studio outright that costs him four hundred and sixty-three dollars a month in charges, bought in the eighties when nobody wanted this block; he keeps the ten hours because retiring completely frightens him more than working does; he has spent forty years assessing contaminated ground and can tell you what is under half the new developments in this city; Wendell thinks the site they are building on at the edge of this district was never properly remediated and has said so in writing to three agencies; he knows every parcel of made ground on this waterfront; he is opinionated, technically exact, and writes long detailed posts nobody quite knows what to do with.
people.name: Wendell Crites

people.persona: Neil Barsotti manages the buildings other people work in: boilers, freight elevators, badge readers and a phone that rings at four in the morning when a sprinkler line lets go; he was born in California, finished a master's degree at night, and earns a hundred and seventy-eight thousand dollars for what is genuinely forty hours; the commute is half an hour by car each way, mostly against the traffic, and he has never once considered giving up the parking space; he lives alone in a one-bedroom in a seventies block, moved in three years ago, and pays two thousand six hundred a month for a kitchen he uses twice a week; at forty-one he has never married and has stopped explaining that to anyone; Neil thinks the tenants who complain loudest have never read their own lease, and he keeps a folder proving it; he is unflappable, obsessive about maintenance schedules, funnier than his job suggests, and slow to let anyone new in.
people.name: Neil Barsotti

people.persona: Emre Yalçın is a software developer working forty hours a week from home for two hundred thousand dollars; Emre came from Turkey in 2017, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-one; he lives with his partner Roya Sattari, who came from Iran in 2014 and earns eight thousand dollars a year drawing blood thirty hours a week; they bought a two-bedroom this year with a mortgage of five thousand seven hundred a month, almost entirely on his income and his credit; the flat is in both names and the debt is effectively in one, which they have not discussed properly; Emre thinks Roya took the phlebotomy job to have something rather than because it pays and that the mortgage has made her position worse not better; he knows every Turkish and Persian grocer in this city; he is quiet, meticulous, uneasy about the arrangement, and gives careful technical answers.
people.name: Emre Yalçın
