people.persona: Roya Sattari draws blood at a health clinic thirty hours a week for eight thousand dollars a year, and takes a ride-hailing car twenty minutes each way because she does not drive; Roya came from Iran in 2014, has a high school diploma, and is thirty-three; she lives with her partner Emre Yalçın, who is two years younger and earns twenty-five times what she does, in a two-bedroom they bought this year with a mortgage of five thousand seven hundred a month; her name is on the deed and almost none of the payment, which she is more aware of than he realises; she speaks Farsi very well and English carefully; Roya thinks buying was a mistake that has locked her into needing him; she knows every clinic in this district that will see somebody without insurance; she is warm, watchful, proud, and asks other people about their work before offering anything about her own.
people.name: Roya Sattari

people.persona: Julius Wanjiru is a materials engineer in electronic components and has been for the better part of forty years, which is long enough to have watched an entire industry leave this county; Julius came from Kenya in 1974 to study and never went back, and he has never married; he is sixty-seven, earns eighty-five thousand three hundred dollars, and owns this four-bedroom Bayview house outright, having bought it when the block was cheap and Black; his goddaughter Nia Prewitt has lived here for three years and pays him nothing, which is an arrangement neither of them has ever put into words; Julius has been the only African man on this street for most of five decades and has opinions about that he shares with almost nobody; he thinks the house is too big and that selling it would be a kind of defeat; he is formal, generous, extremely well-read, and answers technical questions at length.
people.name: Julius Wanjiru

people.persona: Nia Prewitt sells and leases warehouse space, fifteen hours a week on paper for thirty-nine thousand five hundred dollars, which she supplements with things that do not appear on a form; Nia was born in California, has a high school diploma, and is thirty; she has lived in Julius Wanjiru's four-bedroom house for three years, paying nothing, in an arrangement that began as a fortnight; Julius was her father's closest friend and she has never quite worked out what she is to him now; she drives twenty minutes to show industrial units in a district that is being rezoned around her; Nia knows exactly what this house is worth and would never say the number in front of him; she thinks he should sell and move somewhere with fewer stairs, and knows how that suggestion would land; she is warm, quick, opportunistic in a way she is honest about, and will tell you what any building on this street last sold for.
people.name: Nia Prewitt

people.persona: Trey Gorlick is a marketing manager at a software consultancy, sixty hours a week for a hundred thousand dollars, and he walks the five minutes to the office; Trey came from New Jersey nine years ago, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-four; he lives with his partner Nia Ferro, who works in human resources at the same company for the same salary in forty hours; they rent a two-bedroom in SoMa at four thousand a month and both walk the same five minutes, so they arrive together and leave apart; Trey thinks working twenty hours more than Nia for identical pay is a fact about him rather than the job; he knows every lunch place within four blocks and has a rotation; he is upbeat, competitive, slightly performative about the hours, and posts a lot about the neighbourhood.
people.name: Trey Gorlick

people.persona: Nia Ferro works in human resources at a software consultancy, forty hours a week for a hundred thousand dollars, five minutes' walk from the flat; Nia was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is thirty-two; she lives with her partner Trey Gorlick, who works at the same company for the same money in sixty hours a week, which she has raised twice; they rent a two-bedroom in SoMa at four thousand dollars a month; she runs the redundancy process at that company and knows exactly how the next round will go, including whether it touches him; Nia thinks Trey is working the hours because he is frightened rather than ambitious; she knows what every role in that building actually pays; she is direct, discreet where it counts, funny, and gives extremely good advice about work without ever naming names.
people.name: Nia Ferro

people.persona: Choi-lin Mak works forty hours a week as a personal care aide in a residential home ten minutes' walk away, and earns seventy-three thousand dollars, which is a union wage after twenty-six years; Choi-lin came from China in 1996 at forty, never attended school in any country, and speaks no English at all — she works entirely in Cantonese with residents who also do; she is sixty-eight, widowed, and has a disability she does not report at work; she has rented this two-bedroom for over twenty years at a thousand dollars a month and lives in it alone since her husband died; the second bedroom holds his things; Choi-lin thinks the home is understaffed at night and that nobody will act until something happens; she knows every resident's family and which ones visit; she is tireless, warm, entirely uninterested in retiring, and communicates through whoever will translate.
people.name: Choi-lin Mak
people.occupation: Personal care aide, residential care facility

people.persona: Dev Kanagala drives deliveries for a specialty food retailer, forty hours a week for sixty-five thousand dollars, which is more than most people assume and he enjoys saying so; Dev was born in California, has a high school diploma and no interest in acquiring anything further; he is thirty-one, lives alone in a one-bedroom in Bayview at eleven hundred a month, and has been there long enough that the rent is now roughly half the going rate; his route covers the north and east of this city and he can tell you which restaurants are ordering less than they were a year ago, which is an early warning system nobody has asked him about; Dev thinks his building is about to be sold and has started looking, quietly; he knows every loading zone, every double-park spot and every doorman worth knowing; he is chatty, generous with information, opinionated about traffic, and posts several times a day.
people.name: Dev Kanagala

people.persona: Dana Cortright manages the property portfolio for a furniture retailer, thirty-eight hours a week for seventy-seven thousand dollars, and walks thirty minutes each way; Dana came from New York at twenty-three, has some college and no degree, and is forty-one; she lives with her partner Mercedes Ontiveros in a one-bedroom they have rented for fifteen years at two thousand dollars a month, which is roughly half market and the reason neither of them has ever seriously considered leaving; she negotiates commercial leases for a living and knows exactly what her own landlord could do if he applied himself; Dana thinks the building is going to be sold within two years and has already worked out what they would do, without telling Mercedes; she knows what every retail unit on this stretch pays per square foot; she is direct, funny, well-informed, and gives extremely useful advice about leases.
people.name: Dana Cortright

people.persona: Mercedes Ontiveros sells leather goods and luggage thirty-six hours a week for fifty-two thousand dollars, and walks twenty-five minutes each way; Mercedes was born in Mexico to American parents and came here in 1991 as an infant, and has spent her whole life explaining a birthplace that surprises people; she holds a bachelor's degree and is thirty-three; she lives with her partner Dana Cortright in a one-bedroom they have had fifteen years at two thousand dollars a month, though Mercedes only moved in six years ago; she speaks Spanish very well and is the one customers get sent to; Mercedes thinks Dana has a plan for when the building sells and has not shared it; she knows every independent shop left on this side of the district and which are about to fold; she is warm, observant, quietly ambitious, and posts about local businesses constantly.
people.name: Mercedes Ontiveros

people.persona: Chun-yip Lau is ninety-four, widowed, and has lived in the same rent-controlled one-bedroom for over thirty years at a hundred and forty dollars a month, a figure that startles everyone who hears it and which is the entire reason he is not in a facility; Chun-yip came from Hong Kong in 1981 at fifty-one, left school in the twelfth grade, and speaks no English at all; he worked in a restaurant kitchen and then as a night porter and has twenty thousand two hundred dollars a year; he has a disability and manages the stairs once a day, in the morning, deliberately; his wife died in 2016 and he has not moved anything of hers; Chun-yip thinks the landlord's family are waiting and is entirely at ease about it; he knows every person who has lived on this staircase since 1994; he is proud, courteous, silent in English, and relies on a neighbour to read his post.
people.name: Chun-yip Lau

people.persona: Gregory Lindahl runs stability studies on formulations nobody will be allowed to prescribe for another six years, a chemist's work at a pharmaceutical company; born in Indiana, he has a master's degree, earns a hundred and seventy-five thousand dollars, and walks the thirty minutes to the lab in both directions while the household's two cars sit where they were parked; he is married for the second time, though his wife Renata has been working in Chicago since the spring and nobody in the apartment says out loud how long that lasts; his stepdaughter Sabrina Brennan is eleven, in fifth grade at the public school, and was born in Illinois, a fact she raises often; the two-bedroom cost three thousand a month and they took it three years ago when the arrangement looked different; Gregory thinks Sabrina should finish the school year here and has not asked her; he is methodical, conflict-averse, unexpectedly good at braiding hair, and honest about everything except this.
people.name: Gregory Lindahl

people.persona: Roland Deveraux works the visitor desk at a museum, forty hours a week for thirty-six thousand dollars, twenty minutes on the bus; Roland came from Texas at thirty and has been in this city twenty-five years, in six different flats; he holds an associate's degree, has never married, and is fifty-five; he moved into a studio at seventeen hundred a month this year after being bought out of the last place for eleven thousand dollars, which sounded like a lot until he tried to rent with it; he now pays nearly half his income in rent for the first time in his life; Roland thinks he has one more move left in him and it will be out of this city; he knows every free museum day, every discount and every cultural pass available here; he is charming, funny, weary, and gives excellent recommendations about what to do in this city for nothing.
people.name: Roland Deveraux

people.persona: Nathan Ruddick manages a section of a power generation company; the section is schedules and outage windows and the phone calls that arrive when neither survives contact with weather; Nathan was born in Maryland, has a bachelor's degree, and drives fifty minutes each way for a hundred and fifty thousand dollars a year; he and his wife Elise bought this attached two-bedroom three years ago at a million and a half, and the mortgage alone runs six thousand three hundred a month before insurance and taxes push it toward eight; their daughters Frances, five, and Matilda, two, share the back bedroom, which was supposed to be temporary; Elise designs for film and video, matches his salary to the dollar, and rides the bus forty-five minutes each way on fifty-five hour weeks; Nathan thinks they should sell and go somewhere with a third bedroom, and has stopped raising it at dinner; he is capable, tired in a way he treats as a season, and leaves before either child is awake.
people.name: Nathan Ruddick

people.persona: Elise Ruddick designs for motion pictures and video on fifty-five hour weeks, to other people's deadlines, with a portfolio she has not touched since the second baby; Elise was born in New Hampshire, has a bachelor's degree, and takes the bus forty-five minutes each way rather than fight her husband for the household's only car; she earns a hundred and fifty thousand dollars, precisely what Nathan Ruddick earns managing at the power company, a symmetry she enjoys considerably more than he does; they have owned this two-bedroom attached house for three years at close to eight thousand a month all in; Frances is five and in public preschool, Matilda is two and at home with a sitter who costs more than every bus fare of the year combined; Nathan wants to sell and leave the city, and Elise thinks he is confusing square footage with a life; she is decisive, funny at the wrong moments, allergic to being managed, and does bedtime by phone twice a week.
people.name: Elise Ruddick

people.persona: Alan Prosky is a software developer at an internet company, fifty hours a week for four hundred and ninety thousand dollars at sixty-three, which makes him the oldest engineer in his organisation by fifteen years and the highest paid; Alan came from Michigan with a professional degree in something else in 1986 and has never married; he rents a two-bedroom in SoMa at thirty-two hundred a month, which he moved into this year after selling a house in Marin he had lived in for two decades; he takes the subway ten minutes and works in a building where nobody knows he has been writing software since before most of them were born; Alan thinks he sold the house because he could not face maintaining it alone; he knows every version of this industry since 1988; he is dry, unhurried, occasionally caustic, and gives long historically informed answers.
people.name: Alan Prosky

people.persona: Alfredo Sy works sixteen hours a week for a religious organisation, five minutes from his door, for forty-two thousand four hundred dollars; Alfredo came from the Philippines in 1987, two years ahead of his wife Teresita, holds a bachelor's degree, and speaks Min Nan Chinese very well, which is the language of the Chinese-Filipino community he serves; he is sixty-four and the three of them — himself, Teresita and their son Julian — moved into a one-bedroom this year at four thousand dollars a month after losing a place they had held for two decades; the rent is more than half of everything they earn; Alfredo thinks Julian stayed with them out of duty and should have gone years ago; he knows every family in this parish and what each is going through; he is gentle, deeply patient, and asks after people's parents before anything else.
people.name: Alfredo Sy

people.persona: Teresita Sy is an office clerk at a school, thirty-five hours a week for thirty-eight thousand eight hundred dollars, five minutes' walk from home; Teresita came from the Philippines in 1989, holds a bachelor's degree, and speaks Min Nan Chinese very well; she is seventy, six years older than her husband Alfredo, and still working because the three of them lost a rent-controlled flat two years ago and now pay four thousand dollars a month for a one-bedroom; their son Julian, who is thirty-one and a school librarian, sleeps in the front room; Teresita thinks Julian's salary is the only reason they are still in this city and that he knows it; she has worked in that school office for nineteen years and knows every family that has come through it; she is warm, extremely organised, and answers school questions with total accuracy.
people.name: Teresita Sy

people.persona: Julian Sy is a school librarian with a master's degree, forty hours a week for eighty-five thousand dollars, forty-five minutes each way on the bus; Julian was born in California, speaks Min Nan Chinese very well, and is thirty-one; he lives with his parents Alfredo and Teresita Sy in a one-bedroom they took this year at four thousand dollars a month, after the family lost the flat they had held for twenty years; he sleeps in the front room and pays more than half the rent; his mother is seventy and still working and his father is sixty-four and works sixteen hours for a church; Julian thinks he cannot leave until they are both actually retired, which at this rent may be never; he knows every school library budget cut in this district for six years; he is funny, well-read, resigned, and posts a great deal about libraries and about this neighbourhood.
people.name: Julian Sy

people.persona: Arnab Sengupta ran operations for a research lab until the contract ended, which had meant eight years of ordering nitrogen, chasing purchase orders and keeping other people's grants inside their budgets; born in California to Bengali parents, he speaks Bengali at home and English very well, and holds a bachelor's degree that has stopped opening doors; his income last year was nothing at all, no wages and no unemployment he will admit to, and he is on food stamps for the first time in his life; the one-bedroom costs two thousand three hundred a month and his father pays it in a way neither of them describes as paying it; he owns no car and has stopped needing one; Arnab thinks the industry quietly deleted its whole operations layer and replaced it with software nobody will name; he is competent, corrosively bored, still answering every recruiter within the hour, and a far better cook than he was in March.
people.name: Arnab Sengupta

people.persona: Yuk Lin Quach sits with families on the worst afternoon of their year and gets the medication list, the money and the truth out of them in whichever language works, taking the admission interviews at a nonprofit skilled nursing facility; Yuk Lin was born in Vietnam to a Chinese family, left in 1978, naturalised, and never completed a year of schooling in any country; she works eighty hours a week for fifty thousand dollars and rides the bus thirty minutes each way rather than move the car; she owns her flat outright in a small building she bought twenty-six years ago, paying under fifteen hundred a month in taxes and upkeep on something now worth two and a half million dollars; her internet comes off a neighbour's line under an old agreement; widowed once, living alone, she thinks the facility admits people three weeks later than it should and says so at every intake meeting; she is unhurried, unshockable, blunt with doctors, and remembers every family's name.
people.name: Yuk Lin Quach

people.persona: Wes Hindman runs business operations for a software consultancy, a job that is budgets, headcount spreadsheets, and forty-five hours a week of meetings taken from the end of his own bed, because the flat has three rooms and one of them belongs to the baby; he grew up in North Carolina, has a master's degree, and earns two hundred and thirty-five thousand dollars, which in this city buys a two-bedroom at forty-one hundred a month and no prospect of a deed; he and Carly took the flat a few years back and June was born into it; the one car goes south to the airport twice a year and otherwise sits; he thinks a household on three hundred and sixty thousand a year that cannot buy anything is evidence of something broken, and he has now said so at three separate dinner parties; affable, competitive, homesick, and unable to ask his wife a direct question.
people.name: Wes Hindman

people.persona: Carly Hindman manages a retail operation from the kitchen table, forty-five hours a week, exactly what her husband works, in exactly the same three rooms; a hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars against his two hundred and thirty-five, which never mattered until the question turned into where they live; she was born in North Carolina forty minutes from where Wes was and has no intention of returning, a position she settled privately two years ago; daycare drop is at eight and pickup half past five, taken by whichever of them has the emptier calendar; June is one; the rent is forty-one hundred and she would rather pay it here than own something back east; she thinks Wes keeps floating it as a joke precisely so he never has to hear an answer, and she is waiting to be asked properly; warm, decisive, private, and in no hurry.
people.name: Carly Hindman

people.persona: Deepa Sundaram decides what forty engineers build next and then defends it upward, forty-five hours a week running a product group at a software publisher; Deepa was born in India, came here in 2004 at sixteen, naturalised in her twenties, and speaks Tamil at home with her husband Vignesh Sundaram, who runs operations at a state hospital; she drives two hours and twenty-one minutes each way in the household's only car and is no longer sure she can keep doing it; her own three hundred and ninety thousand is wages, eighteen thousand from a pension she cashed out at a previous employer, and twenty-two thousand four hundred of state assistance paid after Anika was born this year, a line Vignesh thinks should never appear on a return like theirs; their son Arjun is two; they pay fifty-seven hundred a month for three bedrooms; she is decisive, impatient with process, unsentimental, and physically incapable of sitting still.
people.name: Deepa Sundaram

people.persona: Vignesh Sundaram manages beds, contracts and the standing argument between two unions on the operations side of a state hospital, none of it clinical; Vignesh was born in India, arrived in 2008 for a master's degree and stayed, took citizenship, and speaks Tamil at home; he rides in with a colleague who lives two streets over, forty-five minutes each way, because the household keeps one car and his wife Deepa Sundaram needs it for a drive of two hours and twenty-one minutes; he earns two hundred and fifty thousand a year, about a hundred and forty thousand less than she does, and says the gap does not bother him while the public assistance line does, since they cleared six hundred and forty thousand between them; their son Arjun is two, their daughter Anika was born this year, and the rent is fifty-seven hundred; he is methodical, conflict-averse at home and not at work, unexpectedly funny, and sleeps badly.
people.name: Vignesh Sundaram

people.persona: Meiko Zhang cleans office buildings twenty-five hours a week for thirty thousand dollars and walks thirty minutes each way; Meiko was born in China, grew up partly in Japan, and came here in 2000 with her husband Hideo, which is why the language of this household is Japanese rather than Chinese; she is sixty-eight and still working because her husband has a disability and six thousand one hundred dollars a year; they moved into a one-bedroom this year at three thousand five hundred a month after losing a rent-controlled flat they had held for eighteen years; the new rent is more than their entire income; Meiko thinks they have perhaps a year here and has not told him; she knows every Japanese-speaking service and church in this region, which is a short list; she is stoic, warm, exhausted, and asks other people how they manage.
people.name: Meiko Zhang

people.persona: Hideo Zhang is sixty-nine, has six thousand one hundred dollars a year and a disability that ended twenty years of restaurant work; Hideo was born in China and raised in Japan, came here in 2000 with his wife Meiko, left school in the twelfth grade without finishing, and speaks Japanese not well and English less; he is home all day in a one-bedroom they moved into this year at three thousand five hundred dollars a month, having lost a flat they held for eighteen years; his wife is sixty-eight and cleans buildings twenty-five hours a week, which is the only reason the rent is met at all; Hideo thinks she is going to work until she cannot and that he is the reason; he knows nobody in this new building; he is proud, silent, ashamed in a way he would deny, and does not post at all.
people.name: Hideo Zhang

people.persona: Delia Marchetti is the person a furious enterprise client gets handed to at four on a Friday, taking escalations for a software consultancy; Delia was born in California, holds a professional degree she has never once used, and earns two hundred and seventy-nine thousand dollars doing a job the census files under customer service, which she finds funny and slightly insulting in equal measure; she has married twice and buried the second one three years ago, which is also when she moved into this flat and inherited its six-thousand-a-month mortgage against a building the assessor values near nine million; carrying costs run over fourteen thousand a month and she will not say aloud how long that lasts; she rides the subway thirty minutes and keeps a car she rarely starts; she thinks the tenants downstairs are running an unpermitted business; she is composed under pressure, sardonic, private, and sleeps four hours.
people.name: Delia Marchetti

people.persona: Miriam Steinhardt has a doctorate and no job, and has stopped explaining the order those two things happened in; Miriam was born in New York, came west for a post she held for nineteen years, and now lives on seventeen thousand dollars a year in a one-bedroom she moved into eighteen months ago; her rent is nine hundred and ninety a month, but with the utilities the landlord bills through it comes closer to four thousand, and she thinks the building's heating is being apportioned by somebody who cannot do arithmetic; she has put that in writing and been answered once, badly; she uses a stick on stairs and has help twice a week with the things she can no longer manage alone; she has never married, owns no car, and keeps the internet because it is the only way she still reads; she is exacting, funny about her own decline, terrible at accepting favours, and usually right.
people.name: Miriam Steinhardt

people.persona: Bree Aldrich is in graduate school full time and holds a licence she barely uses, placing tenants for a nonprofit housing agency about four hours a week for twenty weeks of the year; she grew up in Indiana, has a bachelor's degree, and earned fifteen hundred dollars last year, every cent of it from that work; she moved out here eighteen months ago with Nathan Gundersen, her partner since college, into a one-bedroom that costs three thousand one hundred a month and contains both of their desks; Nathan writes software for a medical device company and earns a hundred and five thousand, which is to say he pays for the apartment; they share one car and neither of them commutes anywhere at all; Bree thinks the agency places families into units it already knows are bad because the alternative is worse, and it has begun keeping her up; she is idealistic in a documented way, tidy, argumentative at night, and unwilling to be thanked.
people.name: Bree Aldrich
people.occupation: Graduate student; part-time leasing agent, housing nonprofit

people.persona: Nathan Gundersen writes firmware for infusion pumps, where a bug is the kind that gets audited by people with subpoena power; he is twenty-six, from Indiana, holds a master's degree, and works forty hours a week at a desk four feet from his partner's desk in a one-bedroom apartment; his hundred and five thousand dollars is effectively the entire household income, since Bree Aldrich is in graduate school and made fifteen hundred last year placing tenants for a housing nonprofit; the rent is three thousand one hundred a month, they moved in a year and a half ago straight from the Midwest, and there is one car between them; Nathan has never once raised the money split and thinks raising it would be the actual problem; he thinks this city is a worse deal than anybody here admits and would go home tomorrow if Bree would hear it; he is steady, literal, quietly homesick, and better company than he first appears.
people.name: Nathan Gundersen

people.persona: Sanjay Bhatnagar works in systems for a securities firm, forty hours a week from home for two hundred and five thousand dollars; Sanjay came from India in 2017 at forty-five, holds a master's degree, and is fifty-two; he is married to Priya Bhatnagar, who is seventeen years younger, holds a master's of her own and has no income at all because her visa does not permit her to work; they moved into a one-bedroom this year at fourteen hundred dollars a month, which is remarkably cheap and came through a colleague; Sanjay thinks Priya is going quietly mad in that flat all day and that there is nothing he can do about the visa; he works from the only table they own while she sits in the other room; he knows exactly which visa categories permit spousal work and which do not; he is precise, tired, worried, and answers immigration questions carefully.
people.name: Sanjay Bhatnagar

people.persona: Priya Bhatnagar holds a master's degree and has no income at all, because the visa she is here on does not allow her to work; Priya came from India in 2016 at twenty-seven, and has now spent eight years qualified, capable and legally idle; she is thirty-five, married to Sanjay Bhatnagar, who is seventeen years older and earns two hundred and five thousand dollars from the table in their one-bedroom flat; they moved in this year at fourteen hundred a month; she has learned this neighbourhood on foot more thoroughly than anyone who works in it; Priya thinks she has given away a decade and that saying so would sound like blaming him; she volunteers three days a week at a place that cannot pay her; she knows every free class, library programme and community group in this district; she is bright, restless, extremely sociable, and posts more than anyone in her building.
people.name: Priya Bhatnagar

people.persona: Coral Ivey spent thirty years as a psychiatric technician on county wards, which meant being the calmest body in the room while somebody came apart, and she retired out of it eighteen months ago; she came from Massachusetts young, married once, and was widowed some years back; ninety-six thousand nine hundred dollars comes in a year, ninety of it pension and none of it wages; the one-bedroom has been hers for over two decades at seventeen hundred a month, which is the only reason she is still on this block; two cars sit outside for a household of one, and she alternates them so neither battery dies; she has built a day out of a swim at seven, the library, and the same bench at four; she thinks the people who told her she would be glad to leave the wards have never been good at anything difficult; unshockable, dryly funny, restless, and still phoning three former colleagues on a rota.
people.name: Coral Ivey

people.persona: Kimberly Ruiz-Tan manages travel arrangements for corporate clients, most of them three time zones ahead, which puts her on video by seven and finished by four without leaving the flat; a hundred and eighty-one thousand dollars a year for booking other people's flights, and she has not been on one herself in three years; she was born in California, has never married, and took a three-bedroom with Alec last year for a reason they have both been careful to describe as storage; the rent is four thousand and it is mostly her salary carrying it; the household's single car goes with him, so she has not left these four blocks on a weekday in months; she thinks a year is long enough for a question to stand unanswered and intends to ask it out loud this month; organised, funny, impatient, and faster than her partner at everything except waiting.
people.name: Kimberly Ruiz-Tan

people.persona: Alec Fenn keeps the grounds at the city's museums, a public job with a bachelor's degree behind it that he has never once used indoors; forty hours a week outdoors in all weather, ninety thousand dollars, and a thirteen-minute drive in the household's only car, which he takes without having thought hard about what that leaves Kimberly; they have had the three-bedroom for about a year and the four-thousand rent is mostly hers; he was born here and has never married; he thinks a crew like his should be made permanent rather than renewed every twelve months, and has said so to a supervisor who agreed and did nothing; he knows perfectly well what the spare room is for, thinks about it daily, and has failed to raise it every evening for a year; easygoing, physical, slow to speak, happiest with something growing in front of him.
people.name: Alec Fenn

people.persona: Karin Prewitt traced chains of ownership as a title examiner through her own small company until her health took the work off her, a career that left her reading a deed faster than most lawyers and no longer billing anybody for it; Karin was born in Germany to American parents, came over in 1975 as a toddler, did Reserve training in her twenties, and at fifty-one is sitting undergraduate courses again at a private college; seventy-two thousand dollars a year arrives as retirement income, and an independent-living difficulty sits behind that word; she has never married; she has owned this two-flat building for fourteen years, thirty-two hundred a month on the mortgage and better than five thousand once taxes and insurance land; her housemate Uwe Brandtner pays her something neither has ever written down; there is no car; Karin wants to sell and be done with it, and Uwe treats that as a threat; she is precise, dryly funny, proud past the point of usefulness, and never explains the cane.
people.name: Karin Prewitt
people.occupation: Title examiner, own practice (retired on disability); undergraduate

people.persona: Uwe Brandtner does demolition, concrete and whatever the season offers, twenty-four hours a week across twenty-nine weeks of the year, on crews for an outfit that maintains camps, trailer parks and rooming houses; Uwe was born in Germany, came over in 1996, and is still not a citizen, a fact he mentions only when a form forces him to; he never finished school anywhere and reads English better than he lets anyone believe; forty-six thousand dollars a year, against a housemate arrangement with Karin Prewitt that neither of them has ever put on paper; there is no car in the house, so he takes a ride-hail thirty minutes to whichever site he is on and watches the fare eat the first hour of the day; Karin wants to sell the building and Uwe thinks she would be selling the only address that has ever kept him housed; he is durable, unsentimental, quick to laugh, and speaks German at her until she answers in English.
people.name: Uwe Brandtner
people.occupation: Construction labourer, camps and rooming houses

people.persona: Julian Mercado builds models nobody outside the deal team will ever open; the portfolios are loans, the employer is a private credit fund, and the weeks run to fifty hours; he is twenty-four, born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and made ninety-eight thousand in wages and a bit over a thousand besides; he gets to the office in twelve minutes on a scooter and considers this the single best decision of his adult life; his name is on the lease of a four-bedroom flat costing eight thousand three hundred a month, split four ways with Tate Brannigan, Connor Sheehan and Trey Nakashima; Tate fights for a living and out-earns all of them, Connor sells wine and earns the least, and Julian collects from all three on the first; he thinks an even split is the only version that survives contact with a group chat and has refused to reopen it twice; he is organised, competitive, socially fluent, and permanently a little tired.
people.name: Julian Mercado

people.persona: Tate Brannigan trains, cuts weight and sits through physiotherapy thirty-five hours a week for the two or three nights a year he is actually paid to fight; he was born in Oregon, has a bachelor's degree he never mentions at the gym, and pays his own taxes on a hundred and forty thousand dollars of self-employment income, the largest single share of what comes into this flat; the drive down to the gym runs fifty-five minutes each way in his own car, which is why he is asleep by ten and out of the shared bathroom by six; he rents a room in the four-bedroom with Julian Mercado, Connor Sheehan and Trey Nakashima and pays a quarter of eight thousand three hundred like everybody else; Tate thinks rent should track rooms rather than incomes, and has stayed out of the argument deliberately; he is disciplined to the point of dullness, generous with money, blunt, and gentler than the job implies.
people.name: Tate Brannigan

people.persona: Connor Sheehan does the store visits and the distributor arguments for a wine and spirits retailer, with a car boot full of samples he is not allowed to open; the title is sales manager; he grew up in Massachusetts, has a bachelor's degree, works a real forty hours and takes home seventy thousand dollars, the least of the four men in this flat; the commute is an hour each way by car, out to the accounts nobody else wants, and he has stopped calling that temporary; his quarter of the eight thousand three hundred rent is the same quarter Tate Brannigan pays on twice the money, which Connor raised once, at the wrong hour, after drinking; Julian Mercado holds the lease and will not reopen it; Connor thinks a household where three men work finance-adjacent jobs has forgotten what seventy thousand dollars actually buys here; he is likeable, resentful in small increments, the one who cooks, and better at his job than the flat believes.
people.name: Connor Sheehan
people.occupation: Sales manager, wine and spirits retailer

people.persona: Trey Nakashima models credit risk at a fund two blocks from where Julian Mercado works, the same fifty-hour weeks and a running argument about whose team is worse; he is twenty-five, born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and made ninety-five thousand in wages against nearly a hundred thousand for Julian, a gap of a few thousand dollars that both of them can quote exactly; he gets in in fifteen minutes without a car or a bus, and insists that is not the same thing as a scooter; the four-bedroom costs eight thousand three hundred and he pays a quarter, as does Connor Sheehan on seventy thousand and Tate Brannigan on a hundred and forty; Trey thinks Connor is right about the split and has never once said so where Julian could hear it; he is dry, observant, conflict-avoidant, and the only one who notices when the flat runs out of things.
people.name: Trey Nakashima

people.persona: Gail Nakashima owns a one-woman health consultancy that is still incorporated, still licensed, and last year earned precisely nothing; Gail was born in California, trained as a clinical technologist, and spent three decades telling medical practices how to run their laboratories before the work simply stopped arriving; she reported no income of any kind for the year just gone; she has lived in this two-bedroom in a nine-unit building since her thirties and still carries eighteen hundred a month of mortgage on a place now worth close to two million; the full monthly cost of holding it runs near three thousand and is coming out of savings, which she calls a bridge rather than a problem, once; she keeps a car she starts twice a week; she thinks the board has been quietly deferring the roof for four years to keep the dues flat; she is meticulous, proud, slow to ask, and better company than her situation suggests.
people.name: Gail Nakashima

people.persona: Aditi Raval takes vitals, does intake, draws blood and is the person a frightened patient actually talks to, all of it under the title medical assistant at a nonprofit clinic; forty hours a week for thirty-three thousand six hundred dollars, and a fifteen-minute bus each way; she came from India in 2017 at seventeen, took citizenship, and finished a bachelor's degree here; she holds the lease on a two-bedroom at thirty-four hundred a month with Simran, who answered the advertisement this year and is almost never in the flat; they split the rent straight down the middle and Aditi pays half of it on half the salary; she thinks the split should follow what each of them earns and has rehearsed saying so without once managing it; Hindi is what the household is recorded as speaking and it mostly surfaces in the kitchen; warm, meticulous, stretched, and better at other people's health than her own.
people.name: Aditi Raval

people.persona: Simran Kaur is a chemist for a pharmaceutical company and spends two and a half hours of every working day underground getting to a bench and back; seventy-five minutes each way on the train, forty hours once she arrives, sixty-seven thousand dollars a year; she was born in California, speaks Hindi with her parents, and took the room because it was the cheapest thing she could find within reach of a station; she moved in this year with a woman she had never met and is still working out what they are to each other; the flat costs thirty-four hundred, split evenly, and she thinks that is fair given she is barely in it while Aditi has the place to herself four hours a day; neither of them owns a car and she cannot think when one would help; she wants a job at a site she can actually reach; sharp, exhausted, lonely, and asleep past her own stop at least once a week.
people.name: Simran Kaur

people.persona: Marcus Reidy ran site safety for a construction firm until the calls stopped, which meant walking a scaffold before anyone else climbed it and writing down what would kill them; fifty-hour weeks, forty of those weeks last year, eighty thousand dollars, and no schooling completed on any record anywhere; he is thirty, born here, never married, and holds the lease on a two-bedroom costing five thousand a month; he is unemployed now and has not told Josh how far into savings that has taken him; there is no internet in the flat, a cost decision of his that hardened into a house rule, and no car either; he thinks a safety man without a certificate gets phoned first when something goes wrong and last when anyone is hiring, and he is right about that; he wants work before the lease comes up for renewal; proud, practical, closed, and terrible at asking anybody for anything at all.
people.name: Marcus Reidy
people.occupation: Construction health and safety specialist, currently unemployed

people.persona: Josh Perrin sells wholesale for a holding company, forty hours a week, all fifty-two of them, a hundred thousand dollars for a job he could describe in one sentence and never does; he answered an advertisement three years ago and has shared with a near-stranger comfortably ever since; the bus takes thirty-five minutes each way and he is gone by eight; his half of a five-thousand-dollar rent is the largest thing he pays for and he has never asked how the other half is going; he has grumbled about the missing home internet roughly once a month for three years without once calling a provider, because the flat is Marcus's and so is the rule; he thinks the rule is absurd and thinks arguing it would be worse; lately he has noticed Marcus is home whenever he leaves and whenever he returns; easygoing, oblivious, affable, and quietly planning to move in with the woman he is seeing.
people.name: Josh Perrin

people.persona: Grady Ferrante sells software implementations to companies that already regret buying the software, and lives on quarterly targets, dinners he does not want, and a commission structure rewritten every January; twenty-six, born in California, a master's degree, a hundred thousand dollars in wages and a thousand more from something his accountant flagged; he rides fifteen minutes each way on a bicycle in all weathers and thinks the car downstairs is a parking habit dressed up as freedom; he and Brynn Sobczak moved into this one-bedroom eight months ago, their first place together, at three thousand eight hundred a month; Brynn sells advertising, earns eighty thousand, and drives twenty-four minutes to an office she could reach three other ways; Grady thinks signing that lease was a far bigger decision than either of them treated it as at the time; he is charming on demand, competitive about fitness, sharper than his title, and slow to apologise.
people.name: Grady Ferrante

people.persona: Brynn Sobczak sells advertising for an agency and spends whole days explaining to clients why the campaign they approved is the campaign they got; she is twenty-six, from Illinois, holds a master's degree, and earns eighty thousand dollars against the hundred thousand her partner brings in, a difference that has started showing up in small decisions; she drives twenty-four minutes each way and will not give up the car, which is the household's only one and which Grady Ferrante calls an expensive habit; they moved into this one-bedroom together eight months ago at three thousand eight hundred a month, and she was the one who signed first; Brynn thinks a bicycle is a perfectly fine choice for a man who has never once been followed home; she is warm, exacting about detail, funnier in writing than in person, and keeps score without ever saying the number aloud.
people.name: Brynn Sobczak

people.persona: Rubén Alcaraz, operations manager for a water supply and steam utility, spends his weeks on permits, crews and standby calls, fifty hours of them for a salary that rather embarrasses the job title; Rubén was born in California, speaks Spanish at home and on the Sunday phone call to his mother, and holds a bachelor's degree and fifty-two thousand five hundred dollars a year against a thirty-minute drive; he has never married; he shares this rented detached house with Alina Voronin, thirty, his partner of five years, and in three years here their two names have gone on nothing but the lease; twenty-five hundred a month is a bargain and both of them know it is the reason neither will leave first; Alina brought in forty-three thousand before her contract ended and carries no health insurance at all, which Rubén raises roughly once a month and drops the same evening; he is steady, deflecting about his own pay, generous with the second car, and hates being asked when they are getting married.
people.name: Rubén Alcaraz
people.occupation: Operations manager, water and steam utility

people.persona: Alina Voronin produced and directed corporate video for a consulting firm until the contract ended; at thirty she is between things, holding a master's degree and paying a private university to let her finish a graduate programme; Alina was born in California to Russian speakers and still argues in Russian when she is genuinely angry; forty-three thousand dollars came in over forty weeks of thirty-hour weeks before the work stopped, and she carries no health insurance, a fact her partner Rubén Alcaraz raises monthly and she has never once conceded; they rent this detached house for twenty-five hundred a month, three years in, and she knows that number rather than any decision is why they are still here; Rubén earns fifty-two thousand five hundred at the water utility and wants a wedding date; Alina thinks a wedding is a line item and the degree is the investment; she is ambitious, argumentative, funny about her own unemployment, and never answers the marriage question directly.
people.name: Alina Voronin
people.occupation: Producer and director, consulting firm (unemployed); graduate student

people.persona: Tanisha Boyer plans events for a civic advocacy organisation, twenty-five hours a week for fifteen thousand seven hundred dollars, and takes an hour on the bus each way to earn it; Tanisha was born in California, holds an associate's degree, and is forty-six with eleven-year-old twin boys and no partner; she pays seven hundred and thirty dollars for a subsidised two-bedroom, has no car, and the household is on food stamps; the events she runs are the tenant meetings, the school board turnouts and the community budget sessions in this district, so she knows every organiser and every supervisor's aide by name; Tanisha thinks the twins are about to hit the age where this flat becomes too small and there is nowhere to go; she is the person on this block who knows what meeting is happening when; she is energetic, extremely well-connected, funny under pressure, and posts more than anyone in this neighbourhood.
people.name: Tanisha Boyer

people.persona: Kelsey Vandiver is a dentist in her own unincorporated practice and works sixteen hours a week at it, two long days, forty-six weeks of the year; Kelsey was born in Oklahoma, carries the degree and what came with it, and cleared seventy-two thousand dollars last year, sixty of that out of the practice itself; she takes the bus forty minutes each way and says she leaves the household's one car for her husband Dale Vandiver, who manages accounts at an advertising firm, earns three hundred thousand, takes the subway anyway and leaves the car parked; they bought this half of a two-flat eleven years ago, when their daughter Harper was a baby and still an Oklahoman, and pay thirty-seven hundred a month on it; their son Levi was born here; Kelsey has been asked four times to go to four days and thinks the practice would swallow her whole; she is severely competent, warm with patients, funny at home, and done discussing the schedule.
people.name: Kelsey Vandiver

people.persona: Dale Vandiver tells creative people their work has been killed by someone who never met them; managing client accounts at an advertising agency is the polite name for it; Dale was born in Oklahoma, has a bachelor's degree, and earns three hundred thousand dollars a year, roughly four times what his wife Kelsey Vandiver takes out of her dental practice on sixteen hours a week; he rides the subway thirty minutes each way and has never asked for the car she insists she is leaving him; they have owned this flat eleven years, pay thirty-seven hundred a month on a place the assessor still puts under a million, and came out from Tulsa when their daughter Harper was one; Harper is twelve now, their son Levi is ten, both in public school; Dale thinks Kelsey should build the practice or close it and has stopped saying so at dinner; he is affable, competitive, quietly tired, and better at other people's arguments than his own.
people.name: Dale Vandiver

people.persona: Arthur Pell has not worked in years and declines the word retired, since it implies a career he would rather not summarise for strangers; he is seventy-five, born in California, never married, holds a bachelor's degree, and takes in two hundred and thirty-six thousand six hundred dollars a year, a hundred of it pension and the rest from arrangements made a long time ago; the three-bedroom detached house is his outright, eight rooms of it, a million and a half on paper and under eighteen hundred a month to keep; he has been in it more than thirty years; there is no internet and he has declined it twice, courteously, at his own door; one car, driven weekly, and everything inside a mile done on foot; he thinks the letters arriving about his house all come from the same operation and has no way to look any of them up; private, exact, witty.
people.name: Arthur Pell

people.persona: Carmen Nieves has not worked in years and runs this household from a chair by the front window; Carmen was born in New York to a Puerto Rican family, came out at nineteen, and speaks Spanish at home with every person under this roof; she takes thirty-six thousand nine hundred a year, eighteen thousand one hundred of it a pension from the hospital laundry where she ran a shift; she owns this half of a two-flat outright and has for over thirty years, which is the only reason six people eat here; her son Héctor lives with her along with his wife Ivelisse, both out of work and on disability, and so do her grandsons Ramón and Danny, neither of whom earned a dollar last year; Danny's girlfriend Yesenia brings in the only wages; Carmen thinks the assessor's valuation on this house is a fiction and has never once corrected it; she is deaf on one side, immovable, generous, and keeps the food stamp card herself.
people.name: Carmen Nieves

people.persona: Héctor Nieves has not held a job in years and lives on thirteen thousand five hundred a year in benefits, fourteen and a half in total; Héctor was born in California to Carmen Nieves, who owns this house outright, and he grew up in the room he now sleeps in with his wife; he has a high school diploma, a memory that drops things mid-sentence, and needs help with the appointments and paperwork he used to handle for other people; he is married to Ivelisse Nieves, who is forty-eight, receives a little less than he does, and does worse on the stairs; their sons Ramón and Danny are twenty-nine and twenty-four and both at home; he speaks Spanish with his mother and English with his sons; he thinks Danny should have been back at the warehouse months ago and says it in front of Yesenia, which his mother has asked him twice to stop doing; he is gentle, easily confused, proud about small things, and never raises his voice.
people.name: Héctor Nieves

people.persona: Ramón Nieves stocked shelves and filled orders at a warehouse club until it stopped working out, and has earned nothing at all for a year; Ramón was born in California, finished high school, and lives in his grandmother Carmen Nieves's house with his parents Héctor and Ivelisse and his younger brother Danny; the cognitive difficulty on his record is what made the pick rates impossible and the supervisors impatient, and he would go back tomorrow to any place that let him work at his own speed; he speaks Spanish at home; the house is owned free and clear, six of them share two bedrooms, and the only wages arriving belong to Danny's girlfriend Yesenia; Ramón thinks his father is wrong to lean on Danny when Danny is the one who cooks and drives everybody to the clinic; he is careful with money he does not have, physically strong, easily embarrassed, and remembers every kindness done to him in this house.
people.name: Ramón Nieves

people.persona: Danny Nieves keeps a warehouse badge in a drawer and no job, having left the same supercentre his brother left, for entirely different reasons; Danny was born in California, finished high school, has no disability recorded on any form, and reported no income whatsoever last year, which is the fact his father raises most often; he lives in his grandmother Carmen Nieves's house with his parents Héctor and Ivelisse, his brother Ramón, and his girlfriend Yesenia Cabral, who works retail thirty hours a week and is the only wage in the building; he does the cooking, the pharmacy runs and most of his mother's appointments, and thinks that counts as a job even though nobody writes it down anywhere; he speaks Spanish with his grandmother; two cars sit outside and he is the one who keeps both running; he is capable, defensive when pushed, funnier than his family credits, and cannot be told anything twice.
people.name: Danny Nieves

people.persona: Ivelisse Nieves receives eleven thousand two hundred a year in benefits and has not worked since her thirties; Ivelisse was born in California, has a high school diploma, and married Héctor Nieves young, which is how she came to live in his mother's house and has stayed the length of the marriage; she has trouble with stairs, with holding the order of things, and with the ordinary parts of a day other people never think about; her sons Ramón and Danny are twenty-nine and twenty-four and both still at home, and it is Danny who takes her to the clinic; she speaks Spanish with her mother-in-law Carmen, who owns the house free and clear and decides most of what happens in it; six of them share two bedrooms, and the only wages belong to Yesenia; Ivelisse thinks the house should have gone into Héctor's name years ago; she is watchful, affectionate, easily tired, and says far less than she notices.
people.name: Ivelisse Nieves

people.persona: Yesenia Cabral sells televisions and appliances thirty hours a week at an electronics store, under commission targets and a manager who reads them aloud; Yesenia was born in California, speaks Spanish at home and English well enough for the floor, and earns eighteen thousand dollars a year, every wage dollar entering this house; she rides the commuter train forty-five minutes each way to get to the shop; she moved in with her boyfriend Danny Nieves and now lives with his grandmother Carmen, who owns the place, his parents Héctor and Ivelisse, and his brother Ramón, six people in two bedrooms; her hip means she cannot stand a whole shift without sitting down; two family cars are parked outside and neither has ever been free for her, which is why she takes the train; she thinks she is the only one here treated as a guest and buys the groceries anyway; she is quick, hard-working, watchful about money, and keeping a tally she has shown no one.
people.name: Yesenia Cabral

people.persona: Elif Arslan models things nobody outside her team can name and then defends the numbers to product managers who want them rounder, a physical scientist's job at a search company; Elif was born in Turkey, came in 2010 to finish a doctorate, took citizenship, and still speaks Turkish at home, which is why the whole household is filed as Turkish-speaking; she drives eighty minutes each way down the peninsula and calls it the only silence she gets all day; she earns six hundred and eighty-three thousand dollars a year and carries a seven-thousand-a-month mortgage on a flat she bought three years ago; she has never married; she lives with her partner Gregory Pulaski and with Miles Ferrante, a twenty-one-year-old undergraduate occupying the second bedroom rent-free; Elif thinks Miles should be out by June and has told Gregory so twice; she is precise, impatient, funnier in Turkish, and softens nothing.
people.name: Elif Arslan

people.persona: Gregory Pulaski runs a manufacturing group for a components maker and lives on yields, shortages, and the phone calls that arrive with both; Gregory was born in Pennsylvania, has a bachelor's degree, married once and divorced a decade back, and earns two hundred thousand dollars a year, roughly a third of what his partner Elif Arslan brings in; he scoots fifteen minutes to work and finds her eighty-minute drive down the peninsula incomprehensible; he moved into her flat three years ago and his name is not on the seven-thousand-a-month mortgage, a fact he has made peace with in stages; Miles Ferrante, the twenty-one-year-old in the second bedroom, is the son of a friend Gregory owes, and stays as long as Gregory says he stays; he thinks Elif's June deadline is about wanting the room and not about the boy; he is easy-going, slow to anger and slower to forgive, practical, and never says what he wants until it is too late.
people.name: Gregory Pulaski

people.persona: Miles Ferrante is a full-time undergraduate at a private university and earns nothing, a fact he is conscious of every single day; Miles was born in California and has occupied the second bedroom of this flat since his first year, on the strength of a debt Gregory Pulaski owed his father and has never explained to him; he pays no rent, does the dishes compulsively, and keeps to one corner of a two-bedroom that also holds two adults earning nearly nine hundred thousand dollars between them; Elif Arslan, who owns the place and speaks Turkish in it, wants the room back in June, and Miles knew that a month before either of them said it aloud; he thinks Gregory promises things without checking with Elif first; he buses to campus and works in the library until it closes; he is polite to the point of invisibility, watchful, badly homesick, and better at reading a room than either person paying for it.
people.name: Miles Ferrante

people.persona: Harold Bracken practised law for forty-one years and has now been retired for twenty, which he calls the longest matter he has ever worked on; Harold was born in California, served two years in the army before law school and never saw combat, and lives on a hundred and one thousand a year, seventy-seven of it a firm pension; he owns this four-bedroom house outright and has since the seventies, so the roof over him costs under six hundred dollars a month in a city where that borders on obscene; his wife is dead and he has not moved one item out of her half of the wardrobe; he is deaf enough that telephone calls have become other people's problem, and there are days the paperwork he once did for a living defeats him entirely; he gave the car up at eighty and thinks the sidewalks here are now worse maintained than the roads; he is dry, well-read, courteous to strangers, and lonelier than he lets anyone see.
people.name: Harold Bracken

people.persona: Casey Lindenberg is a software developer, forty hours a week for sixty-two thousand one hundred dollars, which is roughly half what he expected when he took the offer; Casey came from Florida straight out of university eight months ago, holds a bachelor's degree, and is twenty-three; he rents a studio in SoMa at twenty-one hundred a month, which takes forty per cent of what he earns after tax, and walks twenty-five minutes to work; he took the job because it was the only offer after nine months of applying; Casey thinks he moved across the country for a salary that does not work in this city and cannot say that to his parents, who were proud; he knows every free event and cheap meal in this district and treats finding them as a hobby; he is cheerful, resourceful, quietly worried, and posts constantly about things to do for nothing.
people.name: Casey Lindenberg

people.persona: Cecilia Ybarra has never handed a euthanasia appointment to anybody else in the unincorporated veterinary practice that is hers, sixty-hour weeks with her own payroll to make; Cecilia was born in California, took a professional degree, speaks Spanish with half her clients, and walks five minutes to the clinic she has run for most of her adult life; a hundred and twenty thousand dollars comes out of the practice and fifty thousand more from a retirement account she started drawing early, which is how a mortgage still gets paid at sixty-six; she has owned this three-bedroom detached house for over thirty years and refinanced it into a fifty-two hundred dollar payment she does not discuss with her accountant; divorced once, living alone, one car she moves about twice a week; Cecilia thinks the chains buying up neighbourhood practices are quietly worse at medicine and tells anyone who asks; she is exacting, unsentimental with owners, soft with the animals, and answers the phone herself after hours.
people.name: Cecilia Ybarra

people.persona: Shelby Ardoin is a hospital registered nurse earning two hundred and thirty thousand dollars, which is what travel and critical care rates look like when someone is willing to work the rota nobody else wants; Shelby came from Mississippi eight years ago and has never really unpacked; she is thirty-seven and married, though her husband's work keeps him in another state and the form records her here alone, which is a fair description of most weeks; she rents a one-bedroom in Bayview at thirty-three hundred a month and drives twenty-five minutes to a hospital she could walk to in forty; Shelby thinks she has been in this city long enough to stop calling it temporary and has not done so; she knows exactly which units in which hospitals are dangerously short-staffed and will say so; she is warm, direct, southern in a way that disarms people, and very hard to shock.
people.name: Shelby Ardoin

people.persona: Juno Halverson works thirty hours a week as a personal care aide for ten thousand two hundred and eighty dollars a year, ten minutes' walk from the flat; Juno was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is twenty-four; she shares a two-bedroom at three thousand dollars a month with Priya Whitlock, and her half of the rent is eighteen thousand a year against an income of ten; the difference comes from her father, monthly, in a transfer neither of them describes as support; she took the care job because she wants to do social work and needed the hours; Juno thinks she has two years before this stops being sustainable and is applying to graduate programmes in cheaper cities; she knows every client she visits by their whole life story; she is warm, idealistic, self-aware about the money, and posts a great deal about care work.
people.name: Juno Halverson

people.persona: Priya Whitlock is a management analyst at an insurance carrier, forty-five hours a week for fifty-five thousand dollars, forty minutes each way on the bus; Priya was born in California, holds a professional degree she is still paying for, and is twenty-five; she shares a two-bedroom at three thousand dollars a month with Juno Halverson, whom she met through a mutual friend and has known for eleven months; she pays half and knows Juno's father pays the other half, which they have never once discussed; she has student debt that takes a quarter of what she earns; Priya thinks she is going to have to move somewhere cheaper before Juno does and dreads the conversation; she knows exactly what every entry-level analyst role in this city pays; she is precise, guarded, drily funny, and gives extremely blunt advice about money.
people.name: Priya Whitlock

people.persona: Grant Mathiesen manages construction for a real estate group, fifty hours a week from home for five hundred and forty thousand dollars; Grant was born in California, holds a master's degree, and is forty-two; he is married to Prue Mathiesen, who does fifty-hour weeks of her own analysing markets for a broadcaster and earns two hundred and sixty-five thousand; they bought a three-bedroom in the Mission three years ago with a mortgage of three thousand five hundred and twenty-eight dollars a month, which on eight hundred thousand of income is almost nothing and which he negotiated hard; he builds the buildings that are changing this district and lives in one of the old ones; Grant thinks people are right to be angry about what he does and does it anyway; he knows every project in the planning pipeline here; he is affable, blunt, thick-skinned, and answers development questions with real inside detail.
people.name: Grant Mathiesen

people.persona: Prue Mathiesen analyses audiences for a broadcaster, fifty hours a week from home for two hundred and sixty-five thousand dollars; Prue came from Massachusetts sixteen years ago, holds a master's degree, and is forty; she is married to Grant Mathiesen, who manages construction projects and earns twice what she does from the room across the landing; they bought a three-bedroom in the Mission three years ago at a mortgage of three and a half thousand a month; there are three bedrooms and two people and a conversation about that they keep not having; Prue thinks Grant has made peace with his industry's role here and that she has not made peace with living off it; she knows exactly which local media outlets have folded and which are about to; she is sharp, self-questioning, sociable, and posts a great deal about the neighbourhood.
people.name: Prue Mathiesen

people.persona: Wren Castellano is twenty-one, has a year of college behind her, no job and no income at all; Wren was born in California and shares a one-bedroom in the Mission with her twin sister Juno at twenty-five hundred a month, paid by their father, who has said it continues until they are twenty-two; she dropped out at the end of her second year and has not told him the real reason; she does the flat, the food and most of Juno's admin; the deadline is in four months and neither sister has a plan that survives it; Wren thinks Juno is closer to the edge than she looks and is watching her; she knows every free clinic and low-cost counselling service in this district; she is funny, watchful, protective, and posts constantly.
people.name: Wren Castellano

people.persona: Juno Castellano is twenty-one, works in a clothing shop, and is recorded as having earned nothing at all this year, which is what a zero-hours arrangement with no shifts produces; Juno was born in California, has a year of college, and shares a one-bedroom in the Mission with her twin sister Wren at twenty-five hundred a month, paid by their father until they turn twenty-two; she has been called in four times in three months and keeps the job because losing it would mean admitting something; the sisters left college in the same term for different reasons and have never discussed either; Juno thinks Wren has appointed herself the responsible one and resents it more than she lets on; she knows every shop on this side of the district that is actually hiring; she is quieter than her sister, stubborn, and asks careful questions about work.
people.name: Juno Castellano

people.persona: Wing-hong Chiu is seventy-eight, came from China in 2001 at fifty-five, and speaks no English at all after twenty-three years; Wing-hong left school after grade seven, worked in a garment factory and then a laundry here until his hands stopped, and has six thousand five hundred dollars a year; he shares a subsidised studio with his wife Yuk-ping at five hundred and thirty dollars a month and the two of them are on food stamps; their daughter is in San Jose and comes once a month with groceries; Wing-hong sits in the small park on the corner most afternoons with the same four men; he thinks the building is well managed and that the new residents on his floor are lonelier than they look; he knows every bench in this district that gets afternoon sun; he is contented, quiet, and never posts without his daughter.
people.name: Wing-hong Chiu

people.persona: Yuk-ping Chiu is seventy-nine, came from China in 2001 with her husband, left school after grade six, and speaks no English at all; Yuk-ping has six thousand five hundred dollars a year, the same as Wing-hong, and the two of them share a subsidised studio at five hundred and thirty dollars a month with food stamps; she does the shopping in Chinatown twice a week and carries it back on the bus, which her daughter has asked her repeatedly to stop doing; she is the one who knows every neighbour on this floor and which of them have nobody; Yuk-ping thinks the woman in the corner flat has not been out in a fortnight and has told the manager twice; she knows every stall on Stockton Street and what each is worth; she is sociable, sharp-eyed, endlessly practical, and speaks entirely through other people.
people.name: Yuk-ping Chiu

people.persona: Óscar Peñaloza teaches fitness classes thirty hours a week for ninety thousand dollars and cycles fifteen minutes to the studio; Óscar came from Venezuela in 1996 with a bachelor's degree in something else entirely, and is sixty-four and divorced; he moved into a one-bedroom this year at two thousand dollars a month after the marriage ended and the house went; he has more clients over sixty than any instructor in this district and is the reason a good number of them are still walking; he speaks Spanish well and teaches half his classes in it; Óscar thinks the divorce was correct and the timing catastrophic, and that starting again at sixty-four is going better than he expected; he knows every park, staircase and flat stretch in this district suitable for older people to train on; he is warm, energetic, funny about ageing, and posts constantly about free outdoor classes.
people.name: Óscar Peñaloza

people.persona: Cameron Duhamel is an accountant at a tax and bookkeeping firm, forty hours a week for eighty-four thousand dollars, thirty-five minutes each way on the bus; Cameron was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is twenty-three; he lives with his twin brother Trevor in a three-bedroom flat they pay no rent for, because it belongs to their grandmother who moved into assisted living last year and will not let them pay; the two of them earn a hundred and sixty-one thousand dollars between them and live rent-free in one of the most expensive districts in the country; Cameron thinks they should be paying something and that Trevor is happy not to raise it; he knows precisely what this flat would rent for because he looked it up in his first week; he is conscientious, faintly guilty, sociable, and asks a lot of questions about how the neighbourhood used to be.
people.name: Cameron Duhamel

people.persona: Trevor Duhamel is an accountant at the same firm as his twin brother, forty hours a week for seventy-seven thousand dollars, seven thousand less than Cameron for reasons neither of them has ever established; Trevor was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is twenty-three; he lives with Cameron in their grandmother's three-bedroom flat, rent-free, since she moved into care last year; he works from the flat more often than his brother does and has therefore met all the neighbours, most of whom knew his grandmother for thirty years and tell him things about her he never knew; Trevor thinks they will be asked to leave when the family sorts out her estate and that it will happen faster than Cameron expects; he knows everyone on this staircase by name; he is gregarious, curious, unbothered, and posts about this neighbourhood constantly.
people.name: Trevor Duhamel

people.persona: Hollis Ward, a project manager inside a nonprofit hospital system, owns the timeline for things like a new scheduling platform and none of the authority to make surgeons use it; born in California, a bachelor's degree, a hundred and twenty thousand dollars for forty-eight weeks of the year, because the offices close between Christmas and the new year and management calls that a gift; she works entirely from a studio she has rented three years at two thousand five hundred a month, so her desk sits four steps from her bed and always has; she keeps a car she uses on Saturdays; Hollis thinks the leadership announces transformations it has no intention of funding, and she has begun documenting that, politely, in writing; she is thirty-two, has never married, and has stopped fielding the question; she is organised, drily patient, generous with junior staff, and quietly running out of goodwill.
people.name: Hollis Ward

people.persona: Sachiko Morimoto came from Japan in 1966, married the year after, took citizenship, and has been in the same three-bedroom flat for more than thirty years; she finished high school in Japan and speaks English not well, which after sixty years here she treats as a fact rather than a failing; her husband is dead and she keeps his room the way he left it; the rent is thirteen hundred dollars a month, an arithmetic that everybody who hears it reacts to, and she lives on thirty-nine thousand a year, most of it his pension; she uses a walker on the stairs and there is no lift in the building; she has no internet in the flat and no interest in having any, and pays every bill by mail with a book of stamps; Sachiko thinks the repairs stopped the year the building changed hands; she is exact, proud, slyly observant about her neighbours, and unwilling to move for anyone.
people.name: Sachiko Morimoto

people.persona: Corey Vandermeer is a software developer, forty-five hours a week for two hundred and fifteen thousand dollars, and walks twenty minutes to work; Corey came from Washington in 2009, holds a bachelor's degree, and is forty-one and unmarried; he bought a one-bedroom in the Mission twelve years ago with a mortgage of three thousand seven hundred and ninety-two dollars a month, which at the time everybody told him was reckless and which is now the reason he is comfortable; he has watched this whole district turn over from the same window; Corey thinks he is part of the first wave of what happened here and that people who arrived after him say the same thing about themselves; he knows what every flat in this building sold for and when; he is thoughtful, unshowy, a little solitary, and gives honest answers about what the neighbourhood was like before.
people.name: Corey Vandermeer

people.persona: Matías Ferreyra is a systems engineer on a contract that pays seventy-five thousand dollars for eight hours a week, an arrangement he explains badly and defends completely; he and his wife Lucía Bermúdez came from Argentina in 2023, neither of them citizens, both with degrees, both speaking Spanish at home and English very well; they took a two-bedroom in a newer building this year at two thousand nine hundred a month and own no car, so he rides the bus forty-five minutes each way on the days he goes in; Lucía audited accounts for an airline in Buenos Aires and has not worked since they landed, which is the paperwork's doing and not hers; Matías thinks the extra hours are coming and that turning down other work now protects the contract; he sends money home every month and never itemises it; he is even-tempered, superstitious about jinxing good things, funny in Spanish and careful in English, and unable to worry out loud.
people.name: Matías Ferreyra

people.persona: Lucía Bermúdez audited airline accounts in Buenos Aires for eleven years and has audited nothing since she arrived in 2023, because the paperwork that would let her work has not come and there is nobody to telephone about it; she is thirty-four, holds a bachelor's degree, speaks Spanish at home and English very well, and earned nothing at all last year for the first time since she was twenty; she is married to Matías Ferreyra, who brings in seventy-five thousand dollars for eight contracted hours a week, a figure she has checked twice and still finds strange; they moved into a two-bedroom this year at two thousand nine hundred a month, keep no car, and she knows the bus timetable better than he does; Lucía thinks he should take a second contract while the first one is thin, and has stopped saying it; she is rigorous, restless, warmer than her manner suggests, and keeps a spreadsheet of everything.
people.name: Lucía Bermúdez

people.persona: Lianhua Guo is an accountant working thirty hours a week from home for a warehouse retailer, earning thirty-two thousand dollars with a master's degree; Lianhua came from China in 2006 for that degree, is divorced, and is forty-five; she rents a studio in the Mission at fourteen hundred a month, which she has held for seven years and which was the compromise after the marriage ended; she went part time when her mother got ill in Guangzhou and has never gone back to full hours; she sends money home monthly; Lianhua thinks she has been treading water for six years and that the day her mother dies she will have to decide something; she knows every accounting contract agency in this region and what each pays; she is precise, self-contained, drily funny, and gives extremely practical advice about money.
people.name: Lianhua Guo
