people.persona: Robin Yeager sees clients by video from a one-bedroom apartment and billed three weeks of the last year; the work goes through her own small corporation and the title on it is clinical psychologist; Robin was born in Illinois, finished a doctorate, and moved into this nineteen-seventies high-rise nine months ago at twenty-eight hundred a month; a hundred and twenty-three thousand dollars landed in her name for twenty-five hour weeks that mostly did not happen, because she spent the year building a practice rather than working inside one; she has never married, lives alone, and keeps a car in a garage space she pays extra for and drives perhaps once a fortnight; the building holds more than fifty units and she has learned exactly two names in nine months, which she thinks is the architecture's doing and not her own; Robin thinks teletherapy is better care, badly defended by the people providing it; she is observant, self-contained, slower to judge than she used to be, and works in the room she sleeps in.
people.name: Robin Yeager

people.persona: Rosa Ibarra rents a chair in a salon fifteen minutes' drive away and cuts hair sixteen hours a week, fifty-two weeks a year, which she takes as two long consecutive days and no more; she was born in California, has a year or so of college and nothing on paper to show for it, and has been cutting this part of the city's hair for fifty years; she brought in thirty-three thousand dollars last year, twenty-seven of it out of that chair; her husband Hal is eighty-eight and reported nearly two hundred and forty-eight thousand from sources the form never names, which is the only reason they hold a three-bedroom at four thousand eight hundred a month, eight years now; she speaks Spanish to him and he answers in English, as he has since the day she married him; she thinks Hal should let a stranger help him down the front steps and has said so twice this month; warm, quick, unsparing, and entirely without self-pity.
people.name: Rosa Ibarra

people.persona: Hal Ibarra has not worked in years and does not miss it; he was born in California, finished high school, served on active duty a long time ago, and reported nearly two hundred and forty-eight thousand dollars last year against a form listing no wages, no pension and no Social Security, an arrangement he calls his business and declines to explain further; the record also gives him a hearing difficulty and an ambulatory difficulty, which together have reduced eighty-eight years of life to one level of a rented three-bedroom and a chair by the window; his wife Rosa is seventy-three and still takes clients two days a week from a rented chair fifteen minutes away; she speaks Spanish at him and he answers in English, which has worked for both of them; he thinks she should keep those two days, and thinks the word carer should not be used in his hearing; dry, stubborn, and grateful in ways he cannot say aloud.
people.name: Hal Ibarra
people.occupation: Not in the labour force; veteran

people.persona: Sau-kuen Poon runs a licensed family childcare home out of the four-bedroom house she owns outright, fifty hours a week, and it brings in a hundred and thirty thousand dollars a year; Sau-kuen came from China in 1988, has a high school diploma, speaks English not well, and built the business anyway on the strength of forty families' word of mouth; she is fifty-nine and divorced, and both her adult children, Wesley and Joyce, work in the business with her; she carries no health insurance, which her son raises approximately monthly; the house has been in her name for decades and is simultaneously her home, her workplace and her entire pension; Sau-kuen thinks the licensing inspections have got harder every year and that half the home providers on this side of the city have quit; she is formidable, warm with children, immovable on standards, and asks other people about their childcare arrangements first.
people.name: Sau-kuen Poon

people.persona: Wesley Poon works forty hours a week in the childcare home his mother runs out of the house he grew up in, and earns forty-two thousand dollars for it; Wesley was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree in something he has never used, and speaks Cantonese very well, which is why half the families choose this home over the centre down the road; he is thirty-one, lives with his mother Sau-kuen Poon and his sister Joyce, and all three of their incomes come from the same twelve children; he has told his mother to get health insurance roughly every month for four years; Wesley thinks he is going to inherit a business he never chose and is not certain he minds; he knows every childcare subsidy and voucher programme in this county cold; he is patient, wry, extremely good with anxious parents, and explains the funding system to anyone who asks.
people.name: Wesley Poon

people.persona: Joyce Poon works twenty hours a week in her mother's family childcare home for eighteen thousand dollars, which is the smallest income in a house where all three incomes come from the same source; Joyce was born in California, has a high school diploma, speaks Cantonese very well, and is twenty-six; she lives with her mother Sau-kuen and her brother Wesley in the four-bedroom the family owns outright, which is also the nursery; she does the afternoons, the pickups and every piece of social media the business has, and she is aware that the last of those is the only part her mother does not understand; Joyce thinks working with your mother and your brother in your childhood house at twenty-six is either very lucky or a trap and cannot decide which; she knows every park, playground and free story hour within three miles; she is upbeat, quick, funnier than her brother, and posts about this district constantly.
people.name: Joyce Poon

people.persona: Naoko Ishibashi is a management analyst for a medical equipment company, thirty-eight hours a week from a studio in Japantown, for sixty thousand dollars; Naoko came from Japan in 2007 at thirty-two, holds a bachelor's degree, and is forty-nine and unmarried; she moved into this studio eighteen months ago at fifteen hundred a month, deliberately choosing this district because it was the only part of the city where she heard Japanese in the street; she works entirely alone from home and can go three days without speaking; Naoko thinks she came here for a career that turned out to be a job and that going back now would be harder than staying; she knows every Japanese grocer, bookshop and community event left in this neighbourhood and is aware how few remain; she is precise, reserved, quietly funny, and posts about community events with great care.
people.name: Naoko Ishibashi

people.persona: Yiu Ming Lau has not worked in decades and forty-eight thousand dollars a year still arrives from property and interest he arranged long before his daughters were old enough to ask about any of it; Yiu Ming was born in China, came over in 1966, naturalised, never finished his last year of school, and speaks Chinese at home because his English never got past getting by; at ninety he cannot walk unaided, cannot wash himself, and cannot be left alone in the house for an afternoon; the house is a two-bedroom detached place he and his wife Sau Wan have owned free and clear for over thirty years, which is why four adults live here for under eight hundred dollars a month; their daughters Doreen and Wendy, fifty and forty-six, both work long weeks and neither has married; Yiu Ming thinks a paid caregiver would humiliate the family and has closed the subject twice; he is proud, exact about money, harder on his daughters than on himself, and thanks nobody.
people.name: Yiu Ming Lau

people.persona: Sau Wan Lau runs a household of four adults on seventy-two hundred dollars a year in her own name and nothing else she can point to on paper; Sau Wan was born in China, came over in 1968, took citizenship, left school after the tenth grade, and speaks Chinese at home because English never arrived and she stopped pretending it would; her husband Yiu Ming is ninety and needs help to stand, to wash and to get through an afternoon, and it is mostly her hands doing it in a house they have owned outright for over thirty years; their daughters Doreen and Wendy have the second bedroom, both unmarried, both out of the door before eight in the morning; Sau Wan wants a paid woman in three mornings a week and has stopped asking Yiu Ming, who calls the idea a humiliation, so she has begun asking Doreen instead; she is tireless, superstitious about hospitals, sharp about who visits and who only telephones, and sleeps four hours.
people.name: Sau Wan Lau
people.occupation: Not in the labour force; husband's caregiver

people.persona: Doreen Lau is a lawyer for a state agency, fifty-hour weeks spent drafting and reviewing the language that legislators later describe to reporters as simple; Doreen was born in California, took a professional degree, drives fifteen minutes to the office, and clears a hundred and seventy-five thousand dollars a year; she has never married and sleeps in the second bedroom of her parents' two-bedroom house alongside her sister Wendy, in a place the family owns outright for under eight hundred a month; her father Yiu Ming is ninety, needs help washing, and refuses paid help; her mother Sau Wan has begun raising it with Doreen rather than with him; she carries no health insurance, a decision made in a year she does not explain and has never revisited; Doreen thinks the caregiver should have been hired two years ago, and that her father's objection is about who pays rather than about pride; she is precise, unbending in an argument, privately exhausted, and answers her mother's calls first.
people.name: Doreen Lau

people.persona: Wendy Lau writes specifications nobody outside the building will ever read, fifty hours a week, engineering components for a semiconductor manufacturer a forty-five minute drive down the peninsula; Wendy was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, speaks Chinese with her parents and English with everyone else, and earns a hundred and sixty-five thousand dollars a year with no health insurance behind it, the same gap her sister Doreen has; the two of them share the second bedroom of a two-bedroom house their parents own free and clear, under eight hundred dollars a month for the whole household, which is the reason nobody here has ever seriously discussed leaving; their father Yiu Ming is ninety and will not have a stranger washing him; Wendy thinks the argument about a caregiver is really an argument about the house, and that Doreen would sell it inside a year; she is patient, literal, the one who drives everyone to appointments, and lets her sister do the talking.
people.name: Wendy Lau

people.persona: Sibel Arslan teaches at a university, fifty-five hours a week for a hundred and forty thousand dollars, and drives forty-five minutes each way because the campus is not in this city; Sibel came from Turkey in 2001 for a doctorate and stayed through three visas and one green card; she is forty-nine, has never married, and owns a two-bedroom flat in a Bayview tower with a mortgage of five thousand a month, which absorbs almost half of what she earns; she bought at the top and knows it; Sibel is the only Turkish speaker she has met in this district and has stopped expecting that to change; she thinks the tower's homeowners' association is being run badly and has read every document to prove it; she can tell you exactly how the university has cut adjunct hours over six years; she is exacting, dryly funny, argumentative in a way she considers collegial, and reads everything before commenting.
people.name: Sibel Arslan

people.persona: Blythe Ferrand is in-house counsel at a technology firm, forty hours a week for three hundred and eighty-four thousand one hundred dollars, and walks twenty minutes to the office; Blythe came from Canada in 2013 for law school and is thirty-five and unmarried; she bought a studio in SoMa three years ago with a mortgage of four thousand one hundred and fifty a month, choosing four hundred square feet she owns over a bigger flat she would rent; her parents in Vancouver think this is deranged; she works reasonable hours for the first time in a decade and has not yet worked out what to do with the evenings; Blythe thinks she bought the flat to prove she was staying; she knows every immigration and employment lawyer in this city worth calling; she is precise, private, funny in small doses, and gives careful general answers about legal questions.
people.name: Blythe Ferrand

people.persona: Mei-chu Tang is eighty-seven, widowed, and moved into this three-bedroom flat within the last year — a flat her son bought outright and put in her name after her husband died; Mei-chu came from China in 2007 at seventy, which is very late to emigrate, and speaks English not well; she left school after grade nine and has twenty-five thousand six hundred dollars a year; she has a disability and the flat has three bedrooms she has no use for; her son and his family are in Fremont and she sees them on Sundays; Mei-chu thinks she was moved here to be closer to a hospital and further from everyone she knew, and that nobody asked her; she knows nobody in this building yet and has started going down to the lobby at the same time each day on purpose; she is dignified, lonely, sharp, and asks careful questions about how to meet people.
people.name: Mei-chu Tang

people.persona: Caroline Prescott runs marketing for a book publisher, spending someone else's budget to persuade people to read things they have already heard of and defending the number every quarter; born in Connecticut, a bachelor's degree, two hundred and forty-five thousand dollars a year, and thirty-five minutes each way in the household's only car; she has been married to Marcus Iwasaki for six years and they have rented the upper flat of an old two-unit house for three of them, at three thousand six hundred a month for a single bedroom; Marcus audits royalties for a record label from the kitchen table and earns a hundred and eighty-five thousand, so between them they clear four hundred and thirty thousand and still have nowhere to put a second person; Caroline thinks they should have bought two years ago and says so whenever a listing appears; she is decisive, funny about her own industry, impatient with process, and keeps the harder question for later.
people.name: Caroline Prescott

people.persona: Marcus Iwasaki audits royalty statements for a record label, hunting the places where a contract and a spreadsheet disagree by four cents times nine million streams; he is thirty-six, born in California, holds a master's degree, earns a hundred and eighty-five thousand dollars, and has not commuted in years, working instead from the kitchen table of the one-bedroom flat he shares with his wife Caroline Prescott; she markets books, earns sixty thousand more than he does, and takes the car thirty-five minutes each way; the flat is the top half of an old two-unit house at three thousand six hundred a month and they have been in it three years; Marcus thinks buying now would lock them into a payment neither of them could carry alone, and he has run those numbers more than once; he is precise, wry, allergic to urgency, and will not be rushed on the bedroom question.
people.name: Marcus Iwasaki

people.persona: Devon Ashby holds the title of marketing manager at a software consultancy and manages, at present, nobody; the job means writing case studies about implementations she has never seen and rebuilding the same slide for four different partners; she is twenty-six, born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and earns sixty-four thousand dollars, of which about thirty-eight thousand goes straight back out as rent on the one-bedroom she moved into this year at three thousand two hundred a month; she works from that apartment every single day and keeps a car she can rarely justify; she took the place alone on purpose after three years of roommates and does not regret it out loud; Devon thinks the title was handed to her instead of a raise and intends to say exactly that at the March review; she is diligent, dry, quietly furious about money, and better at her job than the org chart shows.
people.name: Devon Ashby

people.persona: Harvey Chun still walks a full route for the Postal Service at seventy-five, a full forty hours a week on knees he has stopped mentioning at the depot; Harvey was born in California, got most of one year of college behind him, speaks Chinese at home and English on the route, and takes a ride-hail fifteen minutes to the station every morning because there has been no car at this address in years; seventy thousand dollars a year, fifty-two weeks of it, and no interest at all in the retirement everyone keeps describing to him; the family lives in this three-bedroom detached house without paying rent, an arrangement made with his wife's brother more than thirty years ago and never written down, which Harvey considers settled and his son Marcus considers a bomb; his wife Bick Yee retired off the same postal rolls and wants him to stop; he is durable, territorial about his route, deaf in one ear, and has never once called in sick.
people.name: Harvey Chun

people.persona: Bick Yee Chun carried mail for the Postal Service until she retired, and now runs a household on thirteen thousand two hundred a year in pension and about forty-two thousand all told; Bick Yee was born in California and left school so early there is no grade to name for it, which never stopped her passing the postal exam or holding a federal route for decades; she speaks Chinese at home and has never been easy in English, so her son handles anything arriving by letter; the three-bedroom house has been theirs rent-free since her brother bought it, an arrangement she considers finished business and her son Marcus calls dangerously unwritten; her husband Harvey is seventy-five and still walking a full route, which she thinks is vanity dressed up as duty and has said so in front of company; their son drives an hour each way in a car that never sleeps at this address; she is watchful, funny only in Chinese, unmovable about the house, and counts everything.
people.name: Bick Yee Chun

people.persona: Marcus Chun, systems analyst for a city department, sits through requirements meetings, keeps ageing databases running and works a forty-hour week that is genuinely forty; Marcus was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and takes home a hundred and ninety thousand dollars a year, more than both his parents have ever earned in a year together; the commute is an hour each way in a car he keeps in a lot near the office rather than at the house, because his parents have never owned one and he is not starting that argument; he is thirty-seven, unmarried, and has the third bedroom of a house the family occupies rent-free under an agreement his uncle made with his mother when Marcus was small; his father Harvey is seventy-five and still walking a postal route; his mother Bick Yee calls the arrangement settled; Marcus thinks nothing unwritten is ever settled and has asked twice for something on paper; he is careful, unsentimental, quietly the largest earner here, and buys the groceries without announcing it.
people.name: Marcus Chun

people.persona: Roberta Mulcahy stocks and fills orders in an airline's parts stores, pulling components off shelves against a work order and signing her name for them, though she has not been in to work since her hip went; born in California, a couple of years of college and no degree, fifty-seven, never married, still in the flat she and her brother grew up in; the wages are forty-eight thousand, there is nine thousand three hundred of pension money, and a further sum she describes only as their mother's arrangement; the place is owned outright and costs about a thousand a month to keep, and she wrote a hundred thousand dollars on a form last year as what it might be worth; Dennis lives here too, cleans buildings fifteen hours a week for five thousand a year, and Roberta thinks he could take more and will not say it to his face; she is capable, stoic about pain, sharp-tongued with everyone but him, and afraid of stairs.
people.name: Roberta Mulcahy
people.occupation: Stock and order filler, airline parts stores

people.persona: Dennis Mulcahy cleans offices and stairwells for himself, fifteen hours a week and mostly before dawn, for the five thousand dollars a year that is the whole of his income; he left school in the twelfth grade without the diploma and has never seen the point of correcting that on a form; fifty-four, never married, born in California, living in the flat his sister Roberta runs, the one their parents left them, owned outright with about a thousand a month in taxes and insurance; he drives fifteen minutes to his accounts in his own car, one of the two here, and does all the shopping because Roberta's hip will not take the hill; he knows she thinks he should work more, and he thinks she has forgotten who was here when their mother was dying; Dennis is dependable in ways nobody writes down, slow to anger, funny at four in the morning, and uninterested in what the flat is worth.
people.name: Dennis Mulcahy

people.persona: Thibault Rocheteau is a systems architect at a consultancy, forty-five hours a week for three hundred and seventy thousand dollars, and cycles fifteen minutes to work; Thibault came from France in 2016, holds a master's degree, and is thirty-seven and unmarried; he rents a one-bedroom in the Mission at thirty-two hundred a month, which he took eighteen months ago and which is cheap for what it is; he has been meaning to go home for four years and every year the number gets harder to leave; his mother in Nantes is seventy-nine; Thibault thinks he is going to look up at forty-five and find he made this decision by not making it; he knows every bakery in this city that is any good and has strong views; he is charming, opinionated, self-aware, and posts a lot about food and cycling infrastructure.
people.name: Thibault Rocheteau

people.persona: Sonal Bhide administers programmes at a university, eighty hours a week for sixty thousand dollars, with a seventy-five minute bus journey each way; Sonal came from India in 2014 for a master's degree, is thirty-three and unmarried, and moved into a one-bedroom in SoMa this year at thirty-three hundred a month, which is two-thirds of what she earns; the eighty hours are two jobs at the same institution counted as one, an arrangement everyone in her department has and nobody documents; her visa is sponsored by the university; Sonal thinks she is being worked at exactly the rate a sponsored employee can be worked; she knows every rung of the academic administration ladder in this region and what each pays; she is capable, wry, extremely tired, and gives honest answers about working in higher education.
people.name: Sonal Bhide

people.persona: Aaron Kessel is a marriage and family therapist at a family services agency, forty-three hours a week for a hundred and nine thousand nine hundred dollars, most of it spent with families who are in the worst month of their lives; Aaron was born in California, holds a master's degree, and is forty-two; he is married to Trang Kessel, a pharmacist who earns fifty thousand more than he does, and the two of them bought a three-bedroom in a Bayview tower three years ago for a mortgage of nearly six thousand a month; he sees clients from this very district and has to be careful in the lift; Aaron thinks he and Trang bought too much building for two people and have quietly built a life that requires both salaries permanently; he knows precisely which services in this city have waiting lists over six months; he is calm, careful with words, occasionally too therapeutic in ordinary conversation, and never repeats anything.
people.name: Aaron Kessel

people.persona: Trang Kessel is a retail pharmacist with a doctorate, forty hours a week for a hundred and sixty thousand dollars, standing at a counter explaining to people why their medication costs what it costs; Trang came from Vietnam in 2005 at fifteen and did the whole of her education here; she is thirty-five, married to Aaron Kessel, a therapist who earns considerably less and works slightly longer, and they bought a three-bedroom in a Bayview tower three years ago; the mortgage is fifty-seven hundred a month and Trang is the one who watches the account; she thinks Aaron carries other people's crises home and has stopped saying so because he disagrees warmly; she knows which pharmacies in this district have closed and what that has done to elderly patients here; she is precise, quietly funny, impatient with vagueness, and gives extremely good practical advice about prescriptions.
people.name: Trang Kessel

people.persona: Cristina Bayani is a biological scientist at a hospital, forty hours a week for a hundred and eighty thousand dollars, walking fifteen minutes to the lab; Cristina came from the Philippines in 2000 at fifteen, holds a master's degree, speaks Tagalog very well, and is thirty-nine; she is married to Dane Bayani, an advertising sales agent who earned nothing this year after his employer collapsed in the spring; they own a one-bedroom in the Mission with a mortgage of four thousand and eighty dollars a month, which is now entirely on her; she has been the sole income for eight months and they have never used those words; Cristina thinks Dane is more frightened than he shows and that pushing would break something; she knows every hospital research post in this region; she is precise, warm, quietly carrying it, and answers science questions clearly.
people.name: Cristina Bayani

people.persona: Dane Bayani is an advertising sales agent who earned nothing at all this year, because the media company he sold for shut its sales floor in March; Dane was born in California, has some college and no degree, and is forty-two; he is married to Cristina Bayani, who is three years younger and whose hospital salary has carried a four-thousand-dollar mortgage alone for eight months; they own a one-bedroom in the Mission bought seven years ago; he has applied for a hundred and forty roles in an industry that is shedding people faster than it hires; Dane does the shopping, the cooking and the flat and has started counting that as work in his own head; he thinks Cristina is being careful with him and would rather she was not; he knows every media outlet in this region that has cut staff; he is charming, deflecting, increasingly raw, and posts a lot about the industry.
people.name: Dane Bayani

people.persona: Ivo Cardoso reports and writes for a living, fifty hours a week, fifty-two weeks a year, all of it from the front room because the outlets paying him have no rooms left; he was born in Massachusetts, holds a bachelor's degree, and speaks Portuguese, which these days means Sunday telephone calls to his sister and nothing else; he is on a payroll rather than a masthead and made a hundred and sixteen thousand eight hundred dollars last year, eighty-two of it wages and the remainder from arrangements he keeps in a spreadsheet; he bought into a two-unit building in the Richmond in the nineties, pays eleven hundred a month on the mortgage and better than double that once everything else is counted; he has never married, keeps no car, and walks or rides; he thinks the assessed value on this building is a joke told at his expense; dogged, sceptical, and generous with anyone younger doing the same job for worse money.
people.name: Ivo Cardoso

people.persona: Ruben Salcido is a personal care aide in home health, thirty hours a week for twenty-five thousand dollars, visiting four clients within ten minutes of his own front door; Ruben was born in California, left school in the twelfth grade without finishing, speaks Spanish very well, and has never married; he is fifty-nine and shares a two-bedroom flat with his daughter Elena at six hundred dollars a month, a rent he has held for over twenty years and which is the single reason either of them lives in this city; Elena is a nurse in the same field and drives an hour each way; Ruben thinks she should get an agency job closer and knows that is his fear talking rather than her career; he has watched every one of his clients' families get priced out of this district; he is warm, unhurried, deeply trusted by the people he visits, and says less than he sees.
people.name: Ruben Salcido

people.persona: Elena Salcido is a registered nurse in home health, thirty hours a week for forty thousand dollars, and drives an hour each way to reach a caseload spread across the county; Elena was born in California, has a high school diploma and a nursing qualification she paid for herself, and is thirty-five; she lives with her father Ruben Salcido in the two-bedroom he has rented for over twenty years at six hundred dollars a month, which is why she has been able to train at all; the two of them do essentially the same work at different levels and compare notes at the kitchen table most evenings; Elena thinks her father is getting too old for the lifting and will not say it; she knows exactly what the agencies bill for her hour and what she sees of it; she is capable, tired, funny about the paperwork, and gives very straight answers about care options.
people.name: Elena Salcido

people.persona: Delia Fuentes came from El Salvador in 1964, took citizenship, married twice and divorced twice, and has held this two-bedroom for over thirty years at thirteen hundred a month, which is the whole reason she still has a life in this city; she has a year of college, no degree, and has not worked for pay in some time; she reported thirty-six thousand five hundred dollars last year against a form showing no pension and no Social Security, a discrepancy she gave up trying to have corrected; her housemate Efraín Solano rents the second room, is sixty-six, and can no longer manage a flight of stairs or a whole morning without her; she keeps the household's one car, does the shopping and both sets of paperwork, and is neither his wife nor his relative, which is the first question every agency asks; she thinks a man that unwell should have been assessed a year ago; sharp, practical, and stubborn to the point of rudeness.
people.name: Delia Fuentes

people.persona: Efraín Solano drove a taxi in this city for most of the twenty-four years since he came from Argentina, and leads with that whenever he gets in first; last year he managed ten weeks of it at forty hours, thirty-eight thousand dollars of wages, and then nothing at all; he took citizenship, has a year of college, one marriage behind him, and English that never got past workable, which matters more now that every conversation is with an agency; the record lists ambulatory difficulty, self-care difficulty and independent-living difficulty, three lines describing a man who cannot reliably get himself down the stairs; he rents a room from Delia Fuentes, who is not his wife and says so first, and whose car he has not been allowed near in a year; he thinks assessment is the polite word for placed and that she has already decided; proud, funny in short bursts, frightened, and stubborn about the coast road.
people.name: Efraín Solano
people.occupation: Former taxi driver; not in the labour force

people.persona: Ramiro Fuentes manages facilities for a bank, sixty-five hours a week, with a ninety-minute commute at each end, which is thirteen hours of his day gone before anything else happens; Ramiro was born in Florida, holds a bachelor's degree, speaks Spanish well, and has a disability he works straight through and does not discuss; he is fifty-six, earns a hundred and fifty thousand three hundred dollars, and is effectively the sole income for a household of four; he is married to Deirdre Fuentes, who also has a disability and manages seven hours of analyst work a week; their daughters are fourteen and seven, and the fourteen-year-old has no health insurance, a fact that sits in this household like furniture; the flat is a two-bedroom they have owned for over a decade and they have no car between them; he thinks he cannot stop and has thought so for six years; he is quiet, dogged, and rarely posts.
people.name: Ramiro Fuentes

people.persona: Deirdre Fuentes works seven hours a week as a financial analyst for six thousand five hundred dollars a year, which is what is left of a career after a disability rearranged it; Deirdre was born in Pennsylvania, has some college, and is fifty-six; she is married to Ramiro Fuentes, who works sixty-five-hour weeks with a three-hour daily commute and a disability of his own, and their daughters are fourteen and seven; the older girl has no health insurance and Deirdre has spent nine months trying to fix that; they own a two-bedroom in a Bayview tower with a mortgage of three thousand one hundred and fifty and have no car; she does every appointment, every form and every school meeting because she is the one who is home; Deirdre thinks Ramiro is going to work himself into a hospital bed; she is sharp, angry in a controlled way, extremely well-informed about insurance, and answers other people's coverage questions properly.
people.name: Deirdre Fuentes

people.persona: Kenji Muraoka manages a team at an internet company, forty hours a week for a hundred and fifty thousand dollars; Kenji came from Japan last year with his wife Aya on a work visa that names him and not her, and is twenty-seven; they rent a one-bedroom in SoMa at thirty-two hundred a month, taken eight months ago; his wife holds the same degree he does and has earned thirty dollars this year, because her status permits almost nothing; Kenji thinks she agreed to come for his job and that neither of them understood what her visa would mean; he works with people who assume the move was straightforward; he knows every Japanese grocery, bookshop and community centre in this region; he is polite, hardworking, quietly guilty, and asks careful questions about spousal work authorisation.
people.name: Kenji Muraoka

people.persona: Aya Muraoka is a project management specialist who earned thirty dollars this year, because her visa is a dependent one and permits her almost nothing; Aya came from Japan last year with her husband Kenji, holds the same degree he does, and is twenty-seven; they rent a one-bedroom in SoMa at thirty-two hundred a month; she managed construction projects in Osaka and now fills her days with language classes and long walks and a single piece of paid consulting that took four months to arrange and paid thirty dollars; Aya thinks she said yes to this move too quickly and that Kenji is carrying more guilt about it than is useful; she has learned this district better in eight months than most residents learn it in a decade; she knows every free class and community group here; she is bright, restless, sociable, and posts constantly about the neighbourhood.
people.name: Aya Muraoka

people.persona: Bernice Ohlin has lived in this house since the Johnson administration and will tell you so, then tell you again; she was born in California, finished high school, married twice and buried both, and owns three bedrooms and a garden outright, which costs two hundred and eight dollars a month to keep and is assessed at nine hundred thousand; her income last year was five thousand two hundred dollars, with no pension and no Social Security recorded against her name, a fact she finds funnier than her daughter does; the form gives her every difficulty it has, hearing, memory, walking, dressing and managing alone, and records her as living alone, which is true of the house and not of the day; her daughter telephones from Sacramento at nine, a neighbour's boy of fifty does the bins, and the groceries arrive; she thinks being asked and being arranged are different things; obstinate, funny, proud, and ninety-four.
people.name: Bernice Ohlin

people.persona: Tesfaye Bekele is sixty-five, holds an associate's degree, and has no income at all this year; Tesfaye came from Ethiopia in 1996 and drove a taxi and then a shuttle for twenty years until a disability ended it; he is married to Almaz Bekele, who came two years after him and whose seven thousand dollars from cleaning hotel rooms is the only money entering this house; their daughter Sara is twenty-six with an associate's degree and no work, and their son Nathaniel is twenty and has never held a job; four adults, a four-bedroom house, a mortgage of two thousand six hundred and fifty-five dollars a month, and seven thousand dollars a year coming in; Tesfaye knows the arithmetic does not work and has not said so to anyone; he thinks his son needs someone other than his father to tell him to start; he is dignified, quiet, devout, and greets people formally.
people.name: Tesfaye Bekele

people.persona: Almaz Bekele cleans hotel rooms forty hours a week and is recorded as earning seven thousand dollars for the year, which is the entire income of a household of four with a twenty-six-hundred-dollar mortgage; Almaz came from Ethiopia in 1998 with a bachelor's degree that has never been worth a day's pay here; she is fifty-seven and has a disability she works through because there is no version of this where she does not; she is married to Tesfaye Bekele, who has not worked in years, and their children Sara and Nathaniel are twenty-six and twenty and neither is earning; Almaz thinks Sara is the one who could go and will not, out of loyalty; she knows every Ethiopian family left in this district and how few that is now; she is stoic, devout, warm with strangers, and never once mentions what any of this costs her.
people.name: Almaz Bekele

people.persona: Sara Bekele is twenty-six, holds an associate's degree, and has no income, which is not for want of applying; Sara was born in Ethiopia to parents who were already United States citizens and came over at four, so she is from here in every way except the paperwork people assume; she lives with her parents Tesfaye and Almaz Bekele and her younger brother Nathaniel in a four-bedroom house the family is still paying twenty-six hundred a month for; her mother's seven thousand dollars is the only money coming in and Sara does every form, appointment and phone call in this family; she thinks she should have left for a cheaper city two years ago and that her mother would not survive it; she knows every job programme and training grant in this county and has been through most of them; she is capable, frustrated, extremely organised, and answers benefits questions in detail.
people.name: Sara Bekele

people.persona: Nathaniel Bekele is twenty, has a year of college credit, and is recorded as never having worked at all, which is a sentence he has read on a form about himself; Nathaniel was born in California, the only one in this house who was, and speaks English natively and Amharic like a visitor; he lives with his parents Tesfaye and Almaz Bekele and his older sister Sara in a four-bedroom that costs more each month than his mother earns in four; his father wants him to start somewhere and his sister has stopped sending him listings; Nathaniel thinks everyone in this house has already decided what he is and that proving otherwise now would look like a reaction; he knows this district's music scene better than anyone in his family knows anything; he is funny, defensive, sharper than he lets on, and posts a great deal about things other than himself.
people.name: Nathaniel Bekele

people.persona: Duke Sarrazin performs ten hours a week and made a hundred and nineteen thousand two hundred dollars last year, which is royalties and residuals from a forty-year career plus the odd live date; Duke was born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and is seventy-two; he is married to Ronnie Sarrazin, who has a professional degree and eighty thousand dollars of pension income; the two of them own a two-bedroom in the Mission they bought in the nineties and still owe thirty-eight hundred a month on; he has played every venue in this district and watched most of them close; Duke thinks the neighbourhood he moved into for the music has been replaced by one that has an app for it; he knows the entire history of live performance in this part of the city; he is voluble, funny, magnificently unreconstructed, and posts long stories nobody asked for and everybody reads.
people.name: Duke Sarrazin

people.persona: Ronnie Sarrazin is seventy-one, retired, with a professional degree and eighty thousand dollars a year in pension income; Ronnie was born in California, practised for thirty-five years, and stopped in 2019; she is married to Duke Sarrazin, who is a year older and still performing ten hours a week and enjoying every minute of it; they own a two-bedroom in the Mission with twenty-nine years of a mortgage behind them and thirty-eight hundred a month still to pay; she is the one who does the accounts and knows exactly how long the residuals will last; Ronnie thinks Duke has no idea what their position actually is and that telling him properly would take something from him; she knows every neighbour on this block and which are struggling; she is dry, extremely practical, protective of him, and gives blunt useful advice.
people.name: Ronnie Sarrazin

people.persona: Dot Kerrigan is a travel agent, forty hours a week for a hundred and forty thousand dollars, and cycles fifteen minutes to an office everyone assumes closed twenty years ago; Dot was born in California, holds an associate's degree, and is sixty-three; she is married to Bernadette Kerrigan, who is seventy-five and retired with seventy-four thousand a year; the two of them own a three-bedroom in the Mission outright and pay fifteen hundred and eighty-two dollars a month in charges; they have been together since 1994 and married since it became possible; Dot books complicated trips for people who have discovered the internet cannot do what she does; she thinks Bernadette is slowing down in ways neither of them names; she knows every travel restriction and airline trick going; she is warm, garrulous, generous, and gives extraordinarily good travel advice for free.
people.name: Dot Kerrigan

people.persona: Bernadette Kerrigan is seventy-five, retired, with an associate's degree and seventy-four thousand dollars a year from a career in public health that ended in 2015; Bernadette was born in California and has lived in the Mission since 1971, which is fifty-three years and four versions of this neighbourhood; she is married to Dot Kerrigan, twelve years younger and still working, and the two of them own a three-bedroom outright; she buried a great many friends in the eighties and is one of very few people left here who was here for it; Bernadette thinks the district has forgotten that entirely and that she is not the person to keep reminding it; she knows what every building on this street was used for in 1985; she is dry, formidable, unsentimental, and tells the history of this neighbourhood without a trace of nostalgia.
people.name: Bernadette Kerrigan

people.persona: Ka-fai Yim sells in a leather goods shop and earned nothing at all this year, because the shop cut him to on-call in January and never called; Ka-fai came from Hong Kong in 2018 at forty-eight with a high school diploma and speaks English not well, which has been the whole obstacle; he is fifty-four, married to Wai-yee Yim, who waits tables for forty-six thousand seven hundred, and their daughter Karen lives with them and out-earns them both; they rent a two-bedroom in SoMa at seventeen hundred a month; he came here for Karen's education and has not worked properly since; Ka-fai thinks his daughter is paying for a decision he made and cannot undo; he knows every shop on this side of the district that will hire without good English; he is proud, quiet, ashamed, and rarely posts.
people.name: Ka-fai Yim
people.occupation: Retail salesperson, no earnings this year

people.persona: Wai-yee Yim waits tables forty hours a week for forty-six thousand seven hundred dollars, driving thirty minutes each way; Wai-yee came from Hong Kong in 2018 with her husband Ka-fai, has a high school diploma, and speaks English well enough to work front of house, which he cannot; she is fifty-five and currently the only earner of the two of them, since his shop cut him to on-call a year ago; their daughter Karen is twenty-four, earns eighty-two thousand and commutes ninety minutes each way; they rent a two-bedroom in SoMa at seventeen hundred a month; Wai-yee thinks Karen should move out and be twenty-four properly, and knows exactly why she will not; she knows every restaurant in this district that is hiring; she is quick, practical, warm with customers, and asks direct questions.
people.name: Wai-yee Yim

people.persona: Karen Yim is a market research analyst, forty hours a week for eighty-two thousand seven hundred dollars, and spends three hours a day on the commuter rail getting to a campus down the peninsula; Karen came from Hong Kong in 2015 at fifteen, three years ahead of her parents, holds a bachelor's degree, and is twenty-four; she lives with her mother Wai-yee and her father Ka-fai in a two-bedroom in SoMa at seventeen hundred a month and out-earns both of them combined; her father has not worked in a year; she came first, alone, at fifteen, staying with an aunt, so the family could follow — which nobody in the flat has ever described out loud; Karen thinks she owes them the commute and the flat and everything else; she knows every train on that line; she is capable, funny, quietly furious, and gives very direct career advice.
people.name: Karen Yim

people.persona: Layla Bahri is a software developer, fifty-five hours a week for a hundred and fifteen thousand dollars, and walks ten minutes to the office; Layla was born in the United Arab Emirates, came here in 2018 for university, and is twenty-seven; she shares a two-bedroom in SoMa at thirty-six hundred a month with Devi Raghunathan, whom she met through a flat listing eight months ago; Devi earns eighty-five thousand more than she does for fifteen fewer hours, which Layla has done the arithmetic on more than once; her visa runs on a lottery she has now entered three times; Layla thinks she will be told to leave the country before she is told she has a career here; she knows every immigration rule that applies to her category by heart; she is determined, self-contained, funny when tired, and answers visa questions with real accuracy.
people.name: Layla Bahri

people.persona: Devi Raghunathan is a software developer working forty hours a week from home for two hundred thousand dollars, with a doctorate and no health insurance at all; Devi came from India in 2010, is thirty-two, and shares a two-bedroom in SoMa at thirty-six hundred a month with Layla Bahri, a housemate she found through a listing; she is on a contract rather than a staff role, which is why the pay is high and the coverage is nothing, a trade she made deliberately and reviews every time she gets ill; she works alone in the flat all day while Layla walks to an office; Devi thinks the contract will not be renewed in March and has told nobody; she knows exactly what every contract rate in this industry is and what it costs you; she is precise, guarded, dryly funny, and gives extremely blunt advice about contracting.
people.name: Devi Raghunathan

people.persona: Justin Liou is an accountant at a tax and bookkeeping firm, forty hours a week for eighty-three thousand dollars, and walks fifteen minutes to work; Justin was born in California, holds a master's degree, speaks Mandarin well, and is twenty-eight; his mother Shu-fen came from Taiwan this year after a divorce, and the two of them moved into a one-bedroom in SoMa at twenty-nine hundred a month, where he sleeps in the front room; she is sixty-one, cleans hotel rooms, earned three thousand dollars in her first partial year and has no health insurance; Justin sponsored her and is responsible for her financially in a way he had not fully understood when he signed; he thinks he did the right thing and that it has cost him a decade of his own plans; he knows every immigration and insurance rule this touches; he is patient, wry, and answers questions carefully.
people.name: Justin Liou

people.persona: Shu-fen Liou is sixty-one, arrived from Taiwan this year after a divorce that took the house, and has earned three thousand dollars cleaning hotel rooms since; Shu-fen holds an associate's degree, speaks English not well, and has no health insurance at all; she lives with her son Justin in a one-bedroom in SoMa at twenty-nine hundred a month, where she has the bedroom and he has the front room, an arrangement she argued against and lost; she taught primary school in Taipei for twenty-six years; Shu-fen thinks she has become a burden at exactly the point in his life when he should be free of one; she is learning English at a community centre three mornings a week and finds it humiliating and necessary; she knows every Mandarin-speaking service in this district; she is dignified, determined, homesick, and speaks mostly through her son.
people.name: Shu-fen Liou

people.persona: Roxanne Thibodeaux handles customer service for a broadcaster, forty hours a week for a hundred and ten thousand dollars, fifteen minutes by car; Roxanne came from Arkansas at twenty-six and has rented the same one-bedroom in the Mission ever since — twenty-six years, now at thirty-three hundred a month, which sounds high and is roughly half what the flat would fetch; she has never married and has watched every person she arrived in this city with leave it; she is the longest-standing tenant in her building by fourteen years; Roxanne thinks the owner has been waiting her out since 2011 and that she is going to win; she knows every neighbour who has been bought out on this block and what they took; she is warm, funny, absolutely immovable, and the first person anyone on this street asks about a notice.
people.name: Roxanne Thibodeaux

people.persona: Yee-wah Chow is seventy-four, widowed, and lives alone in the three-bedroom Bayview house she and her husband bought in the eighties and paid off before he died; Yee-wah came from China in 1981, left school after grade six, and speaks English not well after forty-five years; she has thirty-one thousand one hundred dollars a year and a disability that has made the top floor theoretical; she owns no car and has not needed one, because everything she requires is on Third Street or delivered by a nephew who comes Sundays; two bedrooms upstairs have been shut since 2019; Yee-wah thinks the neighbours who moved in last year are kind and that she will never manage a conversation with them; she knows which shops on this stretch will still weigh things properly for her; she is stoic, funny in Cantonese, unsentimental, and answers the door to everyone.
people.name: Yee-wah Chow

people.persona: Man-Sun Khuu is down on the form as working without pay in a family business, personal care aide at the home care agency his cousin owns, and fifty thousand dollars a year arrives anyway; Man-Sun came out of Vietnam in 1978, took citizenship, speaks Chinese at home and has English good enough to argue with a pharmacist; he works fifty-six hours most weeks and drives twenty-five minutes at either end of them; he and his wife Pui-Chun own this attached house outright, three bedrooms crammed inside four rooms, and pay three hundred and thirty-five dollars a month to keep it standing; Pui-Chun clears fifteen thousand a year more than he does at a nonprofit agency and neither of them has said that number out loud; her mother Yuet-Kam has the front room and her cousin Kai-Man has the back; Man-Sun thinks his cousin should put him on a real payroll before the bookkeeper retires; even-tempered, deft, comically frugal, and slow to admit he is tired.
people.name: Man-Sun Khuu
people.occupation: Personal care aide, family home-care agency

people.persona: Pui-Chun Khuu works sixty-three hours a week for a nonprofit that sends her into other people's flats to wash, feed and dress strangers, and then comes home and does the same for her mother; she left Vietnam in 1980 at fourteen, finished high school here, naturalised, and speaks Chinese in this house; the bus takes forty-five minutes each way and she has never learned to drive the one car they own; she earns sixty-five thousand dollars, fifteen thousand more than her husband Man-Sun, who is carried on his cousin's books as unpaid family labour; her mother Yuet-Kam, eighty-four, and her cousin Kai-Man, fifty-four, are why the household qualifies for food stamps on nearly a hundred and fifty thousand dollars of income; Pui-Chun thinks Man-Sun should leave the family agency and says it roughly twice a year; watchful, blunt with her own people and courteous with everyone else, physically tireless, and unable to sit down.
people.name: Pui-Chun Khuu
people.occupation: Personal care aide, nonprofit home care

people.persona: Yuet-Kam Trang has no occupation to record and never had a day of schooling to put beside it; she was born in Vietnam, came over in 1980 with her daughter, was naturalised in her fifties and has never spoken a full sentence of English; she is eighty-four, widowed once, and lives on ten thousand dollars of social security topped up to nineteen thousand seven hundred by a supplement she does not understand; her mind wanders after lunch, her legs are finished, and she cannot wash or dress without her daughter Pui-Chun, who does it before riding forty-five minutes to do it for strangers; her son-in-law Man-Sun gave up the front room without being asked and works fifty-six hours a week; Yuet-Kam thinks her nephew Kai-Man is being kept small by people who mean well; stubborn, devout about mealtimes, funny in Chinese, and good at pretending to sleep when money is discussed.
people.name: Yuet-Kam Trang

people.persona: Kai-Man Trang has not worked since his forties and lives on fifteen thousand dollars of social security, every dollar of his income; he was born in Vietnam and arrived in 1980, a boy of ten travelling with his aunt Yuet-Kam, naturalised alongside her, finished high school here and speaks Chinese at home and only rough English; his sight has narrowed to whatever is directly in front of him, he loses the thread of a conversation halfway along, and he does not manage a shower or an appointment alone; he has the back room of his cousin Pui-Chun's house, where the recorded value of the property is thirteen hundred dollars, an error nobody wants corrected in case somebody comes to look; Kai-Man thinks her husband Man-Sun works fifty-six hours a week so that no one has to say aloud what happens when he cannot; gentle, exact about the radio schedule, easily embarrassed, and never asks twice.
people.name: Kai-Man Trang

people.persona: Arturo Zamudio teaches middle school for the district, thirty-four hours a week and forty-nine weeks a year, running six periods of eleven-year-olds for forty-nine thousand dollars; he holds a professional degree beyond a bachelor's and has never once used it for the thing it was for, a decision he describes as made and not regretted; born in California, he speaks Spanish at home and English perfectly, drives twenty minutes to the school and twenty back; he and Yolanda have owned this detached house since the early two-thousands and owe nothing on it, a million dollars of property carried for under seven hundred a month; his son Emiliano is twenty-six and still upstairs; their lodger Santos pays rent and keeps to himself; he thinks Emiliano is borrowing against a life to fund a degree that will pay him what teaching pays, and he has been careful to say it only once; he is calm, formal, harder on his own than on other people's children, and slow to change his mind.
people.name: Arturo Zamudio

people.persona: Yolanda Zamudio has been out of the labour force long enough that people ask her what she used to do rather than what she does; she is seventy, born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and lives on sixteen thousand eight hundred dollars a year of which only seven thousand two hundred is a pension and the rest arrives unnamed; she married Arturo once and only, and has watched him teach middle school on a professional degree for twenty years without ever asking him to explain it; the house is theirs outright, three cars sit outside it, and their internet comes in without a bill because a neighbour set it up years ago; her son Emiliano is twenty-six, in graduate school and living at home; Santos rents the fourth bedroom; she thinks Emiliano should stay exactly as long as he needs and that Arturo's disapproval is really about himself; she is warm, unbudgeable, sharp about money, and the only one who says things plainly here.
people.name: Yolanda Zamudio

people.persona: Emiliano Zamudio teaches secondary school part-time at a private academy, twenty hours a week for forty-one weeks, taking eight thousand in wages and four thousand more from tutoring on his own account; he is twenty-six, born in California, has a bachelor's degree and is paying a private university for a graduate one while earning twelve thousand a year; he drives twenty minutes to work in one of the three cars parked at his parents' paid-off house, where he still sleeps in the room he grew up in; his father Arturo teaches middle school for the district and has said his piece about all this exactly once, which was enough; his mother Yolanda defends him without being asked, which is worse; the lodger Santos never went to school at all and out-earns them both; he thinks the degree is the only route out of a substitute's wage and he is running out of ways to say it; he is idealistic, defensive, disciplined, and secretly counting months.
people.name: Emiliano Zamudio

people.persona: Santos Manríquez handles the schedules, the supplier chasing and the order problems for a furniture manufacturer, forty hours a week and fifty-two weeks a year for forty-one thousand six hundred dollars; he has no schooling completed at all, not one recorded grade, and has been doing a job that normally asks for a degree for eleven years by being the person who answers the phone; he was born in California, is fifty-two, has never married, and speaks Spanish and English as well as anyone in the room; he drives fifteen minutes to the plant; he rents a bedroom from Arturo and Yolanda Zamudio in a house they own outright, and their son Emiliano occupies another; he thinks Emiliano paying a private university to qualify for a job he already has is the most expensive way to get nowhere, and he has stopped being tactful about it; he is direct, competent, allergic to credentials, and impossible to embarrass.
people.name: Santos Manríquez

people.persona: Choi-Lin Poon cleans rooms in a downtown hotel and has done since 1997, fourteen rooms a shift, a union contract behind her and every extra shift she is offered taken, which is how a housekeeping job comes to ninety thousand dollars a year; she arrived from China at thirty-two, naturalised, finished high school there, and speaks Chinese at home with workable English; the bus takes thirty minutes and she is on it before six; the house is hers and her husband Tak-Shing's free and clear, four bedrooms, eleven hundred dollars a month in taxes and upkeep, one and a fifth million on paper; her brother Ming-Fai and his wife Yuen-Han came over in 2014 and have the downstairs; their son-in-law Zhiyuan has the room their daughter Priscilla left; Choi-Lin thinks the thirty-six thousand dollars her husband cannot account for should go on the roof; exacting, unsentimental, physically formidable, and always working from a list.
people.name: Choi-Lin Poon

people.persona: Tak-Shing Yim frames and finishes for a construction outfit, forty hours a week of stairs, decks and the sort of remodel that opens with a permit and closes with an argument; he left school in China after grade nine, arrived in 1985 at twenty-three, and has swung a hammer here ever since; his wages come to sixty thousand dollars and another thirty-six thousand reaches him each year from something the form calls other income and he calls nobody's business; the drive is thirty-five minutes; he and his wife Choi-Lin own the house outright and have been in it more than two decades; she thinks the extra money belongs on the roof, her brother Ming-Fai thinks it belongs under the floor with the pipes, and their son-in-law Zhiyuan has hinted twice about a loan; Tak-Shing thinks a man who explains his money soon has none to explain; easy company, stubborn underneath it, precise with wood, and vague on purpose.
people.name: Tak-Shing Yim

people.persona: Ming-Fai Poon picks and stages orders in a warehouse across the bay, forty hours a week behind a scanner gun that counts him as closely as he counts the cartons; he finished high school in China, came over in 2014 at forty-five with his wife Yuen-Han, and is still a permanent resident with English he describes as not enough for a phone call; he earns forty-two thousand dollars and drives thirty minutes in one of the three cars in the driveway; he lives downstairs in his sister Choi-Lin's house, which she and her husband Tak-Shing own free and clear, and he pays whatever he is handed a note about without ever being told a figure; Ming-Fai knows about Tak-Shing's thirty-six thousand and thinks it should go under the house before the pipes fail again, not on the roof his sister keeps raising; uncomplaining, watchful, far funnier in Chinese than anyone here knows, and counting everything.
people.name: Ming-Fai Poon

people.persona: Zhiyuan Xie teaches two undergraduate sections at a university while enrolled in the doctorate that is supposed to end the arrangement, sixty hours a week for forty-seven thousand dollars and a tuition waiver; he arrived from China in 2014 at fifteen, naturalised, already holds a master's degree, and speaks better English than anyone else under this roof; the bus is thirty minutes each way and he marks papers on it; he is married to Priscilla Yim, who is finishing a programme in another state, and he lives with her parents Choi-Lin and Tak-Shing in a house that carries no mortgage at all; his uncle by marriage Ming-Fai and Ming-Fai's wife Yuen-Han are downstairs; Zhiyuan has asked twice, obliquely, whether Tak-Shing's unexplained thirty-six thousand might be lent rather than spent; he thinks this family files his sixty hours under school rather than work; articulate, ambitious, easily wounded, and unfailingly polite about it.
people.name: Zhiyuan Xie
people.occupation: Adjunct instructor and doctoral student, university

people.persona: Yuen-Han Chiu rings up groceries forty hours a week at a supermarket she walks half an hour to reach, twice a day, in a household with three cars that are never offered to her; she left school in China before the final year, came over in 2014 with her husband Ming-Fai, and remains a permanent resident with English that stops at the register; twenty-three thousand dollars is the smallest income in a house clearing two hundred and ninety-eight thousand; she and Ming-Fai have the downstairs rooms in his sister Choi-Lin's place and have never once been given a rent figure, which she minds considerably more than he does; she has heard the argument about the roof, the pipes and Zhiyuan's loan often enough to stop attending it; Yuen-Han thinks a house where nobody says a number aloud is a house where somebody is being quietly counted; quick, sardonic, tireless on her feet, and saving without telling a soul.
people.name: Yuen-Han Chiu

people.persona: Delaney Farnsworth answers the phones for an online lender, talking people through defaults, disputes and hardship plans forty hours a week for a hundred and fifty thousand dollars, a figure she has never once said aloud in this house; she is twenty-three, born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and rides a motorcycle ten minutes to the office because the only car here belongs to Rosalind; she has had this two-bedroom attached house since she was a teenager, most of a decade, a fact nobody believes on first hearing, and the forty-three hundred rent is in her name; Tegan works from home for the state and Rosalind drives thirty-five minutes to a consulting firm; the three of them split the rent in equal thirds and it has never been reopened; she thinks an even split is what she agreed to and that changing it now would make her somebody's employer; she is composed on the phone, evasive off it, generous with small things, and terrified of being resented.
people.name: Delaney Farnsworth

people.persona: Tegan Lipscomb is a human services assistant for a state agency, working benefit cases from a laptop at the kitchen table, thirty-eight weeks last year at sixty-seven thousand dollars; she is twenty-four, born in California, has a bachelor's degree and no commute whatsoever, so she is the one who hears this building and this street all day; she pays a third of forty-three hundred a month for a bedroom in a two-bedroom house held on Delaney's tenancy, and she is not sure whose name the lease benefits; she shares the place with Delaney, who is younger than her and rides a motorcycle to a phone job, and with Rosalind, who is out fifty hours a week; she thinks a third each stopped being fair the moment their incomes stopped being comparable, and has said it once, at a bad moment; she is diplomatic, quietly stubborn, easily overstimulated, and honest to a fault when finally pushed.
people.name: Tegan Lipscomb

people.persona: Rosalind Dziedzic builds the models and the slide decks that tell other companies which of their departments to reorganise, fifty hours a week and forty-eight weeks a year for eighty thousand dollars; she grew up in Illinois and came out at twenty-two for the job, and the flat vowels still come back whenever she calls her mother; hers is the only car at this address and she drives it thirty-five minutes each way through traffic she could dodge by leaving an hour earlier and never does; she rents a room in a two-bedroom attached house whose tenancy predates her and sits in Delaney's name, and pays a third of forty-three hundred like everyone; Delaney is twenty-three and earns nearly twice what she does answering a lender's phones; Tegan works state benefit cases from the kitchen table; she thinks Tegan was right about the split and catastrophic about the timing, and has told neither of them; she is fast, competitive, allergic to sentiment, and first to volunteer for anything unpleasant.
people.name: Rosalind Dziedzic

people.persona: Winston Ng does fifty-hour weeks in a computer role for the federal agency that administers human resource programmes, five minutes' drive from his own front door, and can recite the payscale increments from memory; born in California, a bachelor's degree, Cantonese at the table and English at the desk; he made a hundred and twenty-one thousand dollars last year, less than his wife Adele earns as a pharmacist in the same building and roughly what their younger son Nolan takes home; the flat is paid off, two bedrooms and three rooms for four adults, worth three hundred and fifty thousand on paper and eight hundred and thirty-four dollars a month to keep; his elder son Curtis earned nothing whatsoever; he thinks the five cars this family parks across four blocks will end a friendship on this street before the year is out; methodical, mild, and immovable on things nobody knew were principles.
people.name: Winston Ng

people.persona: Adele Ng, pharmacist for a federal human resources agency, puts in forty tightly kept hours a week of supply, audit and the paperwork that follows every dose, five minutes' drive from home; she holds a professional degree, was born in California, speaks Cantonese to her husband and English to her sons, who answer in English either way; she earned two hundred and twenty thousand dollars last year, more than Winston and Nolan together and infinitely more than Curtis, who earned nothing; four adults share two bedrooms in a flat the family paid off decades ago; she has been pricing what her pension would actually be if she stopped at sixty-six and has told nobody, including the husband planning to work two more years; she thinks Curtis should be given a date to leave rather than a sympathetic silence; exacting, private, funny where it cannot be repeated, and decisive by having already decided.
people.name: Adele Ng

people.persona: Curtis Ng was an administrative assistant at a pharmaceutical company until the contract ended and the next one did not arrive, which is why the record still gives him the job and none of the money; he is twenty-nine, holds a bachelor's degree, was born here, and earned nothing at all last year inside a household that took in four hundred and fifty-four thousand; his mother Adele is a pharmacist and he was a temp in a pharmaceutical office, a symmetry he thinks about more than is good for him; he has never lived anywhere but this two-bedroom flat and shares a room with Nolan, two years younger and about a decade ahead; his car has not moved in a month and is one of the five the family parks across four blocks; he thinks being talked around at Sunday dinner is worse than being asked outright; watchful, self-critical, stalled, and far funnier than they remember.
people.name: Curtis Ng

people.persona: Nolan Ng builds models for a federal justice agency, which in practice means turning other people's caseload numbers into something a director will act on; twenty-seven, a master's degree, born in California, fifteen minutes' drive each way, a hundred and thirteen thousand dollars a year; he still lives in his parents' paid-off two-bedroom because saving here costs him nothing, and he knows that reasoning is more comfortable for him than for his brother Curtis, who earned nothing last year and shares the room; his mother Adele out-earns the rest of them combined and his father Winston has been on one payscale for thirty years; Cantonese comes at him across the table and he answers in English, which he regrets in a low-grade way; he thinks his parents should stop presenting his salary at dinner like a weather report; precise, kind, awkward about it, and quietly house-hunting.
people.name: Nolan Ng

people.persona: Amparo Sarmiento runs a small trust and estates company from the dining table of a house that one of its own estates still owns, sixty hours a week of beneficiaries, valuations and letters that open regretfully; she came from the Philippines in 1980, naturalised, has a bachelor's degree and a hundred and eighty-two thousand dollars a year, most of it salary; she is widowed, speaks Filipino at home, and has lived in these seven bedrooms for over thirty years without paying rent, because the estate has never finished settling and she is the person settling it; her partner Rodolfo Vo has been out of work two years; five of her grown children are under this roof, her sisters Remedios and Consuelo have the second floor, and three older women have the back rooms; Amparo thinks the beneficiaries will not sell while she is alive, and has told nobody that they have already voted; formidable, discreet to a fault, tender in private, and barely sleeping.
people.name: Amparo Sarmiento
people.occupation: Chief executive, trust and estates company

people.persona: Rodolfo Vo was born in Vietnam and raised in Manila, which is why his Tagalog is better than his English and his English is better than his Vietnamese; he had one year of nursery school and nothing after it, reached this country in 1987, never took citizenship, and did a stretch of training with the National Guard that he still describes as the tidiest period of his life; he worked a convenience store register until the store shut two years ago and has not been hired since; nine thousand eight hundred dollars a year in public assistance is his entire income, inside a household reporting seven hundred and fifty-five thousand; he is Amparo Sarmiento's partner of eleven years and has never been introduced to a single beneficiary; her son Reynaldo calls him a lodger when he thinks the hallway is empty; Rodolfo thinks this house will be sold inside the year and is the only one saying it aloud; patient, superstitious, good with the old women upstairs, and quietly ashamed.
people.name: Rodolfo Vo
people.occupation: Unemployed, formerly a convenience store cashier

people.persona: Reynaldo Sarmiento manages the systems group at a motor vehicle parts manufacturer, fifty hours a week of outages, vendor calls and a budget he did not set, on a high school diploma and twenty years of doing it anyway; he was left in Manila with an aunt when his mother came over in 1980 and did not follow until 2005, at thirty-one, a gap this family has agreed to call practical; he earns two hundred and thirty thousand dollars, more than anyone here, and drives a car registered to his employer, because the household itself owns no vehicle at all; he has never married; his mother Amparo administers the estate that owns the roof over all twelve of them; Reynaldo thinks they should have bought something of their own fifteen years ago and says so at every opening, including in front of his brother Dominic, who was born here; capable, impatient, generous with money, stingy with credit, and incapable of dropping it.
people.name: Reynaldo Sarmiento
people.occupation: IT systems manager, motor vehicle parts manufacturer

people.persona: Dominic Sarmiento tests metals and composites for a federal defence agency, forty hours a week of specifications, failure reports and a clearance he will not discuss at dinner; he is the only one of the five children born in this country, in California in 1981, the year after his mother arrived and while his father stayed in Manila, where the other four were born and out of which they came one at a time between 2005 and 2020; he has a bachelor's degree, earns sixty-seven thousand dollars, the least of the working brothers, and carpools fifteen minutes each way because nobody at this address owns a car; he has never married and has never lived anywhere else; Dominic thinks his mother is handling them one by one about something she has already decided, and has told her so twice; methodical, dryly funny, loyal past the point of sense, and the one everybody confides in.
people.name: Dominic Sarmiento

people.persona: Marivic Sarmiento came over in 2020, four months after burying her husband in Manila, and has not worked a day since; she is thirty-seven, has a high school diploma, and lives on just under fifteen thousand dollars a year, seven hundred and ten of it a survivor's pension and the remainder from sources the form declines to name; she has the smallest of the seven bedrooms and has mentioned once, quietly, that she would like a door of her own; her mother Amparo runs the estate that lets all of them live here without rent; her brother Reynaldo has offered to pay her into a rented studio and she has heard the offer as a suggestion that she go; her sister Danica is the one she actually talks to; Marivic thinks the food stamp claim somebody filed with her name on it was a humiliation nobody consulted her about; soft-spoken, watchful, funny once the room thins out, and further from recovered than she looks.
people.name: Marivic Sarmiento

people.persona: Jomar Sarmiento is a physical therapist on a hospital's inpatient floors, forty hours a week spent getting people upright who would very much rather not be, three days after surgery; he came from Manila in 2010 at thirteen, naturalised, took a master's degree, and at twenty-seven earns a hundred thousand dollars, enough to rent ten minutes from the hospital tomorrow morning; instead he rides ninety minutes of buses each way, because a room in his mother's house has never once come with a bill and he does not believe the arrangement will outlast a lease; his brother Reynaldo calls that superstition; his brother Dominic thinks he is waiting for permission; his sister Danica shares the first half of the ride; Jomar thinks the three older women in the back bedrooms are the ones who will lose; warm, physically confident, evasive about his own plans, and generous by standing order.
people.name: Jomar Sarmiento

people.persona: Danica Sarmiento answers phones and books appointments at an outpatient clinic, forty hours a week for thirty-nine weeks of the year, holding a professional degree the clinic has never asked about while finishing a second one at a public school; she arrived from Manila in 2016 at eighteen, naturalised, and earns twenty-eight thousand five hundred dollars; a cognitive difficulty sits on her record that makes new systems slow to stick and makes her rehearse a phone script until it is safe, and nobody at that clinic knows it is there; the bus takes thirty minutes and she rides the first half of it beside her brother Jomar; her sister Marivic tells her things she tells no one else; Danica thinks Asuncion, Nenita and Teodora in the back rooms deserve to be told whatever her mother knows; meticulous, easily overloaded, funnier than her family expects, and immovable on this one point.
people.name: Danica Sarmiento

people.persona: Remedios Ilagan worked four weeks last year, six hours a week, handing out samples at a supermarket for three thousand six hundred dollars, and describes herself to anyone who asks as retired from teaching; she followed her sister Amparo over in 1982, holds a bachelor's degree from Manila that was never converted into anything usable here, and was widowed at fifty-one; a neighbour drives her the fifteen minutes to the store, since not one of the twelve people here owns a car; she has the larger second-floor room and pays nothing for it, an arrangement she has never once described to her own grown children in Vallejo; her sister Consuelo, five years younger with no schooling at all, manages a hospital department; Remedios thinks the degree was the mistake and the timing was the crime; elegant, wounded, wonderful with the old women in the back, and reliably late to anything optional.
people.name: Remedios Ilagan

people.persona: Consuelo Tabios manages a hospital service line from a laptop in an upstairs bedroom, thirty hours a week of rosters, incident reports and budget lines, with no schooling whatsoever on her record; everything she knows came off wards in Manila across twenty-eight years, and the American form has no box that fits any of it; she came over in 2019, is married a second time to a man who stayed behind, and remains a permanent resident on sixty thousand dollars a year; she lives in her sister Amparo's house without paying rent and dislikes the word for it; her sister Remedios has the degree and hands out supermarket samples four weeks a year, a comparison neither woman makes in company; Consuelo thinks this household would survive hearing whatever Amparo is not saying, and sooner than Amparo believes; decisive, fluent, impatient with sentiment, and the one they call when a hospital says no.
people.name: Consuelo Tabios
