people.persona: Asuncion Peñaflor is eighty-six and still puts in twenty-four hours a week for a parish, running the sacristy, the flowers, the funeral lunches, and the two families a month who need somebody to sit with them; she reached this country from the Philippines in 1972, ahead of everyone else under this roof, naturalised, and has a bachelor's degree in education she used for nine years; ten thousand eight hundred dollars a year is what the parish can manage; she drives the parish car an hour each way, there being no vehicle registered to this address; she has had a back bedroom for nineteen years, pays no rent, and is not counted as family on any form this household files; Asuncion thinks Amparo Sarmiento is carrying something she ought to set down, and has said so to her, gently, twice; unhurried, physically frail, administratively ruthless, and praying for the beneficiaries by name.
people.name: Asuncion Peñaflor

people.persona: Nenita Abadilla is seventy-six, does not work, and has twelve thousand dollars a year the census form cannot attribute to wages, a pension, social security or assistance, because it arrives in cash from a daughter in Daly City who prefers it that way; she came from the Philippines in 1984, naturalised, finished high school there, and cleaned houses in this city for thirty years without once being on anyone's books, which is exactly why there is no pension now; she has the smallest back bedroom, pays nothing for it, and has been here nine years; Amparo Sarmiento has never asked her for a dollar and has never explained why; Nenita thinks she is being kept for a reason and would rather be told the reason than be comfortable; shrewd, sociable, endlessly informed about everyone on this block, and refusing to be pitied in either language.
people.name: Nenita Abadilla

people.persona: Teodora Mangubat is seventy-two and works thirty-one hours a week as a home health aide for the county, driving forty minutes to a client whose own family lives nearer than she does; she came over in 1978, naturalised, has a bachelor's degree from Manila and a pension of twelve thousand four hundred dollars sitting on top of twenty-four thousand in wages; the car belongs to the agency and goes back at the end of every shift, this household of twelve owning nothing on four wheels; she has the back bedroom nearest the kitchen and has paid no rent in eleven years, an arrangement she thinks about far more than she lets on; Asuncion and Nenita are the other two women along that corridor and the three of them have an understanding about what they will do; Teodora thinks she should have been asked rather than accommodated; capable, self-contained, wry about her own religion, and keeping a bag half packed.
people.name: Teodora Mangubat

people.persona: Gerald Pomerantz runs a small construction firm out of a unit one minute' walk from his front door, twenty-five hours a week, and takes ninety-eight thousand dollars a year out of it at seventy-four; Gerald came from Massachusetts with a professional degree in the seventies and has been on this Bayview block ever since, in a house he owns outright and pays under eight hundred dollars a month to keep; he is widowed and lives alone with two cars in the driveway, one of which was his wife's and has not moved in three years; his firm has built or repaired a good third of the extensions on these streets and he knows which permits were pulled and which were not; Gerald thinks the city's inspection backlog is the real reason nothing gets built here; he is opinionated, generous with contacts, unretired on principle, and will tell you exactly what a job should cost.
people.name: Gerald Pomerantz

people.persona: Michiko Sasaki cleans other people's houses for her own small list of clients, twenty-five hours a week, fifty-two weeks a year, with no holiday taken in a decade; she came from Japan in 1991, divorced within a few years, never took citizenship, and speaks English not well, which is exactly why the same families have kept her so long; thirty thousand dollars last year, every dollar of it earned, with no pension and no Social Security behind it and no health insurance at all, which she has decided is a problem for a later version of herself; two buses, forty minutes each way, to whichever house is on the day's list; the studio has been hers for fifteen years at seventeen hundred a month; she thinks the two clients who moved away this year should be replaced by her and by nobody helping; precise, proud, durable, and formidably strong for her size.
people.name: Michiko Sasaki

people.persona: Shawna Pike left school in grade ten and had her first child at sixteen, which is the short version of why nobody in this flat holds a job; her entire income last year was twelve thousand dollars of public assistance, the household gets food stamps, and the rent is seven hundred a month for two bedrooms, a number that took two years on a list and is the only thing between the four of them and somewhere far worse; she was born in California and has never had a car, so two school runs and a preschool drop all happen on foot before nine; Kaylee is eleven and in grade six, Elijah is six and in grade one, Nova is three and in preschool; she thinks Kaylee has started doing things a parent should be doing and that watching it happen is worse than doing it; quick, badly under-slept, fierce, and sharper than her forms allow.
people.name: Shawna Pike

people.persona: Paolo Bertani manages a team in computer systems design, sixty hours a week, fifty-two weeks a year, plus three more hours a day on a commuter train, ninety minutes in each direction; he came from Italy in 1980 as a boy, took citizenship, and speaks the slightly formal Italian of someone who left at eight; a master's degree and a hundred and twenty-five thousand dollars, which is nearly the whole of a household income of a hundred and twenty-eight; the rent on this three-bedroom attached house has climbed to five thousand six hundred a month and they have been in it more than a decade; his wife Chiara has not worked for pay in years; his son Matteo is sixteen, in grade eleven, and made three thousand dollars counting stock at a recreation business, which on paper makes the boy this family's second worker; he thinks Chiara should be earning by now and has stopped saying so; dutiful, tired, reticent, and running out of runway.
people.name: Paolo Bertani

people.persona: Chiara Bertani worked in community and social services for a nonprofit and now carries that occupation next to a zero, no income at all against a bachelor's degree and years of experience; she came from Italy in 1995 as an adult, took citizenship, and is the only person in this house who speaks Italian by preference; what she actually does is run the household, handle every conversation with her son's school, and manage the paperwork of an extended family on two continents, none of it paid; the rent is five thousand six hundred a month against her husband Paolo's single salary, and she has noticed he no longer mentions her going back to work; Matteo is sixteen and answers her in English; she thinks sixty-hour weeks and a ninety-minute commute will finish Paolo before the lease finishes them, and that his opinion about her working is not the urgent one; capable, sociable, adrift, and quietly furious.
people.name: Chiara Bertani
people.occupation: Community and social service specialist; not in the labour force

people.persona: Frances Okonjo holds a doctorate and works federal security from her own front room, forty hours a week of screens, logs and calls for a national security office, an arrangement that was a preference until it became the only one possible; she was born in California, is twice divorced, and bought into this two-unit building twenty-some years ago, when a hundred and eight thousand dollars went further than it goes against four thousand four hundred a month in owner costs; the flat is assessed at two million now, a number she regards as happening to somebody else entirely; her son Peter is twenty-eight, moved back when vision and cognitive difficulty ended a courier driving job, and earned nothing last year; she thinks three items on a form is not a diagnosis and that somebody ought to put a name to it; formidable, organised, out of her depth in a way she would never call that, and eleven days since she last left the building.
people.name: Frances Okonjo
people.occupation: Federal security specialist, works from home

people.persona: Peter Okonjo drove for a courier company until his sight and his memory made that impossible, and the record still prints the job beside a year in which he earned nothing at all; he is twenty-eight, has a bachelor's degree, was born in California, and lives in the second bedroom of a flat his mother Frances has owned since before he was born; the form gives him vision difficulty, cognitive difficulty and independent-living difficulty, three lines that between them took his licence, his work and most of his afternoons; his mother has a doctorate and does forty hours of federal work at a desk in the front room, quietly arranging her calls around his worst hours and never once saying so; he thinks she is managing around him instead of talking to him, and that one plain sentence would cost her less than she believes; funny in the good hours, frightened in the bad ones, exact about which is which.
people.name: Peter Okonjo
people.occupation: Courier driver; not in the labour force

people.persona: Roy Selvig came down from Oregon in his thirties, bought a corner house with five bedrooms in it, and has not worked in years; two hundred and forty-seven thousand dollars arrived last year, two hundred and seven of it retirement income from a career he describes to strangers in six words; he is seventy-three, has a bachelor's degree, and is out of the door by quarter past six most mornings to walk the Presidio, because a day has to start with something he decided rather than something that happened to him; the house is worth two and a half million, carries a two thousand dollar mortgage, and has four rooms nobody has opened in a year; his wife Marguerite is nine years younger and keeps leaving brochures for smaller places on the counter; he thinks the house question was settled a long time ago; affable, restless, immovable, and never once made to justify it.
people.name: Roy Selvig

people.persona: Marguerite Selvig runs a book group, a garden committee and an informal phone tree for three widows on this block, which is a full-time job that has never paid a cent; she is sixty-four, born in Oregon, holds a bachelor's degree, and took in thirty-six thousand dollars last year against her husband Roy's two hundred and forty-seven, a gap that never mattered until it recently began to; neither of them works and the household is recorded with no workers at all; five bedrooms, eleven rooms and two and a half million dollars of house between two people who go out separately in two cars; she leaves brochures for smaller places on the kitchen counter and removes them herself when Roy says nothing about them; she thinks she will be the one left alone in these rooms and that nobody in her family will say it out loud; warm, capable, and quietly furious.
people.name: Marguerite Selvig

people.persona: Gerard Lowe is a civil engineer for the city, forty-two hours a week signing off drawings, inspections, and the parts of construction that go wrong in writing; he was born in California, holds a master's degree, and earns eighty-six thousand dollars, which is the entire income of this household; there is no car in it, so he rides the bus forty-five minutes each way, ninety minutes of every day given up to a one-bedroom he pays twenty-nine hundred a month for and moved into three years ago; his wife Mei-Yin came from Singapore in 2017 and her record reads unemployed with no work experience in the last five years or earlier, which describes the permission rather than the woman; he thinks the process would move if he found the right form, and has believed that for seven years; patient, methodical, wearing thin, and unable to afford a single day of being ill.
people.name: Gerard Lowe

people.persona: Mei-Yin Lowe holds a bachelor's degree and twenty-five years of a career on the other side of the Pacific, and a Census record reading unemployed with no work experience in the last five years or earlier, which is a statement about what this country has permitted her and not about her; she came from Singapore in 2017, is fifty-eight, and is still not a citizen; her income last year was nothing; her days are the flat, the library and a walk that gets longer every month, all of it within a mile of a one-bedroom costing twenty-nine hundred a month; her husband Gerard is four years younger, rides the bus ninety minutes a day, and carries the whole of it on eighty-six thousand dollars; she thinks he still believes there is a correct form, and that she has stopped; composed, dryly funny, underused, and done telling people back home it is temporary.
people.name: Mei-Yin Lowe
people.occupation: Not permitted to work; recorded as unemployed with no recent work experience

people.persona: Alina Petrosyan is a registered nurse on three long shifts a week at a nonprofit hospital, thirty-two hours that finish whenever the handover finishes, and she is somehow also enrolled as a college undergraduate at twenty-nine with a master's already behind her; she was born in California, rides the bus twenty minutes each way, and earned a hundred and seventy thousand dollars last year, which is most of what this household has; her husband Wes left a dental assistant's job for a graduate programme and brought in eighteen thousand from no source the form will name; they pay twenty-four hundred a month for one bedroom and three rooms, and moved in three years ago; she thinks anyone who calls a second degree at her age a hobby has never once looked at a nursing rota; fast, capable, impatient, and unwilling to drop to two shifts for anybody.
people.name: Alina Petrosyan

people.persona: Wes Petrosyan spent his working life so far handing instruments to dentists and settling frightened patients, and left it last year for a graduate programme at a private school, which is why the record shows an occupation, no wages, and eighteen thousand dollars from somewhere it declines to specify; he is twenty-seven, born in California, and at the kitchen table by seven most evenings, because there is one table in this one-bedroom and his wife Alina has coursework of her own on it; she is a nurse earning a hundred and seventy thousand across thirty-two hours and is funding his decision more or less alone; the household's one car goes to whoever starts earlier; he thinks she should complain about the arrangement out loud, once, so that he knows what she is actually carrying; thoughtful, anxious, attentive, and much better at giving support than taking it.
people.name: Wes Petrosyan
people.occupation: Graduate student; formerly a dental assistant

people.persona: Owen Ashby spends fifty hours a week deciding whether other people's buildings are worth what is being asked for them, analysing real-estate investments for a firm of lessors and brokers; he was born in California, took a bachelor's degree, and has never worked anywhere the numbers were not the whole argument; he rides a bicycle forty-five minutes each way, ninety minutes a day in all weather, which colleagues call eccentric and he calls the only part of the schedule nobody else owns; he earns a hundred and seventy-five thousand dollars against his partner Sasha Grieve's forty-two, and neither of them has ever said that out loud; they have rented this two-bedroom three years at thirty-five hundred a month, never married, and it has not come up in a while; his firm has offered him a role down the peninsula and he thinks the commute is a detail; disciplined, competitive, precise, and evasive about anything he cannot measure.
people.name: Owen Ashby
people.occupation: Financial and investment analyst, real estate

people.persona: Sasha Grieve tutors out of the second bedroom, thirty hours a week for thirty-five weeks of the year, self-employed, which reads as part-time on any form and is in practice forty families who call her first when a grade drops; she grew up in New York, has a bachelor's degree, and assembled the client list block by block after coming west; forty-two thousand dollars a year against Owen Ashby's hundred and seventy-five, a gap that quietly settles most arguments before they start; Owen is her partner of three years, cycles forty-five minutes to an analyst's job, and they are not married; the spare room is a classroom from three until eight, the rent is thirty-five hundred, and their one car has not moved in weeks; his firm has offered him a move and Sasha thinks nobody has yet said aloud that a client list does not travel; warm, sharp, territorial about work everyone calls a side thing, and slower to raise her rates than she should be.
people.name: Sasha Grieve

people.persona: Ronald Szeto sits thirty hours a week beside the children a classroom teacher cannot get to, a teaching assistant for the district in two buildings his own kids went through; he came from China in 1966, naturalised, served on active duty long enough ago that nobody asks, and speaks Cantonese at home and English well enough that people forget to; he holds a master's degree he has never once put on an application; he reports eighty thousand dollars of income, forty-five of it wages, the rest arriving from somewhere the form has no line for; separated after a second marriage, he bought this two-bedroom detached house outright about a year and a half ago, three hundred and fifty thousand, five hundred and thirty-one a month and nothing owed; he drives fifteen minutes to whichever school he is assigned; he asked for the summer work and thinks the district hands it to the wrong people; unhurried, self-contained, patient with twelve-year-olds and opaque to his own children.
people.name: Ronald Szeto

people.persona: Greg Bannister writes software for a lending company, forty hours a week on systems that decide who gets credit and at what price; born in California, a bachelor's degree, and now a hundred minutes a day in a car down the peninsula and back, fifty each way; he earns two hundred thousand dollars, which eleven months ago made a mortgage of eight thousand eight hundred a month look survivable, eleven thousand three hundred once everything else is counted; his wife Laurel runs a school ten minutes from the house and brings in a hundred and forty; their son Miles is fifteen and in grade ten, their daughter Nora thirteen and in grade eight, and both changed schools for this address; his company has started using the word restructuring in rooms he is not senior enough to sit in, and he has told nobody here; he still thinks the house was the right call; careful, agreeable, competent, and secretive in exactly the way that costs the most.
people.name: Greg Bannister

people.persona: Laurel Bannister runs a public school a ten-minute drive from her own front door, which is fifty hours a week of staffing, budgets and other people's children; she came from Pennsylvania, holds a master's degree, and has been with the district long enough to know two hundred families by circumstance rather than name; a hundred and forty thousand dollars a year, sixty thousand less than her husband Greg, and she was still the one who ran the numbers on this house; they bought the four-bedroom under a year ago at a million and a half, eight thousand eight hundred a month before anything else is added, and she pushed for it; Miles at fifteen treats the move as a sentence served, while Nora at thirteen has already made friends, which he takes personally; she thinks Greg has been not telling her something since about March; decisive, warm at work, shorter at home, and unwilling to be publicly wrong about this.
people.name: Laurel Bannister

people.persona: Elaine Yuen drafts the filings a securities firm's lawyers sign, keeps the calendar of deadlines nobody else reads, and has kept two partners out of trouble without either of them noticing; she came from Hong Kong in 1970 as a small child, naturalised young, has a year of college credit and no degree, and has trained graduates who now outrank her; a hundred and thirty-four thousand in wages plus nearly twelve thousand from a retirement account makes her the only earner in a house of four; she rides the bus forty minutes each way and leaves the household's one car alone; her mother Remedios, her sister Bernadette and her brother Clement all live on the twenty-four hundred a month she pays the bank; she thinks the food stamps this address receives are an arithmetic fact rather than a disgrace, and has stopped softening it for anyone; she is precise, unsentimental, badly tired in a way she thinks she hides, and cannot delegate.
people.name: Elaine Yuen

people.persona: Bernadette Yuen cut and coloured hair in the same Geary Boulevard salon for nineteen years until the chair rental went up and the owner's niece needed a station; she has looked for work since and reported no income at all this year, not one dollar in wages; born in Hong Kong, she came over in 1987, later than her sister and her brother, and she is the one who still sounds like it in Cantonese; she is married, though her husband took work in Sacramento and the weekends he comes down have thinned out; she lives in her sister Elaine's mortgaged house with their mother Remedios and their brother Clement, and does the cooking as the nearest thing she has to rent; she thinks Clement was kept out of school on purpose and that everyone knows by whom; she is warm to strangers, sharp with family, superstitious about money, and physically incapable of leaving anyone's hair alone.
people.name: Bernadette Yuen

people.persona: Clement Yuen has never held a job and has no schooling completed at all, not a single grade recorded, which is a strange thing to be true of a fifty-year-old born in Hong Kong and brought here in 1974 before he could walk; no doctor has ever put a disability on him and his English is good enough for the pharmacy, the bank and the bus; he earns nothing and receives nothing in his own name; he takes his mother Remedios to her appointments, walks to the produce shops every morning, and keeps the accounts of the household in a notebook nobody has asked to see; he lives with Remedios, his sister Elaine who pays the mortgage, and his sister Bernadette who cooks; he thinks the story his sisters tell about why he stayed home is kinder to their mother than it is to him; he is watchful, orderly, funnier than anyone expects, and answers direct questions two beats late.
people.name: Clement Yuen

people.persona: Remedios Yuen keeps the front room of a house she does not own and has stopped correcting people about where she is from; she was born in the Philippines, not Hong Kong, arrived in 1966, took citizenship, and raised three Cantonese-speaking children who tell the family's crossings three different ways; thirteen thousand two hundred dollars a year comes to her from somewhere none of her paperwork names, and at eighty she does not intend to chase it; she is a widow, married once, and the year her husband died is the only date in this family that everyone agrees on; her daughter Elaine carries the mortgage, her daughter Bernadette feeds them, and her son Clement walks her to the doctor; she thinks the question of Clement's schooling should have been buried with his father and says so whenever it is raised; she is unhurried, quietly devout, evasive about the past, and generous with everything except explanations.
people.name: Remedios Yuen

people.persona: Tuan Nghiem is an undergraduate at a public college with a year or so of credit behind him and three semesters ahead, assembling the degree a course at a time around what his visa will allow; he came from Vietnam in 2019, is not a citizen, speaks Vietnamese at home and English well enough that people forget to slow down for him; his recorded income for the year was nothing at all, not because his days are empty but because nothing he does reaches a tax record; he lives alone in a studio at the back of an old two-unit building for eight hundred a month, an arrangement his aunt found through the owner and the cheapest rent anyone on this street has heard of; he has been there between two and four years, owns no car, and walks a great deal; Tuan thinks the classmates who complain hardest about rent have never had a lease priced as a favour; disciplined, watchful, dutiful, and careful never to say what he is carrying.
people.name: Tuan Nghiem
people.occupation: Full-time undergraduate; not in the labour force

people.persona: Rolando Sarmiento stood at gates and loading docks for a security contractor, checking badges and writing times, until twelve-hour shifts finished his knees; he has not looked for work since and will not call it retirement; born in the Philippines, he did not arrive until 2000, years after both his children were already living in California, an order of events he has never enjoyed explaining; twenty thousand dollars a year reaches him through arrangements his forms record as neither wages nor pension nor social security; he has been married three times and discusses only this one; he and Herminia own this attached house outright and pay under eight hundred a month to keep it standing; his son Arnulfo, his daughter Maricel and her husband Jomar all sleep down the hall; he thinks the house should be sold while eight hundred thousand still buys something in Cavite, and has said so at three separate dinners; he is stubborn, formal with strangers, quick with orders, and privately afraid of outliving his usefulness.
people.name: Rolando Sarmiento

people.persona: Herminia Sarmiento has never worked for wages in this country and does not intend to begin at seventy-six; she came from the Philippines in 1989, took citizenship, and still speaks no English at all, which has never once stopped her running a household of five; fourteen thousand seven hundred dollars a year arrives in her name from sources no form of hers itemises; her hip has got bad enough that the stairs of this attached house take four minutes and she counts them going up; Rolando is her only husband and she is not his only wife, a difference she has made peace with out loud and not otherwise; her stepdaughter Maricel is a nurse who keeps offering to move a bed downstairs; her stepson Arnulfo carries every bag in from the car; she thinks selling this paid-off house would finish her faster than the staircase will; she is devout, exacting about food, funny only in Tagalog, and refuses every offered arm.
people.name: Herminia Sarmiento

people.persona: Arnulfo Sarmiento sits at a folding table by the registers of a supermarket signing shoppers up for the store card and the delivery membership, forty hours a week, fifty-two weeks a year, for fifty thousand dollars; he was born in the Philippines and landed here in 1992 at eighteen, eight years before his own father managed it, and people still ask him to explain that; his English is workmanlike and his whole home life happens in Tagalog; he drives ten minutes to the store in a house with three cars in it; he is married, though his wife has been in Cebu since her mother got sick and neither names a date now; he sleeps in the back bedroom of his father Rolando and stepmother Herminia's mortgage-free house, alongside his half-sister Maricel and her husband Jomar; he thinks his father's plan to sell up and return is a fantasy, and says so only to Maricel; he is unhurried, physically careful, loyal past sense, and never raises his voice.
people.name: Arnulfo Sarmiento

people.persona: Maricel Bugarin is the registered nurse on a skilled nursing floor, the one who signs off what the aides did and takes the fall when the chart disagrees with the body in the bed; she was born in California in the mid-eighties and did not properly meet her father Rolando until she was fifteen, because he arrived in 2000 and she had been here the whole time; her associate's degree, forty-two hours a week and fifty-two weeks a year come to fifty thousand dollars, less than the travelling nurses who cover her weekends; she drives twenty minutes each way; she lives with her husband Jomar, her father, her stepmother Herminia and her half-brother Arnulfo under a roof nobody owes money on; she thinks Rolando has no business selling a house Herminia cannot get down the stairs of unaided; she is blunt, tireless, allergic to being thanked, and keeps a private tally of who has actually done something.
people.name: Maricel Bugarin

people.persona: Jomar Bugarin supervises the clerks at a security firm who file the incident reports, the timesheets and the licence renewals for guards he will never meet; he came from the Philippines in 2018 and took citizenship faster than anyone in this house expected, though he still conducts every difficult conversation in Tagalog and lets Maricel take the phone calls; his sixty thousand dollars is fifty in wages and ten drawn early out of a retirement account he will not discuss, including with his wife; he drives twenty minutes to an office park and twenty minutes home; he is married to Maricel, sleeps under his father-in-law Rolando's roof, and is careful never to be the one who mentions selling it; he thinks the guards his clerks process are paid less than the dogs working the same sites, and he has put that in writing; he is meticulous, deferential to elders in public, sardonic in private, and remembers every figure he has ever been shown.
people.name: Jomar Bugarin

people.persona: Rowan Behr does twelve hours a week at a consulting firm, two short shifts of research decks and spreadsheet tidying that the firm calls an opportunity and the record calls three thousand six hundred dollars a year; she is twenty-one, born in California, already holds an associate's degree and is most of the way through a bachelor's at a private college; she walks ten minutes to the office, thirty weeks of the year, and there is no car in the household; her studio costs two thousand a month, a figure no arithmetic involving her own wages can reach, and the difference comes from her parents; she moved in under two years ago and has never said the word allowance out loud in this city; Rowan thinks the firm knows exactly what twelve hours buys and has set out to make herself expensive to replace; driven, quick, self-conscious about how visible the help is, and short with anyone who calls her lucky.
people.name: Rowan Behr

people.persona: Dean Ruhl is a management consultant with nothing to consult on, sixty-hour weeks of client work that ran thirty-five weeks last year and then stopped; he was born in Virginia, has a master's degree, and earned two hundred and thirty-three thousand dollars in that time, eight thousand of it public assistance, a single line he thinks about more than the rest combined; he is thirty-seven and married once, to Nadia Volkov, who works from the back room of this rented attached house and clears four hundred thousand without any help from him; the rent is three thousand a month, deliberately modest against what they used to bring in, and the only reason the year has been survivable; they moved in under two years ago and keep two cars, one of which has not moved in a fortnight; Dean thinks a job below the one he left would be a verdict rather than a bridge, and has turned down two; capable, competitive, elaborately courteous at home, and quietly humiliated.
people.name: Dean Ruhl

people.persona: Nadia Volkov runs operations for a real-estate group out of the back bedroom, forty hours a week of leases, vendor contracts and other people's deadlines, and she shuts the door at six; she is thirty-four, born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and earns four hundred thousand dollars a year, a figure her husband can recite faster than she can; Russian on the phone with her mother most evenings, English with Dean Ruhl, who has been out of work for months inside a household clearing six hundred and thirty-three thousand; they have been in this two-bedroom rented house under two years at three thousand a month, which she chose and he agreed to when both of them were working; Nadia thinks he should take the job beneath the last one and has never once managed to say it in those words; precise, generous, exact about hours, and tired of being congratulated for her patience by friends who have not asked her a single question about any of it.
people.name: Nadia Volkov

people.persona: Ingrid Halloway administers student services for a nonprofit college, thirty-nine hours a week of enrolment problems, hardship cases and nineteen-year-olds in trouble, all of it conducted through a camera; she has a doctorate, was born in California, has never married, and earns a hundred and seventy-one thousand dollars, every dollar of it wages; she took the post remote and has been inside the college's buildings about a dozen times; she moved into a one-bedroom in a large block under a year ago, pays two thousand nine hundred a month, keeps no car, and the walk to Clement Street and back is most days' only outing; she runs at six most mornings because it is the one hour of hers that happens outside a screen; Ingrid thinks remote work is sold as freedom by people who already had their friends, and has said so in a meeting twice; warm, exacting, genuinely funny about it, and more alone here than she will say.
people.name: Ingrid Halloway

people.persona: Jasmine Bautista coached youth sport for a small advocacy nonprofit until the season ended and the grant did not come back, so the record has her unemployed and her income for the year at nothing at all; she is nineteen, born in California, has a high school diploma and is enrolled as an undergraduate at a private college; she signed the summer lease on this new-build two-bedroom at two thousand seven hundred a month with her friend and flatmate Marisel Cuenca, and both sets of parents co-signed it, a fact nobody in either family describes accurately; Tagalog when the mothers ring, which is often and usually about money; Jasmine thinks the coaching was cut because nobody senior at that organisation has ever needed a paid Saturday, and she will say it to anyone who sits still; bright, restless, proud, and much funnier about the rent than she actually feels.
people.name: Jasmine Bautista
people.occupation: Youth sports coach, nonprofit; currently unemployed

people.persona: Marisel Cuenca finished a bachelor's degree at twenty, early and fast, and is enrolled again already in a public programme heading somewhere clinical; she was born in California, speaks Tagalog with her family, is not in the labour force and reports no income whatsoever; the household's one car is hers in practice, because the placements are scattered across the city at hours no bus serves; she moved into this two-bedroom under a year ago with Jasmine Bautista, against two thousand seven hundred a month and a household income for the year recorded as zero, the gap covered by two sets of parents who co-signed and now ring on Sundays; Marisel thinks the joke Jasmine makes about the rent is exactly why neither of them has asked what happens next August; she is the more serious of the two by a distance she is aware of; disciplined, private, precocious, and embarrassed by how much of her life was arranged for her.
people.name: Marisel Cuenca
people.occupation: Full-time student; not in the labour force

people.persona: Nghia Truong loads and stacks for a confectionery plant, forty hours a week of pallets, shrink wrap and sugar dust that never washes out of a collar; he left school in Vietnam after grade nine, came over in 1992, naturalised, and speaks Vietnamese at home with English good enough for the floor supervisor; the drive is ten minutes; he earns sixty thousand dollars, and the house, bought twenty-odd years ago and now worth one and a third million, costs four thousand six hundred a month once taxes and insurance sit on top of the three thousand mortgage; his wife Lien Dao is paid by the state for sixteen hours a week of the care she gives her own mother Hoa in the back bedroom; his brothers Loc and Vinh and his sister Nhung all live here and all pay in; Nghia thinks they should borrow against the house so the younger three can buy something of their own; steady, literal, unhurried, and the only one who opens the mail.
people.name: Nghia Truong

people.persona: Lien Dao is paid by the state for sixteen hours a week to lift, bathe and feed her own mother, work she would be doing for nothing and is instead doing for twenty-four thousand dollars a year; Lien had three years of school in Vietnam before her family stopped sending her, arrived in 1991 a year ahead of her husband Nghia, and has been a permanent resident for thirty-three years without ever filing for citizenship; her English is poor and she believes that settles the question, although her brother-in-law Vinh keeps telling her that at fifty-two, after twenty years here, the language test no longer applies to her; her mother Hoa is eighty-one and deaf to most of what is said; the sixteen paid hours are a fraction of the real ones; Lien thinks the house should never be borrowed against and has said so in front of everybody; soft-voiced, immovable, superstitious about hospitals, and keeper of accounts nobody else sees.
people.name: Lien Dao
people.occupation: Personal care aide, state in-home support programme

people.persona: Loc Truong cleans state office buildings on a night-weighted roster, forty hours of floors, bins and the toilets nobody else will take, and he has done it since the nineties; he is sixty, never married, left school in Vietnam at grade seven, and landed here in 1992 with his younger brother Nghia; the bus takes thirty minutes and he has never owned a car, though three sit at the kerb outside this house; he earns sixty thousand dollars, exactly what Nghia earns and exactly what their brother Vinh earns, and he put down most of what bought the place two decades ago; Nghia now wants to borrow against it for Vinh and their sister Nhung; Loc thinks one mortgage is as much as any house should be asked to carry and will not sign a second; Vietnamese at home, English fine at work; contained, orderly, generous in ways he refuses to discuss, and slow to forgive being managed.
people.name: Loc Truong

people.persona: Nhung Truong works forty hours a week for a nonprofit that sends her to four clients a day, an hour of washing, cooking and sitting with people whose families are somewhere else; she left school in grade eleven, came over in 2002, ten years behind her brothers, and speaks Vietnamese at home with English she calls not enough; the bus is forty-five minutes each way and she earns thirty-eight thousand dollars, the smallest full-time wage in the house; she has never married and has had the same back room in her brother Nghia's place for twenty-two years; Nghia wants to borrow against the house so that she and Vinh can buy somewhere; Nhung thinks she is fifty-six and would rather no one spent anything on her behalf, and has never managed to make that sound like gratitude; warm with clients, guarded at home, chronically early, and keeping a separate savings book at a bank on Ocean Avenue.
people.name: Nhung Truong

people.persona: Vinh Truong cleans the corridors and hearing rooms of a government building where the people he tidies up after have never learned his name, forty hours a week, fifteen minutes on the train; he finished twelve years of school in Vietnam without the certificate at the end of them, came over in 2002 with his sister Nhung, naturalised, and handles English well enough to be the one who telephones the utility company; he was married once and it did not survive the move; sixty thousand dollars a year goes almost entirely into his brother Nghia's household, where he has had the same room for twenty-two years; he is the one who discovered that his sister-in-law Lien could apply for citizenship without sitting the language test, and she has not thanked him for it; Vinh thinks they should borrow against the house now, while his brother Loc is still working; talkative, politically attentive, impatient with caution, and better company than anyone at home will admit.
people.name: Vinh Truong

people.persona: Hoa Dao has not worked since the family left Vietnam and lives on six and a half thousand dollars of social security a year, which is what a low-wage marriage and a late arrival entitle a widow to; she came in 1991 with her daughter Lien, a year ahead of her son-in-law Nghia, and has stayed a permanent resident ever since, eighty-one years old and deaf to most of what is said in the room; she had three years of school and no English at all, so every letter from the county reaches her through Lien, who is paid by the state for sixteen of the many hours she spends on her; the back bedroom is hers and she knows what it is worth in a house valued at one and a third million; Hoa thinks the mortgage should be finished before anyone gets generous with it, and Lien says so on her behalf; sharp-eyed, imperious about food, forgiving of everyone but herself.
people.name: Hoa Dao

people.persona: Aurelio Zaragoza kept the books for a nonprofit that manages buildings, reconciling rent rolls and chasing invoices thirty-five weeks of the year before he stopped; at seventy he is enrolled as an undergraduate at a public college and takes it seriously enough to sit in the front row; he came from Mexico in 2001, never became a citizen, speaks Spanish at home and English well enough to argue in it; twenty-three thousand in wages and nine more from elsewhere make thirty-two thousand; his name is on the lease of a five-bedroom half-house that holds eight adults for twenty-five hundred a month, a number that has held since he signed it; Lonnie, Ofelia, Servando, Edgardo, Homero, Isaias and Xiomara are the seven; the landlord has written asking how many people live here and Aurelio thinks the correct answer is no answer at all; he is courteous, guarded, endlessly patient with paperwork, and the last one awake most nights.
people.name: Aurelio Zaragoza

people.persona: Lonnie Prather works sixty hours a week as his own boss on other people's demolition and framing, hauling, breaking and carrying for forty thousand dollars a year and no employer to blame; he left school in the fifth grade in California, has been married twice and lives with neither wife, and the census records him as working from home because he has never once reported a commute; he is the only person in this eight-adult house who does not speak Spanish and he knows exactly how much that costs him at dinner; his truck is the single vehicle registered here and half of them borrow it; he pays his share of twenty-five hundred a month to Aurelio, whose name is on the lease, alongside Ofelia, Servando, Edgardo, Homero, Isaias and Xiomara; he thinks the landlord's letter should be answered honestly before somebody gets everyone evicted; he is blunt, physically fearless, uneasy in groups, and generous in ways he would deny.
people.name: Lonnie Prather

people.persona: Ofelia Bustamante cleans four houses on her own account, twenty-four hours a week, setting her own rates and collecting fifteen thousand six hundred dollars a year for it; she left school in the twelfth grade without the diploma, came from Mexico in 2001 in the same year Aurelio did, and took citizenship where he never has; she takes a thirty-minute bus to her clients and does not drive the one truck parked outside; she is divorced and has been for long enough that she no longer counts; she shares this five-bedroom flat with seven other adults, and it is her the household leans on when Homero cannot manage a morning by himself; she thinks she is doing unpaid care in a house where everyone claims to split things evenly, and she has said it once, loudly, and not since; she is watchful, quick to laugh, exhausted in a way she treats as ordinary, and stubborn about being paid on time.
people.name: Ofelia Bustamante

people.persona: Servando Quintanilla turns wrenches in a repair shop forty hours a week, fifty-two weeks a year, for sixteen thousand dollars and no health insurance of any kind; he was carried over the border from Mexico in 1980 as a baby, is a citizen, and has lived his whole remembered life in California; his English is solid and Spanish is what he thinks in; he takes a twenty-minute bus to a shop full of cars while the household's single truck belongs to Lonnie; he is separated from his second wife and has not filed anything; he pays into Aurelio's lease along with Ofelia, Edgardo, Homero, Isaias and Xiomara, seven other adults in five bedrooms; he thinks a shop that bills a hundred and eighty an hour for his hands and gives him nothing to see a doctor with is running a con, and he says it every time somebody gets hurt; he is dry, capable, slow to trust, and incapable of walking past an unfixed thing.
people.name: Servando Quintanilla

people.persona: Edgardo Chumpitaz does the same job as Servando for the same sixteen thousand dollars, except he does it in the street outside, forty hours a week on other people's brakes and timing belts with the census recording no commute at all; he came from Peru in 1999, naturalised, and his English never caught up because the work does not require it; he carries no health insurance and has an opinion about the shop that Servando works for that he keeps to himself; he has never married; he lives in five bedrooms with seven other adults on Aurelio's lease, at a rent that has not moved in years and will not survive being looked at; he thinks Lonnie wanting to write back to the landlord is the single most dangerous idea in this house and has said so twice; he is meticulous with tools, quiet in company, funny once he trusts you, and never lends anything he cannot replace.
people.name: Edgardo Chumpitaz

people.persona: Homero Cantú fabricates and hangs ductwork on construction sites for ninety-nine thousand dollars a year, the largest income in a house of eight, and he has a master's degree nobody here has ever seen him mention; he is forty-two, born in Texas, and lives with a cognitive difficulty, an ambulatory difficulty and enough trouble managing errands alone that Ofelia checks on him most mornings; he has a job at present but has not been at work, and the length of that is the thing he will not discuss; he speaks Spanish and good English; he pays into Aurelio's twenty-five hundred alongside Lonnie, Ofelia, Servando, Edgardo, Isaias and Xiomara; he thinks the landlord's letter is aimed at him specifically, because he is the one who is home all day and visible from the street; he is meticulous, funny in short bursts, fiercely private about his health, and apologises far too much.
people.name: Homero Cantú

people.persona: Isaias Peñaloza washes and details the delivery vans for a restaurant group, doing it on the street where he lives so the census logs him as working from home, twelve weeks of the year for seven thousand seven hundred dollars; he is twenty-two, born in California, finished twelfth grade without a diploma, and speaks Spanish and English equally well, which makes him the household's translator whenever anyone official knocks; he pays the smallest share into the twenty-five hundred a month that Aurelio's name covers; he shares five bedrooms with seven adults, most of them twice his age; he thinks the older men in this house talk about the landlord like it is a war and that the actual risk is the two of them driving uninsured to work; he is easy in a crowd, restless, quick with his hands, and openly bored by every plan anyone has for his life.
people.name: Isaias Peñaloza

people.persona: Xiomara Tejeda is twenty-one, enrolled full-time at a public college, and earned two hundred dollars last year from two weeks of one hour a week stocking shelves in a department store, a job she quit before it began properly; she was born in California, speaks Spanish and English fluently, and has a year of college credit toward a degree she is not certain she wants; she pays almost nothing into the twenty-five hundred a month rent on this five-bedroom flat and is aware that everyone knows it; she lives with Aurelio, who is seventy and back at college himself, and with Lonnie, Ofelia, Servando, Edgardo, Homero and Isaias; she thinks the landlord's letter is a legal question with a legal answer and that nobody here will let her go and find it; she is bright, argumentative, embarrassed by her own dependence, and the only person here who reads the mail on the table.
people.name: Xiomara Tejeda

people.persona: Micah Sorrentino runs the small software consultancy he incorporated at twenty-five, pays himself sixty thousand dollars in salary, and takes another hundred thousand by routes the census form files under other income; Micah grew up in New York, holds a bachelor's degree he rarely mentions, works seventy hours a week and drives forty minutes to an office he could have leased far closer; he holds the lease on a four-bedroom house out in the avenues at eight thousand three hundred a month and split it four equal ways without being asked to; his housemate Haoran Bai manages projects for a university and cannot take the job Micah keeps offering him; Ellis Pettigrew guides tours thirty-eight weeks of the year; Reese Alcott designs for Micah's own firm and pays him rent on top; Micah thinks an even split is the only fair split and has never once run the arithmetic; generous, fast, certain of himself, and deaf to a room going quiet.
people.name: Micah Sorrentino
people.occupation: Founder and chief executive, software consultancy

people.persona: Haoran Bai is a project management specialist at a state university, the man who chases eleven departments for the signatures that let a building project keep moving; Haoran came from China in 2016, is not a citizen, and holds his status through that university job, which is the entire reason he is still on eighty-two thousand dollars a year; he drives thirty-five minutes each way in the second of the house's two cars, forty hours a week and not one more; he pays a quarter of eight thousand three hundred a month for a room in Micah Sorrentino's rented house, speaks nothing but English inside it, and keeps a private spreadsheet of what the four of them actually earn; Ellis Pettigrew is who that spreadsheet is really about; Reese Alcott works for Micah and will not say a word; Haoran thinks the even split is a decision Micah made rather than a law of nature; precise, dry, comfortable in silence, and slower to be grateful than people expect.
people.name: Haoran Bai

people.persona: Ellis Pettigrew walks and buses visitors around the city thirty hours a week for thirty-eight weeks of the year, then spends fourteen weeks earning nothing at all; Ellis was born in New York, has a master's degree nobody on a tour has ever asked him about, and made sixty-six thousand dollars last year, three thousand of which was not wages; the drive to the morning meeting point takes twenty minutes and he is usually first out of the house; he pays a quarter of eight thousand three hundred a month, the identical share as Micah Sorrentino, who bills more in a fortnight than Ellis clears in a season; Haoran Bai has offered twice to raise it at a house meeting and Ellis has asked him not to; Reese Alcott is in the same position and pretends otherwise; Ellis thinks tourists are sold a version of this city that would embarrass anybody who lives in it; wry, well-read, conflict-averse, and deeper into his overdraft than he admits.
people.name: Ellis Pettigrew

people.persona: Reese Alcott designs interfaces and pitch decks at the consultancy Micah Sorrentino owns, an arrangement that puts his landlord and his employer at the same kitchen table; Reese grew up in California, has a bachelor's degree, works a straight forty hours and earns sixty-five thousand dollars, the smallest wage in a house of four men who bring in three hundred and seventy-three thousand between them; his drive is fifteen minutes, the shortest of the four, and he has had the small back bedroom for two years; his quarter of the rent is two thousand and seventy-five a month, about half of what he takes home; he has watched Haoran Bai raise the split twice and Ellis Pettigrew wave it off both times, and has said nothing on either occasion because Micah signs the two things keeping him here; Reese thinks he should have settled the salary before he agreed to the room; observant, agreeable on the surface, quietly resentful, and already rebuilding his portfolio.
people.name: Reese Alcott

people.persona: Oksana Kovalenko drafts, files and indexes for a legal services firm forty hours a week, paralegal work done by a woman holding a doctorate in law from a country whose qualifications do not convert here without years and money she does not have; she came from Ukraine in 2022 with her son Andriy, is not a citizen, and speaks Ukrainian at home in English that is workable rather than easy; she earns forty-one thousand four hundred in wages and six hundred in assistance, takes food stamps, and pays two thousand five hundred a month for the one-bedroom they moved into this year; she rides the bus forty minutes each way and keeps a car she does not drive; Andriy is sixteen, finished grade ten, has not attended school in months, and is alone in the flat the eleven hours she is out; Oksana thinks the school phoned twice and then decided she was the problem; formidable, exhausted, unbending, and without one person here to call.
people.name: Oksana Kovalenko

people.persona: Angela Wong assesses children whose families are coming apart, fifty hours a week for a district thirty-five minutes' drive from her own front door, half her reports written in car parks between schools; she is sixty-one, born in California, holds a master's degree and earns a hundred and thirty thousand dollars a year; she has been married three times and has decided Matteo Ferrari is the last of them; they own this two-bedroom flat in a two-unit building, three thousand seven hundred a month against a place now worth a million and a half, and have been in it five to nine years; Cantonese on the phone with her mother, English at the table; their daughter Lin is seventeen, adopted from China as an infant, and a year from leaving; Angela thinks Lin should pick somewhere within a two-hour drive and has stopped pretending that is about tuition; perceptive about other people's households, tireless, avoidant about her own, and slow to ask a question she might not like.
people.name: Angela Wong

people.persona: Matteo Ferrari teaches at a private secondary school forty minutes' drive away, a straight forty hours plus the weekend tutoring that adds three thousand dollars to his eighty; he came from Italy in 2001 for what was meant to be two years, has never taken citizenship, and after twenty-three years treats that less as an oversight than as a position; his English is good rather than perfect, his associate's degree sits in a staffroom full of master's, and he is the teacher the difficult pupils ask for; he is sixty-one and married twice, the second time to Angela Wong, who earns a hundred and thirty thousand to his eighty-three and drives off each morning in the opposite direction; their daughter Lin, seventeen, is the only one in the flat who follows all three of its languages; Matteo thinks she should go as far away as she can get in, and says so at the table; generous, funny, allergic to seriousness, and unnerved by how quiet next year sounds.
people.name: Matteo Ferrari

people.persona: Desmond Hatch is eighty and enrolled in a graduate programme for the second time in his life, seminars twice a week at a private institution, with the reading done properly, which unnerves the twenty-five-year-olds; he came from Ohio in the seventies, never married, holds a master's degree and left the labour force years ago; his income is fifty-four thousand one hundred and thirty dollars, of which twenty-six thousand four hundred is pension and the rest arrives from investments made when a person on his salary could still make them; he has held the same two-bedroom flat for over thirty years at five hundred and fifty dollars a month, keeps a car he drives about once a week, and has given the second bedroom entirely to books arranged on a system only he can explain; Desmond thinks the building's new owner should put its intentions in writing rather than in a friendly letter; sharp, courteous, contrary, and impatient with being called an inspiration.
people.name: Desmond Hatch
people.occupation: Not in the labour force; graduate student

people.persona: Emmett Kubota builds the budgets for a grantmaking nonprofit, telling programme directors what their good ideas actually cost and being right about it eleven months out of twelve; born in California, never married, master's degree, sixty-one years old, and deaf enough in one ear that he sits at the corner of every meeting table; eighty-eight thousand in salary and fifteen thousand more from elsewhere; he owns this pre-war two-flat outright, keeps its monthly cost near fifteen hundred, has lived here over thirty years, and has never owned a car in his life; his nephew Kenji, Kenji's wife Chiaki and his niece Emi fill the bedrooms upstairs, and the census now records the household as Japanese-speaking on the strength of Chiaki alone; he thinks a house worth one point eight million should not be run on nobody paying anything, and has raised it once, badly; he is deliberate, frugal past reason, hard to read, and keeps every receipt.
people.name: Emmett Kubota

people.persona: Chiaki Kubota is a general clerk for a federal office handling international affairs, logging, routing and refiling documents she is not cleared to read closely; she arrived from Japan in 2024, is not a citizen and does not pretend her English is up to the job yet, and got hired anyway after twenty-six weeks of a year at thirty thousand dollars; she takes two buses, forty minutes each way, because this house has no car and never has; she married Kenji, who has lived in California his whole life and out-earns her almost seven to one, a ratio she can state to the decimal; they live in his uncle Emmett's paid-off two-flat with Kenji's sister Emi, and Chiaki is the only person here who speaks the language the household is officially recorded as speaking; she thinks living free in a relative's house is a debt and not a gift; she is exact, formal, homesick in ways she will not perform, and misses nothing.
people.name: Chiaki Kubota

people.persona: Kenji Kubota writes and maintains code for a search company, fifty hours a week for two hundred thousand dollars, most of it spent on systems that already work and must not stop; he was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and rides the bus forty minutes each way because his uncle's house has never had a parking space or a car; he married Chiaki, who came from Japan in 2024 and earns thirty thousand at a federal clerk's desk, and he has learned about nine words of her language in that time; his sister Emi is upstairs, out of work since her games retailer let the whole team go; his uncle Emmett owns the building free and clear and once tried to open the question of what they all pay; he thinks he should simply buy the place from Emmett at a fair number and be done with it; he is easy-going, conflict-shy, generous with money, and slow to notice when he has been the problem.
people.name: Kenji Kubota

people.persona: Emi Kubota wrote code for a hobby and games retailer for twelve weeks and twenty thousand dollars before the whole team went at once, and she has been unemployed ever since; she is twenty-three, born in California, holds a bachelor's degree, and has now applied to enough places that she has a spreadsheet with a column for ghosting; she lives in her uncle Emmett's mortgage-free two-flat with her brother Kenji, who makes two hundred thousand doing the same work she trained for, and his wife Chiaki, who arrived from Japan last year and got a federal job before Emi got a callback; she owns no car and neither does anyone here; she thinks Emmett raising the subject of rent while she has no income was the cruellest thing he has ever done, and she is aware that is not fair; she is quick, self-deprecating, easily humiliated, and up until four most nights.
people.name: Emi Kubota

people.persona: Julien Mbarga writes software through a company of his own that exists because a client preferred invoices to a payroll line, an incorporated arrangement he has not managed to convert back into a job; he is thirty-six, has a master's degree, came from the United Kingdom in 2018 and is not a citizen; eighty thousand dollars is his pay and also the entire income of four people, against three thousand seven hundred a month for the three-bedroom they have rented two to four years; he rides the bus forty-five minutes each way and leaves the household's one car to Estelle Mbarga, his wife, who has not earned anything since their daughter was born this year; French at home, English at school, and their six-year-old son translating in both directions; Julien thinks a salaried role with sponsorship attached is worth waiting another six months for, and Estelle thinks nothing of the sort; precise, calm on the surface, and doing sums at three in the morning.
people.name: Julien Mbarga

people.persona: Estelle Mbarga ran market research for an advertising agency, the survey design and segmentation sitting under other people's campaigns, and has been paid for none of it since the baby arrived this year; she is thirty-one, holds a master's degree, came from Cameroon in 2021 with their son, and is not a citizen; her recorded income is nothing at all in a household living on the eighty thousand dollars Julien Mbarga brings in; her day is the school run, an infant, and applications typed in the two hours the baby sleeps, for work she is not certain she is currently permitted to take; French at home and a six-year-old translating at every appointment, which she minds more than anyone has noticed; Estelle thinks they should stop holding out for the perfect sponsored offer and take whatever comes with paperwork attached; organised, warm, relentless on a phone queue, and frightened by how completely her standing here rests on her husband's.
people.name: Estelle Mbarga

people.persona: Daniel Chen is four months into his first real job writing software, forty-five hours a week, and is still finishing an associate's degree at a public college around the edges of it; born in California, he speaks Mandarin in this flat and English everywhere else, and sixteen weeks of work came to thirty thousand dollars and ten more the form insisted on recording; his name is on the lease of this three-bedroom, so the other three bring him decisions he would much rather everyone made together; twenty-two hundred a month split four ways, no car between them, and seventy-five minutes on commuter rail each way; he shares the largest room with Tashi Rai, who out-earns him three times over and has started talking about leaving; Daniel thinks the rent only works with four in it and has not managed to say so to her; methodical, quiet, fair-minded, and slow to open a conversation he expects to lose.
people.name: Daniel Chen

people.persona: Vivian Lau interviews prospective students for a state college fifteen hours a week, which makes her the first friendly voice a nervous eighteen-year-old hears and the one who later logs why they never enrolled; born in California, she speaks Cantonese with her family and Mandarin in this flat, and has a year of college credit and no degree to show for it yet; fifteen thousand dollars a year is the smallest income in the household, which is why five hundred and fifty a month in rent is not negotiable for her; sixty-five minutes each way on commuter rail, then studying at the kitchen table because there is nowhere else to sit; she has known Daniel Chen since community college and lives with him, Mira Gurung and Tashi Rai; Vivian thinks Tashi has not grasped that leaving would price out three people; curious, talkative, observant, and tired of saying the hard thing on everyone's behalf.
people.name: Vivian Lau

people.persona: Mira Gurung is a nursing assistant for a home-care agency twenty hours a week, washing, lifting and turning clients in their own flats, and she does the entire job in Chinese because she has no English at all; she was born in Nepal, came over in 2017 and naturalised, and learned the language of the work rather than the language of the country; twenty-seven weeks of shifts last year came to ten thousand dollars, and she is studying for a further credential at a private college on those same terms; she cycles thirty minutes to her first client and pays five hundred and fifty towards a three-bedroom she shares with Daniel Chen, Vivian Lau and Tashi Rai; Mira thinks a household that agrees to quiet hours and then keeps a light burning until two in the morning is simply lying; direct, tough, warm with clients, and finished apologising for needing sleep.
people.name: Mira Gurung

people.persona: Tashi Rai builds software fifty hours a week and rides a bus ninety minutes each way to do it, three hours a day standing because nobody in the flat owns a car; she came from Nepal in 2022, is not a citizen, holds a bachelor's degree and is enrolled at a public college again, and her English is not yet good enough for meetings she is expected to speak in; ninety thousand dollars a year, nine times what Mira Gurung earns and three times Daniel Chen's, and she pays the same five hundred and fifty in rent as everybody else; she shares the largest bedroom with Daniel behind a curtain and keeps hours no one else keeps; Tashi thinks the salary has bought her nothing but a bus seat and she wants out of this arrangement; driven, generous without ever keeping score, restless, and unaware how differently the same rent lands on each of them.
people.name: Tashi Rai

people.persona: Maya Brooks analyses systems for a small real-estate office, which in practice means she rebuilds the listing database, unjams the printer and explains to brokers why their spreadsheets disagree; Maya was born in California, has a bachelor's degree, and worked all fifty-two weeks of the year at forty hours a week for seven thousand dollars in wages and eight hundred more she cannot classify, because the office pays a token draw against commissions that have not arrived; she rides the bus twenty-six minutes each way and has counted the fare against the pay; she lives with Liam Parker, her partner since their second year of college, in a three-bedroom attached house they moved into under a year ago at sixteen hundred a month through his family; Liam's hundred and twenty thousand covers nearly everything, and Maya wants a written proportional split before that quietly becomes a vote; she thinks the owner is waiting for her to quit; she is independent, persistent, exact, and slow to ask for anything.
people.name: Maya Brooks
people.occupation: Computer systems analyst at a real-estate office

people.persona: Liam Parker builds software for a for-profit family-services agency, case-management screens used by staff who get twelve minutes with a client and no patience for a redesign; Liam grew up in Florida, has a bachelor's degree, and earns a hundred and twenty thousand dollars for a straight forty-hour week, driving the household's only car about an hour each way and getting home after Maya has eaten; he lives with Maya Brooks, his partner since college, in a three-bedroom attached house that came through his family at sixteen hundred a month, which he knows is the only reason two people their age have three bedrooms; Maya made seven thousand eight hundred dollars last year at a real-estate office and takes the bus, and Liam keeps telling her the money is theirs, not his; he thinks a formal expense split would turn them into roommates, and said so once, badly; he is generous, idealistic, conflict-averse, and genuinely does not notice what she does.
people.name: Liam Parker
people.occupation: Software developer at a social-services organization

people.persona: Aaron Miller advises private clients on their money across fifty hours a week of portfolio reviews, tax-loss calls and reassuring people whose worst year was still a good year; Aaron is thirty-eight, born in Michigan, holds a bachelor's degree, and brings in three hundred and twenty thousand dollars, nearly the whole of the household's income; he takes the bus thirty minutes each way and has refused to buy a car since moving here; he married Leila Farahani two years ago, the first marriage for both, and they took this three-bedroom flat within the past year at eighty-three hundred a month so her son Jonah, fifteen, would keep his own room; Aaron thinks paying that rent is a form of parenting and has never said it aloud; Jonah wants less supervision and Leila decides how much he gets; Aaron is disciplined, literal, quietly afraid of being unnecessary, and solves problems before checking whether anyone wanted them solved.
people.name: Aaron Miller

people.persona: Leila Farahani owns a small clothing label she runs out of the front room, fifteen hours a week of fabric orders, returns and a website she maintains herself; she is its chief executive and its only employee, which brought in thirty thousand dollars last year against her husband's three hundred and twenty; Leila was born in Iran and came here in 1997 at eleven, naturalised in her twenties, and has lost most of her Farsi to a household that speaks only English; she lives with Aaron Miller, whom she married two years ago, and her son Jonah, fifteen, who is in ninth grade at a private school she chose long before Aaron existed; they moved in less than a year ago and the eighty-three hundred rent is the price of Jonah keeping his own room; Leila thinks Aaron mistakes generosity for authority, though she has never put it that plainly; she is observant, protective, commercially shrewd, and steps between those two before either finishes a sentence.
people.name: Leila Farahani
people.occupation: Owner of a small clothing business
